notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
When White avoids the main systems, challenge the centre with d5 and develop; sharp refutations matter only against a couple…
notes.original: Choice guide: use this section when White avoids the main systems: each branch below gives a safe and a sharp option. Against 2.Bc4 (Hillbilly Attack) and 2.Nc3 d5 3.Qf3 the sharp refutations are important; the other sidelines are harmless if you develop and fight for the centre. Risk level: low unless you misplay the early moves. The rare second moves all give Black an easy game if the usual principle is applied: challenge the centre with ...d5 and develop.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
2.d4 is White's main try; White's third move decides which variation you reach.
notes.original: Part one: the main systems, with pointers only. 2.d4 is White's main try and the backbone of this entire course. Depending on White's third move this transposes into: 3.exd5 cxd5 (Exchange Variation, 🔵 01, 02 and 🟢 01), 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 dxe4 (Classical Variation, 🔵 07 to 10, 🟢 03 and 04), 3.e5 (Advance Variation, 🔵 11 to 14 and 🟢 05 to 07), or 3.f3 (Fantasy Variation, 🔵 18 and 🟢 11). See the Course Map and Scaffolding Guide chapters for the full breakdown of which third move leads where.

notes.text: The Panov gives White an isolated pawn for initiative; stay solid and develop with ease.
notes.original: The Panov Attack is an aggressive opening choice against the Caro Kann. First of all white voluntarily creates an isolated pawn which would be a clear target for Black to take on. Second of all White is willing to create weaknesses in exchange for initiative and attack. Even a pawn sacrifice would not matter if White has enough counterplay. Black's goal is to further fortify the position. Develop the pieces with ease and is looking forward to a great game.

notes.text: The Accelerated Panov has its own chapters; you simply answer with ...d5.
notes.original: 2.c4 is the Accelerated Panov Attack. See 🔵 06 and 🟢 02 for the full treatment. (The main, non-accelerated Panov-Botvinnik Attack, 🔵 03 to 05, arises instead after 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5, with White then playing 4.c4.)

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The Two Knights Attack has its own chapters; here just challenge the centre with ...d5.
notes.original: 2.Nf3 is the Two Knights Attack. See 🔵 15 to 17 and 🟢 08 to 10 for the full treatment (Tartakower, Karpov, Classical, Dano-Russian and ...a6 Variations, and rare third-move tries). No new content here.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
After this, d5 mostly transposes; White's odd early queen sorties are the exceptions, covered next.
notes.original: Part two: sidelines covered elsewhere, in short form, each with its home chapter. 2.Nc3 d5 mostly just transposes (3.d4 = main systems above, 3.Nf3 = Two Knights Attack above), but White also has two odd early queen sorties here, both already fully annotated in 🔵 19, recovered condensed below.

notes.text: This is a quiet, positional try; probably not White's strongest, but it keeps the game calm.
notes.original: 2.d3 is a quiet, positional way to meet the Caro-Kann. White is not after a quick attack. It is probably not his strongest try, but it keeps the game calm.

notes.text: White delays d4 and aims for a King's Indian Attack setup with Nd2, g3, Bg2 and castling.
notes.original: White delays d4 entirely and aims for a King's Indian Attack style setup with Nd2, g3, Bg2 and O-O, keeping the center flexible rather than committing to a specific pawn structure right away. Black's plan: this system lives or dies on Black's central response. Grabbing full central space immediately with ...e5 (rather than waiting) is the single most important practical lesson here - it denies White any chance of a favorable King's Indian Attack-style kingside buildup and leaves Black with at least equal, often slightly better, chances with completely natural development.

notes.text: White's 2.d3 systems have their own chapters; you still answer with ...d5.
notes.original: 2.d3 Systems. See 🔵 19 and 20 for the full treatment (Breyer Variation and the King's Indian Attack & Leela Setup). That same 🔵 19 also contains White's odd 3.Qf3/3.Qe2 queen sorties after 2.Nc3 and the Hillbilly Attack/Gambit after 2.Bc4, both recovered in condensed form below.

notes.text: The Hillbilly Attack is playable but weak: after d4 the bishop cannot stop your ...d5 break.
notes.original: Another variation in this particular opening is the move Bc4 the Hillbilly Attack. This move is complete nonsense against the Caro Kann but it is indeed playable. Its nonsense because after the move d4 the bishop on c4 fails to stop the d5 breakthrough and at the same time once the d5 pawn has been played. The bishop has to reroute back to either e2 or b3.

notes.text: The Hillbilly Attack looks active, but your d-pawn kicks the bishop with tempo.
notes.original: 2.Bc4, the "Hillbilly Attack". Active-looking but the bishop just gets kicked by ...d5 with tempo. Full treatment (including the "Hillbilly Gambit" 3.Bb3!?) in 🔵 19.

notes.text: A quiet fianchetto try that is harmless: just develop normally.
notes.original: 2.b3, a quiet Nimzowitsch-style fianchetto try. Harmless: just develop normally. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: This old, aggressive-looking try overextends White more than it threatens you.
notes.original: 2.f4, the "La Bourdonnais Attack". An old, aggressive-looking try that overextends more than it threatens. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: White fianchettos quietly instead of fighting for the center with d4.
notes.original: 2.g3, a fianchetto try that develops quietly rather than fighting for the center with d4. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: White keeps options open: the knight can go to g3 or later support a d4 push.
notes.original: 2.Ne2, keeps options open (the knight can go to g3 or later support a d4 push). Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: White prepares d4 with extra support from the c3 pawn, a reversed Alapin idea.
notes.original: 2.c3, a kind of reversed Alapin idea, preparing d4 with extra support. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: The e5 push is premature: the pawn lacks real support, so you challenge it at once.
notes.original: 2.e5?!, premature; the pawn gets no real support and Black challenges it at once. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: An eccentric early queen move that gains nothing for White.
notes.original: 2.Qf3?!, an eccentric try, developing the queen far too early for no real gain. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: A quiet developing move that keeps White's options open.
notes.original: 2.Be2, a quiet developing move that keeps options open. Full treatment in the Scaffolding Guide.

notes.text: This flank lunge weakens White's kingside for no real gain, so you just take the center.
notes.original: Part three: other second moves. These ten moves (2.g4, 2.h4, 2.b4, 2.f3, 2.a3, 2.h3, 2.Na3, 2.Nh3, 2.Qh5, 2.Qg4) do not appear anywhere else in this 64-chapter course - this is the first time they have been checked and written up. 2.g4!?, a flank lunge that weakens the kingside for no real gain. Black just takes the center.

notes.text: White's h4 is a flank move with no point yet, since there is nothing to attack on the kingside.
notes.original: 2.h4, a flank expansion with no real point yet, since there's nothing on the kingside to attack.

notes.text: White grabs queenside space with b4 instead of fighting for the centre.
notes.original: 2.b4!?, a wing-gambit-style try, grabbing queenside space instead of fighting for the center.

notes.text: The f3 pawn blocks White's own knight from its natural square and loses time.
notes.original: 2.f3, supports a later e4/d4 setup but blocks White's own king's knight from its natural square and loses time.

notes.text: A pure waiting move with no point against your setup; just develop normally.
notes.original: 2.a3, a pure waiting move with no point at all against the Caro-Kann. Just develop normally.

notes.text: Another waiting move, slightly more useful than a3 since it stops a future bishop pin on g4, but no real…
notes.original: 2.h3, another pure waiting move, slightly more useful than 2.a3 since it at least prevents a future ...Bg4 pin, but still no real try.

notes.text: An odd rim development with no clear follow-up; the knight will need to reroute later.
notes.original: 2.Na3, an odd rim development with no clear follow-up, the knight will likely need to re-route via c4 or c2 later.

notes.text: The knight goes to the rim instead of a natural square, blocking White's kingside pawns and achieving little.
notes.original: 2.Nh3, develops to the rim instead of the natural f3/e2 squares, blocking the kingside pawns and achieving little.

notes.text: The queen has nothing to attack yet, so your central pawn moves will gain time against it.
notes.original: 2.Qh5?!, a very premature queen sortie with no target, Black's center play comes with tempo on the misplaced queen.

notes.text: Another early queen trip that has nothing to attack yet; just keep playing d5.
notes.original: 2.Qg4?!, another premature queen sortie, this time eyeing the kingside with nothing to actually attack yet.

notes.text: White's coming exd5 starts the Exchange Variation, also called the Exchanged Caro-Kann.
notes.original: This is the Exchange Variation (the ECK, or Exchanged Caro-Kann).

notes.text: This is the core of the Caro-Kann: a semi-open game where minor pieces tend to dominate.
notes.original: The core of the Caro-Kann argument lies here. In this semi-open game, minor piece play tends to dominate certain lines. White may handle the resulting tension.

notes.text: Whatever White tries, d5 brings you to a comfortable, well-understood structure.
notes.original: The main Exchange Variation position. See 🔵 01. Everything in this chapter has been a detour around this single, reliable backbone move: whatever White tries on move two, ...d5 (or the matching central break for that specific try) gets Black to a comfortable, well-understood structure.

notes.text: This move order transposes into the Czech Pirc Defence.
notes.original: 2...d6 transposes to the Czech Pirc Defense.

notes.text: Your pawn prepares to fianchetto the kingside bishop.
notes.original: 2...g6, preparing to fianchetto, has been played.

notes.text: The De Bruycker: your knight goes via a6 to the more active c7 square.
notes.original:
2...Na6!? is called the De Bruycker defence. The knight makes its way to c7 via a6.

2...Na6!? is the De Bruycker defence. Black delays playing d5 to first develop their knight.

Having played c6, the usual square for Black's queenside knight is unavailable. Although a6 (being on the rim) is grim, via a6 the knight can reach c7, where it is more active.

Using two tempi to develop the knight this way is an unusual continuation: in the Caro-Kann, Black usually just develops the knight a bit later when they can do so in one move: either to c6 (if it becomes available again, as in the Exchange Caro-Kann) or d7.

Better is for White is to take advantage of the slow move to grab more space, 3.c4, or to develop their own knight more actively 3.Nf3.

notes.text: The Masi invites e5; your knight goes to d5 and, if kicked by c4, to c7.
notes.original: 2...Nf6!? is called the Masi variation. This invites 3.e5!, and the knight relocates to d5 and, if kicked again with 4.c4, to c7.

notes.text: The Exchange Variation is simple and safe for White, so your job is avoiding a passive position.
notes.original: The Exchange Variation removes most of the theory and gives White a simple, safe structure, close to an improvised London System with Black's c-pawn traded off. Black's practical task is to avoid a passive position. This chapter uses the Grunfeld-style setup, which aims at the kingside and the centre at the same time and keeps queenside play optional. The quieter ...e6 route is about as good objectively, so the choice is about structure and playability, not objective strength.

notes.text: White's classical setup is simple; you usually answer with the solid dxe4, since e6 is a dubious sidestep.
notes.original: The classical set-up is simple and flexible for White: development comes easily, and the same formation turns up against the Sicilian, the Philidor and the French as well. Black usually answers with the solid 3...dxe4, among the most heavily analysed Caro-Kann lines. Sidesteps exist, but 3...e6 blocks the c8-bishop and amounts to a French a tempo down, which makes it a dubious choice.

notes.text: The classical set-up is simple and flexible for White, and the same formation appears against other defences.
notes.original: The classical set-up is simple and flexible for White: development comes easily, and the same formation turns up against the Sicilian, the Philidor and the French as well.

notes.text: Answer with dxe4; ...e6 blocks your light bishop and is a dubious choice.
notes.original: Black usually answers with the solid 3...dxe4, among the most heavily analysed Caro-Kann lines. Sidesteps exist, but 3...e6 blocks the c8-bishop and amounts to a French a tempo down, which makes it a dubious choice.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The normal replies are covered elsewhere; deeper in the Classical lines sit a few named gambits.
notes.original: Part three (continued): gambits inside the Classical Variation. The normal replies here, 3.exd5 (Exchange, 🔵 01) and 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 dxe4 (Classical Variation, 🔵 07 to 10, 🟢 03 and 04), are both covered in full elsewhere. Nested a little deeper inside that same Classical tree, though, are three named gambits/sidelines that do not appear anywhere in those chapters or in the rest of this 64-chapter course. Recovered here for completeness.

notes.text: White gains space, but your light bishop gets out before ...e6, giving you queenside counterplay.
notes.original: The Advance Variation is one of the most challenging tries against the Caro-Kann. White gains space and has kingside attacking chances, much as in the French Defence. The principled, classical way to meet it is recommended here: Black makes full use of the bishop on f5 and gets strong queenside counterplay. In the French that same bishop is often the problem piece, and Black may even have to double the b-pawns just to trade it for a White bishop or knight; in the Caro-Kann Black avoids that fate because the bishop is developed before ...e6.

notes.text: The Fantasy Variation: White wants an open f-file and a strong center, and hopes to grab the initiative.
notes.original: This is the Fantasy Variation of the Caro Kann. The Fantasy Variation of the Caro Kann is an aggressive opening choice against the Caro Kann. White actually wants a fantasy land where he has an open f file for his rook to take advantage of. Second to that white wants to get a fortified center following a principled development on the center. So far white just wants an easy play against black but at the same time get the initiative and advantage.

notes.text: With Nd2 you are free to take on e4 and play Bf5, Nf6 or h6, heading back to Classical lines.
notes.original: The Modern Variation is played for exactly this one reason: to avoid the Gurgenidze system. Now White has still the option to play c3, and then a bishop on g7 wouldn't be very effective. With the Nd2 move order. Black is free to take the pawn and play something like Bf5 or Nf6, Nd7 or even h6! Which brings us back to the Classical Caro Kann.

notes.text: This is the quieter move order, and it is how the Alien Gambit is normally reached.
notes.original: The quieter move order; the Alien Gambit below is normally reached this way rather than via 3.Nc3.

notes.text: In the Exchange Variation White plays for a small positional edge, a system used by Carlsen, Caruana and Fischer.
notes.original: With the Exchange Variation, white aims to play for a small positional edge. Again, there are several different approaches here, but I'm going to primarily focus on a setup that has been utilised by both Magnus Carlsen and Fabiano Caruana as white, while the legendary Bobby Fischer was also a pioneer of this line. On reflection, there is no quibbling with the pedigree of this system!

notes.text: Avoid. Recapture with the pawn. The queen comes out early and White gains time with 4.Nc3.
Avoid.
notes.original: Avoid. Without recapturing, Black falls a pawn behind after 4.dxc6, and the development it gets back does not fully make up for it.

notes.text: Avoid taking with the queen: recapture with the pawn, or White gains time with Nc3.
notes.original: Avoid. Recapture with the pawn. The queen comes out early and White gains time with 4.Nc3.

notes.text: Avoid this: without recapturing, you fall a pawn behind after dxc6, and your development does not fully make up for…
notes.original: Avoid. Without recapturing, Black falls a pawn behind after 4.dxc6, and the development it gets back does not fully make up for it.

notes.text: White develops flexibly; you fight for f4 and f5 and try to neutralise the bishop pair.
notes.original: White's most flexible development. From here Black fights for the f4 and f5 squares and looks to neutralise White's bishop pair.

notes.text: White's bishop takes a key square from you; contest f4 at once and neutralise White's bishop pair.
notes.original: Many experienced Exchange Variation players choose Bd3 to take a key square away from Black. Contesting the f4 square at once and neutralising White's bishop pair is the right response.

notes.text: White develops the bishop actively and delays the usual knight and bishop setups.
notes.original: 4.Bf4 - develops actively onto the long diagonal, delaying the usual Nc3/Bd3 setups.

notes.text: White plays a quiet supporting move, keeping d4 defended and preparing Bd3.
notes.original: 4.c3 - a quiet supporting move, preparing Bd3 and keeping d4 well defended before developing the pieces.

notes.text: White accepts an isolated d-pawn for activity; you aim to blockade, trade pieces and keep your structure healthy.
notes.original: The Panov-Botvinnik Attack. After the pawn exchanges White is left with an isolated d-pawn and accepts that weakness in return for open lines, piece activity and attacking chances. Black's task is to blockade, trade pieces and keep the structure healthy.

notes.text: This is an odd move against the London structure, but White still wants e4-e5.
notes.original: An odd move against the London structure, but White is still going for the e4-e5 idea.

notes.text: Many players choose Nf3 here, following their e4 e5 habit of developing the knight.
notes.original: Thus, many players would play something like Nf3 sticking to their e4 e5 principle.

notes.text: Choose this to keep a flexible structure with an early e5 break; White's main tries are h3, Bf4 and c3.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want to meet 4.Bd3 with 4...Nf6 and keep your structure flexible with an early ...e5 break (more active and more varied than the quiet Rubinstein-style play elsewhere in these chapters). Risk level: medium. For a calm, structure-based game stay with 🔵 01 and 02. After 4.Bd3 Nf6 White has 5.h3, 5.Bf4 and 5.c3 as the main tries.

notes.text: White supports d4. You have two sound replies: ...Nf6 as the main line, or ...Qc7.
notes.original: White supports d4. Black has two sound moves here: 5...Nf6 (main line) and 5...Qc7.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Your queen covers f4, leaving White's dark-squared bishop fewer good squares; this is fully playable.
notes.original: Fully playable. The queen covers f4, so White's dark-squared bishop has fewer good squares. Black answers the most accurate 6.h3 with ...e6, ...Bd6 and ...Nge7.

notes.text: Never take on d4 with the knight.
notes.original: Never take on d4 with the knight. White recaptures and wins a piece for a pawn. The same capture fails on moves 6 to 9, whichever White piece recaptures.

notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
notes.original: ...g6 and ...Bg7

notes.text: Taking on d4 with the knight falls into a trap: you drop a piece.
notes.original: Watch out: ...Nxd4? drops a piece on moves 5 to 9.

notes.text: Never take on d4 with the knight: White recaptures and wins a piece for a pawn.
notes.original: Never take on d4 with the knight. White recaptures and wins a piece for a pawn. The same capture fails on moves 6 to 9, whichever White piece recaptures.

notes.text: White develops the bishop before e3 or Nf3, keeping control of e5 and f4.
notes.original: The main move. White develops the bishop before playing e3 or Nf3 and keeps control of e5 and the f4 square.

notes.text: White's h3 rules out your bishop going to g4 for good, before White develops its own bishop.
notes.original: A move-order point worth knowing: rather than develop the bishop right away, White rules out ...Bg4 for good first. Playing Bf4 a tempo later is not weaker in itself. See the note after 7.h3 below for why this move order is the one Black players find hardest to meet.

notes.text: White develops the knight first and plays h3 only once your bishop comes to g4.
notes.original: A third move order: develop the knight first and meet ...Bg4 with h3 only once Black actually plays it, rather than inserting the prophylactic pawn move unprompted.

notes.text: Against the quiet setup, fianchetto, offer a light-bishop trade with ...Bf5, and aim a knight at e4.
notes.original:
Idea: Against White's quiet 4.Bd3 and 5.c3, fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, then offer to trade the light-squared bishops with ...Bf5. The structure is symmetrical, so the game turns on the pieces: aim for a knight on e4 and play on the queenside.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 g6
Watch out: ...Nxd4? drops a piece on moves 5 to 9, and ...Nxc3? or ...Nxf2? do the same later. Recapture on d5 with the pawn, and at move 10 take back with ...gxf5.
Next: 🔵 02 continues the Exchange Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11. Model game: 🟡 Game 15.

notes.text: You choose ...g6 for its Grunfeld-style structure and playability, with play on the kingside and in the centre.
notes.original: Black aims for a Grunfeld-style structure. The bishop on g7 pressures d4, and Black can play on the kingside and in the centre, not only on the queenside. This is about as good as the quieter 6...e6, and 6...Bg4 is slightly better still, so 6...g6 is chosen for its structure and playability.

notes.text: Your knight takes e4, blocks the d3 bishop, then heads to d6 so ...Bf5 can offer a trade.
notes.original: A surprising choice against a White player who has settled for the London-style setup. The knight heads to e4 to use that square, centralise itself and block the d3 bishop's diagonal. From there Nd6 and ...Bf5 become possible, so Black can offer to trade off White's strong light-squared bishop.

notes.text: White plays h3 first, ruling out ...Bg4 and gaining a tempo, so choose your reply carefully.
notes.original: This is the move order that actually gives Black the hardest practical choice in the whole Bf4 plan - and it is the reason some players find Bf4 so awkward to meet, rather than Bf4 itself being a poor idea. With ...Bg4 ruled out for good, White is a free tempo ahead of the main line below for the same eventual kingside expansion, and the question becomes which of Black's two main replies absorbs that extra tempo best.

notes.text: Your bishop invites a trade on f5. It costs a little, but the positions are clear.
notes.original: Black provokes the trade on f5. It costs a little compared with the best moves 9...Bg4, 9...Qb6 and 9...Nh5, but it leads to clear, well-understood positions.

notes.text: One of the best moves here: your knight attacks the bishop on f4.
notes.original: One of the best moves here. It attacks the bishop on f4.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White takes on f5, the critical test; you recapture with the g-pawn.
notes.original: White's best and the critical test. Black recaptures with the g-pawn.

notes.text: White loses a tempo with this retreat, so you get easy development.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop pair but loses time. Black gets easy development.

notes.text: This bishop move just loses a tempo: White must trade bishops or retreat.
notes.original: This pin merely loses a tempo, since White must either trade off the bishop pair or pull the bishop back. It is the line recommended by WGM Sopiko Guramishvili.

notes.text: White's knight jumps to e5, and your knight simply takes it.
notes.original: White's knight jump. Black takes it.

notes.text: Nb3 avoids the trade on f5, but you get an easy game.
notes.original: It avoids the trade on f5, but Black gets an easy game.

notes.text: The queen on e2 gets in the way of White's rook.
notes.original: The queen gets in the way of the rook.

notes.text: You double the f-pawns, but they control e4 and g4, and the open g-file gives you kingside play.
notes.original: Black gives up the light-squared bishop and doubles the f-pawns, but the pawns control e4 and g4 and the open g-file gives Black kingside play. Mueller-Kieninger, Beverwijk 1965, was drawn: Black kept the position solid and White could not make progress.

notes.text: White's knight takes the e5 square and prepares to trade on your c6 knight.
notes.original: White's best. The knight takes the e5 square and prepares to trade on c6.

notes.text: If White trades on c6, you retake with the b-pawn for the open b-file.
notes.original: The main line. It is a little more accurate than 11...Nxe5 and clearly better than 11...Qb6 and 11...Kh8 below. Black keeps the knight on c6 for the moment and meets 12.Nxc6 with ...bxc6, taking doubled c-pawns in return for the open b-file and the bishop pair. White has a wide menu of tries here: 12.Nxc6, 12.Ndf3, 12.Re1, 12.Nd3, 12.Bg5 and 12.Qe2 are all close together, plus the weaker 12.Qf3!? and 12.f3?!, but none of them change the picture much. White keeps a small edge here, which is normal for this chapter.

notes.text: Taking on e5 is sound, but 11...e6 is the main recommendation and this is a backup.
notes.original: Playable and close to 11...e6, so treat 11...e6 above as the main recommendation and this as a sound backup.

notes.text: Slightly inaccurate: White keeps a slightly bigger edge than after Nxe5 or e6.
notes.original: Slightly inaccurate. White keeps a slightly bigger edge than after 11...Nxe5 or 11...e6.

notes.text: A natural waiting move, but it ignores the knight on e5, so it is a little worse.
notes.original: A natural waiting move, but it does not deal with the knight on e5, so it is a little worse than 11...e6 or 11...Nxe5.

notes.text: White's most testing try, but you meet it comfortably with a knight move or the ...a5 break.
notes.original: White's most testing try here, slightly stronger than 12.Nxc6. Black meets it comfortably with either knight move or the queenside break.

notes.text: White's bishop pins your f6 knight to the queen instead of trading on c6.
notes.original: Pins the knight instead of trading it off on c6.

notes.text: White's queen move is playable, but it is not White's most testing try against you.
notes.original: Playable, but not White's most testing try.

notes.text: This loosens e3 and g3 for no gain, and your knight can hit the bishop at once.
notes.original: A real inaccuracy: it loosens e3 and g3 for no gain, and Black's reply hits the bishop at once.

notes.text: Your knight starts a kingside build-up instead of a passive defence.
notes.original: Black starts a kingside build-up instead of a passive defence.

notes.text: The most-played reply, but looser: it trades your strong e4 knight for White's weaker one.
notes.original: The most-played reply in practice, but looser: it trades off Black's strong e4 knight for White's less active one and costs a little compared with retreating.

notes.text: You slowly reinforce your kingside pieces to provoke weaknesses in White's camp.
notes.original: Black slowly reinforces the kingside pieces to provoke weaknesses.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White could have grabbed a7 first and then returned to defend; you still have no way in.
notes.original: White could have grabbed the a7 pawn first and returned to defend. Black has no way in.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the rook on g2 and forces White to retreat.
notes.original: The pawn hits the rook on g2 and forces White to retreat.

notes.text: You switch your rook to the queenside and push c4, but neither side finds a way in.
notes.original: You switch the rook to the queenside and push c5-c4, but White shuffles and finds no way in for either side, so expect equality.

notes.text: White fixed your structure on the queenside, but your rook on b8 targets the bishop on b4.
notes.original: White has used the open queenside lines to fix your structure. After the exchange, the Bd6 jump is annoying, but ...Rfb8 targets b4 and you have a sound game.

notes.text: Your c4 pawn is passed and your c4 and d5 pawns are strong, so you have enough counterplay.
notes.original: White offers the queen trade to head for a rook ending where the b-pawn is a nuisance. Your c4 and d5 pawns are strong and you have enough counterplay.

notes.text: White's knight wants g3 to challenge your e4 knight, then h5 to trade your g7 bishop.
notes.original: Your knight on e4 attacks the bishop on g5, so it has to retreat. White's plan is Ng3 to challenge the e4 knight and then Nh5 to trade off your g7 bishop and leave the dark squares thin.

notes.text: Your king and rook cover g7, so White has no real target and keeps only a small edge.
notes.original: Kh8 and Rg8 cover g7, so Nh5 only wins a trade of minor pieces. When the bishop comes to h6 you just step the rook aside; White keeps a small edge but has no real target.

notes.text: White's quick attack on g7 fails: your knight and bishop trades removed the attackers.
notes.original: White goes for g7 at once, but ...Nf6 and ...Bxh6 trade off the attackers.

notes.text: Your a4 pawn fixes White's queenside and your knight on g6 hits the annoying e5 knight.
notes.original: The pawn on a4 fixes b2 and cuts down the knight. You regroup with Ne7-g6 and Ne4. White's knight on e5 is annoying but not decisive.

notes.text: White's bishop and knights point at your kingside, so you want to trade pieces.
notes.original: Step off the g-file so that ...Rg8 and ...Ng6 can follow and challenge the e5 knight. White's bishop on g5 and both knights are aimed at your kingside, so you want to trade pieces.

notes.text: With a pair of knights traded, White keeps only a small edge.
notes.original: Once you have traded a knight White keeps only a small edge.

notes.text: A calmer set-up: your bishop on f6 hits the e5 knight and offers a trade.
notes.original: A calmer set-up that offers the bishop trade on f6.

notes.text: Your knight chased the e5 knight away, and your pieces are placed sensibly despite White's small edge.
notes.original: Your knight challenges the Ne5, so White retreats it. Then Ng4 trades off the dark-squared bishop and Bf8 covers the dark squares. White has a small edge, but your pieces are placed sensibly.

notes.text: Your rook and queen deal with the strong-looking bishop, and your f6 pawn supports e5.
notes.original: You trade White's best minor piece, then support the e5 square with ...f6. The Bd6 looks strong but Rf7 and Qb6 deal with it. White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Your knight hits the f4 bishop, so White must move it and you seize the initiative.
notes.original: The point: the bishop on f4 has to move, and Black seizes the initiative.

notes.text: Take at once: White's f3 pawn took its own knight's best square, so trading leaves White badly coordinated.
notes.original: Take at once: White's f3 pawn has taken the best square from its own knight, so trading the bishop leaves White's pieces badly coordinated.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn hits the d4 pawn and the f4 knight.
notes.original: ...e5 hits d4 and opens the diagonal for your g7 bishop.

notes.text: Your pieces swarm around d4, e5 and b2 while White's king is stuck behind its pawns.
notes.original: Your pieces swarm around d4, e5 and b2 while White's king is stuck behind its own pawns.

notes.text: Your loose knight on h5 was a target, and White's queen simply takes it.
notes.original: The quiet ...Re8 lets White keep the bishop, and the loose knight on h5 becomes a target.

notes.text: Recapturing with the pawn is also strong, but the e5 pawn needs long-term support; Bxe5 is simpler.
notes.original: Also strong, about as good as 12.Bxe5, but it trades the solid d4 point for a pawn on e5 that needs long-term support, instead of keeping the bishop actively posted there. 12.Bxe5 stays the simpler recommendation.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
Your a-pawn can advance to gain queenside space.
notes.original: Black's structure is solid. Typical Black plans: ...Kh8 and ...Rg8 to use the g-file, ...Ne4 and ...f6 to challenge the bishop on e5, and ...a5 to gain queenside space. Typical White plans: keep the bishop on e5 or f4, bring the knight to f3 and expand with a4-a5.

notes.text: White wants a knight on f3 and the a-pawn pushed forward.
notes.original: Black's structure is solid. Typical Black plans: ...Kh8 and ...Rg8 to use the g-file, ...Ne4 and ...f6 to challenge the bishop on e5, and ...a5 to gain queenside space. Typical White plans: keep the bishop on e5 or f4, bring the knight to f3 and expand with a4-a5.

notes.text: A useful waiting move: your king steps aside so the rook can go to g8 for a kingside plan.
notes.original: A useful waiting move that prepares ...Rg8 and a direct kingside plan. It is as good as 12...e6.

notes.text: White's edge is the better structure, not an attack; you are solid.
notes.original: White's best. 13.Nb3, 13.Bf4 and 13.Qe2 are about as good. Black is solid and White's edge is the better structure, not an attack.

notes.text: A natural move, but not White's most accurate.
notes.original: Natural, but not White's most accurate move.

notes.text: Your knight steps aside so your bishop offers to trade White's strong bishop.
notes.original: Black offers the trade of White's strong bishop.

notes.text: White declines the trade and keeps the bishop.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop.

notes.text: You gain queenside space and prepare to play f6.
notes.original: Black gains queenside space and prepares ...f6.

notes.text: Do not grab material on c3 or f2.
notes.original: Do not grab material on c3 or f2. White recaptures and Black has lost a piece for a pawn. The knight on e4 is a strength, not a target.

notes.text: Don't grab on c3: White recaptures and you have lost a piece for a pawn.
notes.original: Do not grab material on c3 or f2. White recaptures and Black has lost a piece for a pawn. The knight on e4 is a strength, not a target.

notes.text: White's bishop must guard e5, while your f-pawns cover e4 and g4.
notes.original: A typical setup. Black has no weaknesses, and White keeps a small edge. The bishop on f4 has to guard e5, and the doubled f-pawns cover e4 and g4.

notes.text: White's knight heads for d3 to cover e5 and f4.
notes.original: White steers the knight to d3 so that e5 and f4 are covered.

notes.text: Don't wait: your e-pawn hits the bishop and the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Do not wait: ...e5 hits the Bf4 and the d4 pawn and activates your bishop.

notes.text: White attacks your king, but your rook on the b-file gives you counterplay.
notes.original: White opens lines against your king with Qh5 and f4, but ...exd4 and then ...Rb8 give you counterplay on the b-file. White keeps a small initiative.

notes.text: White is winning.
You are a piece down for a pawn, and White consolidates and keeps trading.
notes.original: You are a piece down for a pawn, since the knight on c3 was lost. White consolidates with Re1 and g3 and keeps trading, because your doubled f-pawns and king are not worth the piece.

notes.text: You can pile up on the g-file, but White covers everything.
White trades the good bishop for a knight, giving up part of the edge.
notes.original: This trades White's good bishop for a knight and gives up part of the edge.

notes.text: This loses most of White's remaining edge.
notes.original: Loses most of the remaining edge.

notes.text: White now has only two good moves: g3 and Qh3. The natural Kh1 is a mistake.
notes.original: White now has only two good moves, 18.g3 and 18.Qh3. The natural 18.Kh1? is a mistake: Black is clearly better.

notes.text: White plays g3 to shut your queen and rook battery on the g-file and keep the king safe.
notes.original: The point of g3 is to shut the g-file battery of your Qg8 and Rg6 against g2 and to leave the king safe.

notes.text: You keep the g-file and the f5 pawn, and White's knight is gone.
notes.original: You keep the g-file and the f5 pawn together, and White's knight has gone. The position is close to equal.

notes.text: White's other correct move was Qh3, attacking your f5 pawn.
notes.original: Qh3 is the other correct move, attacking your pawn on f5.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
White's queen attacks your b7 pawn, but this is not White's best move.
notes.original: This attacks b7 but is not White's best.

notes.text: This position was seen in Rasmussen-Sapis, Leningrad 1983.
notes.original: Seen in Rasmussen-Sapis, Leningrad 1983.

notes.text: You are solid, and White keeps only a small edge.
notes.original: Black is solid and White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: White's knight on e5 is held by the d4 pawn, and White keeps only a small edge.
notes.original: White's knight on e5 is supported by the bishop on f4 and the d4 pawn. When f3 kicks your Ne4, you swing the knight to h5 to hit the bishop and then trade queens or regroup. White has only a small edge.

notes.text: Simple and good: the pawn steps out of the queen's attack and leaves White with little.
notes.original: Simple and good. It defends b7 and leaves White with little.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
A direct try, but it gives White a slightly bigger edge than the b6 pawn move.
notes.original: A direct try, but it gives White a slightly bigger edge than 14...b6.

notes.text: You are solid, and White has little to show for the queen move.
notes.original: Black is solid and White has little to show for the queen move.

notes.text: Your rook supports the d5 pawn before it comes under attack.
notes.original: Your rook supports d5 before it is attacked.

notes.text: White grabbed a7, but you win the d4 pawn with active rooks and good counterplay.
notes.original: White grabs a7 but has to allow ...Rxd4 with active rooks. The dark bishops have disappeared and you have good counterplay.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White closes the position, but your kingside attack stays on the board.
notes.original: White closes the position, but the kingside attack stays on the board.

notes.text: Your queen escapes the attack and goes to h3, where it watches the g2 pawn.
notes.original: White hits your queen, so it goes to h3 where it keeps an eye on g2.

notes.text: White closed the centre to reduce your play, but you still have h4 for the attack.
notes.original: White closed the centre with c5 to reduce your play, then trades the knights. You still have ...h5-h4 for the attack, but White's pieces are well placed for defence.

notes.text: The position is equal.
You stack the rooks, trade bishops, then attack the white king.
notes.original: Black stacks the rooks, trades bishops and then attacks the white king.

notes.text: White's d5 blocks your bishop; you aim at the king, but White's queenside majority gives a long-term edge.
notes.original: White trades knights and pushes d5, which blocks your bishop. You answer with ...e5 and bring the rook to g6 and play ...h5, aiming at the white king. Meanwhile White's pawn majority on the queenside gives him the long-term edge.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
A compact move that stops White's queen ideas of reaching c7.
notes.original: A compact move that stops ideas of Qc4-c7.

notes.text: White opens lines with d5; your f-pawns are doubled, so keep the rook and h-pawn harassing the king.
notes.original: White uses the d5 break to open lines and activate the rooks. Your e- and f-pawns are doubled, so keep ...Rg6 and ...h5 going to harass the king.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's knight on h4 attacks your f5 pawn, so keep it protected; the edge is small.
notes.original: After the bishops come off White aims the knight at f5 via h4, so you bring the h5 knight back with ...Nf6 and protect f5 with the rooks. The edge is small.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
This is a mistake: you are already slightly better.
notes.original: A mistake: Black is already slightly better.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your queen is ready to unleash a strong attack on White's kingside.
notes.original: Black is ready to unleash a strong attack on White's kingside.

notes.text: Your rook takes on g3 and the attack is converted into a winning position.
notes.original: Black converted. (Rasmussen-Sapis, Leningrad 1983, 0-1.)

notes.text: White's rook offers a trade on g3 to ease the pressure, but it does not help.
notes.original: White trades off the rook on g3 to relieve the pressure, but it does not help.

notes.text: Your queen checks and your rook hits the knight on g1; White's king is caught in a net.
notes.original: Your queen and rook have the exposed king in a net and White cannot hold the knight on g1.

notes.text: Your rook check on d2 is checkmate, because your queen on h6 guards it.
notes.original: Tempting, but it walks into a mating net.

notes.text: White's c4 is a better try than Kh1, but taking on g3 keeps you fine.
notes.original: 19.c4 is a better try than 19.Kh1, but Black is fine after 19...fxg3 or 19...f6.

notes.text: White takes the pawn, and your knight and rook now press on the g3 pawn.
notes.original: White takes the pawn, and the Nh5 and Rg7 now press on g3.

notes.text: Both sides have chances: your pieces swarm on g3, while White grabs b7 and uses the knight against f7.
notes.original: Both sides have chances. Your rooks and queen swarm on g3, so White grabs b7 and uses the knight to hit f7.

notes.text: The knight sacrifice looks like a trick, but you take everything and stay clearly better.
notes.original: The knight sacrifice looks like a trick, but you take, finish the pawn grab, and stay clearly better.

notes.text: Your rook grabs b2 and your rooks and queen invade quickly.
notes.original: Black's rooks and queen invade quickly.

notes.text: White's rook hits your b2 rook, and the queen on a7 stays safe while your f7 pawn blocks the rank.
notes.original: This is the only move that keeps White clearly ahead: it hits the rook on b2 at once, while the queen on a7 is safe as long as your f7 pawn blocks the seventh rank.

notes.text: Now that the f-pawn has moved, your rook on g7 attacks White's queen.
notes.original: Once the f-pawn moves, your Rg7 attacks the queen.

notes.text: White gave up the queen but wins your b2 rook next, leaving two rooks and a knight against queen and…
notes.original: White gives the queen but wins the rook on b2 next, and two rooks and a knight against queen and knight leave White clearly better.

notes.text: In this line White ends up giving the queen for two rooks.
notes.original: Qg5 hits d2 and g2 together, and White ends up giving the queen for two rooks.

notes.text: White trades knights first, so your central pawn mass becomes the target.
notes.original: White trades knights first so that your central pawn mass is the target.

notes.text: White's queen eyes b7 and d5, but you won the e5 pawn and your central pawns are mobile.
notes.original: White's queen on b3 watches b7 and d5, so he opens the c-file, but you win the e5 pawn and your central pawns are mobile. Everything is level.

notes.text: Trading on g7 earlier gave you the g-file and the easier game.
notes.original: Taking on g7 gives you the g-file and the easier game.

notes.text: White's bishop retreat to f4 is the most testing try here.
notes.original: White's most testing move here.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your knight clears f6 for the queen and keeps e5 under watch.
notes.original: Nd7 clears f6 for the queen and keeps e5 under watch, ready for Qh5 and the Nc5 jump.

notes.text: Your queen protects the f5 pawn while your rooks wait.
notes.original: The queen protects f5 while the rooks wait.

notes.text: White's queen hits your f5 pawn, but your queen guards it and you stay safe.
notes.original: The knight lands on c6 for a moment, but you answer by offering the queens. You are slightly worse but safe, with your doubled f-pawns firmly protected.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's king leaves the g-file, so your rook has nothing to hit, and f3 and g4 come next.
notes.original: White steps off the g-file so that your Rg8 has nothing to hit, and now f3 and g4 are possible.

notes.text: Your bishop offers a trade for White's e5 bishop, the best defender of White's centre.
notes.original: You trade off the dark bishop, which is the best defender of White's centre.

notes.text: White's g4 pawn already hits your f5 pawn, aiming to open the position, but your structure holds.
notes.original: White's plan is f3 and g4 to break your f5 pawn and open the position. A modest White edge remains, but your structure holds.

notes.text: Your knight hits the e5 pawn, the only real try, and keeps your structure together.
notes.original: The only real try, keeping the structure together.

notes.text: Hit the e5 wedge at once; White wants it as a spearhead against your doubled f-pawns.
notes.original: Hit the wedge on e5 straight away: White wants to keep that pawn as a spearhead and use Qh5 and the bishop on f4 against your doubled f-pawns.

notes.text: White keeps the same small, nagging edge through this whole sequence.
White protects b2 and prepares to trade rooks on e4, after which the queen can pester your king.
notes.original: White protects b2 and prepares the simplifying trade on e4, after which Qh6 pesters the king.

notes.text: You trade one pair of rooks and hold the king, so White's edge stays small.
notes.original: You keep the position safe by trading one pair of rooks and holding the king. White's edge is only small.

notes.text: Hitting the rook with the queen looks attractive, but you take b2 and White only has perpetual check.
notes.original: Hitting the rook with Qh5 looks attractive, but you take b2 and White only has perpetual check.

notes.text: Strong and simple; Nd3 is a touch more precise and Rb1 is also fine.
notes.original: Strong and simple. 12.Nd3 is a touch more precise and 12.Rb1 is also fine; the choice between them barely matters in practice.

notes.text: This isn't White's best move, but Black goes wrong later.
notes.original: Not White's best, but Black goes wrong later.

notes.text: This lets most of White's edge slip away.
notes.original: This lets most of the edge slip.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
You grab b2 and aim for an endgame rather than a kingside attack.
notes.original: Black aims for an endgame rather than a kingside attack. 0-1 (56) Baljon-Rosenlund, Bad Meinberg 1975.

notes.text: You have enough defence, and White has at best a perpetual check.
notes.original: Your queen goes pawn hunting on the queenside, so White lifts a rook with Rd3-g3 to pin and trade the Bg7 and bring the queen onto g5. You have enough defence, and White has at best a perpetual check.

notes.text: White keeps a lasting edge, and you have to defend patiently.
notes.original: White keeps a lasting structural edge from the doubled c-pawns, and Black has to defend patiently.

notes.text: You pick up a2 and b2, but your queen is out of play while White's pieces swing to your king.
notes.original: The point of f3 is to kick the knight, and Bh6 trades off your best defender so that the g-file opens for Qg3+. You pick up a2 and b2, but your queen is out of play while White's pieces swing to the king. Defend patiently.

notes.text: Your kingside attack arrives too late when you are already a pawn down.
notes.original: The kingside attack arrives too late for a side that is already a pawn down. (Commons-Denker, Lone Pine 1976, 1-0.)

notes.text: Your queen raid on e2 is counterplay, but White's knight and safe king hold, so White stays a pawn up.
notes.original: You grab the e5 pawn back, but Qxd5 then wins the d5 pawn, so White stays a pawn up. Your counterplay is the Qe2 raid, but the knight and the safe king hold everything together.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
White lifts the rook to h3 to hit h7 while your king sits in the corner.
notes.original: White's idea is a rook lift: Re3-h3 aims at h7 and your g7 bishop while your king sits in the corner.

notes.text: Your bishop offers a dark-bishop trade, and your rook on g7 guards h7. White keeps a clear edge.
notes.original: ...Bf8 and ...Rg7 cover h7 and h6, and trading the dark bishops with ...Bd6 relieves the pressure. White keeps a clear but manageable edge.

notes.text: White can try Ng3-h5 to remove your bishop, but ...Ng6 answers it.
notes.original: Another way to attack is Ng3-h5 to remove your bishop, but ...Ng6 meets it.

notes.text: Your kingside is weakened, but your pieces are active, so this is playable, not a refutation.
notes.original: Black's kingside is weakened, but in return Black has active pieces. White keeps a modest edge, so this is playable rather than a refutation.

notes.text: White trades your active knight, then wants a4-a5 to fix your queenside.
notes.original: White trades your active knight and then fixes the queenside with a4-a5.

notes.text: Your g5 and h6 pawns are looser, so White will aim at them with h4.
notes.original: Your kingside pawns are looser (g5 and h6), so White will aim at them with h4 and the bishop on h2. You answer with the strong Ne4 and ...Bf8-d6 to trade off the bishops.

notes.text: You answer with the strong knight on e4 and ...Bd6 to trade off the bishops.
notes.original: Your kingside pawns are looser (g5 and h6), so White will aim at them with h4 and the bishop on h2. You answer with the strong Ne4 and ...Bf8-d6 to trade off the bishops.

notes.text: If White waits, you trade a pair of minor pieces and your position relaxes.
notes.original: If White waits you trade a pair of minor pieces and your position relaxes.

notes.text: You have the bishop pair and are at least equal.
notes.original: Black has the bishop pair and is at least equal.

notes.text: White offers a queen trade, hoping your queenside pawns become the weakness in the ending.
notes.original: White offers the queen trade to cash in the doubled pawns, since your c-pawns are your only weakness.

notes.text: You have the bishop pair, and ...e5 next frees your pieces so the bishops take over.
notes.original: After the trade you have the bishop pair and a strong centre. ...f6 and then ...e5 free your pieces, so your bishops soon take over.

notes.text: Black is winning.
Your knight escapes with tempo, hitting the knight on d2 and the b2 pawn.
notes.original: The knight escapes with tempo.

notes.text: Recapturing on f5 is the natural move, but 11...Nc4! first is better.
Retaking on f5 is natural, but playing ...Nc4 first is better.
notes.original: Recapturing on f5 is the natural move, but 11...Nc4! first is better.

notes.text: Your position is fine.
notes.original: Black is fine.

notes.text: White's bishop already eyes g6, so White plans h4-h5 to open the h-file.
notes.original: Bc2 already eyes g6, so White plans Qe2 or Qf3 and then h4-h5 to open the h-file.

notes.text: Your h-pawn shuts White's h-pawn down; your c4 pawn cramps White, so follow with ...a5 and ...b4.
notes.original: ...h5 shuts the h-pawn down. Your own trumps are the c4 pawn, which cramps White, and the b5 chain; follow with ...a5 and ...b4.

notes.text: You are comfortable here.
notes.original: You are comfortable.

notes.text: Your f-pawn challenged the e5 wedge, so White had to resolve the tension by capturing.
notes.original: ...f6 is your lever against the e5 wedge; White has to resolve the tension.

notes.text: Rfe1 looks active, but White's e6 pawn already breaks up your centre.
notes.original: Active-looking, but the knight is offside and White's e6 thrust breaks up your centre.

notes.text: White's knight on d2 blocks the queen, so White cannot recapture on d3 and you win a piece.
notes.original: The knight on d2 blocks the queen, so White cannot recapture on d3. Black wins a piece.

notes.text: White cannot win the piece back, so he looks for activity on the e-file.
notes.original: White has no way to win the piece back, so he looks for activity on the e-file.

notes.text: Retreat the bishop, drive off the pressure with Ne8 and Bf6, and keep your extra piece.
notes.original: Retreat the bishop, drive away the pressure with ...Ne8 and ...Bf6, and keep the extra piece.

notes.text: Trading bishops first changes nothing; you still keep the extra piece.
notes.original: Trading bishops first changes nothing.

notes.text: You have no problems in this position.
notes.original: Black has no problems.

notes.text: Push your a-pawn to a4 to chase White's knight, then bring your knight back to f6.
notes.original: White has parked the knight on b3 and keeps developing slowly. You play ...a5-a4 to push it back and complete the plan with ...e6 and ...Nf6.

notes.text: Your knight returns to the centre while White's knight heads for d3; the position is balanced.
notes.original: Your knight comes back to the centre. White's knight heads for d3 and the dark bishops come off. The position is balanced.

notes.text: This is White's best, but you are fine.
notes.original: White's best. White is slightly better, but Black is fine.

notes.text: White's knight jump looks tempting, but it does not win a piece.
notes.original: This looks tempting, but it does not win a piece.

notes.text: A quiet improvement; nothing here changes the overall assessment.
notes.original:
A quiet improvement. White has a slightly more pleasant position, and nothing here changes the overall assessment.
Trap: 14...Qxb2? 15.Reb1 Qxa1 16.Rxa1 Rac8 17.Qb1 Ne4 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on b2 with the queen falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 14...Qxb2? 15.Reb1 Qxa1 16.Rxa1 Rac8 17.Qb1 Ne4 and Black is losing.

notes.text: White reroutes the knight via e3 to g4, and a4-a5 may also chase your queen.
notes.original: White reroutes the knight via f1 and e3 to g4 to trade your Nf6, and a4-a5 may also chase the queen.

notes.text: You meet White's plan with Rac8 and Ne4, putting your knight on a strong blockade square.
notes.original: You meet the plan with ...Rac8 and ...Ne4, putting your knight on a strong blockade square.

notes.text: A normal middlegame where White is a little freer.
White expands with b4 and a5, so you retreat the queen and break in the centre with e5.
notes.original: White expands with b4 and a5, so you retreat the queen and break in the centre with ...e5.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the bishop on f4 and gains time.
notes.original: The knight attacks the bishop on f4 and gains time.

notes.text: This queen move is playable, but the queen move to g5 is stronger.
notes.original: Also playable, but 14...Qg5! is stronger.

notes.text: Black is winning.
Retaking on c6 with your b-pawn would have been a mistake that leaves you losing.
notes.original: Trap: 15...bxc6? 16.hxg5 Rfb8 17.Qxf4 Rxb2 18.Rfc1 Rc8 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on c6 with the pawn falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 15...bxc6? 16.hxg5 Rfb8 17.Qxf4 Rxb2 18.Rfc1 Rc8 and Black is losing.

notes.text: You stand clearly better here.
notes.original: Black has a clear advantage.

notes.text: White retreats the knight to d3 to trade off your strong knight on f4.
notes.original: White retreats the knight to d3 to trade off your strong Nf4.

notes.text: Offering a queen trade is the clean way to cash in your extra pawn.
notes.original: Offering the queen trade is the clean way to cash in the extra pawn.

notes.text: Your e3 pawn cramps White, and the knight on g5 soon has few good squares.
notes.original: The e3 pawn cramps White and the knight on g5 soon has few good squares.

notes.text: White's knight sacrifice was a desperate try to open the b-file; it fails against your queen and knight.
notes.original: A desperate knight sacrifice to open the b-file and lure your rook away. It fails because your queen and knight attack the king.

notes.text: Black is winning.
White protects the b2 pawn first and keeps its pieces together.
notes.original: The knight on b4 is attacked by your queen, so White first protects b2 and keeps its pieces together.

notes.text: The a-pawn kick sent the knight back; your queen and the c-file give you the play, and you are a…
notes.original: The kick ...a5 sends the knight back, and your queen plus the c-file give you all the play. You are a clean pawn up.

notes.text: Seeking a queen trade while leaving b2 hanging just loses the pawn and lets your queen into White's camp.
notes.original: Looking for a queen trade while leaving b2 hanging just loses the pawn and lets your queen into White's camp.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
You have enough counterplay on the queenside.
notes.original: Black has enough queenside counterplay.

notes.text: The loose queenside pawns and the hanging knight on a4 give you the upper hand.
notes.original: The loose queenside pawns and the hanging knight give Black the upper hand. (Kiryushkin-Feofanov, Berdsk 2010, 0-1.)

notes.text: With the knight on a4 attacked twice, White jumps to c5, a square the d4 pawn protects.
notes.original: The Na4 is attacked twice (by Rc4 and Qa3), so White jumps to c5, a square protected by the d4 pawn.

notes.text: You gave a rook for a knight, but you collect two pawns and White's exposed king ties down its queen.
notes.original: You gave a rook for a knight, but you collect two pawns and White's king is exposed, with the queen tied to its defence.

notes.text: White's f5 attack looks tempting, but the knight falls.
notes.original: An f4-f5 attack looks tempting, but the knight falls.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White has to trade queens, since other queen moves leave you clearly better.
notes.original: Other queen moves, such as Qe3, leave you clearly better, so White has to trade.

notes.text: Attack the b5 pawn with your rook; the position is balanced, so play safely for a draw.
notes.original: You pick up b2 but the bishop gets harassed by Rc2 and the knight settles on d4. Now hit the b5 pawn with ...Rfb8: the position is balanced, so play for a draw safely or look for small chances.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Black is clearly better.
White's edge is small and nothing concrete; play patiently with your rook to c8 and the f-pawn to f5.
notes.original: A fully typical position for this whole chapter: White's edge is the bishop pair and a touch more space, nothing concrete. Black's plan from here is simple and reliable: ...Rfc8, ...Nb6xc4 trading off White's good bishop, or ...f5 to gain central space once the knight on h5 has done its job of provoking Be3. There is nothing to fear in this line; it just needs a touch more patience than the main 9...Bf5 trade.

notes.text: White offers to trade the active bishop, and g4 will then drive away your knight on h5.
notes.original: White offers to trade off the active bishop: after Bxd3 the knight sits well on d3, and g4 will drive away the knight on h5.

notes.text: Your knight is back on f6 and White has no concrete target.
notes.original: Your knight returns to f6 and White has no concrete target.

notes.text: Taking on a6 would also leave White with the same small edge.
notes.original: Taking on a6 gives the same small edge.

notes.text: White gave up the bishop pair for nothing, and now you have both bishops.
notes.original: White gives up the bishop pair for nothing. Black is fine.

notes.text: White's rook takes the e-file and eyes your e7 pawn.
notes.original: Rook to the e-file, eyeing e7 and the centre.

notes.text: Push the h-pawn on to h4 to open the h-file against White's king.
notes.original: With your bishop on g4, ...h5-h4 will prise open the h-file against White's king.

notes.text: White's kingside pawns are doubled and wrecked, so your centre pawns can roll forward.
notes.original: White spends his bishop to double your c-pawns, but his own kingside is wrecked and your centre pawns roll.

notes.text: Your bishop recaptures on g4 and stays active on the board.
notes.original: Retreating the bishop lets you keep playing for ...h5-h4.

notes.text: Your f-pawn hits the bishop on e5, winning the initiative.
notes.original: Black wins the initiative and gets a clear advantage.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
If White does not take, your pawn goes to e4 and hits the knight.
notes.original: If White does not take, ...e4 hits the knight and gains space.

notes.text: Your e4 pawn and the g7 bishop now dominate the centre.
notes.original: Your knight on h5 hits g3, so White cannot keep the bishop, and after the trade your e4 pawn and the g7 bishop dominate.

notes.text: A knight sacrifice for two pawns is tempting but unsound; you keep the extra piece.
notes.original: Giving a knight for two pawns and lines against c6 and your king is tempting but unsound; you keep the extra piece.

notes.text: This is White's best move here.
notes.original: White's best.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's knight on c5 hits b7 and e6, and grabbing on b2 would cost you time.
notes.original: The knight lands on an outpost and hits b7 and e6; White also invites ...Qxb2, a pawn grab that costs you time while White develops.

notes.text: Your e-pawn break frees the position, hitting the d4 pawn and the bishop on f4.
notes.original: ...e5 is your freeing break: open the position before White can use the loose queen.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop on f4.
notes.original: The knight hits the bishop on f4.

notes.text: Trading right away looks natural, but with h3 played White's kingside attack is stronger, so be precise.
notes.original: Trading immediately looks natural, but with h3 already in, White's attacking chances on the kingside are better than in the normal main line (compare 9...Bf5 below), so this needs to be handled very precisely.

notes.text: With h3 already played, ...Bg4 is off, so your bishop simply offers the usual trade on d3.
notes.original: Also perfectly playable once h3 has already ruled out ...Bg4 - there is no reason to delay the usual trade on d3 just because the move order changed.

notes.text: The game transposes back to the normal setup, only with White's h3 already played.
notes.original: Transposing back to the normal developing scheme, just with h3 already banked.

notes.text: Keep your light bishop on c8 and head for the central break with e5.
notes.original: The cleaner practical answer to the h3 move order: rather than trade light-squared bishops into White's now-supported g4 push, Black keeps the bishop on c8 for now and heads straight for the standard central break with ...e5, matching the plan already given above in the pure 6.h3 line.

notes.text: Prepare the central break with e5 instead of trading bishops, since h3 gives White a useful extra move.
notes.original: The key practical improvement for this exact move order: rather than the immediate 9...Bf5 trade (see the note just below), Black first prepares a central break with ...e5. Once White has already spent a tempo on h3, trading light-squared bishops hands White an extra supporting move for a later g4 push (compare the 9...Bf5 note), so meeting it with the central break instead is the cleaner practical answer - the actual reason 6.Bf4 can feel notoriously awkward to handle well against this exact move order if Black insists on the normal trading plan regardless.

notes.text: Your central break works because your bishop is still on g7, backing up e5.
notes.original: The central break: with the dark-squared bishop still on g7 instead of having been traded away for White's light-squared one, opening the centre favours Black's better-coordinated pieces rather than inviting a kingside pawn storm.

notes.text: Bb5 is White's most testing try, hitting your knight on c6.
notes.original: The most testing try, pinning the newly-arrived knight before it settles on e5.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your c6 knight, but achieves little because your central pawn is already advancing.
notes.original: Pins the knight, but the pin does not actually achieve much, since Black's central pawn is already rolling forward regardless.

notes.text: You offer a pawn to open lines before White's pieces settle: the most ambitious try.
notes.original: The most ambitious try, offering a pawn to open lines before White's pieces settle.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
This is a comfortable position for you; the ...Nd7 and ...e5 plan works just as well against h3.
notes.original: A typical, comfortable position for Black. The ...Nd7 and ...e5 plan works against h3 just as well as in the main line below.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your g7 bishop, your main king defender, and wants to remove it.
notes.original: White wants to remove your g7 bishop, your main king defender.

notes.text: Trading the dark bishops instead is also fine for you.
notes.original: Rather than avoiding the bishop trade you meet it, then trade rooks on the e-file.

notes.text: You met the bishop trade, then traded rooks on the e-file.
notes.original: Trading dark bishops instead is also fine for you.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
White's knight hits your active bishop and will take it unless you move it or defend.
notes.original: White wants to trade your active bishop or win the d5 pawn.

notes.text: Your c6 pawn is isolated, but the e4 pawn and active queen keep things balanced.
notes.original: You have an isolated c6 pawn, but the e4 pawn and active queen keep the balance.

notes.text: White grabbed a pawn, but your pieces are active and your rook sits on the d-file.
notes.original: White grabs a pawn, but you get activity and a rook on the d-file.

notes.text: White's knight hits your bishop and the b7 pawn, and wants to take on e6 to double your pawns.
notes.original: White's knight attacks the bishop on e6 and the pawn on b7, aiming to double your pawns.

notes.text: After the knight trades your structure is worse, so White keeps a clear edge.
notes.original: White's knights are traded off for your bishop and knight, and your structure comes out the worse. That is why White keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: The trades leave a dead-equal position.
notes.original: Trades down to a dead-equal position.

notes.text: Queens are off and both sides have bishops; White takes b7, you take b2, and it stays level.
notes.original: The queens are off and both sides have bishops. White takes b7, you take b2, and the position stays level.

notes.text: Your bishop pair compensates for the slightly loose queenside pawns, so the position is roughly balanced.
notes.original: Roughly balanced; Black's bishop pair compensates for the slightly loose queenside pawns.

notes.text: Your b4 pawn pressures c3 and the bishop trade eases your queenside, but White keeps a slight initiative.
notes.original: Black plays ...b4 to open lines against c3 and trades a bishop to relieve the cramped queenside; the knight on d4 and the e-file give White a slight initiative.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's queen protects the bishop and hits your b7 pawn at the same time.
notes.original: White protects the bishop and hits b7 at the same time.

notes.text: You are a pawn up with the bishop pair; White's knight on d6 is annoying but your pieces cover the…
notes.original: You are a pawn up with the bishop pair; White's knight on d6 is annoying but your pieces cover the key squares.

notes.text: The position is completely level; trading the dark-squared pieces has simplified things nicely for you.
notes.original: A completely level position; the trade of dark-squared pieces has simplified matters nicely for Black.

notes.text: White's rook lines up on the d-file against your d5 pawn, preparing a knight to d4 and the queen taking…
notes.original: White puts the rook on the d-file against your d5 pawn and prepares Nd4 and Qxb7.

notes.text: White won a pawn, but your rooks and queen are active and White's king is exposed, so it's level.
notes.original: White wins a pawn, but your rooks and queen are active and White's king is exposed, so the position is level.

notes.text: Your rook on the b-file and active queen give you a small plus.
notes.original: An immediate pawn grab gives you the b-file and a small plus.

notes.text: White's g-pawn hits your f5 pawn; the storm against your doubled f-pawns is playable but needlessly sharp.
notes.original: The same idea as above: with h3 already played, this pawn storm has real teeth against the doubled f-pawns. It's still playable for Black, just unnecessarily sharp when the calmer plan is sitting right there.

notes.text: White's g4 hits your f5 pawn, and your doubled f-pawns are now a real target.
notes.original: This is the point: with h3 already played, g4 arrives with full support and real venom, since Black's doubled f-pawns are now a real target rather than just a cosmetic weakness.

notes.text: Your queen hits b2 and forces the knight to b3; counter-attack rather than wait for the storm.
notes.original: Hit b2 and force the knight to b3: with h3 already played the pawn storm has teeth, so counter-attack rather than wait.

notes.text: Your queenside pawns and the knight on e4 give you your own initiative.
notes.original: Your queenside pawns and the e4 knight give you your own initiative.

notes.text: This plan is too slow: White gets the g-file and a strong knight on e5.
notes.original: Too slow: White gets the g-file and the e5 knight.

notes.text: This is the point of h3: White's pawn storm is well supported, and your doubled f-pawns are a lasting target.
notes.original: The point of h3: this pawn storm now comes with full support and real venom, since Black's doubled f-pawns are a long-term target rather than just a structural blemish.

notes.text: This quieter move lets you untangle your pieces comfortably.
notes.original: Quieter, and lets Black untangle comfortably.

notes.text: This is also a fine response for White.
notes.original: This is also a fine response.

notes.text: The critical defence: your rook attacks the g4 pawn down the open file before you try to grab anything.
notes.original: The critical defence: before anything else, Black attacks the g4-pawn down the open file rather than trying to grab material right away.

notes.text: Your queen hits the hanging b2 pawn, but it lets White's attack run ahead unchecked.
notes.original: Tempting, since b2 is hanging, but it lets White's attack run ahead unchecked.

notes.text: Your queen attacks the f5 pawn, so you win it back while developing.
notes.original: Black recaptures next and keeps development going; the rook on g8 has already done its defensive job.

notes.text: Centralising your queen looks natural, but White trades queens and the resulting structure favours White.
notes.original: Centralising the queen looks natural, but it walks into a trade that favours White's structure.

notes.text: You are fine with precise play, but the central-development plan is the recommended answer to h3.
notes.original: Black is fine here with precise play, but 7...Bf5 against h3 is the sharper, more demanding path. That is why the central-development plan below is the recommended answer.

notes.text: Your queen attacks the rook on h1 and the knight on e2 together, so White must castle long.
notes.original: The rook on h1 and the knight on e2 are attacked together. White must castle long so that the rook on d1 covers h1, and Black can castle long as well.

notes.text: White's c4 and d5 advances try to open lines against your king, but your bishop covers e5 and you are…
notes.original: White's c4 and d5 advance tries to open lines against your king; with the king on b8 and the bishop on d6 covering e5, you are fine.

notes.text: White has the safer king and the better minor piece for this ending.
notes.original: White has the safer king and the better minor piece for the ending.

notes.text: Your f-pawn supports the e4 pawn; fix it there and bring your king to f7.
notes.original: This supports the e4 pawn, which cramps White. White's trump is the better minor piece, so fix the pawn on e4 and bring your king to f7.

notes.text: White's only lever was f3, and after the trade the position is close to equal.
notes.original: White's only lever is f3, and after the trade the position is close to equal.

notes.text: The position is level here too.
notes.original: Also level.

notes.text: White's initiative on the kingside and in the centre is now faster than your extra pawn is worth.
notes.original: White's initiative on the kingside and in the centre is now faster than Black's extra pawn is worth.

notes.text: You are a pawn up but passively placed, with real defensive work still ahead.
notes.original: Black is a pawn up but passively placed and still has real defensive work to do - this is a harder version of the position than developing normally.

notes.text: White's rook hits your b7 and d5 pawns, trying to win the pawn back.
notes.original: The rook hits b7 and d5, trying to win the pawn back.

notes.text: Trading the active pieces helps you, and White has lost the right to castle.
notes.original: Trading the active pieces helps you: the extra pawn is easy to hold once White's attackers are gone, and White has lost the right to castle.

notes.text: You recapture on e6, and the queens are already off the board.
notes.original: White offers a queen trade, which suits the side with the extra pawn.

notes.text: The pawn hits your knight on f6 with a gain of time, and White's attack outruns your extra pawn.
notes.original: Gains a key tempo by hitting the f6-knight, and White's attack again outruns Black's extra pawn.

notes.text: This ending is playable but uncomfortable: you are a pawn up, with the worse structure and king safety.
notes.original: A playable but somewhat uncomfortable ending for Black, a pawn up but with the worse structure and king safety.

notes.text: White's knight now hits your e4 pawn and wants to win it right away.
notes.original: White wants to win the pawn on e4 at once.

notes.text: Your king is safe and both sides regained a pawn, so your extra pawn is gone and it's level.
notes.original: Castling gets the king safe. Both sides regain a pawn, so your extra pawn disappears and the position is level.

notes.text: White's e6 break tries to wreck your pawns, but your king reaches f7 in time.
notes.original: Breaking up your structure with e6 is another try, but your king reaches f7 in time.

notes.text: Your king is perfectly safe on the queenside, and the position is fully equal.
notes.original: Fully equal; Black's king is perfectly safe on the queenside.

notes.text: White's knight supports a g4 break that hits your f5 pawn and opens the g-file.
notes.original: White's idea is the g4 break: with the knight on e5 supporting it, g4 hits f5 and opens the g-file.

notes.text: Your knight is centralised, queens are traded, the attack is gone and the ending is level.
notes.original: You centralise with ...Ne4, trade queens, and the attack disappears; the ending is level.

notes.text: Castling long keeps the same balance.
notes.original: Castling long gives the same balance.

notes.text: You have won a pawn, but White's development gives more than enough compensation.
notes.original: Black has won a pawn, but White's development gives more than enough compensation here.

notes.text: Your extra pawn is real, so guard it; White's activity is worth a lot, so be careful.
notes.original: Your extra pawn is real, so guard it: the rook on f7 covers h7 and the seventh rank against the rook lift to h2 and the open g- and h-files. White's activity is worth a lot here, so be careful.

notes.text: After your e5 trade you stay a pawn up and White has no clear break.
notes.original: ...e5 trades off White's central pawn and attacks the bishop; you stay a pawn up and White has no clear break.

notes.text: Too passive: White now takes the open g-file.
notes.original: Too passive: White takes the g-file.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your pawn hits the centre at once, and the lines that follow are balanced.
notes.original: Black hits the centre immediately. After 7.dxe5 Nxe5 8.Qe2 Qe7 the pin-and-trade ideas are balanced.

notes.text: White transposes back to the main plan, just with h3 already played.
notes.original: Transposing back to the main plan, just with h3 already in.

notes.text: An ambitious try: White grabs extra kingside space at once instead of finishing development.
notes.original: An ambitious, more committal try now that h3 is already played: White grabs extra kingside space immediately rather than finishing development first.

notes.text: White develops and prepares to castle; this is a normal Exchange Variation structure, so develop actively.
notes.original: White develops the knight and prepares O-O, Bf4 and Bg5 ideas, avoiding the structure problems of an early g3. It is a natural development move, common in practice (played in about 333,000 games). So the position transposes to a normal Exchange Variation structure and you should develop actively.

notes.text: You have a fully comfortable position that feels equal.
notes.original: A fully comfortable, equal-feeling position for Black.

notes.text: White's bishop aims at your strong c4 knight and wants to remove it.
notes.original: White aims at your strong c4 knight and wants to remove it with Bxc4.

notes.text: You get the e-file and queenside play, so the position is level.
notes.original: The trade doubles your pawns, but you get the e-file and queenside play, so it is level.

notes.text: Your structure and piece activity both look excellent here.
notes.original: Black's structure and piece activity both look excellent here; the bishop pair White kept back on move 7 has not found a real diagonal to use.

notes.text: White's queen hits your b7 pawn and tries to trade queens.
notes.original: White hits b7 and tries to trade queens.

notes.text: Your bishop on d3 and the d4 pawn dominate, so a queen trade leaves you better.
Attacking c6 does not work: your d3 pawn cuts across and White is worse.
notes.original: Attacking c6 does not work: ...d3 cuts across and White is worse.

notes.text: You are fine with precise play, but this version is sharper and more demanding, since White's pawn storm gains extra…
notes.original: Black is doing fine here too with precise play, but it is a sharper, more demanding version of the normal structure than the central-break plan below, exactly because the h3 insertion gives White's pawn storm extra teeth.

notes.text: Your rook comes to the c-file to face White's c5 outpost.
notes.original: Put the rook against the c5 outpost.

notes.text: White's knights press on you; trade pieces and challenge the h4 knight with your knight on g6.
notes.original: White's trumps are the c5 knight, the rook on g1 and the knight on h4 pointed at f5; you must trade pieces and challenge with ...Ng6.
