notes.text: This version is worse for you: White gets a bishop to e5 and attacks.
notes.original: This is worse: White gets his bishop to e5 and attacks.

notes.text: White's g4 aims at your doubled f-pawns; your knight heads from e7 to g6.
notes.original: White plays g4 to break your doubled f-pawns; you trade the dark-squared bishops and bring the knight to e7 and g6.

notes.text: Your h-pawn strikes at the overextended g4 pawn at once, the standard answer to a flank pawn storm.
notes.original: Strikes back at the overextended pawn at once, the standard response to a flank pawn storm, and already starts to turn the position in Black's favour.

notes.text: White keeps the kingside closed, but gives you a completely free hand in the centre.
notes.original: Keeps the kingside closed, but hands Black a completely free hand in the centre instead.

notes.text: Your pieces are far more active than White's, and White's king has nowhere comfortable to go.
notes.original: Black's pieces are far more active than White's, and the king has nowhere comfortable to go - a direct demonstration of why 7.g4 is more risk than reward even with h3 already supporting it.

notes.text: White's knight hits your queen and eyes c7, but gets nothing.
notes.original: Nb5 attacks your queen and c7, but gets nothing.

notes.text: White cannot castle and your pieces swarm in; you are winning.
notes.original: White cannot castle, the bishop on e2 is pinned by your rook, and your pieces swarm in. You are winning.

notes.text: Trying to hit first with Ne5 loses material for White.
notes.original: Trying to hit first with Ne5 loses material.

notes.text: You have an easy, comfortable game: White's g5 pawn is a long-term weakness, not real space.
notes.original: Black has an easy, comfortable game and in fact a clear edge; the g5-pawn is more of a long-term weakness than a real space gain here.

notes.text: Your d4 break hits White's c3 pawn and e3 bishop, and opens lines for your pieces.
notes.original: This central break is stronger than comfort: the pawn hits c3 and e3, and opens lines for the bishop on e5 and the knights.

notes.text: The centre pawns are gone, and you keep a lasting edge.
notes.original: Your knight hits the queen with tempo and the centre pawns are gone, so you keep a lasting edge.

notes.text: This gains activity, but playing ...d4 was more accurate.
notes.original: This gets activity but is less accurate than ...d4.

notes.text: Your bishop hits White's d3 bishop and controls the long diagonal; answer Bb5 with ...Bg7.
notes.original: You exchange or harass White's strongest bishop and keep the long diagonal b1-h7 under control. The point of the move is to meet Bb5 with ...Bg7 and keep the bishop pair safe. Plan: ...Bg7, ...O-O, ...Qc7 to pressure c3 and ...a6 to gain space on the queenside. Avoid passive moves like ...Qc7 first, because White can then play Ne5 with tempo.

notes.text: White's bishop pins your c6 knight to the king, but you simply finish development.
notes.original: The c6 knight is pinned slightly but you finish development.

notes.text: Your pawn asks White's bishop on b5 to move, and you gain queenside space.
notes.original: Time to ask the bishop on b5 a question; it retreats and you have gained space.

notes.text: The position is equal; trade light-squared pieces and play ...e6 to neutralise White's small initiative.
notes.original: The structure is equal, and White has a small initiative that you can neutralise by exchanging pieces on the light squares and playing ...e6. This is a symmetrical pawn structure with White having played h3 and Bd3, so the centre is fairly closed and neither side has a big space advantage. Both kings will go short. Your plan: finish development with ...Bg7, castle, then challenge the c6 pin with ...a6, followed by ...Bf5 or ...Rd8 and ...e6 to trade light-squared pieces. White wants to play Ne5 or Bf1, and tries to build a small initiative using the e-file. You meet it by trading pieces. The risk is allowing Ne5 with tempo, and dropping a pawn on d5. If White deviates with Qb3 or Ne5, keep your pieces coordinated and trade when you can.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the knight on f3 to the queen, so d4 stays under pressure.
notes.original: The pin on the knight keeps d4 under pressure.

notes.text: The knight on e4 is heading to d6; Bg4 and further development follow.
notes.original: The idea behind ...Ne4 is to bring the knight to d6; ...Bg4 and further development can follow.

notes.text: White castles with no direct threat; the d3 bishop eyes your kingside, and Re1 and Bf4 may follow.
notes.original: White finishes development and puts the king away before the pin on f3 starts to matter. It is a very common move in practice (played in about 1.2 million games), so you will meet it often. It carries no direct threat; White wants a calm position with the bishop on d3 aimed at your kingside and the possibility of Re1 and Bf4 later.

notes.text: Retreating to h5 keeps your bishop pinning the f3 knight and avoids an early trade.
notes.original: Retreating to h5 keeps the pin on Nf3 and avoids an early trade.

notes.text: This transposes back to the usual Exchange structures; keep trading dark-squared pieces and aim for the standard breaks.
notes.original: Transposes back toward the normal Exchange Variation structures covered throughout this chapter; nothing about this particular move order changes Black's basic plan of trading down the dark-squared pieces and racing for the standard breaks.

notes.text: Your knight is excellent here, supported by the d5 pawn, and the game is level.
notes.original: The knight is excellent here: it is supported by d5 and forces White to decide the fate of the bishop on f4. If White plays 10.Qb3 you reply ...Bd6, offering a trade of the dark-squared bishops. After 11.Bxd6 you recapture with the queen and your d5 pawn is well defended. The game is level with a very solid position for Black.

notes.text: Your bishop offers to trade White's d3 bishop, even though the queen stands behind it.
notes.original: You swap the dark bishops and then offer the light-bishop trade to avoid a cramped game. White's Qb1 is lined up behind the d3 bishop, but your bishop on g6 trades it off.

notes.text: Your queen now eyes h2, frees d8 for a rook and keeps d5 supported.
notes.original: The queen steps to c7 so that it looks at h2 once the f3 knight moves, and it frees d8 for a rook. It also keeps your d5 pawn well supported without committing the e-pawn yet. Your plan is to answer h3 with ...Bh5, bring the rook to d8 or c8, play ...e6 and then ...Bd6 to swap off White's good bishop, and castle short. Avoid ...e5 too early: after dxe5 your pieces lose their coordination and White's bishops come alive.

notes.text: White's g3 weakens the dark squares, so keep your bishop pinning the f3 knight instead of taking it.
notes.original: White gives the bishop on h5 nothing to attack but weakens the dark squares around h3 and f3, so do not hurry to take on f3. Keep the pin and look for activity.

notes.text: Your knight on e4 hits g3 and c3 and prepares to challenge White's d3 bishop.
notes.original: The knight uses the e4 outpost, eyes g3 and c3, and prepares to challenge the bishop on d3.

notes.text: Your queen steps off the f4 bishop's diagonal and eyes h3, while the knight stays strong on e4.
notes.original: The queen leaves the diagonal of the bishop on f4 and keeps an eye on the kingside, while the knight stays strong on e4.

notes.text: h3 is White's most accurate move here; answer it with ...e6.
notes.original: White's most accurate move.

notes.text: Less accurate but common; you can develop your light bishop before playing e6.
notes.original: Less accurate but common. Black develops the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6.

notes.text: The position is solid and free of weaknesses; White keeps only a small, easily managed edge.
notes.original: A solid, weakness-free position. White keeps a slight, easily managed edge.

notes.text: Your rook joins the center and gets ready for the e5 break.
notes.original: Your rook supports the d5 pawn and the e5 break before White can aim at it.

notes.text: This quiet move takes b5 away from White's knight, so it can't hit your queen there.
notes.original: A useful prophylactic move: White's knight wants Nb5 hitting the queen, and ...a6 takes that square away.

notes.text: White's knight has rerouted to e3 to press d5 and aim for c4, but your pieces cover d5.
notes.original: White is rerouting the knight via c2 and e3 to pile up on d5 and aim for c4. Your pieces cover d5 and the f6/f7 setup keeps everything protected.

notes.text: Bh5 is your most accurate reply; Bxe2 sets a trap, but only if White recaptures the wrong way.
notes.original: 7...Bh5 is the most accurate. 7...Bxe2 sets a trap, but only if White recaptures the wrong way.

notes.text: White's queen heads for h4 or g3; you answer with Nf6, h6 and Bd6 and equalise.
notes.original: White's most testing move: the queen heads for h4 or g3. Black continues with ...Nf6, ...h6 and ...Bd6 and equalises.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White has at most a tiny edge, and you are comfortable.
notes.original: White has at most a tiny edge, within normal opening imprecision. Black is comfortable.

notes.text: White trades your good bishop so f3 can kick your bishop on g4; the edge is tiny.
notes.original: White trades off your good bishop so that f3 can kick the Bg4 and the knight can reroute to c2 and e3. Do not worry: the edge is tiny.

notes.text: If White ever plays g4, you answer Bg6 to trade bishops, and the pawn advance only loosens White's king.
notes.original: If White ever plays g4 here, ...Bg6 trades the light bishops and the pawn advance has only loosened White's king.

notes.text: Your central break e5 is the equaliser, leaving White with no real target.
notes.original: Your central break ...e5 is the equaliser: it opens the e-file in front of the white queen and leaves White with no real target.

notes.text: Black takes the initiative.
Your light bishop has escaped the pawn chain, so White has no pressure and you are slightly better.
notes.original: The light-squared bishop has escaped the pawn chain, so White has no pressure. Black is slightly better.

notes.text: White wants g3 and Nh4 to harass your bishop and so free its own bishop on d3.
notes.original: White wants to harass your bishop with g3 and Nh4 and so free the bishop on d3.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the knight and keeps your bishop alive.
notes.original: Your answer is to attack the knight and keep the bishop alive.

notes.text: Recapturing leaves you with slightly better chances.
notes.original: You get the bishop pair for a knight and slightly better chances.

notes.text: White has swapped off the light bishops, but you keep the better structure.
notes.original: White swaps off the bishop, but you keep the better structure

notes.text: The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
White unpins its knight and is ready for Bf4 hitting your queen, so your bishop on h5 must decide.
notes.original: White unpins the Ne2 and gets ready for Bf4 hitting your queen, so the bishop on h5 must decide.

notes.text: Your queen hits b2 and d4 and forces White to find a clean way to develop.
You have all your pieces out and a healthy structure.
White's queen eyes d5, but your queen and e6 pawn guard it, so the pressure is harmless.
notes.original: Qb3 stares at b7 and d5, but both are guarded and ...e6 settles the matter.

notes.text: Recapturing with the queen loses material, because your knight takes on d4 and wins a pawn.
notes.original: Loses material.

notes.text: Your pawn break opens lines toward White's king, though White still keeps a slight edge.
notes.original: Aims at the white king, but White keeps a slight edge.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Develop with tempo and leave the d5 pawn alone; White's king on f1 needs slow moves to get safe.
notes.original: Declining Be3 leaves White's king on f1 with no castling rights, so White needs a few slow moves to get it to safety. Develop with tempo and do not touch the d5 pawn.

notes.text: White wants Nf3 and then Bf4 to hit your queen.
notes.original: Your rooks belong on the open e-file. White wants Nf3 and Bf4 to hit the queen and cash in the bishop pair, so a quick ...Qc7 is natural.

notes.text: Your rooks belong on the open e-file, so a quick queen move to c7 is natural.
notes.original: Your rooks belong on the open e-file. White wants Nf3 and Bf4 to hit the queen and cash in the bishop pair, so a quick ...Qc7 is natural.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your queen, but it can step away with a useful move.
notes.original: Your queen is hit by the bishop but it steps away with a useful move, and the d5 pawn remains a solid centre.

notes.text: Avoid the queen check on h5: White's g-pawn push drives you back and you end up clearly worse.
notes.original: Trap: 11...Qh5+? 12.g4 Qe5 13.Kf1 Be7 14.Qf3 Qf6 and Black is clearly worse.

notes.text: White's e3 pawn is isolated and the king is exposed, so you are slightly better.
notes.original: Black is better here: White's structure is damaged and the king is exposed.

notes.text: Your queen steps off the e-file so White's king no longer has anything to hit.
notes.original: Your queen steps off the e-file so that White's king no longer has anything to hit.

notes.text: White's queen hits your knight and the a-pawn while the king tucks away on f2, but b7 holds.
notes.original: White's idea is to pressure Nc6 and the a-pawn while the king tucks away on f2, but b7 holds everything together.

notes.text: The e3 pawn is a permanent weakness, so double your rooks on the e-file against it.
notes.original: The e3 pawn is a permanent weakness and the white king cannot castle, so you double on the e-file and keep playing against it.

notes.text: Your knight takes the pawn with tempo, hitting White's queen on e2.
notes.original: The knight takes with tempo.

notes.text: White's knight blocks the a1 rook, so White cannot recapture your queen on c1.
notes.original:
Nb1 blocks the a1-rook, so White cannot recapture on c1. Black is clearly better.
Trap: 9...Qa5+? 10.Nc3 e6 11.a3 Bd6 12.O-O Qd8 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 9...Qa5+? 10.Nc3 e6 11.a3 Bd6 12.O-O Qd8 and Black is losing.

notes.text: White offers a queen trade at once, since it cannot recapture on c1 and must cut its losses.
notes.original: White offers a queen trade at once, since it cannot recapture on c1 and has to cut its losses.

notes.text: Do not hurry: White's king cannot castle and you hold a clean extra pawn, so finish development.
notes.original: Do not hurry anything. White's king has lost castling and you hold a clean extra pawn, so just finish development.

notes.text: White wants Rc1 and a king to e2 to use the c-file.
notes.original: White's only plan is to use the c-file with Rc1 and bring the king to e2. You contest the file with ...Rc8 and keep the pawn.

notes.text: Contest the c-file with a rook to c8 and keep your extra pawn.
notes.original: White's only plan is to use the c-file with Rc1 and bring the king to e2. You contest the file with ...Rc8 and keep the pawn.

notes.text: Your h-pawn gains space and gives the h8 rook a role while White's pieces are still tangled.
notes.original: ...h5 gains space and gives the h8 rook a role while White's pieces are still tangled.

notes.text: White is winning.
White just develops, and the isolated d4 pawn is safe for now.
notes.original: White just develops, and the isolated d4 pawn is safe.

notes.text: There is no compensation here: you are a knight down for just one pawn.
notes.original: There is no compensation: you are a knight down for one pawn.

notes.text: Develop naturally; White's bishop on f4 creates no extra problems for you to solve.
notes.original: 4...Nc6 develops naturally; the bishop on f4 is a reasonable square for White but creates no extra problems for Black to solve.

notes.text: White's c-pawn supports d4 and keeps both Nf3 and Nd2 available.
notes.original: 5.c3 supports the center solidly before developing the knight, keeping options for both Nf3 and Nd2.

notes.text: The bishops are traded and the position stays level.
notes.original: 5.c3 supports the center solidly before developing the knight, keeping options for both Nf3 and Nd2. ...and the position stays level.

notes.text: You are solid, and White will soon need to guard b2 against your queen.
notes.original: You are solid, and White's plan is Rb1 to defend b2 against your queen.

notes.text: Compact development.
Your structure is compact, and you need not worry about bishops since the light-squared ones are traded.
notes.original: A compact structure. You are not worried about the bishops: the light-squared ones are already traded.

notes.text: Your queen hits b2, which forces White to waste time.
notes.original: Hitting b2 forces White to waste time.

notes.text: Your queen hits the b2 pawn and forces White to defend it.
notes.original: Your queen hits b2 and forces White to defend.

notes.text: The position is level; follow with a rook to c8 and knight to a5 for pressure.
notes.original: Level, and you can follow with ...Rac8 and ...Na5 to pressure.

notes.text: Your queen presses b2, your pieces are comfortable, and the symmetrical position is level.
notes.original: Your queen hits b2 and forces White's rook to b1. Your pieces are comfortable and the structure is symmetrical, so it is level.

notes.text: Meet White's play with knight jumps to e4 or b4.
notes.original: Level. You can follow up with ...Rac8 and ...Rfd8 and meet White's moves with ...Ne4 or ...Nb4 ideas.

notes.text: Your knight grabbed d4, but White recaptures: you lose a piece for a pawn.
notes.original: Loses a piece for a pawn, since d4 is guarded twice

notes.text: Simply develop: the tempo White spent on c3 hardly matters once development finishes.
notes.original: 4...Nf6 is simplest; the tempo White spends on c3 is close to a non-factor once development finishes.

notes.text: White develops simply, planning bishops to d3 and f4.
notes.original: The simplest development: Nf3, then Bd3 and Bf4.

notes.text: White's bishop presses your c6 knight, but it can become a target you hit with tempo.
notes.original: White adds pressure on the c6 knight, the defender of your d5 pawn and of e5, hoping to double your pawns or gain time with Ne5. It is a common but slightly speculative move: it develops, yet the bishop may become a target. For you, this is an invitation to hit it with tempo and to use the loose b5 square.

notes.text: You will trade the dark bishops soon and are fine, though White is slightly better.
notes.original: You trade the dark bishops soon and are fine, though White is slightly better.

notes.text: Now you challenge White's good bishop and make the position simple and solid.
notes.original: Now you challenge White's good bishop, making the position simple and solid.

notes.text: Your bishop on h5 pins the f3 knight, and Bd6 offers to trade White's active bishop.
notes.original: Pin the f3 knight and then trade White's active dark bishop with ...Bd6; the extra c3 tempo is not a real factor.

notes.text: You offer to trade off White's good dark bishop and reach a solid, level game.
notes.original: You trade off White's good dark bishop and reach a solid, level game.

notes.text: Your queen hits the bishop and the d4 pawn at once, so White must react.
notes.original: Your queen attacks the bishop and the d4 pawn at the same time, so White must act. This is both a useful developing move and a way to deny White easy play. Your plan afterwards is ...e6, ...Be7, castling short, and ...a6 to push the bishop away when needed. Avoid ...Bg4 without careful thought, since White gets h3 with tempo.

notes.text: You accepted the c4 pawn and finish developing; be ready to give it back if needed.
notes.original: White offers the c4 pawn for quick development. You accept and complete your own development; do not cling to the extra pawn at all costs, but return it at the right moment if needed.

notes.text: Your a-pawn asks the bishop its plans; if White plays d5, recapture with exd5. The line is equal.
notes.original: With ...a6 you ask the bishop what it wants. White's idea is d5 to hit your knight, so be ready to answer it with ...exd5. Hit the bishop with ...Qb6, take the offered pawn calmly, finish development, and keep your position flexible; the line is equal. This is a position with an open centre after the c4 pawn was taken: you have pawns on e6 and a6, White has queen on b3 and bishop on e3, and your queen guards the position. Your plan: finish development with ...Nf6 and ...Bd7, castle short, then return the pawn at the right moment with ...b5. White wants d5 to hit your knight and open lines, so be ready to recapture with ...exd5. The risk is hanging on to the extra pawn when White has a lead in development, and a bishop check can be awkward; if White plays Rd1, keep your king safe.

notes.text: White's queen hits b7 and d5, but your queen covers b7 and your knight guards d5.
notes.original: Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together, but ...Qc8 covers b7 and the Nf6 guards d5.

notes.text: White's queen eyes b7, but your queen on c8 covers it.
notes.original: Qb3 hits b7 and d5 but Qc8 covers.

notes.text: Your queen on c8 guards b7 and the bishop has left f5, so both White ideas are met.
notes.original: White hits b7 with the queen and the f5 bishop with Nh4, but ...Qc8 and ...Bd7 meet both threats.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your bishop gets out before ...e6 and hits the queen, so White must spend a tempo on f3.
notes.original: Get the bishop out beyond the pawns ahead of ...e6, which makes White burn a tempo on f3.

notes.text: White has castled long to attack; your knight trades pieces and your h5 bishop can harass the king.
notes.original: White's plan is to castle long and attack; you trade pieces with ...Nd5 and use the h5 bishop to harass the king.

notes.text: White's bishop to f4 is an equally good alternative here.
notes.original: An equally good alternative.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is a pawn up, so you must open the centre; your e5 pawn hits d4.
notes.original: White is a pawn up, so you must open the centre; ...e5 hits d4 and opens lines for your pieces.

notes.text: You get open lines and quick development, but White keeps the extra pawn.
This is too slow: White consolidates the extra pawn.
notes.original: Too slow: White consolidates the pawn.

notes.text: Taking on e4 does White no good: your d5 pawn recaptures and gets a strong pawn there.
notes.original: 7.Bxe4 dxe4 gives Black a strong pawn on e4 and a free hand in the centre. Taking on e4 does White no good.

notes.text: Your bishop offers to trade White's good bishop; then play e6, bishop to e7 and castle.
notes.original:
Idea: Here you meet 6.Bf4 with 6...Ne4 straight away. The knight drops back to d6 so that ...Bf5 can trade off White's good bishop. Then finish with ...e6, ...Be7 and ...O-O.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 Ne4 7.Nd2 Nd6 8.Ngf3 Bf5
Watch out: ...Nxd4? loses material on moves 5 to 8. ...Nfxd4? loses material on moves 10 to 14.
See also: 🟢 01 covers more of the Exchange Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

notes.text: This completes the Tango move order of the Exchange Caro-Kann, and the position is equal.
notes.original: Tango move order of the Exchange Caro Kann - Complete

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal.
White makes luft and gains queenside space; your knight lands on c4 and the position is equal.
notes.original: White makes luft and uses a4 for queenside space; you counter with ...b6 and ...Na5-c4, planting a knight on the outpost. The position is equal.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn hits d4 and the f4 bishop, challenging White's lone central pawn for enough counterplay.
notes.original: Trying to break through White's one and only central pawn gives Black enough counterplay in the centre.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The knight on e6 forks your queen and rook, so you take it.
White's bishop pair is gone, leaving an equal position.
notes.original: White's queen takes with check and the bishop pair is gone, leaving an equal position.

notes.text: Your king already sidestepped the fork with Kb8, so you are a bit better.
notes.original: If White delays, ...Kb8 sidesteps the fork and you are a bit better.

notes.text: Against Nf3, play Nf6 and follow with Ne4.
notes.original: A fresh way to face the Exchange Variation with Nf3 is the plan ...Nf6 followed by ...Ne4.

notes.text: White castles and keeps the tension; you must choose where your bishop goes.
notes.original: White castles and wants to finish development before deciding on a plan: Re1, c3 or Bg5, and possibly h3 followed by Bf4 and Qb3 against d5. The move is extremely common in practice (played in about 1.4 million games). So White keeps tension in the centre and you must choose where your bishop goes.

notes.text: Taking on e4 gives up White's bishop pair, and your recapture kicks the f3 knight; castling was better.
notes.original: 7.Bxe4 dxe4 gives up the bishop pair, and the new pawn on e4 kicks the knight off f3. It takes White a few moves to sort that out. 7.O-O was the better move.

notes.text: Against Nd2, don't trade knights; retreat to d6 and keep the position dynamic.
notes.original: Against Nd2, ...Nd6 is the answer. Black should not trade knights for White's modest Nd2 and should keep the position dynamic.

notes.text: Bf4 comes before Nd2 so the bishop isn't shut in, but it lets your bishop reach f5.
notes.original: Bf4 comes before Nd2 because otherwise the dark-squared bishop would be shut in. The drawback is ...Bf5, which stabilises the knight on e4.

notes.text: Your queen centralises; plan Bf5, then the strong central break e5.
notes.original: White supports the e4-pawn. Black plans ...Bf5 followed by ...e5, a strong central break.

notes.text: White's e5 pawn is isolated, which is a poor outlook for White.
notes.original: White is left with an ugly isolated pawn, which is a poor outlook.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your rook attacks the e5 pawn, the one thing keeping White a pawn up.
notes.original: You attack the e5 pawn, the one thing keeping White a pawn up.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the rook on f1 and gains a tempo.
notes.original: The bishop hits the rook and gains a tempo.

notes.text: You win the pawn back.
notes.original: The pawn is back.

notes.text: Another tempo: your bishop forks the rook on d1 and the knight on b1.
notes.original: Another tempo: the bishop forks Rd1 and Nb1.

notes.text: You have the bishop pair and White's extra pawn is gone; if White repeats, so can you.
notes.original: You have the bishop pair and White's extra pawn has gone. If White repeats, so can you.

notes.text: Taking f7 looks greedy, but your bishop fork forces White's hand and you regain e5 with active pieces.
notes.original: Grabbing f7 looks greedy, but the Bd3 fork forces White's hand and you regain e5 with active pieces.

notes.text: Your bishop offers a trade; swapping bishops weakens White's light squares on the b1-h7 diagonal.
notes.original: Exchanging bishops helps Black here: White's light squares on the b1-h7 diagonal slowly weaken.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White castles to keep things simple.
notes.original: Castling keeps things simple.

notes.text: Your a-pawn gains queenside space and takes the b4 square away.
notes.original: ...a5 gains queenside space and takes b4 away.

notes.text: You centralised your knight and traded dark bishops; your pieces are active and the position is equal.
notes.original: Centralise ...Ne4 and trade dark bishops with ...Bd6; your c6 pawns are doubled but your pieces are active and the position is equal.

notes.text: A White knight jump to c5 is met by your knight on f5 and bishop on d6.
notes.original: A Nc5 jump is met by ...Nf5 and ...Bd6.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White can't match your Ne4 idea; the simplifying lines leave your knight on e4 intact.
notes.original: White cannot answer with a similar ...Ne4 idea: Nxd5 dxe5 a6 and so on would make the position simpler, with Black's knight on e4 still intact.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Your knight on c5 forks the queen and the bishop on d3, so White must take it.
notes.original: Your Nc5 forks the queen and the bishop on d3, so White must take the knight.

notes.text: Your e5 break comes with the bishop pair.
notes.original: You recapture the bishop and get the bishop pair and the e5 break.

notes.text: The bishop trade did not stop the fork; you won the queen for a knight.
notes.original: The bishop trade does not stop the fork; you win the queen for a knight (over a rook's worth).

notes.text: Your a6 pawn covers b5, so White's bishop cannot pin your queen there.
notes.original: This stops the idea of Bb5 pinning the queen; otherwise Black would be in serious trouble.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is level; your bishop hits e5 and your rook on the open c-file hits c3.
notes.original: The position is level, so you only need a sensible plan. White's pawn on e5 cramps you, but it is also a target: your Bg7 and the open c-file hit it and c3 at once.

notes.text: White's h4 grabs space and hints at h5, and ...h6 is a cheap answer.
notes.original: White's h4 grabs space and hints at h5, and ...h6 stops that cheaply.

notes.text: You are castled, your queen is active and the game is balanced.
notes.original: You are castled, the queen is active and the game is balanced.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the knight on f3 and gets out before e6 shuts it in.
notes.original: You pin the knight and take the c8 bishop out before it is shut in by ...e6. Your plan is ...e6, ...Bd6, ...O-O, with ...Qd7 and a quiet game. The pin on f3 matters because it stops White from playing e5-style jumps and makes h3 a necessity. After 7.c3 e6 8.h3 Bh5 9.Bf4 you can keep the bishop alive with ...Ne4.

notes.text: Recapture on d6 with your queen, then castle and use the knight on e4.
notes.original: This is a fairly open, symmetrical centre: the d5 pawn is solid, White has traded his dark-squared bishop and you have a safe king still to castle. Your plan: castle short at once, play ...Qxd6-style recapture structure with the queen on d6 or d7, then bring the rooks to c8 and e8 and use the knight on e4 as your best piece. White wants the open c-file and the queen on b3 against b7, so keep b7 guarded and watch d5. The risk is hurrying ...O-O into Qxb7 tactics without checking; if White avoids the trade on d6, retreat calmly.

notes.text: The fianchetto with g6 is a little passive; White gets a comfortable edge and your light squares are loose.
notes.original: A natural fianchetto, but it is a little passive: White gets Re1 and Bg5 with a comfortable edge and your light squares are loose. Avoid this if you want a dynamic game.

notes.text: h3 stops Bg4 for good; you answer with Nc6 and then e5.
notes.original: 5.h3 stops ...Bg4 for good and prepares a quiet development. Black replies ...Nc6 and ...e5.

notes.text: Bf4 develops actively and keeps h3 in reserve; Nc6 is the natural answer.
notes.original: 5.Bf4 develops actively and keeps h3 in reserve. ...Nc6 answers it naturally.

notes.text: The engine prefers Nf3, but this quiet pawn move is a favourite of top players; you have one logical reply.
notes.original:
Stockfish prefers Nf3 here, but this quiet pawn push has found favour with both the world number 1 and world number 2 in classical chess.
Either way there is only one logical response for black, even though other moves are playable.

notes.text: White develops the knight and prepares c3 and Bf4 or castling, hoping for a slight pull.
notes.original: White brings out the knight, keeps the bishop on d3 and prepares c3 and Bf4 or O-O. It is very common (played in about 743,000 games). White hopes for a slight pull from the pin ideas and a calm, solid structure.

notes.text: White's knight keeps the f-pawn free and heads for f4, aiming for a quiet game.
notes.original: White develops the knight so that he can keep his structure flexible, and the f1 bishop is on d3 so the knight cannot go to f3 without blocking. The knight on e2 also prepares to go to f4 and keeps the f-pawn free. It is very common in practice (played in about 250,000 games), so you will meet it often. So White is aiming for a quiet game without early pawn tension.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's check forces trades, but you get the easier game.
notes.original: White's check forces simplification but gives Black the easier game.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
Developing the bishop outside the pawn chain solves the problem of your light-squared bishop.
notes.original: This solves black's problems with the placement of the light-squared bishop.

notes.text: White's queen hits your b7 pawn; Qc7 solves the problem.
notes.original: The most testing line: Black's bishop pins the knight and White's queen hits b7, which forces Black to react. ...Qc7 solves the problem.

notes.text: f3 chases your bishop but weakens the e3 square; retreat and you equalise.
notes.original: 6.f3 tries to chase the bishop but weakens the e3-square. Black retreats with ...Bh5 and ...Bg6 and equalises.

notes.text: Ne2 offers a trade; take on e2, then play e6 for a solid, equal position.
notes.original: 7.Ne2 offers a trade on e2; after ...Bxe2 Bxe2 e6 Black reaches a solid, equal position.

notes.text: If White tried Bf4 here, you would take it, and after Qxb7 your queen mates on c1.
notes.original: Not 7. Bf4??, as indicated in the text below.

notes.text: You unpin and head for e5; the position is balanced and your pieces are well placed.
notes.original: Black unpins and heads for ...e5. The position is balanced and Black's pieces are well placed.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
Pin the knight before h3 and aim to trade pieces; avoid g6 here.
notes.original: Pin the knight at once, before h3. The bishop would like to trade itself for the knight, which relieves your cramped position. After h3 retreat to h5, then ...Nc6, ...e6 and ...Bd6 to challenge the strongest white bishop. Your plan is to exchange pieces, keep the d5 pawn solid and castle short. Avoid ...g6 here, which lets White play Bf4 and c3 comfortably with extra space. The position is about level, with a very small plus for White.

notes.text: Less ideal: White can swap bishops and follow with Bf4, leaving you a little passive.
notes.original: Less ideal. After c3 Bg7 h3 Bf5 White can swap bishops and then Bf4 gives a lasting initiative, so you stay a little passive.

notes.text: Your knight pressures the d4 pawn; next come e6 and Bd6.
notes.original: The knight guards d4 and pressures the centre. Your next moves are ...e6 and ...Bd6.

notes.text: Retake on d6 with your queen; if White plays g4, your h5 bishop retreats to g6.
notes.original: After the exchange you have a healthy position with no weaknesses and only a tiny deficit, which is a good outcome in this line. This is a balanced position with symmetrical pawns and a pin from your bishop on h5, where White has recaptured on d6 with the bishop. Your plan: recapture with ...Qxd6, then play ...Bg6 to trade White's bishop on d3, castle short, and bring a rook to e8. White wants g4 to trap or bother the bishop on h5, then Qe2 and O-O-O. If g4 comes, retreat with ...Bg6 and recapture on g6 with the h-pawn. The mistake is ignoring the pin on f3, which you can exploit with ...Bxf3 at the right moment. If White deviates with Qe2, continue ...Bg6.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn supports d5 and prepares Bd6 and castling.
notes.original: You support d5 and prepare ...Bd6 and castling. Your plan is simple: develop ...Nc6, ...Bd7 and ...Bd6 and then castle short, putting pressure on the white queenside with ...Rc8. If White plays Bf4 you must challenge it with ...Bd6 when possible, since trading the dark squared bishops helps you. Avoid ...Bg4 too early unless you check White's reply.

notes.text: Your bishop develops and prepares Nh5 to hit the bishop on f4.
notes.original: The bishop goes to d7 to prepare ...Nh5 which hits the bishop on f4.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop on f4: White must retreat it or give you the bishop pair.
notes.original: You gain the bishop pair or force the bishop to retreat.

notes.text: You have solid development and equal chances.
White wants Nf4 to hit your knight and d5 pawn; be ready to trade on f4.
notes.original: This is a closed centre with the symmetrical Exchange Variation structure: d4 against d5, with White's pieces more active but your bishops trading in your favour. Both kings castle short. Your plan: castle short, play ...Rc8 and ...Qe7, retreat the knight from h5 to f6 when needed, and keep the bishop on d6 well placed against the dark squares. White wants Nf4 to hit your knight and the d5 pawn, and a later Bd3 plan against h7. Meet Nf4 with ...Nxf4 and Bxf4, then ...Bxf4. The risk is leaving the knight stranded on h5 without a retreat, where a pinned or trapped piece loses time.

notes.text: Another fine reply.
notes.original: This is another fine reply.

notes.text: This is another route to the same position.
notes.original: Another route to the same position.

notes.text: This is quite playable, and you can choose a Grunfeld-style or Queen's Gambit Declined set-up.
notes.original: This resembles a Marshall-style set-up and is quite playable, since White's e-pawn is gone. Black has two sensible plans: the Grunfeld-style set-up or a Queen's Gambit Declined structure.

notes.text: This solid answer steers toward a Queen's Gambit Declined, though it blocks your light-squared bishop.
notes.original: This is the Horwitz-style answer to the Panov-Botvinnik Attack, an improvised Queen's Gambit. It blocks the light-squared bishop but lets Black steer towards a Queen's Gambit Declined.

notes.text: This move can transpose to the main line or head into a sideline.
notes.original: Another Panov Botvinnik line, this move could transpose to the main line or go off the sidelines.

notes.text: The Grunfeld-style setup is the preferred answer here: solid, somewhat passive, with no major weaknesses.
notes.original: The Grunfeld-style approach is sometimes called dubious or inaccurate, yet it is the preferred way here to meet the Panov-Botvinnik Attack. Black's position stays solid, if somewhat passive, and has no major weaknesses.

notes.text: Choose Nc6 for a flexible, active reply; White's main moves are Nf3, Bg5 and Bf4.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose 5...Nc6 if you want a flexible, active reply The ...a6 idea covers the d5 square cheaply. For a quieter, structural game see 🔵 03 and 04. After 5...Nc6 White's main moves are 6.Nf3, 6.Bg5 and 6.Bf4. Black replies ...a6 or ...g6 depending on the system.

notes.text: White's queen hits b7 and eyes d5 behind its c4 pawn, so finish development quickly.
notes.original: 6.Qb3 hits d5 and b7 at once. White wants to win a pawn while developing, so Black has to react quickly and finish development.

notes.text: Nf3 prepares White's principled Queen's Gambit plan.
Taking on d5 releases the pressure on the centre, which tends to help you.
notes.original: This variation tends to help Black because the pressure on the centre has disappeared.

notes.text: You need not rush to guard d5; development matters more than safety here.
notes.original: Black need not rush to protect the d-pawn. Even if White wins it, that pawn is weak, with no other pawns to support it, and will probably fall soon. Development matters more than safety here.

notes.text: Don't rush to win the pawn back: bring your knight to b6 and pressure d5.
notes.original:
Idea: Against the Panov you can fianchetto with 5...g6. White grabs the d5 pawn with Qb3 and cxd5. Don't rush to win it back: castle, bring the knight to b6 and put pressure on d5.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 g6 6.Qb3 Bg7 7.cxd5 O-O
Watch out: ...Nxd5? loses material on moves 7 to 9. ...Nfxd5? loses material on move 10.
Next: 🔵 04 continues the Panov-Botvinnik Attack. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

notes.text: White is trying once more to hold on to the d5 pawn.
notes.original: White tries once more to hold on to the pawn.

notes.text: White can let the d-pawn go and develop freely; both sides get what they want, so it is more drawish.
notes.original: White can also let the d-pawn go and develop freely. White keeps full flexibility while Black also develops easily, so both sides get what they want and the outcome is more drawish.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your f6 knight, one of the pieces aiming at the isolated d4 pawn.
notes.original: 8.Bg5 hits the knight on f6, one of the pieces aiming at the isolated d4 pawn, and tries to slow Black down.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks the bishop on f3, the main defender of White's d5 pawn.
notes.original: Black removes the main support of the d5-pawn.

notes.text: White's d6 forces you to retake with the e-pawn, since playing e6 is not sensible here.
notes.original: It matters for two reasons: Black has to retake with the e-pawn, producing an isolated pawn, and since the dark-squared bishop protects d5, ...e6 is not a sensible alternative.

notes.text: You now have an isolated d-pawn, but White's d4 pawn is isolated too, so both can be targeted.
notes.original: Recapturing with the e-pawn leaves an isolated pawn. White seems to have gained something, but both sides now have an isolated d-pawn and each can be targeted. An isolated pawn can serve as an attacking asset too.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's a-pawn attacks your b6 knight, so the queenside pawn majority starts to move.
notes.original: White kicks the b6 knight so the queenside pawn majority starts to move.

notes.text: Your a-pawn covers b5 and keeps the queenside shut.
notes.original: You secure b5 and keep the queenside shut.

notes.text: White's central break opens the position, but your knight has a good square on e7.
notes.original: The central break opens the position but Black's knight has a good square.

notes.text: Both sides hit loose pieces, the f4 bishop and the b7 pawn, so the position is balanced.
notes.original: Both sides now hit loose pieces, the Bf4 and the pawn on b7, so the position is balanced.

notes.text: In this line you are a touch more active.
notes.original: Black is a touch more active.

notes.text: Your bishop develops with Bg4, and you are also doing well here.
notes.original: Black is also doing well here.

notes.text: White attacks your bishop on g4 and wants to gain time to grab b7 with the queen.
notes.original: White attacks the bishop on g4 and wants to gain tempi to grab b7 with the queen.

notes.text: Your bishop returns and defends the knight on d5.
notes.original: The bishop returns and defends d5.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the bishop on c4, and the d2 bishop is loose after Bxe6.
notes.original: The knight attacks the bishop on c4, and the d2 bishop is loose after Bxe6.

notes.text: White has taken a pawn, but your pieces are active, so the game is balanced.
notes.original: White has taken a pawn but Black has activity, so the game is balanced.

notes.text: A simple line that gives you a full game.
notes.original: A simple line that gives Black a full game.

notes.text: You are happy to open the e-file for your rook.
notes.original: Black is happy to get the e file open for his rook to take advantage of.

notes.text: A queen exchange would favour you: White's doubled, isolated d-pawns are likely to fall.
notes.original: A queen exchange would favour Black: White has doubled, isolated pawns that are likely to fall, and Black has enough pieces to attack them. The initiative and the advantage lie with Black.

notes.text: White declines the queen trade, keeps the initiative and wants you to do the defending.
notes.original: White declines the queen trade and hopes for rapid development, unwilling to give up the initiative and wanting Black to defend.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's knight hits b7, f7 and e8. You have the bishop pair, but a ragged structure.
notes.original: White places the knight on d6 to hit b7 and the e8 and f7 squares. Black has the bishop pair but a ragged structure.

notes.text: White hopes to swing the rook to a6 and pressure your b6 pawn.
notes.original: You cement the knight outpost, but White hopes for Ra6.

notes.text: The position is equal, and your doubled f and b pawns are not a real worry.
notes.original: Equal, and the doubled f6 and b4 pawns are not a real worry.

notes.text: White's a-pawn now hits b6, but you are fine and a touch better.
notes.original: A pawn push that hits b6, but Black is fine and a touch better.

notes.text: White's a4 pawn is a target: your queen, bishop and knight all press on it.
notes.original: The a4 pawn is a target for Black. White's position is slowly crumbling: it is defensible, yet White is under constant pressure and may not enjoy defending it.

notes.text: White's knight comes to e3 to cover c4 and guard the d5 pawn, since a4 is under pressure.
notes.original: White regroups the f1 knight to cover c4 and d5, because the a4 pawn is under pressure.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the knight and gains space.
notes.original: You kick the knight and gain space.

notes.text: You keep pressing on the kingside with ...h4 ideas and stay slightly better.
notes.original: Black keeps pressing on the kingside with ...h4 ideas. Black stays slightly better.

notes.text: Your passed pawn on c2 is a monster that White must watch.
notes.original: If White lets a4 fall, the passed c2 pawn is a monster.

notes.text: Bg5 is imprecise: White wants to take on f6 and win d5, but you can defend.
notes.original: Bg5 is imprecise: White intends to take on f6 and then win the unprotected pawn on d5, but this can be defended.

notes.text: If White takes your knight, your queen, knight and bishop all attack the d4 pawn.
notes.original: White cannot capture the knight, because this would open lines for three black pieces to attack the d-pawn.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
Black is winning.
You are a pawn up with a monster queen on d4; White's rook guards b2.
notes.original: Black is a pawn up with a monster on d4. White tries to keep the b2 pawn and the queen.

notes.text: You kick the bishop first.
You have the extra pawn and a solid central majority.
notes.original: Black has the extra pawn and a solid central majority.

notes.text: You just roll the kingside pawns forward, and you are winning.
notes.original: Black just rolls the kingside pawns, winning.

notes.text: White cannot regain the pawn, and you are winning.
notes.original: White cannot regain the pawn and Black is winning.

notes.text: Be6 looks odd but is fine: it defends d5 and is no longer shut in.
notes.original: ...Be6 may look poor but it is fine. The d-pawn is under attack and must be defended; ...e6 would shut in the light-squared bishop behind the pawn chain, so ...Be6 is better as the bishop is no longer barricaded.

notes.text: White wants to expand on the queenside with b4.
notes.original: White wants to expand on the queenside! b4 would soon be played but White first has to take care of his knight since h4 would only hang his knight.

notes.text: White's Nxd5 is playable, and your bishop can simply take back.
notes.original: Nxd5 is playable, but it fixes Black's attention on the isolated d-pawn.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's idea: after you take on e4, a pawn move to d5 forks your bishop and knight.
notes.original: White has a clear idea here: a later pawn move could fork the bishop and a knight.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White opens the centre by taking on d5.
notes.original: White opens the centre.

notes.text: Trading your knight on c3 relieves the pin on your c6 knight.
notes.original: You trade the knight to relieve the pin.

notes.text: You grab a pawn, and the bishop is safe enough: if White plays Rb6, you answer Rfe8.
notes.original: Black grabs a pawn, and the bishop is safe enough because Rb6 can be met by Rfe8.

notes.text: Black is slightly better here.
notes.original: Black is slightly better.

notes.text: Your knight wins a pawn, and your position is comfortable.
notes.original: Black wins a pawn and the position is comfortable.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White eyes the c-file and Qd2; the bishop pair makes up for the weak d4 pawn.
notes.original: White prepares to fight for the open c-file and to attack with Qd2. The bishop pair compensates for the weakness on d4.

notes.text: Your knight takes the d4 pawn and wins a pawn.
notes.original: You grab the d4 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the queen on d2, and you keep a small edge.
notes.original: The knight attacks the queen on d2 and Black keeps a small edge.

notes.text: This alternative also costs White the d4 pawn.
notes.original: An alternative that loses the d4 pawn as well.

notes.text: Your light-squared bishop is finally out of the pawn chain, which favours you.
notes.original: The light-squared bishop is finally out of the pawn chain, which is favourable.

notes.text: White pulls the bishop back out of the way, covering c4 and e2.
notes.original: White retreats the bishop to get it out of the way, covering c4 and e2.

notes.text: Your rook lines up on the c3 pawn behind your knight.
notes.original: You target the c3 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight on c4 is a thorn for White, and you have good play.
notes.original: The knight on c4 is a thorn and Black has good play.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
notes.original: Slightly better for Black.

notes.text: Grabbing the pawn is fine, but check for tricks; Black is a bit better.
notes.original: A pawn grab, but check for tricks. Black is a bit better.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's queen eyes the e-file, and the f3 pawn weakens White's king.
notes.original: The queen eyes the e-file and White's idea is to use the bishop pair to attack the king. The f3 pawn weakens the white king.

notes.text: Your queen hits the c4 and f3 pawns.
notes.original: You hit c4 and f3.

notes.text: White's pawns are shattered and the c1 bishop is passive, so you keep a slight edge.
notes.original: White's pawns are shattered and the bishop on c1 is passive, so Black keeps a slight edge.

notes.text: The rook raid fails: your rook attacks the one on e7, and you are better.
notes.original: The rook raid fails and Black is better.

notes.text: You have tripled e-pawns but are still a pawn up, and ...e3 is even possible.
notes.original: Black has tripled e-pawns yet is still a pawn up and can give back material for the initiative. Pushing ...e3 is even possible: if White captures, the e-file is shut so the rook cannot go after the doubled pawns, and White's own pawn structure stays damaged. (Gusev-Muratov, Novgorod 1961, 0-1.)

notes.text: White's bishop on g4 hits your e6 pawn and ties your king down.
notes.original: White pins down your king with the bishop on g4 which eyes e6.

notes.text: Your queen attacks the b2 pawn.
notes.original: The queen attacks b2 and the bishop on g4.

notes.text: Your bishop blocks the check, White's attack runs out of steam, and you keep a slight edge.
notes.original: The bishop blocks the check and White's attack runs out of steam, so Black keeps a slight edge.

notes.text: This is another tough defence, and you hold the initiative.
notes.original: Another tough defence, Black has the initiative.

notes.text: White can reach the same structure with another move order, playing the bishop first.
notes.original: Another move order for White

notes.text: A queen on an exposed central square can be harassed, so it is risky to leave it there.
White's queen attacks yours with tempo and hopes to follow with Be3.
notes.original: The queen on d5 is exposed, so White develops with tempo, attacking it and hoping to follow with Nb5 or Be3.

notes.text: Your bishop guards the queen and offers a trade; your pieces are more active.
notes.original: Offer the trade. Black's pieces are more active than White's.

notes.text: White's d4 pawn is isolated and your bishop is safe on c6, so you keep a small edge.
notes.original: The d4 pawn is isolated and the bishop is safe on c6. You keep a small edge.

notes.text: This is another way to harass the queen, but you are comfortable.
notes.original: Another way to harass the queen, but Black is comfortable.

notes.text: Remember this set-up whenever White plays Bc4.
notes.original: This set-up is worth remembering whenever White plays Bc4.

notes.text: White sets a trap: the knight hits e6 and f7, and if you ignore it, Nxe6 wins a pawn.
notes.original: White sets a trap. The knight eyes e6 and f7, and the bishop on c4 supports both. If you ignore it, Nxe6 wins a pawn.

notes.text: Your knight comes to e7 to meet White's pressure on e6.
notes.original: The knight guards e6.

notes.text: White sacrifices the knight on f7, attacking your queen, to try to break through.
notes.original: White tries a combination to break through.

notes.text: White gave two minor pieces for a rook and two pawns, so material is about level and the position is…
notes.original: White has given two minor pieces for a rook and two pawns, so material is about level and the position is balanced. It is critical to keep the bishop b7 on the long diagonal.

notes.text: This quieter alternative for White leads to an equal position.
notes.original: A quieter alternative, equal.

notes.text: You must choose: quiet Be7, or the more popular and principled Bb4.
notes.original:
Both sides continue with regular knight deployment, but black has a decision to make here. The quiet Be7 is perfectly playable, but the Nimzo-Indianesque Bb4 can be considered more popular, and arguably more principled.
But we will examine both lines, and their particular idiosyncrasies.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White pins your f6 knight, so be careful about your d5 pawn.
notes.original: White pins the f6 knight so that you cannot easily play ...dxc4 or ...Ne4, and prepares Nf3 with Rc1 and a pull on d5. It also eyes the possibility of c5, gaining space on the queenside. This is a very common move and is not especially dangerous, but you must be careful about the d5 pawn.

notes.text: White opens the c-file to pressure your d5 pawn; recapture sensibly and keep your king safe.
notes.original: White gives up the tension in the centre to open the c-file and put the pressure on your d5 pawn. It is very common in practice and leads to a symmetrical pawn structure with a slight pull for White. As Black you need to recapture sensibly and to keep your king safe.

notes.text: This is playable and simpler, but discouraged because it is hard to play against the Panov this way.
notes.original: ...e6 is another good alternative, although it is difficult to play against the Panov this way and is discouraged; players who want a simpler, safer game may find it acceptable.

notes.text: Bd6 is playable, but Bb4 is the more accurate square for your bishop.
notes.original: Playable, but Bb4 is more accurate.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the c3 knight at once; you needn't trade it, just ease White's central pressure.
notes.original: Pinning the knight right away, as usually seen in the Bogo Indian Defence. Black doesn't necessarily have to exchange bishop for knight. Black just need to ease up white's forces on his central fortification.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's bishop eyes your kingside and prepares castling; it is the most natural developing move.
notes.original: White develops the bishop to d3, where it eyes your kingside and prepares castling. He is ready to answer ...dxc4 with Bxc4 and ...O-O with cxd5. This is the most natural developing move (played in about 134,000 games). It keeps the structure flexible.

notes.text: Both sides now have an isolated d-pawn, a slightly odd structure.
notes.original: Bg5 is also a pleasant idea here, but creating this slightly weird double-isolated d-pawn structure is best.

notes.text: White's bishop check is one of two good choices here; the other is Bd3, and both are covered.
notes.original: White has two acceptable options here, Bb5+ and Bd3, and both are covered in this study.

notes.text: White's bishop clears the way for kingside castling; little else needs adding.
notes.original: Bd3 prepares kingside castling; little needs to be added.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's bishop pins your f6 knight to the queen and threatens to take it and wreck your pawns.
notes.original: White pins the f6 knight against the queen and threatens to wreck your pawns with Bxf6.

notes.text: You answer the pin with a pin of your own: your bishop pins the f3 knight to the queen.
notes.original: You answer the pin with a pin of your own on the f3 knight.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the bishop, so White must retreat and you gain time.
notes.original: The pawn thrust gains time because the bishop has to retreat.

notes.text: Your knights head for f5 and e4, aiming at White's weakened c3 pawn.
notes.original: Black heads for Nf5 or Ne4, using the weakened c3 pawn as the target.

notes.text: White gave up the bishop to open lines, but you keep a healthy centre.
notes.original: White gives up the bishop to open lines but Black keeps a healthy centre.

notes.text: Your h-pawn stops Bg5, a prudent move; Nc6 is also playable.
notes.original: Preventing Bg5 is prudent here. Nc6 is also playable.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White keeps the bishop pair by avoiding ...Nxc4, and the bishop eyes your f7 pawn.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop pair and avoids ...Nxc4, which would give it up. The bishop also x-rays f7.

notes.text: You threaten ...a4 to harass the bishop on b3.
notes.original: You threaten ...a4 to trap or harass the bishop on b3.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the bishop on d2 and hits the f2 pawn.
notes.original: The knight attacks Bd2 and hits f2.

notes.text: White keeps the bishop pair and a slight space edge, but g4 loosened the kingside.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop pair and a slight space edge, but the kingside is loosened by g4.

notes.text: White chose a more modest retreat, and you are fine here.
notes.original: A more modest retreat, Black is fine here.

notes.text: Take the pawn now, before White plays cxd5; then castle early, since it is your king's safest square.
notes.original: Capture now, before White can play cxd5 and Nb5 type ideas. After Bxc4 White has used time and you get a good development. Follow with ...O-O, ...b6 and ...Bb7. Do not wait too long with ...O-O: it is the safest square for your king.

notes.text: Castling here is also playable.
notes.original: Also playable.

notes.text: Bring your bishop to b7 to fight for e4, and avoid ...Nc6, which blocks it.
notes.original: You aim to put the bishop on b7 and fight for the e4 square. Avoid ...Nc6 here: it blocks the b7 bishop idea.

notes.text: Trading your dark bishop for the knight removes the piece that guards d5 and e4.
notes.original: You trade your dark bishop for the knight to remove the piece that guards d5 and e4.

notes.text: Equal: fight for e4 with ...Bb7, then ...Nbd7 or ...Qc8 and ...Ne4, while avoiding ...Nc6.
notes.original:
White has a pawn structure with c3 and d4 weaknesses, but good bishops. Equal, with an easy plan of ...Nbd7 and ...c5 or ...Qc8 and ...Ne4.
This is a Panov-type position with an isolated-looking centre: White has pawns on c4 and d4 against your d5, and after the trade on c3 he has doubled c-pawns. The centre is semi-open and kings will castle short. Your plan: play ...b6 and ...Bb7 to fight for the e4 square, trade the dark bishop on c3 to remove the defender of d5, then play ...Nbd7 and ...c5 or ...Qc8 and ...Ne4. White wants to use his bishops and the c4 and d4 pawns to attack. You meet it by pressing on c3. The risk is playing ...Nc6, which blocks the b7 bishop. If White deviates, keep control of e4.

notes.text: You get a normal isolated-pawn position, with your bishop well placed on d6.
notes.original: You get a normal isolated pawn position with the bishop on d6 well placed.

notes.text: Another possible move for you here is b6.
notes.original: Also possible: b6.

notes.text: Castling is the best move here, ahead of two decent alternatives.
notes.original: The same position as in 🔵 03 (Fianchetto Defence). Castling is the best move here, ahead of two decent alternatives.

notes.text: Ne4 is another possible move here.
notes.original: Also possible: Ne4.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your bishop develops and covers b5, so White's knight on a4 is offside and you needn't hurry.
notes.original: Black develops the bishop and covers b5, and the White knight on a4 is offside, so there is no hurry.

notes.text: Your knight hits the d4 pawn and prepares to jump to g4.
notes.original: Black hits d4 and prepares ...Ng4.

notes.text: Your queen steps off the c-file before White's rook arrives on c1.
notes.original: The queen steps off the c-file before White's rook arrives on c1.

notes.text: The position is equal, and you have easy play against the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Equal. Black has easy play against d4.

notes.text: Striking with the e-pawn is a more direct break, and it is also fine for you.
notes.original: A more direct break, also fine for Black.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Trade off White's active bishop; the pin on d7 loses its sting and you are comfortably equal.
notes.original: You trade White's active bishop. The pin on d7 loses its sting once the bishop on b5 is exchanged, and Black reaches a comfortable equal position.

notes.text: Your queen eyes the b2 pawn and the knight on a4.
notes.original: The queen eyes b2 and the a4 knight.

notes.text: White gains queenside space, but you have no weaknesses and the position is equal.
notes.original: White gains queenside space but Black has no weaknesses. Equal.

notes.text: White's knight lands on b6 with tempo on your a8 rook; weakening b6 like this was a mistake.
notes.original: The knight lands with tempo on the a8 rook and White gets the upper hand. Do not weaken b6 like this.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The right square: from c7 your queen watches the e5 knight and prepares castling.
notes.original: The right square. White's Ne5 hits the queen and the c6 and f7 squares, but from c7 the queen keeps an eye on e5 and prepares castling.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks the d4 pawn while your knight stays powerful on e4.
notes.original: The bishop attacks the d4 pawn and you keep the powerful knight on e4.

notes.text: You grab kingside space, but White keeps a small edge thanks to the pawn centre.
notes.original: Black grabs space on the kingside. White has a small edge, thanks to the pawn centre.

notes.text: Now your king has lost castling, and White is clearly better.
notes.original: Now the king has lost castling and White is clearly better.

notes.text: The immediate b6 was just as good, but this quieter bishop move is fine too.
notes.original: The immediate b6 is equally good, but I chose the quieter path.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Offering a bishop trade is fine, since your light-squared bishop is somewhat restricted here.
notes.original: Exchanging bishops is acceptable, as the light-squared bishop is somewhat restricted here.

notes.text: Simple development with Nf3 first is the most accurate move order and keeps White's options open.
notes.original: The main line's Nb5 idea (aiming for Nd6+) is well known, but simple development with Nf3 first is actually the most accurate move order, keeping options flexible rather than committing the knight early.

notes.text: Your follow-up is to undermine White's centre gradually and make d4 a target.
notes.original: Black's follow-up would have been to undermine the white centre gradually; the isolated d4-pawn would then be a target.

notes.text: Recapturing with the a-pawn gives you a half-open a-file against White's queenside.
notes.original: You open the a-file against Ra1.

notes.text: Your pieces keep pressing d4, and you have a modest edge.
notes.original: Your pieces keep pressing d4 and c3. A modest edge for Black.

notes.text: White's pawn ran forward, but your rook wins it.
notes.original: The pawn runs forward but falls.

notes.text: The position is very close to equal either way, but Nf3 is slightly more accurate and worth knowing.
notes.original: Very close to equal either way; the main line's chosen try is perfectly reasonable in practice, but Nf3 is slightly more accurate and worth knowing about.

notes.text: White gains queenside space with b4 and b5, and your f5 pawn supports your knight on e4.
notes.original: White gains queenside space with b4 and b5. You counter with ...f5, supporting your Ne4.

notes.text: White's c6 pawn cramps you, but it is also a target.
notes.original: The c6 wedge cramps you but is also a target. Near equal.

notes.text: Your b6 pawn hits the c5 pawn to undermine White's centre.
notes.original: ...b6 aims to undermine the white centre. White can either maintain the broad pawn centre or release it.

notes.text: The position is equal.
If White's knight grabs the c5 pawn, you win the a1 rook and come out on top.
notes.original: Trap: 13.Nxc5? Rxa1 14.O-O Ra7 15.Ne5 Nxe5 16.dxe5 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on c5 with the knight falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 13.Nxc5? Rxa1 14.O-O Ra7 15.Ne5 Nxe5 16.dxe5 and White is losing.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's bishop attacks your rook on d8, so the rook steps over to d5.
notes.original: Bg5 hits Rd8, so the rook goes to d5.

notes.text: Your pieces are active and your knight pressures d4; aim for ...Qe7 and ...Rd8, and avoid ...Ne4 for now.

notes.text: Challenge the centre with ...dxc4 at the right moment, keep d5 well supported, and don't hurry ...Ne4.
notes.original: Unpin with ...Be7, castle, then challenge the centre with ...Nc6 and ...Bd6; the position is equal and balanced. This is a closed, balanced position with pawns on d5 and e6, where White has c4 and d4 and you have just developed your pieces on active squares. Your plan: castle short, complete development with ...Nc6 and ...Bd6, then challenge the centre with ...dxc4 or ...Rd8. White wants to push d5 or capture on c4 and play Bxc4 with an initiative, so keep your knight and pawn on d5 well supported. The risk is hurrying ...Ne4 or ...dxc4 before you have castled, since White gets Bxc4 with a lead. If White avoids Bd3, keep calm, develop and castle.

notes.text: The natural recapture gives you a healthy centre; avoid the passive ...Bd7 and ...Nbd7.
notes.original: The natural move: you get a healthy centre and an easy plan. After Bb5+ you answer ...Nc6 and then ...Bd6, ...O-O and ...Bg4 to pin the knight on f3. Your aim is to trade pieces and play ...a6 against the bishop on b5 only when it helps you. Avoid ...Bd7 and ...Nbd7, which are passive.

notes.text: The position is balanced and you can play for equality with simple moves.

This is a symmetrical, open-centre position with your pawn on d5 against White's d4, both kings castled short, and a roughly balanced game. Your plan: play ...h6 to ask the bishop on g5 a question, consider ...Bxf3 to remove a defender of d4, then bring the rooks to e8 and c8 with ...Re8, ...Qd7 and ...Rac8. White wants to pile up on d5 with Qb3, Rc1 and Bxf6 followed by Nxd5 ideas, so keep d5 guarded before moving the f6 knight. The risk is passive play with ...Bd7 or a careless move that lets Bxf6 win a pawn; if White drops the bishop back, trade pieces calmly.

notes.text: A solid, low-risk way to meet the Accelerated Panov: White can keep the pawn or regain material.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want to meet the Accelerated Panov (2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.exd5 Nf6) with calm development: ...Nbd7, ...g6, ...Bg7 and ...O-O. It is solid and low-risk. After 4...Nf6 White can keep the pawn with 5.Qa4+, or play 5.Nc3 and regain material.

notes.original: Rather than capture the knight (which fixes White's structure, since the isolated d-pawn is repaired by recapturing), Black can develop with ...Nf6.

notes.text: You win the pawn back; White can grab on c6, but your queen and bishop will aim at g2.
notes.original:
Idea: After 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.cxd5, play 4...Nf6 and win the pawn back with ...Nxd5. White can grab the c6 pawn with Bb5, Qa4 and Qxc6+, but you get active pieces for it: after ...Qxd5 and ...Be4 your queen and bishop both point at g2.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.cxd5 Nf6 5.Nc3 Nxd5 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.d4 Bf5
Watch out: ...Nxc3? loses material on move 9. ...Qxd7? loses material on move 14.
See also: 🟢 02 covers more of the 2.c4 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

notes.original: The knight on d7 is deep in your camp and would be trapped after ...Rd8 or ...Bf6, so White trades queens to rescue it and keep the extra pawn.

notes.original: Takes e5 and g5 away from the knight and gives the king f7.

notes.original: Your bishop and queen swarm round the uncastled king.

notes.original: 7.Bb5 pins the newly-developed knight to the king immediately instead of castling first. ...and Black untangles with normal development.

notes.original: Blocks the long diagonal and covers c6.

notes.original: The doubled c-pawns are ugly, but you have the bishop pair and no weaknesses to attack, so the position is level. Aim for ...Qd6 and ...Rfd8.

notes.original: Black's Queen is dangerous in the middle of the center, especially when it cannot even be disturbed by White's minor pieces.

notes.original: Only a small improvement, and the position remains close to balanced - useful to know, but not a serious gap in the existing repertoire coverage.

notes.original: White must retake with the pawn: the f-pawns are doubled, but the g-file opens and the queen on b3 eyes both d5 and b7.

notes.original: Guards the knight so Qxd5 is not a threat; the b7 pawn is the price.

notes.original: Now ...Nc2+ would fork king and rook, so White needs the next check.

notes.original: You offer a queen trade into an equal position. Your king is a little awkward on e7 but nothing is aimed at it.

notes.original: Looks active, but you win the g2 pawn with a hit on the rook and stay well ahead.

notes.original: The f-pawn stays a target for White, so Black should watch for threats there.

notes.original: The point: you recapture on e7 with the knight, which also hits the bishop on d5.

notes.original: The queens are off and your pieces are well placed. White keeps a small edge but you have no weaknesses and can play for ...Rfd8.

notes.original: Your knight on d5 is a rock and the bishop retreats with a solid camp. White keeps a small edge but there are no targets, so just complete development with ...Rc8.

notes.text: You now have an isolated d5 pawn to look after, but White gets little.
notes.original: This gives you an isolated d5 pawn to look after, but White gets little.

notes.original: White would try to hold unto the pawn in case black ever tries to pressurise it.

notes.original: 6.Nc3 develops naturally after the check, heading for a kingside fianchetto setup with g3 and Bg2.

notes.original: You have won the isolated pawn, but the rook on the seventh and the queen on c5 give White real activity, so keep your back rank guarded with ...Re8 and ...Rac8. The edge is modest.

notes.original: The biggest problem for White is the e-pawn: the isolated pawn cannot be held, so a piece ends up being lost.

notes.original: Effectively winning a piece.

notes.original: Challenges the centre at once, because the queen on d5 and the bishops on b7 and g7 would otherwise dominate.

notes.original: Takes the pawn back with the queen, which hits both the bishop on b5 and the queen on b3 and also releases the pin on f6, so White has no time for Bxf6 tricks. The plan after that is simple: trade pieces and convert.

notes.original: Offers to swap White's last active piece.

notes.original: The queen swap kills White's last chance of an attack, and with the better structure you are close to winning. Finish by doubling rooks on the b-file.

notes.original: 6.Nc3 develops naturally after the check, heading for a kingside fianchetto setup with g3 and Bg2. ...reaching a level position where Black's development lead compensates for the slightly exposed king.

notes.original: The standard answer to a queen on a4: the pawn hits it with tempo.

notes.original: Hits the queen again and attacks the d5 pawn, which has lost its support.

notes.original: The bishop on d3 attacks Ne2 and cramps White. The position is level; keep the pressure on d5 and the long diagonal.

notes.original: 5.Bb5+ inserts the check immediately rather than developing with Nc3 or Qa4+ first, hoping to provoke a weakening ...Nbd7/...Bd7. ...and Black untangles comfortably.

notes.text: Fianchetto and castle first, so a bishop trade on d7 can be answered by your knight.
notes.original: Do not play on the queenside with the knight still pinned: Bb5 and Qa4 already pile up on d7. Fianchetto and castle so that Bxd7 can be answered by Nxd7.

notes.original: The pin is gone and ...b5 gains space with a threat to the queen. Level; White's Qh4 achieves little.

notes.original: The queen has lost two tempi to Bf4 and White keeps a comfortable edge.

notes.original: 3...d4! is the simplest answer: the pawn grabs space and takes the c3-square away from White's knight, so White has to spend time on an awkward plan like f4/d3 instead of normal, comfortable development.

notes.text: Placing the bishop outside your pawn triangle felt natural, but Stockfish says d4 is much better.
notes.original: Having never faced this move order, it seemed natural to place the bishop outside of my yet to be formed pawn triangle. But Stockfish notes that d4 is much better here.

notes.text: White supports e5 with f4, Nf3 and d3, hoping the extra space tells.
notes.original: The pawn on e5 needs support, so White builds a chain with f4, Nf3 and d3 and hopes his extra space tells.

notes.text: White hopes to defend the pawn and develop, but the knight blocks the f-pawn and e5 is hard to hold.
Your knight heads for f5, where it eyes the e3 square.
notes.original: The knight heads for f5, where it eyes d4 and e3.

notes.text: Your f-pawn now hits the e5 pawn, giving you a clear way to open the centre.
notes.original: Your plan is to undermine the e5 pawn with ...f6. The structure is level and you have a clear way to open the centre.

notes.text: A tempting trick: the pawn eyes f7 and d7 while White's queen hits your b7 pawn.
notes.original: The tempting trick: the pawn threatens to take on d7 or f7 and the queen hits b7.

notes.text: Your knight steps to d7, where White's e6 pawn can take it.
notes.original: Your knight takes on e6 or attacks the pawn.

notes.text: White grabbed b7, but the queen is far from home and you are slightly better.
notes.original: White grabs b7 but the queen is far from home and you are slightly better.

notes.original: White's queen is far from home and has nothing to show for it, so you are a bit better.

notes.text: Your queen is active on a5, and you develop naturally into an easy, equal position.
notes.original: 4...Qa5+ is simplest: the check forces White to block with a piece (usually Nc3 or Bd2) rather than gaining any time, and Black develops naturally from there with an easy, fully equal position.

notes.text: White's knight develops and defends the e5 pawn.
notes.original: 5.Nf3 develops and defends the e5 pawn, rather than the sharper d4 push some sources prefer immediately.

notes.text: Even after d4, your active queen and central pressure give you a lasting edge.
notes.original: 5.Nf3 develops and defends the e5 pawn, rather than the sharper d4 push some sources prefer immediately. ...and Black's active queen and central pressure give a real, lasting edge.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn solidifies d5 and frees your pieces; queen and bishop stay active.
notes.original: You solidify the d5 pawn and develop. The queen on a5 and Bg4 are active.

notes.text: A solid move: your e6 pawn supports d5 and opens the way for your bishop to b4.
notes.original: Solid: it supports d5 and gives the bishop on f8 access to b4.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the c3 knight against White's king.
notes.original: Pins the knight on c3 against the king, since the queen on a5 already eyes it.

notes.text: You have a pleasant, harmonious position.
notes.original: Black has a pleasant, harmonious position.

notes.text: The pins are resolved and you are a shade more comfortable; aim for Bf5 and Rc8.
notes.original: The pins are resolved and you are a shade more comfortable. You can aim for ...Bf5 and ...Rc8.

notes.original: A tactical simplification: the knight on d5 is attacked and you are about equal.

notes.text: This simplifying alternative is comfortable for you.
notes.original: A simplifying alternative that is comfortable.

notes.original: Both sides play natural moves; White stays a pawn up for a moment but ...Qxe3 equalises material.
