The position is equal.
Taking on e4 is the main move: it removes White's e4/d4 pawn centre, and White nearly always retakes with the…
notes.original: Against the Classical Variation, 3...dxe4 is the main move. It takes away White's e4/d4 pawn centre. 3...g6 would transpose to a Modern Defence, and 3...e6 reaches French-style positions. White almost always recaptures 4.Nxe4, though a few gambit tries exist.

notes.text: Taking on e4 is the most reliable answer; e6 shuts in your light bishop.
notes.original: The most reliable answer to the Classical set-up is to take on e4. ...g6 transposes into a Modern Defence, while ...e6 shuts in the light-squared bishop and is harder to handle.

notes.text: Taking on e4 is your only good move, and it denies White the e4 and d4 pawn center.
notes.original: 3...dxe4 is black's only good move. Other moves are not in the spirit of this opening. This move also denies white his e4/d4 pawn center. White almost invariably responds with 4. Nxe4, but a few gambit continuations do exist.

notes.text: You prepare ...Bg7 to hit the d4 pawn; White can stop the ...Bg4 pin with h3.
notes.original: Black prepares to fianchetto the bishop on g7, in order to attack White's d4 pawn. There's also the usual pin Nf3 Bg4 incoming, so White can play h3 now to prevent it or one move later after Bg7. The c6-c5 break is not supported by the dark-squared bishop, so the knight has to do this job by going to d7.

notes.text: This is the sharper Gurgenidze Counterattack: you skip the fianchetto and strike on the queenside immediately.
notes.original: The real "Gurgenidze Counterattack": Bukhuti Gurgenidze's own sharper answer to White's knight development, alongside the quieter ...g6 fianchetto covered in the rest of this chapter - the same named idea, not an unrelated one. Black skips the fianchetto entirely and strikes on the queenside immediately.

notes.text: Your knight hits e4 and tempts White into e5, giving a closed Advance-style centre they may not know.
notes.original: 3...Nf6 is called the Campomanes attack. This induces White to play 4.e5, kicking the knight to d7.Black has induced White to play with a closed centre, resembling an advance variation Caro-Kann, perhaps not a line they were prepared to play.

notes.text: The calm choice trades on f6 and accepts a small White edge; the sharper tries carry more risk.
notes.original: Choice guide: Choose 5.Nxf6+ exf6 6.Bc4 Bd6 7.Qe2+ Be7 IF you like a calm, solid structure and expect White to play for a small edge (low risk). Choose 5.Ng3 h5 (the Bronstein-style reply) or the 5.Ng5 c5 trap lines only if you are comfortable with sharper play (higher risk). Each branch is marked below. After 4...Nf6 White can trade on f6 (the normal choice) or play the sharp 5.Ng5 and 5.Ng3.

notes.text: White recaptures; your main choices are the Classical Bf5, or Nd7, while Nf6 risks doubled pawns.
notes.original: 4. Nxe4 is an obvious recapture. Black has 3 main alternatives. The Classical Variation, 4...Bf5, usually sees the bishop controlling the light diagonal from g6. The Smyslov/Karpov variation delays the development of the light bishop, with Nd7, while Nf6 risks doubled pawns for an open file. None of the other alternatives have seen significant usage.

notes.text: White skips the recapture and tries to blast the centre open while a pawn down.
notes.original: The Rasa-Studier Gambit (ECO B15): instead of recapturing the pawn immediately, White tries to blast the center open while still a pawn down.

notes.text: The same pawn sacrifice, but White's bishop aims at f7 and e6 instead of opening with f3.
notes.original: The Von Hennig Gambit (ECO B15): the same pawn sacrifice, but aiming the bishop at f7/e6 instead of trying to open the center with f3.

notes.text: Your bishop gets out before ...e6 can block it in; White usually answers Ng3 to chase it back.
notes.original: Known as the Capablanca Variation, this is a deviation from the standard classical move order. Black wants to play e6, but in order to avoid his bishop from being stranded on the chain of light square pawns, he must instead play f5. White may, and almost always does, keep to the standard line, which consists of Ng3 and forces the bishop to retire; nevertheless, the risky Nc5 and aggressive Burris Gambit have given white with surprising victory.

notes.text: Your knight challenges the e4 knight, but Nxf6 exf6 would double your pawns.
notes.original:
4...Nf6, developing the knight instead, leads to 5.Nxf6+ exf6, the Tartakower variation. This is perfectly playable but Black has to accept doubling their pawns.

Nf6 is played at all levels, but is slightly more common in amateur play, and offers a trade of knights.

notes.text: Your d7 knight heads for f6 to trade White's central knight, and you can recapture without doubling pawns.
notes.original:
4...Nd7 is the Smyslov or Karpov variation. This looks slower, as the knight will have to move again before the light-square bishop can enter the game. If Black ends up trading their knight on f6, they may recapture with another knight rather than double their pawns: 5.Nf3 Ngf6 6.Nxf6 Nxf6.Otherwise, the main move is 5.Ng5.

By developing his Knight rather than the Bishop, Black aims to trade for White's central Knight, without compromising his pawn structure.

At one time named after the first world champion Wilhelm Steinitz, nowadays the variation is more often referred to as the Smyslov Variation after the seventh world champion Vasily Smyslov who played a number of notable games with it, or the Karpov Variation, after the twelfth World Champion Anatoly Karpov, in whose repertoire it appeared quite often. The short-term goal of 4...Nd7 is to ease development by the early exchange of a pair of Knights without compromising the structural integrity of his position. Play is similar to the Classical Variation except that Black has more freedom by delaying the development of his bishop, and is not forced to play it to the g6 square. However, this freedom comes at a cost as White enjoys added freedom in taking up space in the center, and often plays the aggressive 5.Ng5!? where Black's development is brought into question as well as the positional weakness of the f7-square. The famous last game of the Deep Blue-Garry Kasparov rematch where Kasparov committed a known blunder and lost was played in this very line.

notes.text: Your h6 makes a retreat square for the light bishop, but it is usually seen as an inaccuracy.
notes.original: With move 4...h6 Black creates escape square for light squared bishop's later use. It is usually considered as an inaccuracy and it is therefore rarely seen in higher levels. White's most usual respond is 5. Nf3. Natural development move 5. Bc4 is also played often and usually with an aim to sacrifice bishop in f7.

notes.text: Your bishop is attacked; retreat it to g6, the only sensible square.
notes.original:
= 5.Ng3 · Caro-Kann Defence:Classical Variation =

Bg6 is almost always played as the only sensible place for the bishop to retreat to, although defending the bishop with g6 is a very rare alternative, leaving black with an inferior pawn structure.

notes.text: White's knight hits your b7 pawn but is badly placed; answer with e5.
notes.original: Rarely seen, but the knight's poor positioning on c5 must be punished. White wants to win a pawn since Black's b pawn is hanging. However after e5! White is pretty much force to take the b pawn or retreat the knight and lose material.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's knight eyes f7 and Qf3 is coming, but this is one of White's less dangerous tries.
notes.original: White jumps with the knight to threaten f7 and Qf3 ideas, hitting your bishop on f5. It is very common (played in about 507,000 games). The point is to gain time if you respond carelessly, but it is one of the less dangerous moves for you.

notes.text: White's f3 guards the knight and prepares Ng3 or Qd2; it weakens e3 and g3, so it's level.
notes.original: White protects the knight on e4 so that your bishop cannot simply harass it, and prepares to bring the knight to g3 or the queen to d2 and castle long. It is very common, played in about 440,000 games, but f3 weakens the e3 and g3 squares and blocks the f-pawn, so the position is level.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
White's bishop develops toward the long diagonal, eyeing e6 and f7.
notes.original: 6.Bc4 develops toward the long diagonal rather than the more common Nf3/f4 setups, eyeing f7 and e6.

notes.text: White grabs kingside space and wants f5 to hit your bishop on g6.
notes.original: 6.f4 grabs extra kingside space immediately, intending f5 to hit the bishop on g6 before Black can secure it.

notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
notes.original: ...Nf6 and ...e5

notes.text: You must challenge the d4 pawn at once, or h4-h5 will trap your bishop on g6.
notes.original: You must challenge d4 at once. If you delay, h4-h5 traps the bishop on g6.

notes.text: Against Nh3, strike at once with Nf6 and e5; after queens come off, the ending is equal.

Idea: The classical 4...Bf5. Against 6.Nh3 strike at once with ...Nf6 and ...e5. After the queens come off you reach an equal ending with active pieces.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5.Ng3 Bg6 6.Nh3 Nf6 7.Nf4 e5 8.dxe5 Qa5+
Watch out: ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 5 to 7. ...Qxd4? loses material on move 4.
Next: 🔵 08 continues the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 02. Model games: 🟡 Game 05, 🟡 Game 06.

notes.text: Check with the queen is the right way; ...Bb4+ instead runs into c3, a queen trade and trouble on f2.
notes.original: Trap: 8...Bb4+? 9.c3 Qxd1+ 10.Kxd1 Ng4 11.cxb4 Nxf2+ and Black is in big trouble.

notes.text: Checking with the bishop on b4 falls into a trap: you are in big trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 8...Bb4+? 9.c3 Qxd1+ 10.Kxd1 Ng4 11.cxb4 Nxf2+ and Black is in big trouble.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's queen offers a queen trade on the e-file.
notes.original: The queen blocks the check and offers a trade instead of blocking with a knight.

notes.text: Your bishop develops and hits the f2 pawn.
notes.original: Hits f2 and develops.

notes.text: The queens are off, the bishops are active and the position is level.
White's knight on e2 is pinned against the king, and you are much better.
notes.original: The knight on e2 is pinned against the king and you are much better.

notes.text: White returns to the Nh3 manoeuvre; review that move order if it is unfamiliar.
notes.original: This returns to the Nh3 manoeuvre; review that move order if it is unfamiliar.

notes.text: Your queen checks the king and regains the pawn.
notes.original: Regains the pawn with check.

notes.text: Queens are off and the structure is level; aim for Bc5 and Nd5.
notes.original: Queens are off. The structure is level and you can aim for ...Bc5 and ...Nd5 with the open h-file in reserve.

notes.text: White castles quickly because the h-pawn push has already driven your bishop to e4.
notes.original: The reason to hurry: h4-h5 forces your bishop to e4.

notes.text: Be careful that your bishop on g6 isn't trapped when White's pawn reaches h5.
notes.original: As in the Advance Variation, black has to be careful here to ensure that the light-squared bishop isn't trapped.

notes.text: White follows h4 with f4, grabbing more space instead of developing the knight first.
notes.original: 8.f4 follows up the h4 advance with more space rather than developing with Nf3 first.

notes.text: White's knight heads to f4 to attack your bishop on g6.
notes.original: 8.Nh3 reroutes the knight toward f4 instead of the more natural Nf3, aiming to hit the bishop on g6 directly.

notes.text: White's pawn hits your bishop and will take it; retreat at once, because only one square really works.
notes.original: White attacks your bishop at once with a pawn push and tries to win time or even trap it. It is common in practice (played in about 850,000 games). So the bishop must go to a safe square immediately, and only one square really works.

notes.text: White offers the light-squared bishop trade at once, a move earlier than most main lines.
notes.original: 10.Bd3 offers the trade of light-squared bishops immediately, a move earlier than most main lines which delay it with h5 first.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White prepares to castle queenside so the h-pawn storm can begin.
notes.original: This is the major route. White prepares to castle queenside, so a kingside pawn storm with h2-h4-h5 is natural. After 11...Ngf6 or 11...Be7 Black keeps improving, and then castling kingside is the only option. If both sides race pawns toward the enemy king, a sharp fight follows. To counter it, Black can try queenside castling: 11...Qc7 takes control of the b8-h2 diagonal and 12...O-O-O lets Black fight for the initiative.

notes.text: To counter the storm, bring your queen to c7 and castle queenside to fight for the initiative.
notes.original: This is the major route. White prepares to castle queenside, so a kingside pawn storm with h2-h4-h5 is natural. After 11...Ngf6 or 11...Be7 Black keeps improving, and then castling kingside is the only option. If both sides race pawns toward the enemy king, a sharp fight follows. To counter it, Black can try queenside castling: 11...Qc7 takes control of the b8-h2 diagonal and 12...O-O-O lets Black fight for the initiative.

notes.text: Your check pushes White toward c3, which ends queenside castling, though White still keeps the upper hand.
notes.original: This move asks White to play c3, which removes any queenside castling and ends the kingside attack. Even so, White tends to keep the upper hand because the kingside attack usually continues undisturbed.

notes.text: White castles, so the kingside pawn storm is postponed and his assault is weakened.
notes.original: Whats the point of launching a pawn storm on the kingside only for White to castle? This would effectively weaken white's assault on the kingside and it's pretty much postponed for now.

notes.text: Your a-pawn advances to break open White's queenside.
notes.original: The a-pawn advances to break open White's queenside, with an all-out attack.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
White lifts the rook to join the attack along the third rank and the g-file.
White's bishop attacks your a3 pawn, but your bishop on e7 guards it.
notes.original: Attacks the pawn on a3, but your Be7 guards it.

notes.text: White has a small edge: your pawn structure is better, but White's rooks are more active.
notes.original: Small White edge. You have the better pawn structure but White has more active rooks; keep ...Nf6 and ...Rc8 handy.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your rook comes to the c-file while your a3 pawn stays in place.
notes.original: Develops the rook to the c-file while keeping your a3 pawn in place.

notes.text: The position is level; your a3 and b4 pawns cramp White and restrain his attack.
notes.original: Level. Your a3 and b4 pawns cramp White and keep him from attacking freely.

notes.text: White's rooks are lining up on g7, and your king comes under pressure.
notes.original: White's rooks aim at g7 and your king comes under pressure.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White puts a rook on the d-file and prepares to play the bishop to e5.
notes.original: White puts a rook on the d-file and prepares Be5.

notes.text: You offer a pawn to open the queenside and free your pieces.
Your knight hits White's bishop on f4.
notes.original: Your knight hits the bishop on f4.

notes.text: White has won a pawn, but your pieces are active; bring a rook to c8 to regain activity.
notes.original: White has grabbed a pawn, but your pieces are very active and the position is close to level. Look for ...Bd6 and ...Rac8 to regain activity.

notes.text: White blocks the check with a pawn rather than a piece.
notes.original: 12.c3 blocks the check with a pawn rather than interposing a piece, keeping the knight on b1 flexible for d2 or a3.

notes.text: After c3, White's king is less safe castling long, risking h5 and ...g5 hitting it.
notes.original: After c3 White's king becomes less safe if it castles queenside, so White is discouraged from castling long, or else risks being hit by something like h5 and ...g5.

notes.text: White centralizes the knight and offers to trade light pieces.
notes.original: 13.Ne4 centralizes the knight immediately after the bishop interposes the check, offering a trade of light pieces.

notes.text: White's pawns now hold more space than yours.
notes.original: White holds more space.

notes.text: White castles long into the centre, accepting a sharper middlegame.
notes.original: 15.O-O-O castles into the center rather than the more modest Kb1 some sources prefer, accepting a sharper middlegame.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's rook takes the open e-file to harass your queen and the bishop behind it.
notes.original: White puts the rook on the open e-file to harass the queen and bishop.

notes.text: Your queen takes the centre and offers to trade queens.
notes.original: Centralises and offers to trade.

notes.text: The endgame is equal, but White's king on f1 is awkward, so aim for ...Rd8.
notes.original: The trades leave an equal endgame. White's king on f1 is slightly awkward, so you can play for ...Rd8.

notes.text: The position is double-edged but balanced.
notes.original: 15.O-O-O castles into the center rather than the more modest Kb1 some sources prefer, accepting a sharper middlegame. ...reaching a double-edged but balanced position.

notes.text: Your rook goes behind the d-file and prepares the ...c5 break.
notes.original: Puts the rook behind the d-file and prepares ...c5.

notes.text: You strike in the centre before White's pawn storm gets going.
notes.original: Strikes in the centre before White's pawn storm starts.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks White's queen.
notes.original: The pawn hits the queen.

notes.text: Take on g5 with your h-pawn and bring your pieces back to defend.
notes.original: Level and sharp. Open the h-file with ...hxg5 and bring pieces back to defend.

notes.text: This is an alternative break, and the position stays level.
notes.original: An alternative break, level.

notes.text: White grabs the b7 pawn, but you still hold comfortably.
notes.original: 13.Ne4 centralizes the knight immediately after the bishop interposes the check, offering a trade of light pieces. ...and Black holds comfortably.

notes.text: You force matters with check, because the knight on b7 attacks your queen.
notes.original: Forces the issue with check, since Nb7 attacks the queen on a5.

notes.text: Your queen hits both the knight on b7 and the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Hits both the knight and d4.

notes.text: The knight escapes with a hit on your f7 pawn, and the position is level.
notes.original: The knight escapes with a hit on the f7 pawn, and the position is level.

notes.text: You end up a pawn down.
Your active pieces give you a real edge once the position opens up.
notes.original: 12.c3 blocks the check with a pawn rather than interposing a piece, keeping the knight on b1 flexible for d2 or a3. ...and Black's piece activity gives a real edge once the position opens up.

notes.text: The simple answer: you win the bishop.
White's queen attacks your knight on f4.
notes.original: Hits the knight on f4 and b7 at once.

notes.text: You are a pawn up; tuck your king away, play ...Rd8 and trade pieces.
notes.original: You are a pawn up. The price is a slightly exposed king, so tuck it away with ...Ke8 and ...Rd8 and trade pieces.

notes.text: White gets ahead in development here, so be careful.
notes.original: The natural recapture lets the bishop escape and White gets ahead in development.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
White retreats the knight to f1 to fuel the kingside attack.
notes.original: Retreats back the knight on the 1st rank to fuel white's attack on the kingside.

notes.text: White tucks the king away on b1 before starting the g4 pawn storm.
notes.original: Before starting the kingside pawn storm with g4, White's most precise move is actually the prophylactic Kb1 first, tucking the king away from any future ...Na4 or queenside counterplay.

notes.text: Your queen offers a queen trade on e2 to keep the position level.
notes.original: Trying to keep the position equal by exchanging queens.

notes.text: White trades queens to keep equality, ending both the g-file attack and your queenside threats.
notes.original: This is how White keeps equality: he trades queens, which ends any attack on the g-file and your threats on the queenside.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop on d2.
notes.original: Attacks the bishop on d2 and eyes the g-pawn.

notes.text: Pawns are traded on both wings and it is level; your knight on h5 guards g7.
notes.original: Pawns have been swapped on both wings and the position is level. Your knight on h5 guards g7 so Bxg7 is not a worry.

notes.text: White has given up a pawn for nothing, so you are a pawn up.
notes.original: White has given up a pawn for nothing.

notes.text: This is a small move-order tweak: your position stays sound, but White's attack is slightly safer.
notes.original: A small improvement in move order rather than a real change - Black's position stays sound, but White's attack flows slightly more safely after Kb1 first.

notes.text: White prepares c4 and Ne5, and keeps the a-pawn from being rolled up.
Your knight challenges the strong White knight on e5.
notes.original: Challenges the strong knight on e5.

notes.text: Your queen checks and forces matters; White's g-pawn storm is dangerous, but your pieces dominate the centre.
notes.original: The check forces matters. White's g-pawn storm is dangerous but your pieces dominate the centre; White is only a shade better.

notes.text: White gives up a pawn for a wedge on h7 and the d5 break; roughly level, so watch your king.
notes.original: Gives up a pawn for a wedge on h7 and the d5 break; it is roughly level but be careful with your king.

notes.text: White offers a knight trade to remove your key kingside defender on f6.
notes.original: Trying to get rid of black's major defences on the kingside to get a upper hand on white's assault on the kingside.

notes.text: Your queen offers a queen trade on e2.
notes.original: Offering a queen trade. The doubled b-pawns are actually a strength, since they claim d5 for the knight and open the c-file.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's bishop points at your h6 pawn, and the h5 pawn keeps cramping you.
notes.original: White points the bishop at the h6 pawn, which your h-pawn push left weak, and keeps h5 as a cramping wedge.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop on e3 and the f2 pawn at once.
notes.original: Hits the bishop and f2 at once.

notes.text: Your knight returns to guard h7 and d5.
notes.original: Returns the knight to guard h7 and d5.

notes.text: White's h5 pawn cramps your kingside, so aim to free your game with ...c5.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge: the pawn on h5 cramps your kingside. But your position is sound, so aim for ...Rfd8 and ...c5 to free it.

notes.text: Your queen stops White's d5 thrust and eyes the a2 pawn.
notes.original: White plays Qd5 to avoid any tactical sequences with d5 thrust for white and also threatening to take white's a2 pawn.

notes.text: White's c4 looks active, but it weakens the king on c1 and invites your queenside attack.
notes.original: 16.c4 looks active, but it weakens the white king on c1 and invites Black to attack on the queenside.

notes.text: The position is balanced; watch for ...f4, since a knight jump to f2 could fork White's rooks.
notes.original: An even keel has been reached here. This is favorable for black Since Bxf4 Nxf2 forks the two rooks, f4 is the primary danger at the moment.

notes.text: White lines up the e-file and avoids ...f4 tricks.
notes.original: White prepares to take over the e-file and avoids ...f4 tricks.

notes.text: White plans to expand with a5; your rook on c8 is the answer.
notes.original: A quiet position with a small White edge. White's plan is to pressure b7 and expand with a5; you hold the c-file and play ...Rc8 to meet it.

notes.text: The king walk looks crazy, but the position is roughly level.
notes.original: The king walk looks crazy but is roughly level.

notes.text: A famous branch point: White keeps only a small, long-explored edge, nothing that should worry a prepared Black.
notes.original: One of the most analysed positions in the Classical Variation: the queen drops back to c7 after the usual bishop trade, before White decides where to put the king. This exact move order runs a little differently from our main Classical repertoire choices elsewhere in the book, so treat this as supplementary deep-theory reference for one of the position's most famous branch points rather than a required addition to your main lines. All three of White's top tries here keep only a small, well-known and long-since-fully-explored edge - nothing that should concern a well-prepared Black player.

notes.text: White can also develop the bishop to d2 here.
notes.original: Also possible: Bd2.

notes.text: White can also play the bishop to e3 here.
notes.original: Also possible: Be3.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White had to retake with the queen, which now stands on e4.
notes.original: White has to recapture with the queen.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen again and gains a tempo.
notes.original: Hits the queen again and gains a tempo.

notes.text: Your knight takes the pawn on g4.
notes.original: Takes the pawn.

notes.text: Your f5 pawn supports the knight on g4, and White's attack is slow.
notes.original: Supports the knight on g4, so Rg1 attacks nothing. White's attack is slow and he keeps a small edge.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White retreats the bishop and keeps a compact structure, with a small edge.
notes.original: Retreats the bishop and keeps the structure compact, with a small edge for White.

notes.text: This is your freeing break: the c5 pawn strikes the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Your freeing break, striking the d4 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight hits White's queen on d3.
notes.original: Hits the queen.

notes.text: Your king is in the centre but safe in this endgame.
notes.original: An equal-looking endgame with a small White edge. Your king is in the centre but it is safe in this endgame: aim for ...Ke7 and ...Rc8.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's queen leaves e4 and lands on h4, pressuring your knight on f6.
notes.original: The queen has to leave e4. Qh4 adds pressure on f6 and h6 while keeping the queen safe.

notes.text: Your knight offers a trade for the bishop on e3.
notes.original: Offers a knight for the bishop.

notes.text: Your bishop develops with a hit on White's queen.
notes.original: Hits the queen.

notes.text: Your pawns are damaged and White is slightly better; aim to bring your rook to g8.
notes.original: The pawns are damaged and White has a small edge. Play for ...Rhg8 and keep the knight routes open.

notes.text: You win the queen first, and your knight on f2 forks both rooks.
notes.original: Counterattacks the queen on c7, but you win it first and the knight forks the rooks.

notes.text: With the bishops traded, the position is very level with fewer pieces.
notes.original: 10.Bd3 offers the trade of light-squared bishops immediately, a move earlier than most main lines which delay it with h5 first. ...reaching a very level position with simplified piece count.

notes.text: You develop the knight and keep ...c5 in reserve.
notes.original: Develops and keeps ...c5 in reserve.

notes.text: Your c-pawn counters in the centre, striking the d4 pawn.
notes.original: The counter in the centre.

notes.text: White storms your king; open lines with hxg5 and bring pieces back to defend.
notes.original: White has a pawn storm against your king, so the position is sharp but balanced. Open lines with ...hxg5 and bring pieces back to defend.

notes.text: White's knight drops back to g3, which is also fine for you.
notes.original: Also fine for you.

notes.text: White develops the knight, and the position stays level with chances for both sides.
notes.original: 8.f4 follows up the h4 advance with more space rather than developing with Nf3 first. ...and the position remains level with chances for both sides.

notes.text: The thematic freeing move: your pawn challenges d4 and opens the way for your pieces.
notes.original: The thematic freeing move: it challenges d4 and opens the way for your pieces.

notes.text: White's knight on d4 is strong, but you have easy development and a healthy structure.
notes.original: The position is level. White's knight on d4 is strong, but you have easy development and a healthy structure.

notes.text: White's position is a touch more pleasant, but not dangerous for you.
notes.original: 8.Nh3 reroutes the knight toward f4 instead of the more natural Nf3, aiming to hit the bishop on g6 directly. ...reaching a position that's actually a touch pleasant for White without being dangerous.

notes.text: Solid: your e6 pawn blocks the c4 bishop's diagonal and opens your bishop's diagonal.
notes.original: Solid: it blocks the diagonal of the bishop on c4 and opens the f8-a3 diagonal for your bishop.

notes.text: White's knight jumps to h5, hitting your knight on f6 and the g7 pawn.
notes.original: White jumps in to hit f6 and g7.

notes.text: Your rook guards the g7 pawn, so White's knight jumps on f6 and g7 win nothing.
notes.original: Defends g7 so that Nxf6+ and Nxg7+ do not win a pawn.

notes.text: You traded the dark-squared bishops and the position is level.
notes.original: You trade the dark-squared bishops and the position is level.

notes.text: Your bishop retreats to h7, still watching the long diagonal and safe from further harassment.
notes.original: The bishop retreats to h7, where it still watches the long diagonal b1-h7 and cannot be harassed again. This is the only sensible reply, and your plan afterwards is simple: develop with ...Nf6, trade the bishop pair by ...Bxd3 when White commits the bishop to d3, play ...e6 and ...Be7, then castle short and use ...c5 to open lines. Avoid any retreat to f5 or any capture on c2.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn fixes the dark squares and opens the diagonal for your f8 bishop.
notes.original: Trading White's strong bishop removes the danger of Bxh7 ideas and costs you nothing. The e6 pawn fixes the dark squares and opens the way for the kingside bishop.

notes.text: Bf4 is also possible, inviting Qa5+; it gives White no real edge and you are well placed.
notes.original: Bf4 is also possible here, which can be considered an open invitation to play Qa5+. This doesn't result in an a tangible advantage, but the black side is undoubtedly well-placed.

notes.text: White castles long to attack along the h-file; keep your pieces flexible and your king safe.
notes.original: You have a fully developed, flexible position, only slightly behind in space, and ...c5 or ...Nbd7 with ...c5 is your plan. This is a semi-open position with White's pawn on h5 next to an advanced h-pawn structure; the centre is open and White has a small space edge on the kingside. Both sides may castle on opposite wings, White long and you probably short or even queenside. Your plan: trade the light-squared bishops with ...Bxd3, develop with ...e6 and ...Be7, then strike in the centre with ...c5 or ...Nbd7 followed by ...c5. White wants a quick attack with Bd2, O-O-O and the h-file, using the pawn on h5. You meet it by keeping your pieces flexible and your king safe. The risk is leaving the bishop on g6 loose, because White can hit it, and an early ...h5 weakens you. If White deviates, avoid weakening moves and trade the strong bishop.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes e6 and f7, but you complete development without difficulty.
notes.original: 6.Bc4 develops toward the long diagonal rather than the more common Nf3/f4 setups, eyeing f7 and e6. ...and Black completes development without difficulty.

notes.text: Your bishop guards e5; White wants f5 to hit your g6 bishop and e6 pawn.
notes.original: Guards e5 and prepares ...Qc7 and ...Nbd7. White's plan is f5 to hit both the bishop on g6 and the e6 pawn.

notes.text: The h-file opens for your rook, pointing at White's h2 pawn.
notes.original: The h-file opens for your rook.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes e6 and f7, but your structure holds. Aim for ...c5 or ...b5.
notes.original: White's pieces watch e6 and f7 but your structure holds, so the position is level. Aim for ...c5 or ...b5.

notes.text: White got f4 and f5 in quickly.
notes.original: White gets f4 and f5 in quickly.

notes.text: White's f-pawn wants f5 against your g6 bishop, but normal development keeps things balanced.
notes.original: 6.f4 grabs extra kingside space immediately, intending f5 to hit the bishop on g6 before Black can secure it. ...and the position stays balanced once Black meets the pawn storm with normal development.

notes.text: Your bishop guards e5; White's idea is f5, hitting both your g6 bishop and the e6 pawn.
notes.original: Guards e5 and prepares ...Qc7 and ...Ne7. White's idea is f5, which attacks both the bishop and e6.

notes.text: You gave up both bishops for knights, so White has the bishop pair, but the position is level.
notes.original: You have traded both bishops for knights. White has the bishop pair but you get d5 and f5 for the knights and the structure is stable, so the position is level.

notes.text: Had White taken on e5 instead, that would have been a mistake: you win with a queen trade and ...Bxc5.
notes.original: Trap: 6.dxe5? Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 Bxc5 8.f4 Na6 9.Bxa6 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on e5 with the pawn falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6.dxe5? Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 Bxc5 8.f4 Na6 9.Bxa6 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d4 now would be a mistake: White's knight takes your queen and you end up worse.
notes.original: Trap: 6...exd4? 7.Nxd8 Kxd8 8.Nf3 Ke8 9.Qe2+ Be7 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d4 with the pawn falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...exd4? 7.Nxd8 Kxd8 8.Nf3 Ke8 9.Qe2+ Be7 and Black is losing.

notes.text: You win the pawn back, and White is behind in development and a little cramped.
notes.original: Black eventually wins the pawn back, but White is behind in development and a little cramped. Black dominates.

notes.text: White's bishop takes control of e4, hits your f5 bishop and hopes for Bxh7.
notes.original: White uses the bishop to take control of e4 and hopes for Bxh7.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop and gains space.
notes.original: Kicks the bishop and gains space.

notes.text: Taking b2 is possible, but your queen is far from home and White leads in development, so it's level.
notes.original: Grabbing b2 is possible, but your queen is far from home and White's lead in development gives him chances, so the position is level.

notes.text: A solid alternative, and the position is level.
notes.original: The solid alternative, level.

notes.text: You win the d-pawn, but White gets good compensation for it in this playable gambit.
notes.original: However, this is one of the more playable gambit lines in the Caro-Kann, in my humble opinion. White gets good compensation for the d-pawn.

notes.text: Avoid grabbing on e4 here: White recaptures on d4 and you end up losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Bxe4? 7.Nxd4 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 e5 9.Nf5 g6 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on e4 with the bishop falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Bxe4? 7.Nxd4 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 e5 9.Nf5 g6 and Black is losing.

notes.text: White gets big attacking chances for the pawn, but if you defend accurately you end a pawn ahead.
notes.original: Safe or risk-free? Not quite: White gets big attacking chances for the pawn, similar to the Smith-Morra Gambit in the Sicilian. White leads in development, but if Black defends accurately Black ends up a pawn ahead after a short attack.

notes.text: Your knight comes out to solidify your position.
notes.original: Trying to solidify the position.

notes.text: With your light-squared bishop gone, you have shed a burdensome piece and the position is level.
notes.original: The light-squared bishop is off the board, which removes a burdensome piece and can change the outcome of the game.

notes.text: Don't fear the bishop lined up on your queen; there is no hidden tactic behind it.
notes.original: Black need not fear the bishop eyeing the queen; there is no hidden tactic behind it.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White trades the strong knight for yours, and the bishop on d3 now eyes h7.
notes.original: White trades off the strong knight and goes for a sharp sequence against h7.

notes.text: Your rook hits the queen and the second rank, giving you counterplay; the wild sequence ends level.
notes.original: A wild sequence that ends level: White regains his pawn and takes on b7 with the rook, but ...Rd2 gives you counterplay against the queen and the second rank.

notes.text: White has just lost time, so you are slightly better.
notes.original: White just loses time and you are better.

notes.text: Trade the light bishops with ...Bxd3 and hit the centre with ...c5; avoid ...Nf6 too early because of Qf3.
notes.original: Solid and good. It opens the way for the f8 bishop and takes away the threat on e6 by the knight. Your plan is to develop with ...Nf6 and ...Be7, trade the light-squared bishops with ...Bxd3, and challenge the centre with ...c5. Castle short. Avoid ...Nf6 too early without taking care of Qf3, since the queen can bother f5 and f7 together. The position is balanced with a tiny edge for you.

notes.text: Also fine: after the bishop trade, h6 drives the knight back, then e6 and Be7.
notes.original: Also fine. After Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 h6 you drive the knight back, then play ...e6 and ...Be7 with a clear plan.

notes.text: The light bishops are traded and your structure is solid; castle short next.
notes.original: You trade the pair of bishops and develop with a solid structure. Next is castling.

notes.text: White hopes to gain time with Nh4 against your f5 bishop, but its g5 knight has no good square.
notes.original: White wants to retreat the knight from g5 only after bringing the other knight out, and hopes to gain time with Nh4 against your bishop on f5. It is very common in practice, but the knight on g5 is stuck with no good square, which makes the move a little dubious.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White has lost two knight moves for nothing, and the game is level.
notes.original: White has lost two knight moves for nothing and the game is level.

notes.text: Prepare Ngf6 to trade White's strong knight, then break with e5; avoid an early e6.
notes.original: Develop the knight to d7 so that ...Ngf6 trades off the strong e4 knight. Your plan is ...e5, which challenges d4 and opens lines for your bishops; the c8 bishop is already outside, so ...e5 is your natural break. Avoid ...e6 too early, which shuts in your f5 bishop.

notes.text: Strike at once: the e4 knight shields your f5 bishop from Bd3, so the e5 break is safe.
notes.original: Strike at once. The f5 bishop is shielded by the knight on e4, so you can afford the break.

notes.text: Take back with the queen so your f5 bishop stays guarded against White's bishop on d3.
notes.original: Recapture with the queen so f5 stays protected after the discovered attack from d3.

notes.text: Your knight retakes in the centre, and your queen on f6 keeps defending the bishop on f5.
notes.original: You retake the pawn with a knight that jumps to the centre; the queen on f6 keeps defending f5. Do not recapture with the queen on e5, which would allow Bxf5.

notes.text: Play ...Bd6, castle long, then use ...Rhe8 and ...Nc4 for pressure while your e5 knight stays strong.
notes.original: After the trades you have a comfortable, active position with the queen on f5 and a good knight on e5. This is an open, active position where your queen on f5 and knight on e5 are well placed, and the position is level. It is White's move, so he may play f4 or Nd4 to hit your queen. Your plan is, first, to develop ...Bd6 and castle long, bringing the rooks to the d-file. Second, keep the knight on e5 strong. Third, use ...Rhe8 and ...Nc4 for pressure. If White plays f4, retreat ...Ng6 or ...Nc6, and if he plays Nd4, move the queen to g6. The risk is losing a tempo to attacks on the queen or on the knight.

notes.text: This is the normal trade: take back with the e-pawn and accept a slightly doubled f-pawn for a comfortable game.
notes.original: The normal move, and the reason 5.Ng5 is only a sideline. White trades the knight that has just recaptured on e4 and Black accepts a slightly doubled f-pawn, getting the bishop pair and a very comfortable game in return. White loses nothing here. The Alien move does the opposite: it spends a tempo on an attack that Black can switch off with one pawn move.

notes.text: White keeps the knight for imbalance, but ...h5 gives you a strong kingside initiative.
notes.original: Ng3!? White wants to preserve his knight hoping to find some more sophisticated game and to keep things imbalanced. However after the move h5! Black gets a strong initiative on the kingside.

notes.text: White's knight tries to provoke ...h6 and weaken your kingside, though Nxf6+ would be stronger.
notes.original: 5.Ng5 tries to provoke ...h6 and unsettle Black's kingside. After 5...h6 Black's kingside is a little weaker and White gets some initiative, but 6.Nxf6+ was the stronger follow-up.

notes.text: The Alien Gambit: White's knight eyes an eccentric, mostly-for-fun sacrifice on f7.
notes.original: The "Alien Gambit": an eccentric, mostly-for-fun knight sacrifice on f7, occasionally seen in blitz and rapid play.

notes.text: White brings the queen out early and invites a trade of knights on e4.
notes.original: 5.Qd3 brings the queen out early, offering a trade of knights on e4 to simplify toward an endgame-leaning structure.

notes.text: White develops and leaves the d4 pawn for you to grab, which leads to a sharp fight.
notes.original: 5.Bd3 develops immediately, offering Black the chance to grab the d4 pawn with ...Qxd4 for a quick, sharp fight.

notes.text: Play Bd6, castle, then route your knight through d7; White's queenside majority is the long-term issue.
notes.original:
Idea: 4...Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6 gives you a very solid kingside and easy development. Bishop to d6, castle, rook to e8, and reroute the knight via d7 to f8. White's queenside majority is the long-term issue, so keep your pieces active.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Bxh2? loses material on moves 7 to 8.
Next: 🔵 09 continues the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 02. Model game: 🟡 Game 13.

notes.text: Korchnoi often played exf6; it is sounder than gxf6 and gives you rapid development.
notes.original: B15 Caro-Kann Defense: Tartakower Variation Viktor Korchnoi has played 5...exf6 many times (including in a world championship match). 5...exf6 is sounder than 5...gxf6!? of the Bronstein-Larsen Variation and offers Black rapid development.

notes.text: Taking with the g-pawn gives you the open g-file and attacking chances, but your doubled f-pawns mean you must stay…
notes.original:
Idea: 5...gxf6 is the fighting choice. You use the open g-file, castle long after ...Qd5, ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O, and play for an attack. Your structure is worse, so you have to stay active.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ gxf6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Qxf3? loses material on move 7.
Next: 🔵 10 continues the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plans: 🟠 Plan 02, 🟠 Plan 10.

notes.text: Your plan is queen to d5 and bishop to g4, then castle long and attack.
notes.original:
Idea: 5...gxf6 is the fighting choice. You use the open g-file, castle long after ...Qd5, ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O, and play for an attack. Your structure is worse, so you have to stay active.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ gxf6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Qxf3? loses material on move 7.
Next: 🔵 10 continues the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plans: 🟠 Plan 02, 🟠 Plan 10.

notes.text: Your doubled f-pawns weaken the kingside, but you get the half-open g-file; taking with the e-pawn is more accurate.
notes.original: The Bronstein-Larsen Variation is the most aggressive way to play against the Classical Caro Kann. First and foremost black weakens his kingside and voluntarily makes a double pawn but in exchange of a dangerous attack on the kingside. The g file is open and further play would be met on the kingside or on the center. Playable, but exf6 is more accurate.

notes.text: Avoid ...Be6, which would weaken your kingside badly; develop the bishop to e7 and castle instead.
notes.original: This dislodges the bishop; ...Be6 is not possible because it would weaken the kingside badly. ...Be7 and ...0-0 are the right follow-up.

notes.text: White offers a pawn for quick development; you needn't suffer, just play Bd6.
notes.original: Bd3 is another idea, offering a pawn for early development and aggression. There is no need to suffer through the defence: just play ...Bd6 and follow the standard procedure of the Korchnoi Variation.

notes.text: White develops quietly and prepares Qd2, keeping the bishop off an exposed diagonal.
notes.original: Be3 - develops to a quiet square instead of the main c3/Bc4/Bd3 tries, preparing Qd2 or long castling without committing the bishop to an exposed diagonal.

notes.text: White develops the knight instead of the sharper setups, aiming for a quick castle.
notes.original: 6.Nf3 develops instead of the sharper c3/Bd3 setups, heading for a quick O-O.

notes.text: White's bishop takes its best square and asks how you will meet it; e5 and d6 are key.
notes.original: White develops the bishop to its best square before playing Nf3 or Ne2, and so asks you how you want to deal with it. With your pawn on f6 the e5 and d6 squares are the key points.

notes.text: Bd6 starts the usual set-up; castle next and you will most likely be fine.
notes.original: There is little to add about the Tartakower: follow the usual ...Bd6 and ...0-0 set-up and you will most likely be fine. Other interesting lines in the Tartakower are included as well.

notes.text: Aim for Re8, Be6, Nd7, Nf8 and h6 if needed; this is the set-up to reach.
notes.original: Black plans ...Re8, ...Be6, ...Nd7, ...Nf8 and ...h6 if necessary - the set-up Black should always aim for here.

notes.text: White's queen lines up behind the bishop toward h7, and this is arguably the main line.
notes.original: 8.Qc2 is the most common try here, eyeing h7 and preparing to meet ...Re8+ by developing rather than castling queenside immediately. This is arguably the main line here, not just a sideline alongside 8.Ne2.

notes.text: Your rook eyes the e-file, but White's knight on e2 shields the king, so there is no check.
notes.original: Contrasting case: compare this to the 8.Qc2 move-order, where the same ...Re8 IS check. Here White played 8.Ne2 first, and that knight now physically sits on the e-file between the rook and the king, so ...Re8 is just a normal developing/centralizing move, not a check. The lesson: whether a rook lift on the open e-file comes with tempo depends entirely on whether White's knight has already occupied e2, not on the rook move itself.

notes.text: White castles at once to finish development instead of playing the queen to c2 first.
notes.original: 9.O-O completes development immediately instead of delaying with Qc2 first.

notes.text: The h-pawn move is the logical, safer choice; the more ambitious f5 is also possible.
notes.original: ...h6 is the logical and safer choice; the more ambitious ...f5!? is also possible.

notes.text: Your h-pawn stops Ng5 ideas and gives your king some luft.
notes.original: 9...h6 stops any future Ng5 ideas and gives the king some luft before continuing with ...Nd7/...Bf5/...c5 depending on White's setup.

notes.text: Your h-pawn aims at White's kingside, where the king may come under real danger.
notes.original: ...h5 aims at White's kingside. With the help of the bishop pair, White's king will be in real danger once the attack gets going.

notes.text: White castles, connecting the rooks and getting the king safe before choosing a plan.
notes.original: 10.O-O connects the rooks and gets the king fully safe before deciding how to use the extra space; Black meets it with the natural developing ...Nd7, and now White has a real choice of four plans at move 11.

notes.text: Your knight can head for b6, depending on White's next bishop move.
notes.original: 10...Nd7 heads for b6 or f8 depending on which bishop move White chooses next.

notes.text: Or your knight can head for f8, depending on White's next bishop move.
notes.original: 10...Nd7 heads for b6 or f8 depending on which bishop move White chooses next.

notes.text: White develops the bishop to support d4 and prepare a later d4-d5 break.
notes.original: 11.Be3 is the most natural square for the bishop, eyeing c5 and supporting a future d4-d5 break.

notes.text: White's knight eyes f5 and h5 and leaves open which bishop White develops next.
notes.original: 11.Ng3 eyes f5/h5 and keeps options open about which bishop develops where.

notes.text: White offers to trade dark-squared bishops right away instead of keeping them on.
notes.original: 11.Bf4 offers the trade of dark-squared bishops immediately rather than keeping it on the board.

notes.text: White keeps the bishop flexible while preparing a rook to e1.
notes.original: 11.Bd2 keeps the bishop flexible (can still swing to e3, c1, or stay put) while preparing Rae1.

notes.text: Your knight on f8 keeps your options open, just as it did against other bishop moves.
notes.original: 11...Nf8 keeps flexibility, just as against Bf4/Bd2.

notes.text: White's rook contests the open e-file that your rook took earlier.
notes.original: 12.Rfe1 contests the open file Black opened back on move 8.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the knight on e2 and eyes f3, preparing queen or rook development.
notes.original: 12...Bg4 develops actively, hitting f3/e2 and preparing ...Qd7 or ...Rad8.

notes.text: This knight move is White's strongest try here, stronger than Rad1.
notes.original: White's strongest try here, stronger than Rad1.

notes.text: Grabbing the a2 pawn is a trap: White's b3 and queen recapture leave you in serious trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 13...Bxa2? 14.b3 Qc7 15.Qxa2 Bxh2+ 16.Kh1 Rxe3 and Black is in serious trouble.

notes.text: The opening phase is over and your position is fine.
notes.original: The opening phase is over and Black is fine.

notes.text: Taking the a2 pawn is tempting, but after b3 and f5 White's attack leaves you clearly worse.
notes.original: Trap: 14...Bxa2? 15.b3 f5 16.Nxf5 Bxh2+ 17.Kh1 g6 and Black is clearly worse.

notes.text: Taking on a2 with the bishop falls into a trap: you are clearly worse.
notes.original: Trap: 14...Bxa2? 15.b3 f5 16.Nxf5 Bxh2+ 17.Kh1 g6 and Black is clearly worse.

notes.text: White's knight retreats to reroute via e3 and free the e2 square for the rooks.
notes.original: The knight retreats to reroute via e3 and free the e2 square for the rooks.

notes.text: White gains queenside space; he plans b4 and c5 to give his bishops room.
notes.original: White gains queenside space; the plan is b4 and c5 to give the bishops room.

notes.text: Push the h-pawn on to fix g3 and take kingside squares from White's knight.
notes.original: Fix g3 and take the kingside squares from the knight.

notes.text: You stand solid: your knight lands on e6 and the f6 pawn controls e5 and g5.
notes.original: Black stands solid. Your knight lands on e6 and the doubled pawn on f6 controls e5 and g5.

notes.text: White develops the bishop before castling, an alternative to castling at once.
notes.original: 9.Be3 develops the bishop before committing the king, an alternative to the immediate O-O or h3 tries at the same node.

notes.text: White develops the bishop flexibly and keeps both ways of castling open.
notes.original: 9.Bd2 develops the bishop flexibly, keeping the option of O-O-O alongside the more common O-O.

notes.text: White prepares to castle long; your c5 strike hits the centre and gives you counterplay.
notes.original: 10.Bd2 prepares O-O-O. ...c5 hits the centre and Black gets counterplay.

notes.text: White offers a trade of dark-squared bishops right after castling.
notes.original: 11.Bf4 offers the trade of dark-squared bishops right after castling, instead of developing the queenside pieces first.

notes.text: Your bishop offers a trade; exchange pieces to avoid complications on the kingside.
notes.original: The opening phase is over and Black is fine. Pieces should be exchanged to avoid complications on the kingside.

notes.text: This is the idea: trade every piece that could attack your kingside, starting with the knight on f4.
notes.original: This is the idea: trade every piece that could attack your kingside. After the knight on f4 disappears there is nothing to your king.

notes.text: The position is equal.
notes.original: Equal.

notes.text: White's attempts to keep the bishops lead to a queen trade and a level ending.
notes.original: White's tries to keep the bishops lead to a queen trade and a level ending.

notes.text: White's bishop trade offer leaves the position balanced.
notes.original: 11.Bf4 offers the trade of dark-squared bishops right after castling, instead of developing the queenside pieces first. ...and the position remains balanced.

notes.text: Your blockading knight on d5 hits the c3 pawn and the bishop on f4, inviting a bishop trade.
notes.original: A blockade on d5 trades the bishops and hits the c3 pawn.

notes.text: White's c4 and d5 gain space, but you traded the light bishops and your structure is fine.
notes.original: White's c4 and d5 try to gain space, but you trade the light bishops and the structure is fine.

notes.text: White's rook move is also playable here.
notes.original: Also playable.

notes.text: White grabs space with g4, but the position stays close to level.
notes.original: 9.Be3 develops the bishop before committing the king, an alternative to the immediate O-O or h3 tries at the same node. ...and the position stays close to level.

notes.text: Keep the h-file shut: the g4 pawn becomes a target and your knight can later use g6.
notes.original: Keep the h-file shut. The pawn on g4 becomes a target and your knight can later use g6.

notes.text: Your b-pawn push starts counterplay on the queenside.
notes.original: Counterplay.

notes.text: The position is level.
notes.original: Equal.

notes.text: Grabbing the pawn opened the h-file for White's rook, and your bishop is now out of play.
notes.original: Grabbing the pawn opens the h-file for White's rook and your bishop is out of play.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White tucks the king away on b1, and the position stays close to level.
notes.original: 9.Bd2 develops the bishop flexibly, keeping the option of O-O-O alongside the more common O-O. ...and the position stays close to level.

notes.text: Develop your last minor piece; White's pawn storm will meet your h5 pawn, already in the way.
notes.original: Develop the last minor piece. White has castled long, so he will start a pawn storm with f4 and g4, but your h5 pawn already stands in the way.

notes.text: Push your b-pawn: you start your own pawn storm against White's king.
notes.original: Counterplay against the king with your own pawn storm.

notes.text: The position is dynamically balanced.
Pushing the b-pawn looks natural, but it opens lines near your king and gives White a small edge.
notes.original: The pawn thrust looks natural, but it opens lines against your own king and gives White a small edge.

notes.text: White trades bishops, heading for a calm position like the other Ne2 lines.
notes.original: 9.O-O completes development immediately instead of delaying with Qc2 first. ...reaching a calm position similar to the chapter's other Ne2 tries.

notes.text: Take back on d6 with your queen right away.
notes.original: Recapture at once.

notes.text: Your h-pawn stops White's h-pawn from advancing and keeps your kingside closed.
notes.original: Stops h5 and keeps your kingside closed.

notes.text: Recapture with the rook and the game is level.
notes.original: Then recapture with the rook and the game is level.

notes.text: Never skip the recapture on d6, or White's bishop takes your knight on f8 and you lose a piece.
notes.original: You must never skip the recapture on d6: White's bishop would then take the knight on f8 and you would be a piece down.

notes.text: Your rook checks down the open e-file, forcing White to block it.
notes.original: 8...Re8+ is the natural, forced response, using the open e-file with tempo before White's king finds safety. Contrasting case: compare this to the 8.Ne2 move-order elsewhere in this chapter, where the identical-looking move ...Re8 is not check. The difference has nothing to do with the rook move itself: here White has not yet moved the e1-knight, so the e8-e1 file is completely open and ...Re8+ is a real check; in the 8.Ne2 line, that same knight already sits on e2, blocking the file, so ...Re8 there is just a normal developing move with no check. Whether a rook lift on an open file comes with tempo depends entirely on what already occupies the file, not on the rook move itself. Choice guide: choose this if you want a very solid pawn structure with easy plans (doubled f-pawns that guard e5 and g5) and the bishop pair in some lines (low risk, medium theory). The queen check on e8 forces White to decide how to block it: 9.Ne2 and 9.Be3 are the main choices.

notes.text: White develops the bishop first, supporting d4 and keeping Ne2 or Ng3 open for the knight.
notes.original: 9.Be3 develops instead of the knight, keeping the knight's own route (Ne2 or Ng3) open for later and eyeing c5/d4 support.

notes.text: Your knight hits d5 and c4, and your bishop can come out to e6 next.
notes.original: 11...Nb6 hits d5/c4 and prepares ...Be6 or ...Bf5 next.

notes.text: White commits the dark-squared bishop and often follows with a rook to e1 for a slow central squeeze.
notes.original: 12.Bd2 finally commits the dark-squared bishop, often followed by Rae1 and a slow central squeeze.

notes.text: Your last minor piece comes out comfortably, completing your development.
notes.original: 12...Be6 completes development comfortably.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop on d2 and the b2 pawn, heading for weak squares.
notes.original: The knight hits the d2 bishop and heads for the weak e3 and b2 squares.

notes.text: Trade your bishop for the knight so that taking back on g3 ruins White's pawn structure.
notes.original: Trade your bishop for the knight so that hxg3 ruins White's pawn structure.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks the rook on d1, and the position is level.
notes.original: The bishop attacks the rook on d1. Equal.

notes.text: White's bishop trip to h7 wins nothing, so you are level.
notes.original: The Bh7+ check is harmless: the king steps to h8 and the bishop must return, so White wins nothing and you are level.

notes.text: Your knight sidesteps and stays flexible for a later jump to g6 or e6.
notes.original: 11...Nf8 sidesteps and keeps the knight flexible for ...Ng6 or ...Ne6 later.

notes.text: White takes your dark bishop; you simply recapture with your queen.
notes.original: 12.Bxd6 cashes in the bishop pair since Black can't avoid the recapture without losing time.

notes.text: Recapturing with the queen gives a very level position.
notes.original: 12...Qxd6 recaptures with the queen, reaching a very level structure.

notes.text: Your g6 pawn takes f5 and h5 away from White's pieces.
notes.original: Takes f5 and h5 away from White's pieces.

notes.text: White's knight hits your queen and your f6 pawn, so the queen steps aside.
notes.original: The knight hits your f6 pawn and queen, so the queen steps aside.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the knight away from e4.
notes.original: Kick it away.

notes.text: White's knight has no good retreat and must trade for your bishop, leaving you solid.
notes.original: The knight has no good retreat and White has to trade it for your bishop. You keep a solid structure and no weaknesses.

notes.text: Your knight again keeps its options open instead of committing to b6.
notes.original: 11...Nf8 again keeps the knight's options open rather than committing to b6 right away.

notes.text: White centralizes the last rook, eyeing e-file pressure or a later knight to f4.
notes.original: 12.Rae1 centralizes the last piece and prepares a timely e-file pressure or a later Nf4.

notes.text: Your last minor piece develops to a safe, useful square.
notes.original: 12...Be6 develops the last minor piece to a safe, useful square.

notes.text: Strike in the centre now, before White's knight jumps to f5 or e4.
notes.original: Strike before White's knight reaches f5 or e4.

notes.text: White's bishop on b5 attacks your rook on e8 through the open c6 square.
notes.original: The bishop now attacks your rook on e8 through the open c6 square.

notes.text: Trading your bishop for the dangerous knight keeps the game level and stops the pressure on f6.
notes.original: You trade your good bishop to remove the dangerous knight and stay level. White's plan was to play Ng3-f5 or Ne4 to hit your f6 pawn.

notes.text: White's f4 and g4 lever tries to open the kingside, but your f5 pawn and h4 knight keep it blocked.
notes.original: White can also try the f4 and g4 lever to open the kingside. ...f5 and the knight jump to h4 keep it blocked.

notes.text: You offer to trade dark bishops; your doubled f-pawns are healthier without pieces that could attack them.
notes.original: White steps off the g1-a7 line and you trade off the dark bishops: your doubled f-pawns are healthier without the pieces that could attack them.

notes.text: White hopes to push a5 and clamp the queenside, but your rooks cover the d- and e-files.
notes.original: White hopes to push a4-a5 and clamp the queenside, but your rooks cover d-file and e-file.

notes.text: Giving your bishop for the knight left White with doubled g-pawns, which are now the weak ones.
notes.original: If White kicks the bishop, retreat to g6 and give up the bishop for the knight so that his pawns become the weak ones.

notes.text: Your f-pawn push opens the position; if White takes on f5, trades follow and it is equal.
notes.original: Black hits the bishop and opens the position. After Bxf5 Nf6 O-O Ng4 the pieces are traded and the game is equal.

Your g6 pawn prepares a bishop move to f5 or a knight move to d7.
notes.original: 9...g6 prepares ...Bf5 or ...Nd7 while keeping the long diagonal closed to future Bc4/Bb5 tries.

notes.text: White finally routes the knight to safety, intending Ng3 or castling long next.
notes.original: 10.Ne2 finally routes the knight to safety, intending Ng3 or O-O-O next.

notes.text: Your knight completes development naturally, heading for b6 or f8.
notes.original: 10...Nd7 completes development naturally, heading for b6 or f8.

notes.text: Your f5 pawn takes e4 from White, blocks the d3 bishop and gives your rook and queen more scope.
notes.original: A small but important point: ...f5 takes e4 away from White, blocks the d3 bishop and gives your rook on e8 and the queen more scope.

notes.text: Your bishop and queen both point at the h2 pawn.
notes.original: Bishop and queen both point at h2.

notes.text: White's g3 pawn blocks the diagonal, so your bishop and queen no longer hit h2.
notes.original: White blunts that battery.

notes.text: Your pieces are developed, so this thematic strike hits d4 and opens the centre.
notes.original: The thematic strike. Your pieces are developed, so open the centre.

notes.text: The position is equal.
notes.original: Equal.

notes.text: White's h-pawn push targets your g6 pawn; answer with f5 and Nf6 to keep your structure together.
notes.original: White tries to rip open the g6 pawn with h4-h5. Meet it with ...f5 and ...Nf6 and keep the structure together.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
White opens the kingside at the cost of safety; take on g4 and bring your queen to a5.
notes.original: White opens the kingside at the cost of safety; ...hxg4 and ...Qa5 give Black counterplay.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
The e6 knight is hit by rook and bishop, so you hit the d2 bishop to deflect White.
notes.original: The point: the e6 knight is hit by both the rook and the b3 bishop, so you hit the d2 bishop to deflect White's pieces.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge with the h4 lever; you aim for active play with queen and rooks.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge. The h4 pawn is a lever to attack your kingside pawns, while you aim for active play with your queen and rooks.

notes.text: White develops quietly, then castles short and plays Re1; he has no space edge after the exchange on f6.
notes.original: White develops the knight and prepares short castling, then Re1 to challenge the e-file. After the exchange on f6 he has no space advantage, so the move is a quiet, developing one. It is very common (played in about 143,000 games).

notes.text: The position is equal.
A model solid line: your doubled f-pawns control e5 and g5 while the pieces come out smoothly.
notes.original: A model solid line: Black's doubled f-pawns control e5 and g5 and the pieces come out smoothly.

Castle: your king is safe and your bishop stays well placed on the long diagonal; skip early Qc7 or Nc6.
notes.original: Castling is the clear and simple answer. The king is safe, the rook gets the e-file and your Bd6 stays well placed on the h2-b8 diagonal. Avoid grabbing space too early with ...Qc7 or ...Nc6, because piece development matters more.

notes.text: A useful waiting move, but it is slower than developing.
notes.original: A useful waiting move to stop Bd3 ideas, but it is slower.

notes.text: A solid main line: your structure is safe, and ...Nd7-b6 gives you play on the queenside.
notes.original: The solid main line: Black has a safe structure and ...Nd7-b6 gives play on the queenside.

notes.text: The rook trade eases your cramped position; now bring the knight to f8, then e6 or g6.
notes.original: You trade a pair of rooks, which eases your cramped position. The knight comes out to d7 and then to f8 and e6 or g6.

notes.text: Bring the bishop to f5, the knight to e6, and the queen to d7; avoid ...Nb6.
notes.original: The knight goes to f8 and then e6 or g6 to control central squares. You also want ...Qd7 and ...Bf5 or ...Ne6. Avoid ...Nb6 which lets White gain time with Bd3 or Bb3.

notes.text: White grabs space but leaves d4 a bit loose; aim your knight at it via e6.
notes.original:
White grabs space but leaves d4 a bit loose. An equal position where you have solid pieces and no weaknesses, and you should aim for ...Ne6 and ...Qf6.
This is a closed centre where White has traded the f-pawn structure and you have pawns on c6, d6 and f6, so the position is solid with no space advantage for either side. Both kings will castle short, you may wait. Your plan: bring the knight round with ...Nf8 and then ...Ne6 or ...Ng6, play ...Qd7 and ...Bf5, then castle short. White wants to push c4 and make space but this leaves d4 a little loose. You meet it by targeting d4 with ...Ne6 and ...Qf6. The risk is playing ...Nb6, which lets White gain time with Bd3 or Bb3. If White deviates with Re1, stay solid and complete development.

notes.text: You get play on the queenside.
The position is equal and your king is safe on g7.
notes.original: Equal. Your king is safe, the dark bishops are traded and ...Bg4 stops the knights from hopping into e4.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
If you take on d5, White retakes the bishop on g4 and leaves you an isolated d5 pawn.
notes.original: The point of Nd5: if ...cxd5 then hxg4 and White has won the bishop back for the knight, leaving you with an isolated pawn on d5.

notes.text: White keeps a small plus: your isolated d5 pawn and broken kingside are long-term weaknesses.
notes.original: White keeps a small plus: your isolated d5 pawn and broken kingside are the long-term weakness.

notes.text: White can also trade down here and keep a small edge.
notes.original: White can also trade down for a small edge.

notes.text: Your bishop eyes the h2 diagonal and you are ready to castle without weaknesses.
notes.original: ...Bd6 (Solid & Optimal) - simple, natural development that eyes the h2-b8 diagonal and prepares to castle without creating any weaknesses.

notes.text: Your queen hits b2 and d4 at once, so White must defend instead of developing.
notes.original: ...Qb6 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - immediately pressures b2 and d4, forcing White to spend a move defending rather than finishing development, at the cost of some tempo for Black's own king safety.

notes.text: Your rook lines up on the e3 bishop, so White must keep it guarded.
notes.original: The rook lines up against the e3 bishop, so White has to keep the bishop guarded.

notes.text: White wants c4 and then d5 to gain space and open lines.
notes.original: White wants c4 and then d5 to gain space and open lines. You keep the centre closed with ...Bc7 and the Nd7-f8 reroute, and the edge stays small. Your doubled f-pawns are safe because the e-file and the h2-b8 diagonal give your pieces real activity.

notes.text: Keep the centre closed with Bc7 and reroute your knight to f8; the edge stays small.
notes.original: White wants c4 and then d5 to gain space and open lines. You keep the centre closed with ...Bc7 and the Nd7-f8 reroute, and the edge stays small. Your doubled f-pawns are safe because the e-file and the h2-b8 diagonal give your pieces real activity.

notes.text: Develop your bishop and keep the h2 diagonal in view.
notes.original: Develop and keep the h2-b8 diagonal in view. White's idea with Qe2 is to hit the e-file against your king and prepare long castling.

notes.text: White's queen eyes your f6 and c6 pawns.
notes.original: The queen eyes the f6 and c6 pawns.

notes.text: Swing your queen toward White's castled king and use the a-file.
notes.original: Your counter: swing the queen to the long-castled king and use the a-file.

notes.text: Your position is fine here.
notes.original: Black is fine.

notes.text: Taking on b2 is playable, but White gets development and open lines while your queen is far away.
notes.original: The pawn grab on b2 is playable, but White gets development and open lines for it, and your queen is far from the rest of your army.

notes.text: White has castled and the position is clean and level.
notes.original: 6.Nf3 develops instead of the sharper c3/Bd3 setups, heading for a quick O-O. ...reaching a clean, level position.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight to the queen and develops at once.
notes.original: Pin the f3 knight and develop at once.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes c8 and covers g6, so you cannot trade there.
notes.original: The bishop keeps the pin-like pressure on c8 and stops a trade on g6.

notes.text: The position is equal: you have developed everything and the e-file is traded off.
notes.original: Equal. You have developed everything and the e-file is traded off.

notes.text: Your bishop challenges the f4 bishop; a trade is fine for you, but don't castle too early.
notes.original: Your bishop challenges the one on f4 at once. If White trades on d6 you recapture and have no problems, since your structure is solid. If he avoids the trade you play ...Na6-c7 and ...Be6 to complete development. Do not castle too early if White has Qd2 and long castling in mind, because your f6 and h7 pawns make a hook for a later g4 attack.

notes.text: Expand on the queenside with your b-pawn to gain space and attack White's long-castled king.
notes.original: You hit out on the queen side, using the b-pawn to gain space and to attack White's king after long castling. The knight on c7 supports ...Bd5 or ...Ne6.

notes.text: Recapture on d6, keep your king safe from a pawn storm, and equality is easy to hold.
notes.original: You have a sound position with an easy plan: queen side expansion, a queen trade or two and equality. This is a semi-open position in which White has just traded the dark-squared bishop on d6 and your queen side expansion ...b5 is in the air. Your plan: recapture ...Qxd6 or ...cxd6, castle short, and push ...b4 and ...a5 to gain space on the queen side. White wants to castle long and attack with g4 and h4, so keep your king safe and do not castle too early. The risk is a pawn storm against your king; if White avoids the trade, play ...Nc7 and ...Be6. You have a sound position and equality is easy to maintain.

notes.text: A calm set-up: your bishop is on e7 and you have castled short against White's c4.
notes.original: Another calm set-up where you develop the bishop to e7 first and castle short.

notes.text: White pushes the h-pawn at once, hoping to provoke a weakness before you finish developing.
notes.original: 10.h4 - grabs the h5-pawn's support square immediately instead of the main 10.Bc4, trying to provoke a weakness before Black finishes developing.

notes.text: White's knight on f3 guards the d4 pawn and gives the g3 knight a retreat to e2.
notes.original: White develops the knight to a natural square and protects d4. It also keeps the knight on g3 safe from ...h4 only indirectly, because the knight can later step to e2.

notes.text: Risky: the h-pawn may fall, but once the h-file opens you get a strong kingside attack.
notes.original: This move is risky: the h-pawn may fall in a couple of sequences, but once the h-file opens Black gets a strong kingside attack.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Open the position now, while your h3 pawn keeps White's kingside frozen.
notes.original: Open the position while White's kingside is frozen by your h3 pawn.

notes.text: White's bishop pins your c6 knight to your queen, so your king steps off the c-file.
notes.original: Bb5 pins the c6 knight to your queen, so the king steps off the c-file. White's pieces have no targets while your h3 pawn cramps g3 and h2.

notes.text: Black has a clear edge here.
notes.original: A clear Black edge.

notes.text: If White plays Nh4, you answer ...Rh5, and the pressure on f3 and g4 keeps White in trouble.
notes.original: Nh4 meets ...Rh5, and the pressure on f3 and g4 keeps White in trouble.

notes.text: You grab central space at once, aiming for a sharper, imbalanced position with chances for both sides.
notes.original: 10...c5 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - grabs central space immediately instead of pinning first, heading for a sharper position with chances for both sides rather than a quiet equalizing line.

notes.text: A solid, standard developing move: White's h4 cost a tempo, and your bishop already hits the queen.
notes.original: 10...Bg4 (Solid & Optimal) - the standard, well-tested developing move; the h-pawn advance costs White a tempo that Black uses to pin the knight and complete development comfortably.

notes.text: White develops naturally and keeps the central tension instead of taking on c5.
notes.original: 13.Nf3 develops naturally rather than taking on c5 immediately, keeping central tension.

notes.text: White takes on c5 right away, heading for a queen trade instead of the sharper Nf3.
notes.original: 13.dxc5 resolves the tension immediately, trading into an endgame-leaning structure rather than the sharper Nf3 try.

notes.text: The position is double-edged, but White's setup remains sound.
notes.original: 13.Nf3 develops naturally rather than taking on c5 immediately, keeping central tension. ...reaching a double-edged but sound position for White.

notes.text: White's c3 pawn supports d4 and gives the queen a safe route after you take on d4.
notes.original: Supports d4 and gives the queen a safe route after ...cxd4.

notes.text: You trade your bishop for the knight on f3 before things get uncomfortable.
notes.original: Trade before the knight pins you.

notes.text: The game is level: White's doubled f-pawns are balanced only by the bishop pair.
notes.original: Level: White's pawns are doubled and the bishop pair is the only compensation.

notes.text: Trading queens with dxc5 lets you play ...e5-e4, and you stay comfortable.
notes.original: Trading queens with dxc5 allows ...e5-e4, which hits the knight and keeps you comfortable.

notes.text: Bb5 would be a mistake: your queen check on a5 wins material.
notes.original: 8.Bb5 would be a mistake: ...Qa5+ wins material.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Black is winning.
