You keep a real, if modest, edge here.
notes.original: 13.dxc5 resolves the tension immediately, trading into an endgame-leaning structure rather than the sharper Nf3 try. ...reaching a position where Black's extra central space gives a real, if modest, edge.

notes.text: Your a-pawn undermines the b4 pawn that is propping up c5.
notes.original: Undermine the b4 pawn that is propping up c5.

notes.text: Your knights are more active and White's king on d1 is awkward, though the edge is tiny.
notes.original: You have the more active knights and White's king on d1 is slightly awkward, though the edge is tiny.

notes.text: Strike the centre: after dxc5 your queen faces White's queen on the d-file and the queens come off.
notes.original: Strike the centre: your bishop and queen face the d1 queen, so after dxc5 the queens come off.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the c5 pawn, and White's king is stuck on e2.
notes.original: The pawn on c5 falls back, and White's king is stuck on e2.

notes.text: If White kicks your bishop, retreat and fianchetto; White's f3 weakened e3. The position is equal.
notes.original: If White kicks the bishop, retreat and fianchetto: White's f3 weakens the e3 square. Equal.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the g3 knight; next develop with ...Bg4, ...Nbd7, then ...Qa5+.
notes.original: Push the pawn and force the knight back. This gains space on the kingside and takes away the g3 square. Your plan after that is to trade your c8 bishop for the knight with ...Bg4, develop ...Nbd7 and later play ...Qa5+ or ...e6.

notes.text: This break is tempting, but your bishop and queen aren't ready, so White is slightly better.
notes.original: A tempting break, but White gets slightly the better game because your king's bishop and queen are not ready.

notes.text: Take the knight: if White recaptures, the pawns in front of the king get wrecked.
notes.original: Take the knight, because White's pawns on f2 and g2 will be wrecked.

notes.text: Your queen gives check, so you gain time.
notes.original: With check, you gain time.

notes.text: The position is equal: your queen pins the d2 bishop, so White must break the pin or castle.
notes.original: This is equal. White has the bishop pair and a doubled pawn, and you have easy development. This is a closed-centre structure where you have grabbed kingside space with ...h4 against White's d4 and doubled f-pawn setup. You have pinned White's bishop on d2 with ...Qa5, and White still has to castle or play c3. Your plan: add pressure with ...Bb4, challenge the centre with ...e5, and then castle short once your pieces are out. White wants c3 to break the pin, castle and use the bishop pair. Do not allow your queen to be trapped on a5; if White plays c3, retreat with ...Qc7. The risk is overextending on the kingside, so only push ...h3 if it wins something clear.

notes.text: Challenge the centre with ...e5 once your pieces are out, then castle short.
notes.original: This is equal. White has the bishop pair and a doubled pawn, and you have easy development. This is a closed-centre structure where you have grabbed kingside space with ...h4 against White's d4 and doubled f-pawn setup. You have pinned White's bishop on d2 with ...Qa5, and White still has to castle or play c3. Your plan: add pressure with ...Bb4, challenge the centre with ...e5, and then castle short once your pieces are out. White wants c3 to break the pin, castle and use the bishop pair. Do not allow your queen to be trapped on a5; if White plays c3, retreat with ...Qc7. The risk is overextending on the kingside, so only push ...h3 if it wins something clear.

notes.text: White has the more active position here.
notes.original: White has a more active position.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the knight, but some White players answer with the dubious Alien Gambit knight sacrifice on f7.
notes.original:
However, many players with White, especially followers of Witty Alien or even Eric Rosen, usually have a sneaky idea with this move; after the natural 5...h6 by Black, White intends to sacrifice the knight for the f7 pawn with 6.Nxf7??, entering the dubious but incredibly scary Alien Gambit.

= Caro-Kann Defense, Classical Variation: 5...h6 = Black naturally looks to kick the knight away with h6.Best in this position is 6.N5f3, retreating the knight to safety. However, this move of 5...h6 actually encourages many players, especially followers of chess content creator Witty Alien, to play 6.Nxf7??, the dubious but scary Alien Gambit.

notes.text: In the Alien Gambit White sacrifices a knight on f7, but your king is safe and the extra piece wins.
notes.original: The Alien Gambit: White sacrifices a knight on f7 for an attack. Black's king is safe after ...Kxf7 and ...Kg8 and the extra piece wins.

notes.text: Also good: you develop, and White's knight attacks nothing that matters, so it must spend another move retreating.
notes.original: Also perfectly good: Black develops. The knight on g5 attacks nothing that matters (f7 is guarded by the king and the e4 pawn is already gone), so White has to spend another move bringing it back.

notes.text: White sacrifices a knight for a long attack on your king; it's a fun idea for blitz.
notes.original: 6.Nxf7 is a knight sacrifice for a long attack on the black king. It is a fun idea for blitz and bullet.

notes.text: The knight sacrifice looks alarming, but it just isn't sound.
notes.original: Watch out if you're on the Black side and haven't seen this before: it looks alarming, but it just isn't sound.

notes.text: Just keep developing by ordinary opening principles; you will be fine.
notes.original: Another option is to carry on with ordinary opening principles and develop; Black will be fine.

notes.text: White retreats the knight and drops the gambit, so the position is level.
notes.original: The natural retreat and White's best by a wide margin. The gambit idea is dropped and the knight goes back to a normal square. The net result is that White has spent two knight moves (Ng5 and back) and Black has spent one pawn move (...h6) that is mildly useful, so the position is level. Everything that follows with 6.Nxf7 is White trying to avoid admitting this.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White threatens Nxf7, but it is too slow: you can simply take the knight.
notes.original: A classic trap in reverse: White threatens Nxf7, but it is too slow.

notes.text: Taking the knight is right; the tempting queen check on a5 instead leaves you losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Qd5 8.Nxh8 Bf5 9.Nf3 g5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Take the knight back and carry on; the sacrifice is unsound, but your exposed king invites traps.
notes.original: Simplest and best: take the knight back and get on with the game. The sacrifice really doesn't work objectively, but this exposed king creates real, concrete traps over the next few moves - worth knowing, since several natural-looking replies below throw back most or all of the advantage, and one even loses outright.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Qd5 8.Nxh8 Bf5 9.Nf3 g5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Declining with the queen looks active, but White simply takes the rook and wins material by force.
notes.original: Declining the sacrifice looks active (the queen hits g2 and c4 is covered) but it loses material by force.

notes.text: White develops first, before deciding what to do about the missing piece.
notes.original: White's most natural try, developing before deciding what to do about the missing piece.

notes.text: White checks at once instead of developing the knight first.
notes.original: The immediate alternative, checking at once rather than developing the knight first.

notes.text: White builds the attack quietly, developing the bishop and keeping Nf3 and Ne5 ideas in hand.
notes.original: A quieter way to build the attack: develop the bishop to a square where it eyes the kingside, keep Nf3 and Ne5+ ideas in hand, and avoid giving a check Black can answer comfortably.

notes.text: Slightly more precise than e6, but White's reply leaves you only one exact good answer.
notes.original: Slightly more precise than 7...e6, but White's reply forces Black onto one exact square, and several natural-looking alternatives there throw the advantage away or worse.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn shuts out White's bishop check from c4 for good, but watch the knight check on e5.
notes.original: The practical recommendation: this blocks White's Bc4(+) idea along the long diagonal for good. It does not stop every check, though - White's other knight can still jump into e5 with check, and that one needs care (see below). Slightly less precise than 7...c5, but safer, because it avoids the Bc4+ tricks after 7...c5.

notes.text: Your bishop blocks the c4 diagonal for good and heads for d5.
notes.original: A sound alternative to 7...e6 and 7...c5. The bishop blocks the c4 diagonal for good and heads for d5.

notes.text: Pinning the knight is a blunder: Ne5 checks, then White's knight takes your loose bishop.
notes.original: Pinning the knight is the most natural developing move in the world, and it is a blunder here.

notes.text: The bishop checks again: even here your king stays exposed.
notes.original: The point: this check is still available even here, and it comes with real sting.

notes.text: White's knight jumps in with check before you can coordinate.
notes.original: Same idea as in the main line: the knight jumps in with check before Black can coordinate.

notes.text: Block the check with the pawn; it is the only move that keeps your full advantage.
notes.original: The only move that keeps the full advantage - block with the pawn and nothing else.

notes.text: Watch out: this natural king retreat gives back almost all of your advantage.
notes.original: Watch out: the natural-looking king retreat gives back almost all of Black's advantage.

notes.text: Watch out: this looks natural (blocking the check while centralizing the queen) but it just hangs the queen outright.
Blocking the check with your queen looks natural, but the bishop simply takes it.
notes.original: Watch out: this looks natural (blocking the check while centralizing the queen) but it just hangs the queen outright.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White's pawns start a storm against your king, with g5 and h4 coming.
notes.original: 12.g4 starts a pawn attack against the black king.

notes.text: You have an extra piece for a pawn and White has little real pressure.
notes.original: Black has an extra piece for a pawn and White has not developed much real pressure. 7...Be6 is simpler, but this is perfectly good.

notes.text: Your knight lands on d5 and you are doing fine.
notes.original: Black is doing fine.

notes.text: Your rook joins the game; White's last try is g5, but your king can retreat.
notes.original: Bring the other rook into play. White is making a last attempt at an attack with g5, but your king can retreat.

notes.text: You are clearly better: your king is safe on d8 and White's sacrificed knight is still missing.
notes.original: Black is clearly better: the king is safe on d8 and White's sacrificed knight is still missing.

notes.text: Trading pieces on e5 didn't help White, and you have already won the h4 pawn.
notes.original: Trading pieces on e5 does not help White: you can even take the h4 pawn.

notes.text: You hit the centre at once; White's bishop is still at home and queens will come off.
notes.original: Black hits the centre at once. Because White's king's bishop is still at home and the queens will come off, Black has no problems.

notes.text: Your knight challenges the e5 knight at once.
notes.original: Challenge the knight at once.

notes.text: Your queen checks, gaining a tempo, and also hits the e5 knight.
notes.original: The check gains a tempo and the queen hits the e5 knight.

notes.text: Level: your bishop hits the annoying e5 knight and can trade it off, so there is no danger.
notes.original: Level. White's knight on e5 is annoying but you can trade it off, so there is no danger.

notes.text: A quieter alternative, and the position stays balanced.
notes.original: A quieter alternative, equally balanced.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal: your active knight on e4 means White has no lasting pressure.
notes.original: Equal. Once the queens are traded, ...Bxc5 regains the pawn and the knight on e4 gives you active play, so White has no lasting pressure.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.

Black is slightly better.

notes.original: 5.Qd3 brings the queen out early, offering a trade of knights on e4 to simplify toward an endgame-leaning structure. ...and the position is dead level after the natural sequence of trades.

notes.text: White plans Bd3 and a knight to f4 to lean on your d5 pawn.
notes.original: The recapture is forced and good: you get a healthy symmetrical centre and the c8 bishop is free. White has no real initiative here. His plan is Bd3 plus Ne2-f4 to lean on d5, and yours is to trade the light bishops and develop calmly.

notes.text: Your plan is to trade the light bishops and then develop calmly.
notes.original: The recapture is forced and good: you get a healthy symmetrical centre and the c8 bishop is free. White has no real initiative here. His plan is Bd3 plus Ne2-f4 to lean on d5, and yours is to trade the light bishops and develop calmly.

notes.text: Recapture with the c-pawn: the structure is symmetrical and your c8 bishop is freed.
notes.original: Always recapture with the c-pawn here: the structure is symmetrical, your c8 bishop is liberated and White has no way to exploit the early queen trade.

notes.text: Your g6 pawn keeps f5 free for your light bishop.
notes.original: Keeps f5 free for the bishop.

notes.text: Your doubled f-pawns look ugly, but they control e4 and g4, and you get the g-file.
notes.original: The doubled f-pawns look ugly, but they control e4 and g4 and your rook gets the g-file.

notes.text: White's knight hits your d5 and e6 pawns; answer with ...Nd7 and ...Bd6 and the game stays level.
notes.original: White's knight eyes d5 and e6. Meet it with ...Nd7 and ...Bd6 and the game stays level.

notes.text: White's knight eyes your d5 and e6 pawns, but your solid pawns and ...Bd6 keep it level.
notes.original: White's knight heads for d5 and e6 targets. Your solid pawn mass and the quick ...Bd6 bring a level game.

notes.text: You are a whole queen down: you had to recapture on d5 at once.
notes.original: Never delay: White's queen just took yours on d5, so any other move leaves you a whole queen down.

notes.text: You have no queen here, so any move other than recapturing on d5 leaves you a queen down.
notes.original: Any other move leaves you a queen down.

notes.original: Trap: 6...Nxe4? 7.Nxd4 Nc5 8.Bc4 Nbd7 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Careful: grabbing on e4 with your knight here leaves you losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Nxe4? 7.Nxd4 Nc5 8.Bc4 Nbd7 9.O-O Nb6 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on e4 with the knight falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Nxe4? 7.Nxd4 Nc5 8.Bc4 Nbd7 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 and Black is losing.

notes.original: Trap: 6...Nxe4? 7.Nxd4 Nc5 8.Bc4 Nbd7 9.O-O Nb6 and Black is losing.

notes.original: Trap: 6...Nxe4? 7.Nxd4 Nc5 8.Bc4 Nbd7 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 and Black is losing. ...and the position is level after the natural queen trade.

notes.original: Trap: 6...Nxe4? 7.Nxd4 Nc5 8.Bc4 Nbd7 9.O-O Nb6 and Black is losing. ...and the position is level after the natural queen trade.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight against the queen; trade it and you are slightly better.
notes.original: Pin the f3 knight against the queen and trade it: you are slightly better.

notes.text: Trade the knights first, then bring your queen to h5.
notes.original: Trade the knights first, then the queen steps to h5.

notes.text: Recapture with your knight; the queens come off and the ending is balanced.
notes.original: Then recapture with the knight; the queens come off and the ending is balanced, with your Black structure sound.

notes.original: Pinning the knight is slightly more accurate.

notes.text: This is just a simpler alternative for White.
notes.original: A simpler alternative.

notes.original: The queen on h5 is a bit exposed, but White has no easy way to chase it.

notes.original: The main line is c3, which supports the d-pawn.

notes.text: Your queen can swing to h5 or g5 if White attacks on the kingside; after c4 you have a check.
notes.original: ...Qd5 is the usual main move; its value depends on how White plays, but the queen can swing to h5 or g5 if White attacks on the kingside. After c4!? Black has ...Qa5+.

notes.text: White is slightly better.

notes.original: ...Rg8 is the main idea of the Bronstein-Larsen Variation: it creates chaos and attacking chances on the kingside, and the queen can go to h5 or g5. ...h5 is also possible.

notes.text: White's g3 answers the rook's attack on g2, but you keep pressing on its kingside.
notes.original: g3 answers the attack on g2 by the rook, but Black keeps attacking White's kingside.

notes.text: White develops and heads for a kingside attack; keep pressure there, but finish your development first.
notes.original: 8.Be3 develops a piece and heads for a kingside attack. Black should keep up the pressure on White's kingside even without castling, but must finish development before committing to an attack.

notes.text: See how easily your queen swings across to support the kingside attack.
notes.original: Note how easily the queen swings across to support the attack on the kingside.

notes.text: This resembles the Stafford Gambit but is better: you aren't committed to a pawn sacrifice and develop flexibly.
notes.original: A key attraction of the Bronstein-Larsen Variation is that it resembles the Stafford Gambit but is better, since Black is not committed to a pawn sacrifice and develops flexibly. White keeps an edge here.

notes.text: Your queen offers a trade on the diagonal and stays active.
notes.original: Offers a queen trade on the diagonal and keeps the queen active.

notes.text: White's queenside pawn storm against your king keeps a real edge, and your e5 pawn is the counterweight.
notes.original: White's plan is a pawn storm against your long-castled king with b4-b5, which keeps a real edge. Your ...e5 and knight on d5 are the counterweight.

notes.text: The natural Bd2 lets you play e5 in time, and White's edge shrinks.
notes.original: The natural Bd2 allows ...e5 in time, and White's edge shrinks.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White intends to castle queenside, where its king is safer, rather than kingside.
notes.original: White's intention is clear: not to castle kingside but queenside, where the king is safer. If every option runs out, the king can stay in the centre or tuck away on f1.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White wants h5 to harass your bishop on g6, which has few squares.
notes.original: White wants h5 to harass the bishop on g6, which has few squares.

notes.text: Your h-pawn steps aside so the bishop on g6 gets the h7 square.
notes.original: Gives the bishop the h7 square.

notes.text: White's queen is far offside on a3, so you have counterplay.
notes.original: White has won a pawn but the queen is far offside, so you have counterplay.

notes.text: White can also trade queens and push on the kingside instead.
notes.original: White can also trade queens and push on the kingside.

notes.text: The queens are off, and the endgame is roughly fine for you.
notes.original: Endgame is roughly alright for Black

notes.text: Your bishop grabs the pawn, but now White tries to trap it.
notes.original: Your bishop grabs the pawn, but then White tries to trap it.

notes.text: You are ahead in pawns, but White's time and open files keep it roughly balanced.
notes.original: You have won a pawn, but White gets time and open files for it, so the position stays roughly balanced.

notes.text: Bd3 develops first and immediately points along the diagonal at your bishop on f5.
notes.original: Developing the bishop to d3 first, rather than Nf3 as in the main line, is a small improvement, since it eyes the h7-b1 diagonal immediately and keeps the knight's best square flexible.

notes.text: White's queen hits your b7 pawn and forces you to decide at once.
notes.original: Rather than g3, White's sharper and more testing try is Qb3, hitting both b7 and d5 at once and forcing Black to make an immediate decision.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's pawn hits your queen, so you trade queens on d2.
notes.original: The pawn hits your queen, so you trade queens on d2.

notes.text: White is slightly better because of your doubled f-pawns, but your position is solid.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge thanks to the bishop pair and your doubled f-pawns, but you are solid.

notes.text: Trading queens on c3 ruined White's pawns: they are doubled and split apart.
notes.original: Trading queens on c3 ruins White's pawns.

notes.text: This is the most critical test in the chapter, and White keeps a lasting edge.
notes.original: This is the most critical try in the whole chapter and keeps a real, lasting edge for White. It's worth having in the course precisely because it's the position's real test, not a cosmetic improvement.

notes.text: White spends a tempo on a3 to slow your queenside play, keeping b4 in reserve.
notes.original: White spends a tempo on a3 to slow your queenside play and keep b4 in reserve.

notes.text: White keeps a lasting edge, and your doubled f-pawns remain a weakness.
notes.original: White keeps a lasting edge: his bishop on g2 hits c6 and your doubled f-pawns remain a weakness.

notes.text: White's c5 gains space, but it is slightly less accurate than the main line.
notes.original: Gaining space with c5 is slightly less accurate.

notes.text: Avoid ...Qb4+ here: White grabs the initiative and you end up in big trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 9...Qb4+? 10.Bd2 Qxb2 11.Bxf5 e6 12.Qb1 Qxd4 and Black is in big trouble.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on b4 falls into a trap: you are in big trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 9...Qb4+? 10.Bd2 Qxb2 11.Bxf5 e6 12.Qb1 Qxd4 and Black is in big trouble.

notes.text: White keeps a modest edge; your doubled f-pawns are a long-term structural concession.
notes.original: This keeps a modest, normal opening edge for White (doubled f-pawns for Black are a long-term structural concession), consistent with the rest of this variation - not a new problem, just a more accurate move order.

notes.text: Develop the knight; later it can go to b6 and hit the queen.
notes.original: Develop the knight, which can later go to b6 to hit the queen.

notes.text: White is a pawn up with a real edge, but your king hits the rook and his king is exposed.
notes.original: White wins the c6 pawn, so he keeps a real edge, but your knight and king chase the rook and White's king is not entirely safe either.

notes.text: In this line you are only a little worse.
notes.original: If White hurries with Bxg6 you are only a little worse.

notes.text: Answer Ng5 with Ngf6, the safe and most popular reply; avoid h6 because of Ne6.
notes.original: This is an interesting move, with chances to blow Black off the Board. Even Kasparov got blown with a crushing knight sacrifice. Choice guide: after 5.Ng5 the safe and most popular reply is 5...Ngf6 (about two games in three), which is safe and positional and leads to a small White edge. 5...e6 and 5...Ndf6 are balanced alternatives that score about the same. 5...h6 is the one to avoid: it scores worst for Black because of 6.Ne6!. The new sidelines below cover every sixth move White tries after 5...Ngf6: 6.Bd3 (main line), 6.Bc4, 6.N1f3 and the knight sacrifice 6.Nxf7.

notes.text: White's bishop aims at f7, so finish your development before starting pawn breaks.
notes.original: White develops the bishop at once to aim at f7 and prepares Ng5 or Qe2 so that the bishop and the e4 knight work together against your kingside. It is very common in practice (played in about 296,000 games). So f7 is the sensitive square, so finish developing before you start pawn breaks.

notes.text: Beware this trap: don't play the g8 knight to f6, because the e7 pawn is pinned and Nd6 is mate.
notes.original: White puts the queen on the e-file behind the e4 knight, setting a famous trap and preparing Nf3 and long castling. It is very common in practice (played in about 287,000 games), so you must know the trap. So one knight move is forbidden.

notes.text: White could develop with Qe2, but capturing on f6 is the most logical continuation.
notes.original: White could also develop further here, possibly with Qe2. But this capture is the most logical continuation.

notes.text: The engine likes exf6, but recapturing with the knight is more natural for a human.
notes.original: Stockfish likes exf6 here, but surely more natural for a human player is to recapture with the knight.

notes.text: The Kasparov Attack keeps the knights on; White avoids a trade because you would happily simplify.
notes.original: The Kasparov Attack keeps the knight and builds tension in the centre. White does not want to trade knights, since that would favour Black, who is happy to simplify and head for an endgame.

notes.text: The game returns to a Classical Caro-Kann structure.
notes.original: The game returns to a Classical Caro-Kann.

notes.text: White's knight eyes e6, and this line usually leads to an immediate sacrifice there.
notes.original: An interesting move which usually devolves into an immediate sacrifice on e6.

notes.text: Trade knights on e4 at once, so White's knights never get to jump to g5.
notes.original: White develops quickly and eyes the h7 square, hoping you will recapture badly on e4 so that Neg5 becomes dangerous. In practice it is very common and fairly harmless if you take on e4, because the knight trade leaves White with a mere slight initiative. The key is to trade knights at once and not allow the white knights to jump to g5.

notes.text: Recapture with a piece to keep your pawns healthy, then play Bf5, e6, Bd6 and castle short.
notes.original:
Idea: 4...Nd7 prepares ...Ngf6, so if White trades knights you recapture with a piece and keep your pawns healthy. Then ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Bd6 and castle short.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5.Nf3 Ngf6 6.Nxf6+ Nxf6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 4 to 7. ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 8 to 9.
See also: 🟢 03 covers more of the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 02.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes f7, and the queen can soon join in.
notes.original: This is one of the most common moves in the database. White develops a bishop against f7 and can soon add a second attacker in the form of the queen.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White grabs space with the c-pawn, so you must fight back toward the centre.
notes.original: White gains space by expanding in the centre with the queenside pawn, and Black has to fight back towards the centre.

notes.text: Bf4 is another option; White simply follows basic opening principles.
notes.original: Bf4 is another option; White sticks to basic opening principles.

notes.text: White has many options here, but this solid pawn move fits the Exchange Variation spirit.
notes.original: White has numerous options here, but this sturdy pawn move, in the spirit of the Exchange Variation, is as worthy as any.

notes.text: White's knight hits your bishop to trade it off, but this is not good.
notes.original: White wants to remove the light-squared bishop, but this is not good.

notes.text: White's knight hits your bishop on f5, but it fails to win it.
notes.original: White wants to eliminate the light-squared bishop at once but fails to do so.

notes.text: White develops easily and the position stays flexible for both sides.
notes.original: White develops with ease, position remains flexible for both opposing sides.

notes.text: White's f3 pawn hits your bishop, but you still get a comfortable position.
notes.original: White desperately tries to eliminate the light-squared bishop and may succeed, but Black gets a very comfortable position in return.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White takes the d-file and wants to bring the h4 knight back to f3.
notes.original: White has traded off a pair of minor pieces and now wants to use the d-file and bring the h4 knight back into play before your bishops dominate.

notes.text: Your light bishop looks toward the kingside and controls the d3 square.
notes.original: Your light bishop eyes the kingside and the d3 square.

notes.text: You traded your bishop for White's best knight, so the position is balanced and both kings are safe.
notes.original: Trading the bishop for the knight cuts out White's best minor piece for use on e5; the position is balanced and neither king is under pressure.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White's f-pawn moves give the knight a base but leave the e3 square weak.
notes.original: White wants to give the h4 knight a stable base and grab space, but f3 and f4 have left e3 and the e1-h4 diagonal weak.

notes.text: You win a pawn.
Your queen defends the d4 pawn and hits White's b2 pawn.
notes.original: Defend the pawn, hit b2 and pin White to the long diagonal.

notes.text: Your central pawns roll forward and you keep the extra pawn with a clear edge.
Opening the centre doesn't help White: your bishop lands on d4 and White's king has few defenders.
notes.original: Opening the centre does not help either: your queen lands on d4 and White's king is short of pieces nearby.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White retreats to b3, where the bishop still lines up against f7.
notes.original: Your ...b5 would hit the bishop on c4, so White retreats it to b3 where it still aims at f7.

notes.text: You gain queenside space and prepare a knight to d5 or a pawn to c5.
notes.original: Gain space on the queenside and prepare ...Nd5 or ...c5.

notes.text: Your queen lines up on the long diagonal, with White's b3 bishop in mind.
notes.original: Aim at the long diagonal and the b3 bishop.

notes.text: You trade your good bishop for the one eyeing your kingside and take the c-file; the game is balanced.
notes.original: You trade your good bishop for the one that eyes your kingside and take the c-file, so the game is balanced.

notes.text: Don't check with the queen on a5 here: after Bd2 and Nxf5 you end up losing.
notes.original: Trap: 8...Qa5+? 9.Bd2 Qb6 10.Nxf5 Ne4 11.Ne3 Qxd4 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Avoid giving your bishop for the knight; head for d5 and swap bishops instead.
notes.original: Black should avoid giving up bishop for knight and prefer the bishop-for-bishop exchange.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
This is already fine for you.
notes.original: This is already fine for Black.

notes.text: c4 is a bad move, since Black has a tactical idea.
c4 is a bad move: you take it, and the check on b4 wins a pawn.
notes.original: c4 is a bad move, since Black has a tactical idea.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's f-pawn moves weaken the e3 square and the diagonal toward h4.
notes.original: White tries to support the knight on h4 with f4, but f-pawn moves weaken the e3 square and the e1-h4 diagonal.

notes.text: Strike at the d4 pawn right away.
Your bishop hits the f3 knight, with the g2 pawn lined up behind it.
notes.original: Your bishop hits the f3 knight and g2 and you keep the better pieces.

notes.text: You have a modest edge, with the d-file and the centre in your hands.
Black is winning.
White offers a queen trade, but you are a pawn up and the d4 pawn and h4 knight are loose.
notes.original: White offers a queen trade to ease the pressure and to open the b-file against b7, but you are a pawn up and White's pieces on d4 and h4 are loose.

notes.text: Your knight on d5 blocks the d-pawn and cannot be kicked away.
notes.original: The knight on d5 blocks and dominates.

notes.text: White's pawns are broken and yours are healthy, so you are clearly better.
Here f4 cost White even more material, since the d4 pawn fell too.
notes.original: Playing f4 loses even more material because the d4 pawn also falls.

notes.text: Castling queenside is double-edged: you have kingside counterplay against White's king, and White may do the same.
notes.original: Take care when castling queenside: Black has enough counterplay on the kingside to attack the king, and White might do the same.

notes.text: White's f4 leaves the d4 pawn short of protection, and your queen already eyes it.
notes.original: White tries to keep the h4 knight defended with f4, but this leaves the d4 pawn short of protection.

notes.text: Your queen takes the d4 pawn with check, since the king on g1 sits on that diagonal.
notes.original: The queen takes with check because the d4 pawn falls and the g1 king is on the diagonal.

notes.text: Your rook goes after the c2 pawn.
notes.original: The rook goes after the c2 pawn.

notes.text: You stay a clean pawn up with active rooks, and your king is safe.
notes.original: You stay a clean pawn up with active rooks, and your own king is not under any threat after trades.

notes.text: Even without f4 you stay better, since your central pawns advance.
notes.original: Not playing f4 still leaves you better since your central pawns advance.

notes.text: Playing e6 is the better option: it guards against attacks on both b7 and f7.
notes.original: ...e6 is the better option, preventing the attack on both b7 and f7.

notes.text: This line is dangerous because White can play Qb3, hitting b7 and f7.
notes.original: This variation is dangerous because White can play Qb3, hitting b7 and f7.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White cannot take the pawn because a tactic would be unleashed.
Black is winning.
White must deal with the attack on h4 first, and two pawns do not make up for the lost knight.
notes.original: White has to deal with the attack on h4 first, and the two pawns on a7 and b7 do not make up for the lost knight.

notes.text: Retreat with tempo and keep the extra piece.
Your bishop offers a trade that removes White's best piece.
notes.original: The bishop trade removes White's best piece.

notes.text: White's queen is out of play on a6, and you are clearly better.
notes.original: The queen is out of play on a6 and you are clearly better.

notes.text: Taking more material only exposes the king, and you win easily.
notes.original: Grabbing more material only exposes the king and you win easily.

notes.text: Your queenside pawn advance gives you enough counterplay to play for a win.
notes.original: Black has enough counterplay on the queenside to play for a win.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White wants the g-file open against g7, using the queen on e4 and bishop on g5 while your king is…
notes.original: White wants to open the g-file against g7: with Qe4 and Bg5 the g7 pawn comes under fire while your king is still uncastled.

notes.text: Your pawn shuts the g-file before White's queen and bishop arrive on e4 and g5.
notes.original: Shut the g-file before Qe4 and Bg5 arrive.

notes.text: You grab the h2 pawn, and your bishop now attacks the rook on g1.
notes.original: Black snatches the pawn and now the g1 rook is attacked.

notes.text: White counterpunches: the bishop on f6 attacks your rook on h8.
notes.original: White's counterpunch: the bishop hits the h8 rook.

notes.text: Rooks are swapped and you have an extra pawn, but both kings are loose, so you are only slightly better.
notes.original: Rooks have been swapped and you have an extra pawn, but both kings are loose, so the line stays only slightly better for you.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
This is the critical test: White grabs a pawn and heads for a6 with tempo against your development.
notes.original: This is the critical test of your setup: White grabs a pawn and heads for a6 with tempo against your development.

notes.text: Your bishop returns to the big diagonal, and White's queen is far from the kingside.
notes.original: Your bishop returns to the big diagonal and White's queen is far from the kingside.

notes.text: You lead in development with a safe king; the pawn grab is roughly level, so play for activity.
notes.original: You have a lead in development and a safe king, and the grab is roughly level, so play for activity and not for a quick refutation.

notes.text: Retreating instead leaves you pleasantly placed.
As soon as White's knight lands on f3, pin it to the queen.
notes.original: As soon as the knight lands on f3, pin it.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight to the queen; next come e6, a bishop move, Qc7 and castling.
notes.original: Now your light-squared bishop leaves the c8-h3 diagonal to pin the f3 knight before you play ...e6. Your plan is ...e6, ...Be7 or ...Bd6, ...Qc7 and short castling, with the break ...c5 as the long-term idea. If White plays h3 at once, drop back to h5 and keep the pin; trade on f3 only when it helps your structure.

notes.text: White's h3 just drops a pawn: take on f3, then grab d4 with your queen.
notes.original: h3 is not possible unless white wants to lose a pawn.

notes.text: White's c3 pawn defends d4, which your queen was attacking.
notes.original: White has to defend the pawn or otherwise gain a disadvantageous position.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White gets the king safe and plans Rd1 to harass your queen, which nothing hits yet.
notes.original: White gets the king safe and plans Rd1 to harass the queen. Your queen is far from home but nothing hits it yet.

notes.text: Centralise your queen so that a bishop move to e3 can't hit it.
notes.original: Centralise and avoid being hit by Be3.

notes.text: Your king goes long and your queen covers squares on the d-file.
notes.original: Your king goes long and the queen covers d-file squares.

notes.text: You are a pawn up with a safe king, so avoid casual queen raids and develop.
notes.original: You are a pawn up with a safe king, so avoid casual queen raids and play for development.

notes.text: Taking the knight stops White from playing Ne5, an idea even Petrosian liked.
notes.original: Even Tigran Petrosian liked this idea, since it prevents White from playing Ne5.

notes.text: Finish development, castle short and break with c5; keep your bishop safe on h5 or g6.
notes.original: Trade the e4 knight, pin on f3 and develop calmly; White has a small lead in space but no real attack. You should aim to castle and play ...c5 when ready. This is a semi-open position with White holding a small space edge in the centre. White has pawns on c3 and d4, you have c6 and e6, and you have pinned the f3 knight and just played ...Bh5. Your plan: complete development with ...Be7 or ...Bd6, castle short, then break with ...c5 when ready. White wants to castle and use Bd2 and Qe2 to build a kingside attack, so keep your bishop safe on h5 or g6. The risk is trading too early on f3 and losing time; if White plays g4, retreat the bishop to g6 and keep calm.

notes.text: In this structure your bishop is worth more than White's knight, so you kept it instead of taking on f3.
notes.original: Notice that Black does not take on f3 with the bishop. In this structure the bishop is worth more than White's knight, so Black keeps it.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's queen and bishop both attack your f6 knight, and only your g7 pawn guards it.
notes.original: White piles up on the pinned f6 knight: Qf3, Bg5 and Ne5 all target it.

notes.text: Moving your knight to h7 gets it out of the pin on f6.
notes.original: Unpin by moving the knight.

notes.text: Take White's strong knight on e5 with your bishop before it does damage.
notes.original: Trade off the strong knight before it does damage.

notes.text: Your rook challenges the centre, and your doubled g-pawns are solid, so White's small edge is not dangerous.
notes.original: Your rook challenges the centre and your doubled g-pawns are solid, so White's small edge is not dangerous.

notes.text: Your queen faces White's queen, aiming for quick simplification.
notes.original: Aiming for quick simplification.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White gains space and prepares d5; your task is to avoid a long-term passive position.
notes.original: White gains space and prepares d5 with the bishop pair behind. Your task is to avoid a long-term passive position.

notes.text: Your bishop steps out of d5's way, and you prepare to push your g-pawn.
notes.original: Get the bishop out of the way of d5 and prepare ...g5.

notes.text: Your g-pawn gains kingside space and gives White's f3 bishop something to worry about.
notes.original: You gain space on the kingside and give the f3 bishop an opponent to worry about.

notes.text: White's bishops give a slight edge, but you have counterplay and no real weakness.
notes.original: White has a slight edge thanks to the bishops, but you have counterplay and no real weakness.

notes.text: White declines to fight your f5 bishop and keeps the central tension.
notes.original: White declines to fight the bishop on f5 and keeps the tension in the centre. He sticks to the d4 plan.

notes.text: White's pawn attacks your bishop; retake with the bishop, since retaking the other way would hang your queen.
notes.original: ...c5 is not possible here because Bxc5 is a problem, and Black cannot retake with the pawn since the queen would hang.

notes.text: Rd1 is another option for White here.
notes.original: Another option for White.

notes.text: White missed that taking back with the d-pawn hangs his queen to yours.
notes.original: Has White missed this tactic? Yes.

notes.text: Retreat your bishop to b6.
notes.original: Retreat the bishop.

notes.text: Your queen offers White a queen trade.
notes.original: Offer a queen trade.

notes.text: You are clearly better: your extra pawn is safe.
notes.original: Black is clearly better: the extra pawn is safe.

notes.text: White's pawn push hung his queen, and you win it for just a bishop.
notes.original: White's pawn push only hung his queen: Black wins the queen for a bishop.

notes.text: You are bringing enough reinforcements to attack White's central pawns.
notes.original: Black is bringing enough reinforcements to attack White's central pawns.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your rook joins in, bringing enough reinforcements to attack White's central pawns.
notes.original: Black is bringing enough reinforcements to attack White's central pawns.

notes.text: White stacks rooks on the d-file to keep it stable and use it.
notes.original: White chooses to stack up rooks and to keep the d file stabilise for White to take advantage of.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn keeps the position closed.
notes.original: Keeping the position closed.

notes.text: You have enough pieces to guard the e4 pawn, and may later give it up for activity.
notes.original: Black has enough reinforcement to guard the e pawn. Black is looking forward to sacrifice that pawn in exchange for something to target on.

notes.text: Your e4 pawn kicked the rook off d3, and e3 is its only comfortable retreat.
notes.original: The rook has to leave d3 because your e4 pawn attacks it, and Re3 is the only comfortable retreat.

notes.text: Support the e4 pawn with f5 so it becomes a wedge, not just a pawn to sacrifice.
notes.original: Back up the e4 pawn so it becomes a wedge instead of a pawn that can only be sacrificed.

notes.text: Swing your queen to the kingside, where White's pieces are short of space.
notes.original: The queen heads to the kingside where White's pieces are short of space.

notes.text: White had to open the position with f3, so you cash in the wedge pawn and keep the more active…
notes.original: White has to open the position with f3, but you cash in the wedge pawn and keep the more active pieces.

notes.text: After White's rook walked into Bxg3 and lost the exchange, your pawn drives forward to e3.
notes.original: Walking into ...Bxg3 costs the exchange and your pawn then drives forward with e3.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's centralised knight offers a trade on d7 and eyes f7; the position is balanced, so don't give it a…
notes.original: White centralises the knight: it offers a trade on d7 and, together with Qf3, aims at f7 and b7. The position is balanced, so just avoid giving the knight a free hand.

notes.text: Your knight dodges the trade and unmasks your d8 rook against White's rook on d4.
notes.original: Your knight dodges the trade and also unmasks the d8 rook against White's d4 rook.

notes.text: Trade off White's active rook before it can double on the d-file.
notes.original: Trade the active rook before White can double on the d-file.

notes.text: Kick the knight away with f6; if White doesn't take on d8, you hold f7 and b7.
notes.original: Kick the knight; if White doesn't take on d8 you hold f7 and b7.

notes.text: Step your queen aside; White's knight is offside and your c5 knight is sturdy, so you equalise comfortably.
notes.original: Ng6 attacks your queen, so step aside. The knight is offside there and your c5 knight is a sturdy defender, so you have no weaknesses and equalise comfortably.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's bishop blocks the d-file, eyes a7 and supports the e5 pawn.
notes.original: White centralises the bishop to block your d-file rook and keep an eye on a7; it is also the natural way to give the e5 pawn some support.

notes.text: Taking the bishop looks like it wins material, but White has a reply that evens things up.
notes.original: You take the bishop with the rook, which looks like winning material.

notes.text: Your bishop forks the rooks on d4 and a1, so material comes back even.
notes.original: The point of White's setup: this fork hits the d4 rook and the a1 rook, so material comes back even.

notes.text: Everything has traded evenly; you contest the d-file and the position is level.
notes.original: Everything has been traded evenly. You contest the d-file and the e5 pawn is the only slightly loose point, so the position is level.

notes.text: White expands on the queenside with a4, so you need a5 to counter it.
notes.original: With a4 White expands on the queenside and would gain counterplay there, so ...a5 is needed to counter it.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Trading your bishop for the knight is roughly fine for you.
notes.original: The exchange of knight for bishop is roughly alright, white gets four pawns vs three on the kingside.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's pawn gains space and chases your d6 bishop; your doubled f-pawns guard e4, so regroup calmly.
notes.original: White uses the bishop pair to gain space and chase your d6 bishop; Ra3-b3 will then target b7. Your doubled f-pawns guard e4 but give you a tight structure, so you need to regroup calmly.

notes.text: Your rook guards the b7 pawn and covers the seventh rank.
notes.original: The rook defends b7 and the seventh rank.

notes.text: After the bishop-for-knight trade your doubled pawns stop mattering; White keeps a small edge but has no concrete threat.
notes.original: After the trade of a bishop for a knight the doubled pawns stop mattering. White keeps a small edge, but there is no concrete threat.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White has no weaknesses to hit, so free your game with ...c5 before White gets a bind.
notes.original: White gives the king air and waits; Black has no weaknesses, so your task is to free your game with ...c5 before White gets a bind.

notes.text: This is the freeing break, and it opens the c-file for your queen.
notes.original: The freeing break, which also opens the c-file for your queen.

notes.text: Offer a bishop trade for White's dark-squared bishop, the best defender of the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Offer to trade your bishop for White's dark-squared bishop, which is the best defender of the d4 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight takes back on c5 next, and with your active queen the game is level.
notes.original: The knight takes back on c5 next and your queen is active, so the game is level.

notes.text: You are already doing fine here.
notes.original: Black is already doing fine.

notes.text: Black is winning.
White's rook hits your queen, so you have to trade queens.
notes.original: White refuses to trade queens because of the fork threat and instead takes the d-pawn. Black has to exchange queens here.

notes.text: Taking your queen would allow a fork: your knight checks the king and hits the queen.
notes.original: The queen capture would allow a fork.

notes.text: White's king step is forced because your knight on e2 attacks the queen.
notes.original: The king step is forced.

notes.text: Black is winning.
You are up material and your knight on d4 is a monster.
notes.original: You are a clean pawn up and the knight on d4 is a monster. White's knight on d6 looks scary but your ...b6 hits it.

notes.text: White controls the d-file, but you are a pawn up and a draw is acceptable.
notes.original: White controls the d-file, but Black is a pawn up and the position is manageable; a draw would be an acceptable result.

notes.text: A solid reply: you keep the extra pawn, though White's active d-file rooks make it about equal.
notes.original: A solid reply: you keep the extra pawn and fix the queenside, although White has enough play to make it about equal. White's d-file rooks are active, so a draw is a fine result.

notes.text: White's rook invades, but you hold.
notes.original: White invades with the rook but you hold.

notes.text: You are a pawn up; your d-file rooks and d4 knight hold everything.
notes.original: Black has won queen for queen and a pawn; White's c5 and Nc4 push is only compensation. Your rooks on the d-file and the knight on d4 hold everything.

notes.text: Your light bishop is blocked now, but ...b6 and ...Bb7 can make it a good bishop.
notes.original: Although the bishop is blocked by the e6-pawn, it can be fianchettoed via the queenside and become a good bishop. On b7 in the Karpov Variation it eyes g2 and the Nf3 knight, unlike in the Queen's Indian, where it sees less counterplay; here it gets real play along the b7-h1 diagonal, since White's kingside is exposed in the endgame.

notes.text: Against Ng3, develop with e6 and Be7, castle, then play b6, Bb7 and break with c5.
notes.original:
Idea: 4...Nd7 and ...Ngf6, as in 🔵 10. When White keeps the knights on with Ng3, develop with ...e6, ...Be7 and ...O-O, then ...b6 and ...Bb7, and break with ...c5.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5.d4 Ngf6 6.Ng3 e6
Watch out: ...Qxd2+? loses material on move 4.
Next: 🔵 17 continues the Two Knights Attack.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Bc4 is a famous move in the Karpov Variation; White just follows sound opening principles.
notes.original: Bc4 is quite a famous move in the Karpov variation of the Caro Kann Defence. White is sticking to his principled opening fundamental.

notes.text: h4 is inaccurate; strike in the centre and storm the queenside before White's attack gets going.
notes.original: h4 is a rather inaccurate move: White wants kingside space and will castle queenside while attacking on the kingside. Black should not let that develop, and instead strike in the centre and launch a queenside pawn storm before White's attack gets going.

notes.text: White gains space, but you can strike back in the centre at once with c5.
notes.original: 7.c4 gains space, but Black can fight back in the centre straight away.

notes.text: Be7 is preferable, because otherwise the Bg5 pin would cause you problems.
notes.original: ...Be7 is preferable, as the Bg5 pin would cause Black problems.

notes.text: This bishop pressures your knight but achieves little; if it takes on f6, you get the bishop pair.
notes.original: White pins the knight with no real purpose beyond giving up the dark-squared bishop. The move is a little inaccurate: it poses no challenges, White will have to retreat later and lose a tempo, and to keep the extra tempo must take on f6, which hands Black the bishop pair.

notes.text: White simply defends d4; you castle, fianchetto your bishop and play c5, like Owen's Defence.
notes.original: A sensible, safe move: White defends the d4-pawn at once. For Black the aim is to castle kingside safely and fianchetto the bishop on b7, then play ...c5, similar to Owen's Defence but without White's space advantage.

notes.text: The f3 knight protects White's centre, so trading it off removes a key defender.
notes.original: The knight on f3 protects White's centre. Trading it off removes a key defender.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White tucks the king away and cramps you with the h5 pawn; Bf5 will hit your d7 knight.
notes.original: White steps the king off the back rank before the g-file opens and uses the h5 pawn to cramp your pieces. Bf5 will hit the d7 knight.

notes.text: Your knight guards h7 and heads for e6.
notes.original: The knight steps back to guard h7 and heads for e6.

notes.text: You trade off the bishop that was cramping you.
notes.original: You trade off the bishop that cramps you.

notes.text: This break hits the f3 pawn and the rook on d3, and White's slight edge is not dangerous.
notes.original: This break strikes at f3 and the rook on d3, and your rooks stay active, so White's slight edge from the doubled f-pawns is not dangerous.

notes.text: White's queen eyes g7 and tries to force kingside concessions, instead of the slower b4 plan.
notes.original: Instead of the slower queenside expansion with b4 in the main line, White's strongest try is the direct Qg4, eyeing g7 and inducing weakening kingside concessions from Black.

notes.text: Keep this idea in mind; it will also help in tournament games.
White's bishop lines up on e6 so a sacrifice there becomes possible.
notes.original: The bishop lines up on d5 and e6 so that a sacrifice on e6 becomes possible.

notes.text: White sacrifices a knight on e6 to rip open the lines to your king.
notes.original: A thematic sacrifice that rips open the lines to your king.

notes.text: White has won a knight for pawns, but your knight hits the queen with tempo; roughly balanced.
notes.original: White has won a knight for pawns for the moment, but your knight hits the queen with tempo. The line is sharp but roughly balanced.

notes.text: White keeps a lasting initiative here; this is the most testing try, so know it.
notes.original: This keeps a lasting initiative for White - the most testing try in the Karpov Variation covered here, and worth knowing rather than assuming the quieter b4 will be played.

notes.text: The bishop attacks your rook; answer it before White plays h5 to open the h-file.
notes.original: The bishop controls the g7 diagonal and attacks your rook, so you must answer it before White follows up with h5 to open the h-file.

notes.text: Your central counter gives your knight the f6 square.
notes.original: Your central counter; the pawn closes the e6 square and gives your knight f6.

notes.text: Your knight on f6 blocks the long diagonal.
notes.original: Blocks the long diagonal.

notes.text: White gave up a bishop for two pawns and keeps a lasting initiative; defend with care.
notes.original: White gave up a bishop for two pawns and has a lasting initiative; defend with care.

notes.text: The quieter h5 lets you trade queens and relax.
White's kingside attack is short-lived: you defend with Re8 and Nf8, and h7 has three protectors.
notes.original: White has build a potential kingside attack but would be short-lived since Black has that defensive idea of Re8 followed by Nf8. The h pawn is fully protected by three pieces.

notes.text: White rushes a kingside attack, which is a poor plan.
notes.original: White rushes the kingside attack, which is a poor plan.

notes.text: Your light bishop is free; play on the queenside, or put a rook on the d-file, and welcome an endgame.
notes.original: The light-squared bishop is finally free. Black aims for queenside play while keeping the king safe; there are enough pieces to build a kingside fortress with ...Nd7-f8 if White attacks quickly, and putting a rook on the d-file is another plan. Black is happy to head for an endgame.

notes.text: White heads for a bishop trade.
notes.original: White heads for a bishop trade so your knight on f8 can no longer rely on its pair.

notes.text: White's knight on b5 forks your queen and attacks the a7 pawn.
notes.original: The knight forks your queen and attacks a7.

notes.text: You traded the light-squared bishops and took the c-file, so the position is level.
notes.original: You trade the light-squared bishops and occupy the c-file, so the position is level.

notes.text: Your light bishop is finally free; play on the queenside, keep your king safe, and happily head for an endgame.
notes.original: The light-squared bishop is finally free. Black aims for queenside play while keeping the king safe; there are enough pieces to build a kingside fortress with ...Nd7-f8 if White attacks quickly, and putting a rook on the d-file is another plan. Black is happy to head for an endgame.

notes.text: White keeps the pieces coordinated and the d-pawn under control.
Your bishop sees the long diagonal now, and you have a half-open c-file.
notes.original: You open the c-file and the diagonal for your bishop.

notes.text: Offer the bishop trade: your bishop hits the f4 bishop, White's main attacker on your kingside.
notes.original: Offer the bishop trade, since the f4 bishop is the main attacker on your kingside.

notes.text: Everything is traded evenly and your king is safe, so the game is equal.
notes.original: Everything is traded off evenly and your king is safe, so the game is equal.

notes.text: Opening lines wrecked White's kingside pawns, so you stay slightly better.
notes.original: Opening lines this way wrecks White's kingside pawns and you stay slightly better.

notes.text: Keep your rooks on open files or in the centre; if the position opens, they dominate the d- and e-files.
notes.original: In the Karpov Variation, keep the rooks on open files or in the centre: if the position opens up, Black gains the advantage because the rooks dominate the open d- and e-files.

notes.text: Your light bishop is free; play on the queenside, keep your king safe, and happily head for an endgame.
notes.original: The light-squared bishop is finally free. Black aims for queenside play while keeping the king safe; there are enough pieces to build a kingside fortress with ...Nd7-f8 if White attacks quickly, and putting a rook on the d-file is another plan. Black is happy to head for an endgame.

notes.text: White's rook and bishop both press your d5 knight, the piece shielding your centre and king.
notes.original: The rook swings to d4 where the knight on f3 and the bishop on c4 back it up; all three aim at your d5 knight, the piece that shields your centre and king.

notes.text: Your a-pawn takes b5 away and prepares b5 to kick the bishop.
notes.original: Take b5 away and prepare ...b5 to kick the bishop.

notes.text: Put your rook on the d-file so White's rook on d4 cannot dominate it.
notes.original: Put your rook on the d-file so Rd4 cannot dominate it.

notes.text: Your h-pawn now covers g5, so White's knight cannot land there.
notes.original: Stops Ng5 before it lands.

notes.text: White's knight eyes g7 and f6, but your pieces guard the king, so the initiative is mild.
notes.original: Nh5 hits g7 and f6 but your pieces guard the king, so White keeps only a mild initiative.

notes.text: White is building a kingside attack; disturb it and the attack stays at bay.
notes.original: White is building up for a kingside attack, and Black should not let White develop easily. Disturbing White's kingside operation is enough to keep the attack at bay.

notes.text: White has the bishop pair but a shaky kingside; focus on development instead of grabbing pawns.
notes.original: White has the bishop pair, but the kingside pawn chain has weaknesses and White is far from reaching his goals. Black has no time to grab pawns and must focus on development, or else suffer from White's piece activity.

notes.text: With b6 and Bb7 coming, you are roughly fine.
notes.original: With ...b6 and ...Bb7 coming, Black is roughly fine.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes b7 and h7, and the rook on d1 now challenges your rook on the d-file.
notes.original: White's bishop on e4 is strong and aims at b7 and h7, so White contests the d-file.

notes.text: Your bishop leaves c8 so it can go to c6 and challenge White's strong bishop.
notes.original: Step the bishop off c8 so it can challenge the Be4 from c6.

notes.text: Your bishop finds a safe post and you have no weaknesses, so the game is level.
White has an isolated pawn on d4, which is a long-term weakness.
notes.original: White has an isolated pawn;

notes.text: Playing the knight first keeps it flexible before White commits the queen; it is very slightly more accurate.
notes.original: A minor move-order point: Nc3 first (rather than Qc2) is very slightly more accurate, keeping the knight flexible before committing the queen.

notes.text: White's kingside build-up has failed; White's d-pawn is isolated and your position is rock solid.
notes.original: White's reinforcement for a kingside attack has failed. Black now has the advantage: White has an isolated d-pawn, and Black's position is rock solid.

notes.text: White has to take the knight, since otherwise ...Nxc3 would damage the pawn structure.
Your knight on d5 threatens to take on c3 and wreck White's pawns, so White must capture it.
notes.original: White has to take the knight, since otherwise ...Nxc3 would damage the pawn structure.

notes.text: Your check drives the king off the diagonal from e1 to h4.
notes.original: This check knocks the king off the e1-h4 diagonal.

notes.text: You put pressure on White's isolated d4 pawn.
notes.original: You put pressure on the isolated d4 pawn.

notes.text: Your queen and rook dominate, the h-file rook has no targets, so White's attack failed and you are better.
notes.original: Your queen and rook dominate and the h-file rook has no targets, so White's attack failed and you are better.

notes.text: Avoiding the trade keeps your pieces dominating.
notes.original: Avoiding the trade leaves your pieces dominating.

notes.text: Either move order is equal; this one changes nothing practical.
notes.original: Equal either way; included for completeness rather than because it changes anything practical.

notes.text: White wants the c-file, then the knight to g5 aiming at h7, but you have an easy answer.
notes.original: White wants to take the c-file and then bring Ng5 and the h-pawn to bear on h7, but you have an easy answer.

notes.text: Your knight covers h7 against White's knight on g5.
notes.original: Your knight covers h7 and challenges the bishop. As the note above says, stay clear of the h4 pawn.

notes.text: The position is equal.
notes.original: Equal.

notes.text: White's h-pawn thrust gains nothing.
notes.original: White's pawn thrust gains nothing

notes.text: Your bishop on b7 gives you a good position.
notes.original: Black stands well.

notes.text: The pawn hits your queen and starts queenside expansion, while White's knight eyes e6 and b5.
notes.original: The pawn hits your queen with tempo and starts queenside expansion, while the Nd4 outpost eyes e6 and b5.

notes.text: Your queen is safe on e7 and keeps the e6 pawn protected.
notes.original: A safe square that keeps e6 protected.

notes.text: Your a-pawn hits the b4 pawn, so White cannot build a queenside clamp.
notes.original: Undermine b4 so White cannot build a queenside clamp.

notes.text: Your knight lands on a strong central post and eyes the c4 pawn.
notes.original: Your knight lands on a strong central post and eyes c4.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen and the f2 and h2 pawns; White's edge is tiny.
notes.original: You hit the queen and the f2 and h2 squares again; White's edge is tiny and you are well coordinated.

notes.text: White gains space, but the d-pawn may become isolated; fight the space advantage and create complications.
notes.original: White gains space, which is not necessarily bad but has drawbacks: the d-pawn may become isolated, which is a liability, and Black is encouraged to attack the space advantage. Black's aim is to fight against it and create complications for both sides.

notes.text: Castling queenside can be risky, but it is fine when White has no major queenside attack.
notes.original: Beware of castling queenside, sometimes it is alright to castle queenside if White does not have any major attack on the queenside.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's rook joins the e-file to prepare c4 and a knight jump to e4.
notes.original: White puts a rook on the e-file to prepare c4 and Ne4.

notes.text: Your queen offers a trade of queens so you can untangle.
notes.original: Offer a queen trade so you can untangle.

notes.text: White's c4 kicked your knight, but you get a solid setup.
notes.original: White's c4 kicks the knight but you gain a solid setup.

notes.text: You expand on the kingside, and the position stays balanced.
White recaptures with the g-pawn, since taking with the bishop would lose the c4 pawn.
notes.original: White has no other choice other than to take back with the g pawn since other options would not be necessary since the pawn will hang.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White's queen hits your c4 knight to regain the pawn, but the knight can retreat safely.
notes.original: White hits the c4 knight to regain the pawn, but your knight has a safe retreat.

notes.text: Fianchetto your bishop on g7 to guard the long diagonal.
notes.original: Fianchetto the bishop to guard the long diagonal.

notes.text: You are a clean pawn up and White has little to show for it.
White's king is dragged out and White falls further behind.
White is slightly better.
White has the bishop pair; Be3 and Qd2 prepare Qa5 against your queenside.
notes.original: White has the bishop pair and the g-file; Be3 and Qd2 prepare Qa5 against your queenside.

notes.text: Strike at the centre before White consolidates; your pawn hits d4.
notes.original: Strike at the centre before White consolidates.

notes.text: You reach an endgame with sound pawns, and White keeps only a tiny edge.
notes.original: You reach an endgame with sound pawns and White keeps only a tiny edge.

notes.text: A calm reply: play Bd6 and h6 after White's moves and you reach the main line.
notes.original: The calm reply: after Bd3 Bd6 and Qe2 h6 the game transposes to the main line of the chapter.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the knight, and White has no good retreat except Nh3.
notes.original: The ambitious reply - kick the knight at once. White has no good retreat: 7.Bd3? hxg5 wins a piece and 7.Nxf7 Kxf7 just gives the knight away. The best White can do is 7.Nh3, after which Black takes space on the kingside. This is a sharp but balanced choice that scores better for Black in practice than the main-line ...e6.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's rook takes the e-file and backs up a knight jump from f3 to e5.
notes.original: White supports the Ne5 jump and the e-file.

notes.text: This freeing break hits the d4 pawn and opens up your pieces.
notes.original: Freeing break that opens the bishop.

notes.text: Your bishop offers a trade of White's e5 knight's neighbour, easing the pressure on that knight.
notes.original: You offer the bishop trade to kill the pressure on the e5 knight.

notes.text: Next you develop the bishop to b7; White's edge is tiny and there are no concrete threats.
notes.original: You then develop the Bb7; White's edge is tiny with no concrete threats.

notes.text: Take the knight, and after White retakes on e4, return with ...Nf6 to kick the bishop.
notes.original: Take the knight, and after Bxe4 return with ...Nf6, kicking the bishop. This removes the dangerous white knight and keeps your position sound.

notes.text: This runs into White's knight jump to g5, hitting h7 and e6, and White keeps the initiative.
notes.original: This looks natural but runs into 7.Neg5, with threats on h7 and on e6, and White keeps a clear initiative.

notes.text: Better was to trade knights first, then win a tempo on the bishop with your knight.
notes.original: It was better here to exchange the knights and then win a tempo on the bishop with Nf6.

notes.text: White's main move is Bd3, but Bc4, N1f3 and the Nxf7 sacrifice are also common.
notes.original: What White plays next: 6.Bd3 is the main move and the line given above. 6.Bc4 and 6.N1f3 are the two other common moves, and 6.Nxf7!? is the speculative knight sacrifice that is seen a lot in online play. Each is covered below, with the one reply Black should remember.

notes.text: White answers with the knight leap to e6; move your queen and White trades for your bishop.
notes.original: This move seems logical, as Nxf7 doesn't work. However, White can get a slight edge with Ne6! and can win quickly if Black makes a blunder. A grandmaster lost to this trap. The e8-h5 diagonal is slightly weakened, and so is f7. The main line is Ne6! Qb6 (Wisely avoiding fxe6?? Qh5+ g6 Qxg6#) Nxf8 Nxf8 with two Bishops and a slight edge.

notes.text: Never take that knight: the queen check on h5 leads to mate on g6.
notes.original: This move seems logical, as Nxf7 doesn't work. However, White can get a slight edge with Ne6! and can win quickly if Black makes a blunder. A grandmaster lost to this trap. The e8-h5 diagonal is slightly weakened, and so is f7. The main line is Ne6! Qb6 (Wisely avoiding fxe6?? Qh5+ g6 Qxg6#) Nxf8 Nxf8 with two Bishops and a slight edge.

notes.text: White sacrifices a knight to drag your king out; just take it with the king.
notes.original: The knight sacrifice. White gives up a whole piece to drag the king into the open. In online games it scores a little over half, because Black has to find a few accurate moves, but it is unsound. Choice guide: this is White's gamble, not yours - just take the knight and then follow the rules in the notes below.

notes.text: Bishop and knight both hit f7, so ...h6 would lose to mate; reply with ...e6.
notes.original: The bishop eyes f7 at once. It is the second most common move after 6.Bd3. The structure is normal and White keeps a small plus, but there is one big trap: ...h6? loses on the spot to Bxf7#. Choice guide: the safe and standard reply is 6...e6; 6...Nd5 is a good, slightly sharper alternative.

notes.text: White's other knight now supports the g5 knight, and Bd3 and Qe2 usually follow.
notes.original: A flexible developing move: the other knight comes out so that the g5-knight is supported. White usually follows with Bd3 and Qe2. Choice guide: 6...e6 is the safe and positional reply and transposes to the main line; 6...h6 is the more ambitious reply that actually scores slightly better for Black and is the most accurate move.

notes.text: Careful: this scores worst, because White's knight leaps to e6 and can't be taken profitably.
notes.original: Watch out: this is the move that scores worst for Black here (White wins two-thirds of the games). The point is 7.Ne6! and the knight cannot be taken profitably.

notes.text: White develops the queen first; after Bd6 the game usually transposes to the main line.
notes.original: A second main move: White develops the queen first and keeps the choice of knight development for later. After ...Bd6 N1f3 h6 Ne4 Nxe4 Qxe4 Qc7 the position transposes to the main line. White plays 7.Qe2 about once in five games here.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
This knight sacrifice is unsound; simply take it back with your f-pawn.
notes.original: The sacrificial try: the knight takes on e6, offering a piece. Black recaptures - a piece for two pawns is not enough. Played in about one game in five here and it scores a little over half for White in practice, but it is not sound. Choice guide: the safe and correct answer is 9...fxe6.

notes.text: This knight sacrifice fails: just take it with your king and carry on developing.
notes.original: Another sacrifice that does not work. Black takes the knight and then develops.

notes.text: The knight retreats to the rim, White loses the edge, and you castle or play Qc7.
notes.original: The knight retreats to the rim and White loses the edge. Black castles or plays ...Qc7 and is slightly better.

notes.text: Your e5 break hits the d4 pawn and loosens White's grip on the centre.
notes.original: The problem with the Ng5 knight manoeuvre, black if black knows what he is doing black tendencies might even get an edge since this would allow black to play for this e5! Breakthrough. Effectively dislodging white's grasp on the center.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your bishop swings to h3, covering g2 and f1 beside White's king.
notes.original: The bishop hits the rook on f1.

notes.text: The position is level, so stay alert to White's other moves.
notes.original: Level. Take care with White's other moves: your Be5 and queen aim at h2.

notes.text: The bishop sacrifice on h2 dragged White's king out, and your active rook on e4 gives you the advantage.
notes.original: The point: Bxh2+ drags the king out and the pin on the e-file gives you the advantage.

notes.text: Checking first is a mistake: after c3 and fxe6, Bg6 check wins your b4 bishop.
notes.original: Watch out: checking first is a mistake. After c3 fxe6 Bg6+ Black loses the bishop on b4 and the king is exposed.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White is winning.
Black is clearly better.
White's pawn attacks your queen, and White keeps a clear edge.
notes.original: The queen is attacked and White keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: Taking with the king is the only move; any other reply lets White's knight take your queen.
notes.original: The only move - Black takes the knight with the king. Any other reply (for example ...e6 or ...h6) allows Nxd8 and White wins the queen. After the king capture White has two serious tries: 7.Nf3 (developing first) and 7.Bc4+ (check at once).

notes.text: Not recapturing is a blunder: the knight on f7 simply takes your queen.
notes.original: Watch out: not recapturing is a blunder because the knight on f7 takes the queen.

notes.text: White develops the knight and keeps Bc4+ in reserve, but your exposed king has time to consolidate.
notes.original: The most common move: bring the knight out and keep the Bc4+ idea in reserve. Black's king is exposed, but every White piece is still on its starting square, so Black has time to consolidate.

notes.text: White checks at once; you have three answers: ...e6 is safest, ...Nd5 is most active, ...Ke8 scores worse.
notes.original: The immediate check. Black has three sensible answers: ...e6 (safest), ...Nd5 (most active) and ...Ke8 (playable but scores worse in practice).

notes.text: Your e6 pawn shuts the bishop's diagonal for good, and your bishop can later come out to d6.
notes.original: The simplest setup: the e6 pawn shuts the c4-g8 diagonal for good, so Bc4 is no longer check, and the bishop can later come out to d6.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your e6 pawn; ...Nd5, ...h6 or ...Nb6 all leave you clearly better.
notes.original: White attacks the e6 pawn and aims at the king. Black has three equally good replies: ...Nd5, ...h6 and ...Nb6, all clearly better for Black. The one move to avoid is 8...Qa5+?!, which lets White trade queens and lose the least.

notes.text: Your knight takes the sting out of Bb3; with ...Bd6 and ...h6 your king is safe.
notes.original: Black centralises the knight and takes the sting out of Bb3. After ...Bd6 and ...h6 the king is safe on f7 and Black keeps the extra piece.

notes.text: Your knight kicks the bishop right away; after Bb3 and ...Bd6, watch for the Ng5+ check.
notes.original: Kick the bishop right away. After Bb3 Bd6 Black should watch the Ng5+ check but remains clearly better.

notes.text: A useful waiting move: your pawn stops Ng5+ for good and gives your king the h7 square.
notes.original: A useful waiting move that stops Ng5+ forever and gives the king the h7 square.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
The solid reply: your pawn blocks the check, and you plan ...Nb6, ...Be7 and ...Kg8.
notes.original: The solid reply, and the one most players choose. The pawn blocks the check and Black plans ...Nb6, ...Be7 and ...Kg8.

notes.text: Your knight blocks the check and keeps your pawns intact; it is not best, but it scores best.
notes.original: The most active reply, blocking with the knight and keeping the pawn structure intact. It is not the best move but it scores best for Black in practice.

notes.text: Also good, but White scores better in practice with your king back in the centre; know the line first.
notes.original: Also good objectively, but in practice White scores better here because the king is back in the centre and Black has to find ...Nb6 and ...c5 to free the position. Choose this only if you know the line.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
White is winning.
Your pawn shuts the bishop's diagonal to f7 and prepares ...Nb6 to kick the bishop.
notes.original: The reply played in nearly every game - the pawn guards f7 and prepares ...Nb6 to kick the bishop.

notes.text: Your e-pawn blocks the bishop's diagonal to f7 and prepares Be7.
notes.original: This blocks the bishop's diagonal and prepares ...Be7.

notes.text: Your knight blocks the bishop's path to f7 and keeps the e-pawn flexible; White keeps a modest edge.
notes.original: A good alternative to 6...e6: the knight blocks the bishop's path to f7 and Black keeps the e-pawn flexible. White keeps a modest edge.

notes.text: Natural-looking ...h6 loses at once: Bxf7 is mate, since the knight on g5 guards the bishop.
notes.original: Watch out: the natural-looking ...h6?? loses at once to Bxf7# - the knight on g5 guards the bishop and the king has no square.

notes.text: This loses a pawn and more: Bxf7 check wins material because the knight on g5 supports it.
notes.original: Watch out: this one loses a pawn and more - Bxf7+ wins material because the knight on g5 supports the capture.

notes.text: White piles up on e6; you answer with ...Nb6 and ...h6 for a normal Caro-Kann position.
notes.original: White adds pressure to e6 and prepares to develop. Black answers with ...Nb6 and ...h6, getting a normal Caro-Kann position.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop with tempo, so White must spend time retreating.
notes.original: Now your knight hits the bishop with tempo and heads towards d5 or c4, so White has to spend time retreating.

notes.text: You have gained queenside space, and the game is balanced.
notes.original: Black has gained queenside space and the game is balanced.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is winning.
White is winning.
The knight steps back to the edge, which is awkward but best.
notes.original: The knight steps back to the edge, the awkward but best move.

notes.text: You have expanded on both wings while White spent many moves on that knight.
notes.original: Black has expanded on both wings and White has spent a lot of moves with the knight.

notes.text: This is your only good move; taking on e6 with the f-pawn gets you mated.
notes.original:
The only good move which actually holds the position onwards.
Trap: 6...fxe6? 7.Qh5+ g6 8.Qxg6# and Black gets mated.

notes.text: Taking on e6 with the pawn falls into a trap: you get mated.
notes.original: Trap: 6...fxe6? 7.Qh5+ g6 8.Qxg6# and Black gets mated.
