notes.text: Retake with the knight; a queen check on b4 or a5 instead leaves you losing.
notes.original:
Trap: 7...Qb4+? 8.c3 Qd6 9.Nxd7 Bxd7 10.Nf3 O-O-O and Black is losing.
Trap: 7...Qa5+? 8.Bd2 Qa4 9.Nxd7 Qxd4 10.Bc3 Qe4+ and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on b4 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 7...Qb4+? 8.c3 Qd6 9.Nxd7 Bxd7 10.Nf3 O-O-O and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 7...Qa5+? 8.Bd2 Qa4 9.Nxd7 Qxd4 10.Bc3 Qe4+ and Black is losing.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your c-pawn hits d4 to break open the centre.
notes.original: Break open the centre.

notes.text: White's bishop pair gives a small edge, but your knights are active.
notes.original: White's bishop pair gives a small edge, but your knights are active and you can chip at d4 with ...c5.

notes.text: White's early a-pawn push lost time, and you have equalised.
notes.original: An early a4 push loses time and you equalise.

notes.text: Your knight challenges the e4 knight; follow with e6, Be7, castling short, then c5.
notes.original: You challenge the e4 knight and develop at the same time. The other knight stays on d7 in reserve, because ...Nb6 can later hit the bishop with tempo. Your plan is ...e6, ...Be7, castle short and then free your game with ...c5. If White trades on f6, recapture with the knight and keep your healthy structure. White keeps only a small edge here.

notes.text: This is less accurate: White keeps the strong knight with Ng3, and your h-pawn pushes cost time.
notes.original: This looks natural but is less accurate: after Ng3 White keeps his strong knight and your ...h5 and ...h4 pawn advances cost time while the kingside gets loose.

notes.text: White's bishop and knight both hit f7, and the knight eyes h7; stay calm and keep pieces covered.
notes.original: White doubles up on f7 and eyes h7. Stay calm and keep the pieces covered.

notes.text: Kick the knight away so your kingside stays safe.
notes.original: Kick the knight away so that your kingside stays safe.

notes.text: This freeing break hits d4; next finish development with Be7 and castling.
notes.original: This is the freeing break. You complete development with ...Be7 and ...O-O next.

notes.text: White's advanced knight relies on the d4 pawn, which your c5 pawn already challenges.
notes.original: White gets an advanced knight, but you can challenge it with ...Nbd7 or ...Bd6 ideas. Your pieces are safe and ...c5 gives you real counterplay. This is an open-centre game with a pawn on d4 for White and your c5 pawn already challenging it, and both bishops still to develop. White's knight on e5 is advanced but needs support from d4. Your plan: challenge it with ...Nbd7, finish development with ...Be7 and ...Bd7 or ...O-O, and take on d4 when it wins time. White wants to keep the knight on e5, add Be3 and pressure f7 and the h-file. The risk is f7, where Nxf7 and Qh5 tricks appear if you neglect it, and opening the d-file with ...cxd4 before you castle. If White deviates by playing Bxe6, recapture with the f-pawn or bishop calmly.

notes.text: Challenge the knight with Nbd7, then finish development.
notes.original: White gets an advanced knight, but you can challenge it with ...Nbd7 or ...Bd6 ideas. Your pieces are safe and ...c5 gives you real counterplay. This is an open-centre game with a pawn on d4 for White and your c5 pawn already challenging it, and both bishops still to develop. White's knight on e5 is advanced but needs support from d4. Your plan: challenge it with ...Nbd7, finish development with ...Be7 and ...Bd7 or ...O-O, and take on d4 when it wins time. White wants to keep the knight on e5, add Be3 and pressure f7 and the h-file. The risk is f7, where Nxf7 and Qh5 tricks appear if you neglect it, and opening the d-file with ...cxd4 before you castle. If White deviates by playing Bxe6, recapture with the f-pawn or bishop calmly.

notes.text: The safe reply: trade on e4, then play ...Nf6, ...g6 and ...Bg7. White keeps only a small edge.
notes.original: This is the safe reply: the d7 knight steps to f6 and the g8 knight stays home, so you are ready to trade on e4. The point is that you never leave the e7 pawn pinned in front of your king. Your plan is ...Nxe4, ...Nf6, then ...g6 and ...Bg7 or ...Bf5 ideas, with ...Qa5+ as a useful resource against the d2 square. Keep the structure flexible and trade pieces. White keeps only a small edge here.

notes.text: This knight move is the trap: your e7 pawn is pinned, so White's knight mates on d6.
notes.original: This is the trap. The queen pins the e7 pawn against your king, so the knight jumps in with mate:

notes.text: Trade off White's strong knight on e4.
notes.original: Trade off the strong knight.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen with tempo.
notes.original: With tempo you hit the queen.

notes.text: Your bishop is heading to g7, and your queen can use a5.
notes.original: Your bishop will go to g7 and the queen can use a5.

notes.text: Your check forces White to block on d2, which hampers his own development.
notes.original: This check forces White to put a piece on d2, which hampers his own development.

notes.text: Never grab the a2 pawn with your queen: the rook simply takes it.
notes.original: A calm, solid position where you complete development with ...Bg7 and ...O-O and aim for ...c5. This is a quiet, semi-open structure with White's pawn on d4 and your solid c6, e7 and g6 pawns. You will castle short with your bishop on g7. After the check, your queen on a5 is attacked, so retreat it with ...Qd5 or ...Qb6, then play ...Bg7, ...O-O and ...Bf5 to hit the queen on d3. Aim for the freeing break ...c5 once you are castled. White wants to castle long or short, play c4 and use his space and the d4 pawn. The big risk is at the fifth move, where ...Ngf6?? loses to Nd6 mate, so always play ...Ndf6. Never grab the a2 pawn with the queen.

notes.text: The standard reply: your bishop gets outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in.
notes.original: 3...Bf5 is the standard reply to the Advance Variation. The bishop gets outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in.

notes.text: White's Nd2 and c4 tries delay Nf3; just develop, challenge the centre with c5, and finish development first.
notes.original: The standard Short Variation setup covered in the main Advance Variation chapters. This chapter covers two respectable independent tries White has instead of the main 4.Nf3: 4.Nd2 and the immediate 4.c4. Black's plan against both: these sidelines avoid committing the king's knight to f3 immediately, but they don't change Black's fundamentals - develop the e7-knight (toward f5 or g6), challenge the center with ...c5 (or accept a favorable structure if White trades on d5/c4 first), and use the extra tempo White spends on these knight/pawn maneuvers to finish development slightly ahead of schedule.

notes.text: Your c-pawn hits White's centre at once; White must hold it together or take the pawn.
notes.original: An interesting move that gives the position a French flavour. Black strikes at the centre at once and starts undermining White's Advance set-up. White must either keep the centre together or release it by taking the pawn, in which case Black spends several moves chasing the c- or e-pawn.

notes.text: The most natural reply: White plans to castle short and keep the bishop pair.
notes.original: Nf3 is the most natural reply: White will castle kingside and develop the bishop pair. Sidelines such as c4?! are treated in this chapter as well.

notes.text: White offers the immediate trade of light-squared bishops before developing anything else.
notes.original: 4.Bd3 offers the immediate trade of light-squared bishops before developing anything else, a distinct system from the Nf3-first approach the chapter otherwise builds around.

notes.text: White develops flexibly, keeping the option of Ng3 or Nf4 depending on your setup.
notes.original: 4.Ne2 develops flexibly, keeping the option of either Ng3 or Nf4 depending on Black's setup.

notes.text: White's c3 supports the centre quietly, keeping both Nf3 and f4 available later.
notes.original: 4.c3 supports the center quietly before committing the king's knight anywhere, keeping options for both Nf3 and f4 later.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes d4 and c5, preparing Nd2 and Nf3 without blocking the c-pawn.
notes.original: 4.Be3 develops toward c5/d4 immediately, preparing a later Nd2-Nf3 setup without blocking the c-pawn.

notes.text: Nc3 keeps c3 free and covers e4; after ...e6 and g4, White gets dangerous play.
notes.original: A strong Advance Variation sideline: Nc3!? first, with c3 not strictly needed since White can hold the centre anyway. Delaying c3 keeps the square free for the knight, which can cover e4 in lines where Black tries to place a bishop there (typical of the Bayonet Attack with g4, here delayed until Nc3 has been played). After ...e6 g4! White gets dangerous play. Despite the age of the idea, it remains effective.

notes.text: If White times g4, your bishop steps back to g6 and then h7, relocated to a safe long diagonal.
notes.original: The Shirov Variation - a flexible try that develops a piece and keeps the option of a later g4 pawn storm in reserve. Black's plan: whichever way White times the g4 advance (immediately, as in the 4.g4!? branch below, or after Nc3 first), the bishop steps back to g6 and then h7 - it is never actually trapped, just relocated to a long, safe diagonal. Once that is settled, Black's normal freeing break ...c5 followed by ...Nc6/...Ne7 and, if White grabs the h5-pawn, a well-timed ...cxd4 tactical point (explained below) give Black completely comfortable, often better, positions in practice.

notes.text: The early c4 is a bit inaccurate: your solid centre is unbreakable, so just meet it with e6.
notes.original: The early c4 move is rather a bit inaccurate since Black's fortified center is unbreakable. The early c4 move would be met with e6.

notes.text: White challenges the centre at once, without developing the king's knight first.
notes.original: A pure, immediate challenge to the center, associated at the top level with Magnus Carlsen. White doesn't bother developing the king's knight first at all.

notes.text: This move order of the Bayonet Attack exposes White's kingside at once, but it hides a few traps.
notes.original: This move order of the Bayonet Attack is not good, since it exposes White's kingside at once, but it contains a few traps, so be prepared.

notes.text: The Bayonet pawn hits your bishop and will take it unless you retreat.
notes.original: The Bayonet Attack - a completely different try from the Tal Variation above. Instead of preparing the pawn storm with h4 first, White goes straight for the point: a pawn on g4 attacks the Bf5 bishop directly (gxf5 is a real threat next move), forcing an immediate decision. Black has three reasonable retreats - 4...Be4, 4...Bg6, and 4...Bd7 - each covered below. Black's general plan across this whole branch: none of the three retreats loses material or the game by force; the practical difference between them is how much central/kingside space Black concedes versus how active the bishop stays, and whether Black is willing to meet White's typical e5-e6!? pawn sacrifice by capturing (...fxe6, opening the f-file for a rook) or declining it (...Qd6, keeping the structure intact at the cost of a tempo).

notes.text: White's pawn hits your bishop and takes away its retreat square; step back to g6.
notes.original: The immediate, more committal try - grab the bishop's retreat square before Black can complete development at all.

notes.text: Be careful with e6 now: White's g- and h-pawns chase your bishop and grab lots of space.
notes.original: 4.h4 gains space and prepares g4. Black has to be careful with ...e6 here: after 5.g4 Bg6 6.h5 the bishop is driven back to h7 and White gains a lot of space.

notes.text: The Tal Variation pushes the h-pawn first while your bishop sits on f5; it is a serious, popular try.
notes.original: The Tal Variation, named for Mikhail Tal. It is a different system from the Bayonet Attack covered later in this chapter: here White pushes the h-pawn first while the bishop can still sit on f5, instead of hitting it at once with g4. It is a serious, popular try, not a minor sideline.

notes.text: White plans Nb3 next, eyeing c5 and d4 and keeping f3 free for the other knight.
notes.original: An idea popularized at the top level by Wesley So. Rather than the natural-looking 4.Nf3, White routes the knight to b3 instead, eyeing c5 and d4 while keeping f3 open for the other knight or a future f4 push.

notes.text: Your pawn chain is very solid, you are comfortable, and you can look for middlegame activity.
notes.original: Black has locked in the position with a very solid pawn chain, is comfortable defensively and positionally, and can look for activity in the middlegame.

notes.text: White offers a bishop swap; answer with ...c5 and then castle short.
notes.original: 5.Bd3 swaps the light-squared bishops at once and simplifies. Black fights back in the centre with ...c5 and then castles kingside.

notes.text: Carlsen played this against Firouzja in 2021; it hits your centre but is defensible.
notes.original: This was the move Magnus Carlsen played against Alireza Firouzja at the 2021 World Rapid and Blitz Championship; Firouzja went on to lose after errors in the middlegame. It hits Black's centre immediately, but the position is defensible and less worrying than other move orders. Caro-Kann players should be ready for such surprises.

notes.text: A slightly unusual move; White probably wants to follow with c4.
notes.original: Perhaps this move is a bit unorthodox but white probably wants to play c4.

notes.text: White can keep the tension with Be2 and simplify, since trades would calm the position.
notes.original: White does have to option to play Be2 to keep the tension on the center and make the position less complicated since an exchange would help simplify the position.

notes.text: Some players avoid theory with c3, and White may well succeed in that.
notes.original: Other players of this line may play c3 to avoid theory, and White may well succeed in that.

notes.text: White's knight pressures d5; decide where your knights go, since your bishop is already outside the chain.
notes.original: White develops the knight to pressure d5 and prepares Bd3 or Be2 without losing control of e5. White does not mind trading bishops on d3 if the pawn recapture is useful. For you the question is where to put your knights while your light-squared bishop is already outside the chain.

notes.text: Trading bishops was prudent; your position is very solid, so finish development and castle next.
notes.original: This Bd3 manouevre is often played in this line, and it's usually prudent for black to exchange the bishops. This is already a very solid position for black; the next priority is to complete development and castle.

notes.text: Against Nf3, play ...e6, take the bishop on d3, and use ...c5 and ...f6 as your breaks.
notes.original:
Idea: Against 4.Nf3, play ...e6, take the bishop if White offers it with Bd3, and bring your knights to d7 and f5. Your breaks are ...c5 and ...f6 against White's centre.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nf3 e6 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.Qxd3 Nd7
Watch out: ...Nxe5? loses material on moves 7 to 12. ...Nxd4? loses material on moves 9 to 10.
Next: 🔵 12 continues the Advance Variation. Plans: 🟠 Plan 06, 🟠 Plan 08. Model games: 🟡 Game 01, 🟡 Game 02.

notes.text: From d7 your knight can head to f8 to defend h7 if White attacks on the kingside.
notes.original: ...Nd7 is useful in case White attacks on the kingside: from d7 the knight can go to f8 and add another defender of h7, forming a fortress.

notes.text: Your c-pawn strikes at d4 at once, the pawn the e5 pawn depends on.
notes.original: With the light-squared bishops traded, you strike at d4 at once: the e5 pawn depends on it, and your pawn chain on d5 and e6 stays solid.

notes.text: Your c-pawn hits d4 at once; trade there, then develop with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7.
notes.original: You have already traded your light bishop, so ...c5 hits d4 at once. White wants to support e5 with Be3 and f4 and keep a space edge. You trade on d4 and develop with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7.

notes.text: White wants Be3 and f4 to support the e5 pawn and keep a space edge.
notes.original: You have already traded your light bishop, so ...c5 hits d4 at once. White wants to support e5 with Be3 and f4 and keep a space edge. You trade on d4 and develop with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7.

notes.text: The d4 break is the standard way to free your game after the bishop trade.
notes.original: The break at d4 is the standard way to free your game and fits the simplified structure after the bishop trade.

notes.text: Challenge the d4 pawn now, before White finishes development; this break frees your position.
notes.original: Challenge d4 now, before White completes development with c3 and Nbd2. The pawn break is the thematic way to free your position.

notes.text: Your check comes first and forces White to block; a knight on d2 would then be pinned.
notes.original: An in-between check that makes White decide how to block it. The knight on d2 ends up pinned along the diagonal, which is why Qa6 is playable next.

notes.text: This is White's strongest try here, stronger than Nc3.
notes.original: White's strongest try here, stronger than Nc3.

notes.text: This is playable, but the ...c5 break is more accurate.
notes.original: Playable, but c5 is more accurate.

notes.text: You switch to queenside counterplay with a6, instead of attacking on the kingside.
notes.original: Another plan is to focus on the queenside rather than the kingside and find counterplay there. Note that ...c5 is not possible because of the Nb5 threat, after which a knight outpost on d6 would cause great problems for Black.

notes.text: White is playing with fire: his pawn hits your knight, and his own kingside is at risk.
notes.original: White is playing with fire: the kingside is at risk, but White can play Kh1 and stack rooks on the g-file to launch an attack.

notes.text: If White skips g4, castle, play c5, then storm the queenside with your a-pawn.
notes.original: If White does not play g4, Black can castle, play ...c5 and then storm the queenside with ...a7-a5.

notes.text: A quiet alternative is ...g5, starting a pawn storm against White's kingside.
notes.original: Other quiet moves are possible, such as ...g5, when Black attacks the white kingside with a pawn storm.

notes.text: If White retreats the knight, your h-pawn can jump to h5 and attack the king at once.
notes.original: If White retreats the knight, ...h5 lets Black attack the king at once.

notes.text: The f-file opens for your rook whether or not White takes, and your bishop on h4 adds to the attack.
notes.original: The f-file will be open for Black's rook whether or not White takes the f-pawn. Black is better because White's kingside is weak with little counterplay, and White lacks pieces to switch to the queenside. With the open f-file and a bishop on h4, Black gets a very dynamic attack on the king.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Answer with ...Qf8, then bring rooks to e8 and f7, keeping your pieces coordinated around the loose h4 bishop.
notes.original: White wants to use the queen on the e-file and the bishop on f4 to pile up on e5 and the d-file, since your knight on d7 is the key defender. You reply with ...Qf8, which defends the f-file and keeps an eye on f2, then bring the rook to e8 and f7. The position is level, so keep your pieces coordinated around the loose bishop on h4.

notes.text: Your h6 answers both White ideas, and ...Nxe5 is the central break.
notes.original: Be5 aims to trade your good knight, and f4 gains space. Both ideas are met by ...h6 and the central break ...Nxe5.

notes.text: A sharper try: if White takes on h5, your queen recaptures with active play against the king.
notes.original: A sharper try: after 18.gxh5 Qxh5 you get active play against the king.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White wants its bishop on g3 to double on the f-file, while its queen eyes your a7 pawn.
notes.original: White wants to bring the bishop to g3 and double on the f-file, while the queen eyes the loose a7 pawn. You answer with ...Rf7 to guard the seventh rank and prepare ...Raf8. When the dark bishops come off on g3, a lone knight on d7 is enough to keep e5 under pressure.

notes.text: Guard the seventh rank with your rook, then bring the other rook to the f-file.
notes.original: White wants to bring the bishop to g3 and double on the f-file, while the queen eyes the loose a7 pawn. You answer with ...Rf7 to guard the seventh rank and prepare ...Raf8. When the dark bishops come off on g3, a lone knight on d7 is enough to keep e5 under pressure.

notes.text: You take the pawn because White's knight on d4 gives very little in return.
notes.original: You take the pawn only because the knight on d4 gives White very little in return.

notes.text: You win the e5 pawn: White spent a tempo on the king, and the queens are gone.
notes.original: If White spends a tempo on the king, the e5 pawn falls once the queens leave the board.

notes.text: Your h-pawn starts the kingside pawn storm, with the knight on h4 helping.
notes.original: 11...h5 starts the kingside pawn storm, with the knight on h4 helping.

notes.text: White cannot take on d4: your bishop would pin the queen to the king and win it.
notes.original: White cannot take due to the Bc5 pin.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Retreat the bishop to d8 to keep guarding h4, then bring a rook to c8 and on to c4.
notes.original: White offers a queen trade and covers b2, hoping to take the sting out of your extra pawn. Do not worry: the d4 pawn cramps White and the knight on h4 is annoying, so you retreat ...Bd8, which still guards h4 along the diagonal, and bring a rook to c8. Then ...Rc4 hits the weak g4 pawn while keeping d4 alive.

notes.text: White has piled up on the f-file, but you are safe and a pawn up.
notes.original: White has piled up on the f-file but you are safe and a pawn up.

notes.text: You take back on b6 after the queen trade.
notes.original: Hitting the d4 pawn at once

notes.text: This is a sharper option that leads to the same main line after Rad1.
notes.original: ...g5 is an option for those who prefer a more dangerous line; it leads to the same thing after Rad1, the line covered in this course.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
White's rook eyes your king down the c-file, and the knight on e2 defends d4.
notes.original: White puts the rook on the c-file against your king on c8, while the knight on e2 covers d4.

notes.text: Your queen steps out of the d-pawn's attack and offers a queen trade.
Your pawn hits d4 and stops White's pawn storm from opening the file.
notes.original: You hit d4 and stop White's pawn storm from opening the file.

notes.text: The balance is level, and White's e3 pawn is split from the others.
notes.original: The balance is level, with White's pawns on e3 split.

notes.text: Your rook takes White's queen first, so the queens just trade.
notes.original: Taking the queen looks free, but the d-pawn is pinned to the queen on d3 by your rook on d8, so ...Rxd3 comes first and the queens just trade.

notes.text: The position is messy and a little dangerous, but you have enough pieces near the kingside to hold.
notes.original: The position is messy and a little dangerous, but Black has enough pieces near the kingside to hold.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your rook on d8 and wants to trade off your active bishop on b4.
notes.original: White hits your rook on d8 and wants to trade the active bishop on b4.

notes.text: Your rook hits the bishop on g5 and keeps watch over the g-file.
notes.original: The rook attacks the bishop on g5, which must retreat, and keeps the g-file under watch.

notes.text: Your rook returns to the d-file, lined up behind the knight against d4, and your king stays safe.
notes.original: Back to the d-file to pressure d4, with the king still safe on c8.

notes.text: Your g4 and h3 pawns cramp White's king, and every trade makes your fortress easier to hold.
notes.original: Your chain on g4 and h3 cramps White's king, and every trade makes your fortress easier to hold.

notes.text: White's Rab1 let you take on e3, and the recapture fxe3 weakened White's king.
notes.original: Rab1 allows ...Nxe3, and fxe3 weakens White's king.

notes.text: White prepares g4 or Ng3 to challenge your knight on f5, and clears c3 for the c-pawn.
notes.original: White prepares g4 or Ng3 to challenge the knight on f5 and clears c3 for the c-pawn.

notes.text: You start your queenside play and hit the d4 pawn, as planned.
notes.original: You start your queenside play and hit the d4 pawn, as you planned.

notes.text: White's g4 kicked your knight, but you traded it off and keep a healthy position.
notes.original: White's g4 kicks your knight, but you trade it off and keep a healthy position. The bishop on h4 takes aim at the king's rook.

notes.text: If White retreats the bishop and plays g4, the game becomes a tactical melee that is roughly equal.
notes.original: If White retreats the bishop and plays g4, the game turns into a tactical melee that is roughly equal.

notes.text: Bring your queen to c7, prepare with c5 or f6, then castle long and continue the kingside attack.
notes.original: Black has enough counterplay on the kingside and is aiming for mate, though the attack will not be immediate. The queen must go to c7 first; castling queenside is perhaps dangerous, so ...c5 or ...f6 should come first, and once the position is less complicated Black can castle long and continue the kingside attack.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's rook lines up on the c-file against your c6 pawn and king, while the knight eyes d6.
notes.original: White brings the rook to the c-file against the c6 pawn and your king, while Nc4 eyes d6 for a check on c8.

notes.text: Your king steps off the c-file and out of the knight-check on d6.
notes.original: The king steps off the c-file and out of the Nd6+ check.

notes.text: You trade a pair of knights, and your knight on d5 is a monster in the centre.
notes.original: You trade a pair of knights and the knight on d5 is a monster in the centre.

notes.text: You have a small edge: your pieces are active and your king is safe on b8.
notes.original: You have a small edge: your pieces are active and the king is safe on b8.

notes.text: Your queen lands on d5, centralised and facing White's queen on e4.
notes.original: Qe4 hits g4 and c6, but ...Nb6 trades the knight and your queen finds d5.

notes.text: You pressure the c5 pawn with knight and bishop, and White cannot hold it much longer.
notes.original: Black pressures the c-pawn, and White cannot hold on to it much longer.

notes.text: Your queen adds another attacker on the c5 pawn, which will soon fall.
notes.original: Black adds another attacker on the c-pawn, which will soon fall.

notes.text: White grabbed a pawn but left the knight on the rim hanging to your queen.
notes.original: Blunders the knight on the rim.

notes.text: After the trades, you are doing fine here.
notes.original: Black is doing fine here.

notes.text: White's queen leaves b3 before your knight jumps in with tempo, and still guards the knight on a4.
notes.original: The queen leaves b3 because your Ne5 was about to jump to c4 or d3 with tempo, and Qd1 still protects the knight on a4.

notes.text: Your queen hits the knight on a4, the c5 pawn and the b2 pawn at once.
notes.original: Your queen hits the knight on a4, the c5 pawn and b2.

notes.text: After the bishop trade, White's c5 and d4 pawns need constant protection against your pieces.
notes.original: Bd4 protects c5 and hits the knight, so you trade it off, leaving White with c5 and d4 pawns that need constant protection.

notes.text: Your bishop pressures d4 and White's advanced c5 pawn is passive; White is only slightly better.
notes.original: Your bishop pressures d4, and White's advanced c5 pawn is passive. White is slightly better but you are doing fine.

notes.text: Black is winning.
You are a knight up; White's queen returns to b3 to challenge yours.
notes.original: White is a knight down after ...Qxa4, and the queen on b7 can be harassed by ...Rb8. Qb3 brings it back and challenges yours.

notes.text: Offer the queen trade yourself: simplifying is good when you have an extra piece.
notes.original: You offer the queens yourself: simplification is your friend with an extra piece.

notes.text: Taking the pawn is safe, because your knight returns to c6 when White attacks it.
notes.original: Taking the pawn is safe, since the knight returns to c6 after Rab1.

notes.text: You are a knight up for two pawns, and the position is simple to handle.
White's c4 and b4 pawn pushes only opened lines for your pieces.
notes.original: Opening lines with c4 and b4 only helps your pieces.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Retake on h4, then bring a rook to d8 to hit the d4 pawn.
notes.original: White removes the knight that was eyeing f3 and g2, and after ...Qxh4 your queen is exposed to Nc3-e4 and g3 tempo moves. Your rook goes to d8 to hit the d4 pawn, and the knight on d5 later blocks the centre.

notes.text: You have a comfortable position with a good knight on d5, but White keeps the extra space.
Castling long leaves you fine, and the position is equal.
notes.original: If White keeps the queens on, the ...f5 break undermines e5 and you are fine.

notes.text: Bishop check is recommended: it develops a piece and lets you castle quickly.
notes.original: ...Bb4 is recommended, since it lets Black castle quickly.

notes.text: White tries another setup here; you stay flexible and keep developing.
notes.original: Another line for White.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White prepares b4 and a3 for a queenside clamp, and the queen eyes a5.
notes.original: White prepares b4 and a3 to build a queenside clamp with the c5 pawn, and the queen eyes a5.

notes.text: The standard undermining move; ...b6 follows to attack White's c5 pawn chain.
notes.original: You answer with the standard undermining move: ...a5 and ...b6 attack the c5 chain from both sides.

notes.text: Your rook goes behind the b-pawn lever.
notes.original: The rook goes behind the b-pawn lever.

notes.text: Your a-file is now half-open for the rook, and the position is balanced.
notes.original: You open the a-file for the rook and the position is balanced.

notes.text: If White is slow with Qc3, your b6 lever comes at once and hits c5.
notes.original: If White is slow with Qc3, ...b6 comes at once and hits c5.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White has the bishop pair and wants to trade off your light-squared bishop, so the knight hits it.
notes.original: White has the bishop pair and wants to remove your light-squared bishop, so Nh4 attacks the bishop on f5.

notes.text: You strike at the centre while White's knight is offside on h4.
notes.original: You strike at the centre while the white knight is offside on h4.

notes.text: White keeps the bishop pair, but your knights are active, your rook takes the c-file, and it's level.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop pair, but your knights are active, your rook takes the c-file and the position is level.

notes.text: A quieter way: your knight lands on d5 and the c5 break comes easily.
notes.original: A quieter way: your knight lands on d5 and the ...c5 break comes with ease.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White stops ...b5 and prepares a rook lift to e1, e4 and g4, aimed at g7.
notes.original: White stops ...b5 and prepares a rook lift with Re1-e4-g4 aimed at g7.

notes.text: You fix the pawn on a4 and keep b4 free for your pieces.
A luft move: your king gets air, so the rook lift to e4 won't come with tempo.
notes.original: A luft move: the king is no longer short of air and Re4 will not come with tempo.

notes.text: Your rook on g8 guards g7 against the rook on g4; White is only slightly better.
notes.original: You step off the g-file, and the rook on g8 covers g7. White keeps a small edge but there is no direct threat.

notes.text: White's queen on e4 hits h7, but your knight trade on c3 and the c5 break equalise.
notes.original: Qe4 hits h7 and eyes the centre, but ...Nxc3 and the ...c5 break equalise.

notes.text: From here, your c-pawn must challenge the centre.
notes.original: From here ...c5 is needed to challenge the centre.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Supporting the centre with c3 is usual; after other tries you can simply take on d4.
notes.original: c3 is usual here. Be3 has also been tried several times in my games, after which black can simply take on d4, with less central control for white resulting.

notes.text: White takes the pawn, but it isn't a real sacrifice; White usually can't keep it anyway.
notes.original: White takes the pawn, this isn't really a pawn sacrifice since white usually do not keep the pawn anyway. Any move orders that tries to saves the pawn would end badly for White.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Two knights hit the e5 pawn while a knight and bishop hit c5, so one pawn likely falls.
notes.original: Two knights bear down on the e-pawn while a knight and a bishop target the c-pawn, so one of these pawns is likely to fall.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's knight hits your c6 knight to break your pawns; castle, then answer with ...Qd5 and ...Bd3.
notes.original: White attacks the knight on c6 so that after ...O-O Nxc6 bxc6 your pawns are broken. Then Bxc5 and Nc4 attack the weak c-pawns. You answer with ...Qd5 and ...Bd3, using your active bishop to hit the e2 bishop.

notes.text: White's knight hits your c6 knight, so castling allows a trade that wrecks your pawn structure.
notes.original: This is the same idea as in the 7.dxc5 move order: White hits c6 so that ...O-O Nxc6 bxc6 wrecks your structure. Bxc5 and Nc4 then pick on the c-pawns, while ...Qd5 and ...Bd3 are your counterplay against the bishop on e2.

notes.text: White keeps a slight edge.
You are a bit worse, but White has no big threats.
notes.original: You are a bit worse but White has no big threats.

notes.text: If White trades the dark bishops at once, you can steer into a level endgame.
notes.original: If White trades dark bishops at once, you can steer into a level endgame.

notes.text: You are happy here, striving for the initiative and the pawn back.
notes.original: Black is happy here, striving for the initiative and the pawn back.

notes.text: Your queen wins back the pawn on d5, leaving you a pawn up.
notes.original: Achieving a significant victory against a pawn

notes.text: White hits your e5 knight; trade the active knights, keep the queen safe and push g5 to free the f-pawn.
notes.original: White hits the knight on e5 and plans Bf3 and a rook on d1 to use the open files against your queen. Your extra pawn is a doubled f-pawn, so it is worth less than it looks. You trade the active knights, keep the queen safe and push ...g5 to get the f-pawn moving.

notes.text: You keep a small edge: after the trades, your extra pawn becomes useful.
notes.original: You keep a small edge: after the trades the extra pawn becomes useful.

notes.text: Your bishop takes on d4, and the position stays level.
notes.original: Putting the knight on

notes.text: White's most testing try is calm development, answering your pawn grab on b2 with active pieces.
notes.original: One of the most debated modern lines of the Advance Variation: 5.Be2 c5 6.Be3 Qb6, where Black grabs the b2 pawn and White gets active pieces in return. This is a different branch than our main recommendation (which meets 4.Nf3 e6 with the calmer 5.Bd3, trading light-squared bishops immediately) - it's included here purely as supplementary reference, so you understand the objective status of the sharper try too, in case you ever want it or face it from the other side of the board. White's most testing try is this calm developing move, meeting the pawn grab with active pieces instead of rushing.

notes.text: Castling is another option for White here.
notes.original: Also possible: O-O.

notes.text: Pushing the c-pawn is another option for White here.
notes.original: Also possible: c4.

notes.text: White's knight heads for a flexible square, keeping b3 available depending on your reply.
notes.original: Nbd2 - routes the knight to a flexible square instead of the main lines with c4 or castling, keeping the option of Nb3 or Nb1-c3 open depending on how Black continues.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your queen on b2 is now the target; the point is a bishop pin that leads to trading queens.
notes.original: Recapturing is forced. Now your queen on b2 is the target: White threatens Rb1 and a knight attack. The cunning point is ...Bb4, pinning the knight against the queen on e1, so that after ...Bxc3 the queens come off and you keep the bishop pair.

notes.text: Your king is displaced, and White's lead in development gives a slight edge.
notes.original: You have the bishop pair but a displaced king, and White gets a slight edge from the lead in development.

notes.text: Your knight takes the bishop with check; ignoring your knight on d4 loses that bishop.
notes.original: Any attempt to ignore the knight on d4 loses the bishop on e2 with check.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Castle long and centralise your knight on d5, covering c3 and e3.
notes.original: White wins the pawn back and opens the position against your king, while your queen on b2 is away from the action. You should castle long and centralise the knight on d5, which stops White from using c3 and e3. This is the same structure as in the 7.c4 line.

notes.text: Castle long and land the knight on d5 to cover c3 and e3; sharp but level.
notes.original: White regains the pawn and opens lines against your king while the queen is out of play on b2. You castle long, and the knight lands on d5 to cover c3 and e3. The sequence is sharp but level.

notes.text: Your knight forks the queen and rook, which balances the line.
notes.original: The knight fork on the queen and rook balances the line.

notes.text: Your knight forks the queen and rook, keeping things level.
notes.original: The final knight fork on the queen and rook keeps things level.

notes.text: Grabbing the pawn on c5 gives you a strong initiative.
White's attempt to trap your queen backfires and leaves you clearly better.
notes.original: Trying to trap the queen backfires and leaves you clearly better.

notes.text: Simple, natural development: your knight keeps pressure on d4 without risk.
notes.original: ...Nc6 (Solid & Optimal) - simple, natural development that keeps pressure on d4 without taking any risks; the safest route to a normal, comfortable middlegame.

notes.text: You grab the pawn at once; White gets some initiative for it, but nothing immediately decisive.
notes.original: ...Qxb2 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - grabs the offered pawn at once, accepting a sharper position where White gets some initiative for the material but nothing immediately decisive.

notes.text: White lets you grab on b2; you can win two pawns but must give one back.
notes.original: White lets you grab at b2, with the idea of dxc5 and Rc1 so that your queen runs out of safe squares near a3. In return your pieces on the kingside are undeveloped. You can take two pawns, but you must give one back.

notes.text: Your queen is tied up, yet White has no immediate win.
This simple setup leaves you with a small edge.
notes.original: This simple line gives you a small edge.

notes.text: White wants Nb3 to hit c5 and Rb1 to chase your queen, so develop quickly.
notes.original: White opens the centre while your queen is far from home. The knight will go to b3 to hit c5, and ...Qxb2 gets hunted by Rb1. Your solution is to develop quickly with ...Ne7, ...Nbc6 and ...O-O-O, so the queen has support.

notes.text: Chasing your queen lets you trade queens and stay a little better.
notes.original: Chasing the queen allows you to trade queens and stay a little better.

notes.text: Against other move orders, such as Be2, you play Nd7, Ne7, then c5.
notes.original: Other move orders, such as Be2, are met by the recommended set-up: ...Nd7, ...Ne7, then ...c5.

notes.text: White's queen threatens to take your b7 pawn.
notes.original: A threat to seize the b pawn.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White tries to save one of the pawns but would fail eventually.
Your b-pawn attacks c5 and breaks up White's over-extended pawns.
notes.original: Effectively breaking up white's over-extended pawns.

notes.text: White had to take, since your b6 pawn attacked c5; ignoring it lets bxc5 wreck White's chain.
notes.original: White has to take, because ...b6 attacks the c5 pawn. If White does nothing, for example with Bf4, ...bxc5 wrecks the pawn chain and you are better.

notes.text: The queens come off and your knight is active on b6 against White's loosened queenside.
Your knights are well placed and your bishop has targets, but White's pieces are fine too.
notes.original: Your knights are well placed and the bishop has targets, but White's pieces are fine too.

notes.text: The loose pawns on c5 and b4 fall, and White's structure collapses.
notes.original: The loose pawns on c5 and b4 fall and White's structure collapses.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White's queen attacks your b4 knight, and your bishop can't guard it because the c5 pawn blocks.
notes.original: The knight on b4 hits both Qd3 and a2, so the queen has to move. Qd4 attacks the knight in return, because your bishop on f8 cannot protect b4 while the pawn on c5 blocks the diagonal.

notes.text: Your knight escapes with a gain of time, since it now hits the queen.
notes.original: The knight escapes with a gain of time, since it now hits the queen on d4.

notes.text: Your knight takes the c5 pawn, and White cannot keep it.
notes.original: The knight from d7 takes the pawn on c5, and White cannot keep it.

notes.text: You gain space with h5, your rook swings out, and White's pieces are loose.
notes.original: You gain space with h5, the rook swings out, and White's pieces are loose; you are clearly better.

notes.text: Your bishop on c5 protected the knight and won the c5 pawn.
notes.original: Qb3 attacks b4 too, but ...Bxc5 protects the knight and wins the c5 pawn.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's queen had to leave, and from g3 it hits both e5 and g7.
notes.original: The queen must leave the knight's attack on d3, and from g3 it hits both e5 and g7.

notes.text: Your knight guards the kingside and heads for f4.
notes.original: The knight guards your kingside and heads for f4.

notes.text: Your bishop develops to e7, ready to trade off White's bishop.
notes.original: You trade the bishop.

notes.text: White's doubled c-pawns are weak, so you are slightly better.
notes.original: Your pawns on d5 and e6 are passed, because White has no d- or e-pawns, and White's doubled c-pawns are weak. That is why you are slightly better.

notes.text: White's Qe2 let your knight jump to c4, and ...axb4 won you a pawn.
notes.original: Qe2 lets the knight jump to c4 and you pick up a pawn with ...axb4.

notes.text: Your knight supports e5 and prepares ...c5; bring the other knight to e7 too.
notes.original: Prepare ...c5 and support e5. Plan: ...Ne7 and ...Nf5, then ...c5 to hit d4. Keep the center pawns on e6 and d5 safe, and do not hurry to castle before you see what White does with the dark-squared bishop. If White plays Bf4 you answer with ...Ne7 and ...Nf5 anyway.

notes.text: This is also fine for you, and it keeps ...Nf5 in mind.
notes.original: Also fine, and it keeps ...Nf5 in mind.

notes.text: The bishops are traded, and White's pawns on d3 and d4 are doubled.
notes.original: Trade the bishop; White's pawn on d3 is a slightly worse structure for White.

notes.text: Equal and comfortable: develop with ...Be7, hit d4 with ...c5, and avoid an early ...g5.
notes.original: This is a useful lever: you will play ...h4 or ...Be7 and aim for ...c5. Avoid playing ...g5 too early without a knight on f5. Equal and comfortable. This is a closed French-style position where your light-squared bishop has been traded for White's d3 bishop, so White has doubled pawns on d3 and d4, and you have good squares on f5 and g6. Your plan: complete development with ...Be7, then hit d4 with ...c5 and, with the knight on f5, use ...h4 to cramp the kingside. White wants Ng3 to challenge your knight, then Nxf5 and exf5, or Qd2 with Bg5. Meet Ng3 calmly and recapture with the e-pawn. The mistake is ...g5 early, because it weakens the light squares without support. If White plays Ng3, retreat only if needed.

notes.text: Trade bishops on d3; the tempting queen check on a5 instead loses for you.
notes.original: Trap: 4...Qa5+? 5.Bd2 Qb6 6.Bxf5 e6 7.Bd3 Qxd4 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 4...Qa5+? 5.Bd2 Qb6 6.Bxf5 e6 7.Bd3 Qxd4 and Black is losing.

notes.text: With the bishops traded, the position is simplified and very level.
notes.original: 4.Bd3 offers the immediate trade of light-squared bishops before developing anything else, a distinct system from the Nf3-first approach the chapter otherwise builds around. ...reaching a simplified, very level position.

notes.text: The bishop trade has simplified things into a very level position.
notes.original: Trap: 4...Qa5+? 5.Bd2 Qb6 6.Bxf5 e6 7.Bd3 Qxd4 and Black is losing. ...reaching a simplified, very level position.

notes.text: White supports d4 so the c5 break cannot undermine the centre; the tension resolves soon, so place pieces with that…
notes.original: White supports the d4 pawn with a pawn so that the c5 break does not undermine the centre, and it frees c2 for the queen or a knight. It is a natural, solid move that is common in practice (played in about 872,000 games). So the tension on d4 is going to be resolved soon, so choose your piece placement with that in mind.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the white knight on d4 that cements the centre.
notes.original: Attack the knight that is cementing the centre.

notes.text: White's f4 will support e5, so you trade the knight before it settles.
notes.original: White supports e5 with f4, so trade the knight before it settles.

notes.text: White keeps the centre with f4, and you trade off a pair of knights.
notes.original: White keeps the centre with f4 and you trade off a pair of knights.

notes.text: Your knight heads to f5, where it will pressure the bishop on d4.
notes.original: White's bishop on d4 aims at g7 and f4 holds e5, but ...Ne7 covers g7 and heads to f5.

notes.text: Your knight on e7 prepares ...Nf5 to hit the bishop on d4.
notes.original: The bishop aims at g7, but ...Ne7 covers it and prepares ...Nf5 to hit the bishop.

notes.text: The position is level; ...Nc6 hits the bishop on d4.
notes.original: The position is level. Your plan is ...Nc6 or ...Qb6, hitting the bishop on d4 and the pawn on b2.

notes.text: Or play ...Qb6, hitting the bishop on d4 and the pawn on b2.
notes.original: The position is level. Your plan is ...Nc6 or ...Qb6, hitting the bishop on d4 and the pawn on b2.

notes.text: The position is balanced.
The position is balanced: you have the half-open c-file, and White has a little extra space.
notes.original: A balanced position. You have the half-open c-file, and White has a little extra space.

notes.text: White has more space, but you develop easily and own the c-file, so the position is level.
notes.original: White has a space edge on e5, but you have easy development and the c-file, so the position is level.

notes.text: The main plan of attacking the d4 bishop is just as good.
notes.original: The main plan of attacking d4 is just as good.

notes.text: Your knight watches e5; bring the other knight via e7 to c6 and prepare the ...f6 break.
notes.original: The knight heads for the best square at once: from d7 it adds another attacker to d4, keeps e5 under watch and leaves c6 free for your other knight, which will come via e7. You plan ...cxd4 followed by ...Bb4+ to force White to use a knight on d2, then ...Ne7 and ...Ba5 to keep the bishop active on the a5-e1 diagonal. Aim for the knight to land on c6 or f5 and for the ...f6 break to challenge e5.

notes.text: Your check drags the b1 knight to d2, blocking the c1 bishop and leaving d4 short of support.
notes.original: The check is useful because it drags the b1 knight to d2, where it blocks the bishop on c1 and leaves the d4 pawn short of support.

notes.text: Develop, then ...Nc6 follows; don't take on d4 with a knight too early.
notes.original: Develop, and ...Nb6 or ...Nc6 follow. Avoid taking on d4 with the knight too early; the pawn is poisoned only when everything else is ready.

notes.text: White has more space, but d4 is your target and your position is healthy.
notes.original: White has more space, but you have a healthy position and targets on d4; ...Nc6 and ...f6 are your breaks. This is a closed Advance structure with White's pawn chain on d4 and e5 and yours on c5, d5 and e6. White has more space, but d4 is your target. Your plan: finish development with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7, castle short, then keep hitting d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 and prepare the break ...f6 to open the position. White wants to hold d4 with c3 and Nbd2 and to keep the centre closed while his space tells. You meet that by trading pieces and attacking the base of his chain. The risk is playing ...cxd4 too early, which frees his game and gives him the c-file. If White plays Bb5 or Qe2, just castle and keep your knights coordinated.

notes.text: Your queen eyes c4 and offers a queen trade on d3.
notes.original: Hit the c4 square and offer a queen trade.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the d2 knight to the king again.
notes.original: Pin the knight again.

notes.text: Checking first and offering the queens is fine, but a little less precise.
notes.original: Checking first and offering the queens is fine but a little less precise.

notes.text: Checking with the bishop is a bit slower and leaves White a small edge.
notes.original: The check is a bit slower and gives White a small edge.

notes.text: This is another sound way to equalise.
notes.original: Another sound way to equalise.

notes.text: The knights are swapped off, leaving a simplified, level position.
notes.original: You swap off the knight, and the position is simplified and level.

notes.text: White's knight keeps its options open, and you equalize comfortably with normal development.
notes.original: 4.Ne2 develops flexibly, keeping the option of either Ng3 or Nf4 depending on Black's setup. ...and Black equalizes comfortably with normal development.

notes.text: White's c3 pawn supports d4, so your c5 break can be met calmly.
notes.original: Quiet development: c3 supports the d4 pawn so that ...c5 can be met calmly.

notes.text: White's knight on g3 prepares h4-h5 to chase your bishop on g6.
notes.original: Ng3 prepares h4-h5 to chase your bishop on g6. Your answer is ...c5, hitting d4, and Bb5+ is met by ...Nc6. White cannot easily keep an edge.

notes.text: Answer with ...c5 to hit d4; if Bb5+ comes, block with ...Nc6.
notes.original: Ng3 prepares h4-h5 to chase your bishop on g6. Your answer is ...c5, hitting d4, and Bb5+ is met by ...Nc6. White cannot easily keep an edge.

notes.text: White's c3 protects d4, and the knight on g3 controls h5 and f5.
notes.original: White builds a quiet centre: c3 protects d4 and gets ready for Bd3 or Bb5+. The knight on g3 also eyes h5 and f5.

notes.text: White's next h-pawn push would chase your bishop off g6 and gain space with tempo.
notes.original: A thematic thrust: h5 next would chase your bishop off g6 and let White gain space with tempo.

notes.text: White's bishop aims at yours; if it takes on g6, you recapture with the h-pawn.
notes.original: Bd3 aims at your bishop. If White takes on g6 you recapture hxg6 and gain the half-open h-file.

notes.text: Your c-pawn strikes at d4 at once, before White can consolidate with Bd3.
notes.original: You strike at the centre immediately, before White can consolidate with Bd3.

notes.text: Strike at d4 with your c-pawn before White has castled.
notes.original: Strike at d4 before White has castled.

notes.text: Your rook comes to the c-file, eyeing White's c3 and d4 pawns.
notes.original: Your rook comes to the half-open c-file against the d4 and c3 pawns.

notes.text: White gave up a bishop for a knight, so you hold the bishop pair and the game is equal.
notes.original: White has traded off a bishop for a knight, so you hold the bishop pair and a solid structure: equal.

notes.text: The position is level, and your pieces are active.
notes.original: Level, with your pieces active.

notes.text: White gave up the bishop and your rook lands actively on c6; your pieces are better placed.
notes.original: White parts with the bishop and your rook lands actively on c6. Your pieces are better placed and there is nothing to fear.

notes.text: A quieter route that also levels the game.
notes.original: A quieter route that also levels out.

notes.text: Your h-pawn stops White's h-pawn dead, so the knight on g3 can't harass your bishop.
notes.original: Stop the pawn dead. Now h4 is fixed and the knight on g3 has no way to harass your bishop.

notes.text: Your h5 pawn stops White's h-pawn from chasing your bishop on g6.
notes.original: h4 threatens h5 to chase the bishop, so you stop it with ...h5.

notes.text: Answering h4 with ...h5 earlier kept your bishop on g6 from getting trapped.
notes.original: Meeting h4 with ...h5 stops the bishop from getting trapped.

notes.text: Your pieces are active and the pin on your knight is harmless, so equality is easy to hold.
notes.original: The structure is symmetrical with an isolated d5 pawn, but all your pieces are active and the pin is harmless. Equality is easy to hold.

notes.text: White's sharper try is h4-h5 to trap your bishop; answer with ...h5 and you stand fine.
notes.original: The sharper try is h4-h5 to trap your bishop. Answer with ...h5, and you stand fine.

notes.text: White's bishop challenges yours on f5; trading is fine, since your structure stays sound.
notes.original: White develops the bishop to challenge your light-squared bishop on f5. If you trade, the advanced pawn on e5 loses its protector, but your structure remains sound. It is a very common move (played in about 776,000 games).

notes.text: White's setup is quiet and flexible, and the position is level.
notes.original: 4.c3 supports the center quietly before committing the king's knight anywhere, keeping options for both Nf3 and f4 later. ...reaching a level, flexible position.

notes.text: Your knight protects the queen on b6, so a queen trade does not damage your pawn structure.
notes.original: The knight protects your queen on b6, so a queen trade does not damage your pawn structure.

notes.text: Skip the queen trade: play ...h5-h4 to cramp White, then ...Ne7-g6 to hit e5.
notes.original: White offers a queen trade on b6 to open the a-file for you, which does you no harm. Instead of trading, you develop the knight and plan ...h5-h4, which cramps White's kingside so that g4 is never possible. Then ...Ne7-g6 attacks e5.

notes.text: Qb3 offers a queen swap that would leave you passive; keep queens on and prepare ...c5 and ...h5.
notes.original: Qb3 hits b7 and offers a queen swap that would leave you passive. Keep the queens on: the knight supports ...c5 and ...h5, and your queen stays active on b6.

notes.text: Quiet development: your bishop eyes g5, and White's queen on b3 has no real targets.
notes.original: Quiet development. The bishop eyes g5 and prepares castling, since White's queen on b3 has no real targets.

notes.text: Fix the kingside with the h-pawn before developing; it stops White expanding and keeps your knight move and h4 in…
notes.original: Fix the kingside before you develop. This stops White expanding and keeps ...Nd7 and ...h4 in reserve.

notes.text: Your h-pawn controls g4, so g2-g4 cannot harass the bishop on f5.
notes.original: The h-pawn stops g2-g4 from harassing the bishop on f5.

notes.text: Your plan is ...h4, which stops White expanding on the kingside and makes your bishop safe.
notes.original: The plan is ...h5-h4, which stops White from expanding on the kingside and makes your bishop safe on f5.

notes.text: Your h4 pawn takes g3 away from White's knight, so your bishop keeps its diagonal.
notes.original: Now Ng3 is no longer possible either, so the bishop keeps its diagonal.

notes.text: Your knight on g6 pressures the e5 pawn and also guards your h4 pawn.
notes.original: The knight on g6 pressures e5 and also guards the h4 pawn.

notes.text: Pushing to h3 cramps White's kingside and forces a weakening reply.
notes.original: Pushing the pawn to h3 cramps White's kingside and forces a weakening reply.

notes.text: Your knight on g6 hits e5; the position is level, and Rc8 with c5 challenges d4.
notes.original: The h4 pawn has fixed White's kingside and your knight reaches g6, pressuring e5. The position is level, and ...Rc8 with ...c5 is your way to challenge d4.

notes.text: The position stays level and is easy to play.
White shuffles the knight back to prepare f4; your structure is sound with no weaknesses.
notes.original: White shuffles back to prepare f4. You have a sound structure and no weaknesses to worry about.

notes.text: This setup is equally fine for you and keeps the queens on.
notes.original: Equally fine and keeps the queens on.

notes.text: Your h-pawn fixes the kingside so White cannot expand there.
notes.original: Fix the kingside before White can expand.

notes.text: Your knight develops to h6, heading toward f5 to challenge White's bishop on e3.
notes.original: The knight heads to f5 to hit the bishop on e3.

notes.text: This is another safe setup with the same balance.
notes.original: Another safe setup with the same balance.

notes.text: White's c4 here is also fine and keeps everything solid.
notes.original: The bishop move is also fine and keeps everything solid.

notes.text: Your pieces are flexible and your king is safe, so the position is level.
notes.original: Your pieces are flexible and your king is safe. The position is level.

notes.text: Your knight heads for f5 after the bishop trade, to pressure d4, with c5 to follow.
notes.original: You develop the knight to e7 so that, after the bishops are exchanged, the knight can reach f5 and pressure the d4 pawn. The plan is ...Bxd3, then ...h6 to deny the knight on g5, ...Nf5 and finally ...c5 to hit the d4 pawn. Keep the knight flexible and castle short when ready. Avoid retreating with ...Bg6 without a plan, since White can then play h4 with attacking ideas. The position is level.

notes.text: Trading at once is fine; after the queen retakes, aim for c5 and Nc6 with a free game.
notes.original: Trading at once is also fine. After Qxd3 you aim for ...c5 and ...Nc6 with a free game, then ...h6 and ...a6 as useful waiting moves.

notes.text: Your h-pawn denies White's pieces g5 and prepares the knight's trip to f5.
notes.original: Stops any Ng5 or Bg5 tricks and prepares ...Nf5.

notes.text: Your knight on f5 hits d4; bring the other knight to d7, castle, then challenge with c5.
notes.original: Your knight sits happily on f5, you hold the e4 and d5 squares and your structure is sound, so the game is equal with plenty of play for you. This is a closed French-style position where White has more space with pawns on e5 and d4, but your knight on f5 attacks d4 and you hold the e4 and d5 squares. Your plan: bring the other knight to d7 to hit e5, play ...Be7 and castle short, then challenge d4 with ...c5. White wants Nc3 and Ne4 to reach d6, or Qb3 to hit your pawn on b7. If Qb3 comes, defend with ...Qb6 and keep your pieces coordinated. The mistake is leaving b7 hanging while you develop. If White plays Bd2, continue ...Nd7.

notes.text: White develops toward d4 and the position stays balanced.
notes.original: 4.Be3 develops toward c5/d4 immediately, preparing a later Nd2-Nf3 setup without blocking the c-pawn. ...and the position stays balanced.

notes.text: Your knight hits the e5 pawn and backs up the ...f6 break against White's space.
notes.original: You add a defender for the ...f6 break: the pawn on e5 is the base of White's space, so attack it and the advantage becomes a liability.

notes.text: Your queen is awkward on b6, so prepare ...f6 to chip at e5 and send it back to d8.
notes.original: Your queen on b6 is awkward: c5 will gain a tempo on it, and the bishop on f5 is exposed to Nc3-b5. So you prepare ...f6 to chip away at e5 and let the queen go back to d8. After the exchange on f6, c5 is not dangerous.

notes.text: White spent time covering b2; your knight supports d5 and prepares the usual ...f6 lever against e5.
notes.original: Be3 and Qc1 exist only to cover b2 against your queen, so White has already spent time before c4 hits d5. Developing the knight supports d5 and prepares the usual ...f6 lever against e5.

notes.text: White's c4 pawn hits your d5 pawn, and your knight meets that without blocking the queen.
notes.original: White's c4 questions your d5 pawn while Qc1 keeps b2 safe. The knight supports d5 and keeps the queen free.

notes.text: Hit the head of White's pawn chain at once, before White has a developed centre.
notes.original: The immediate lever. Be3 and Qc1 only protect b2, so you attack the head of the chain at once before White has a developed centre.

notes.text: Strike at the head of the pawn chain right away with your f-pawn.
notes.original: Strike at the head of the pawn chain right away.

notes.text: Recapture with the knight so your pieces stay compact.
Your queen leaves b6, your pieces develop smoothly, and White's c5 pawn no longer pressures d5.
notes.original: The queen must leave b6, but your pieces develop smoothly and White's c5 pawn has given up the d5 pressure.

notes.text: White's c5 gained time on your queen, but it gave up control of d4 and b4, so the retreat costs…
notes.original: c5 gains time on your queen, but it also gives up control of d4 and b4, so the retreat costs you very little.

notes.text: c5 gains a tempo on your queen but gives up control of d4 and b4, so the retreat costs little.
notes.original: c5 gains a tempo on your queen, but it also gives up control of d4 and b4, so the retreat costs you little.

notes.text: You have a comfortable game, and your d5 pawn is still intact.
notes.original: Black has a comfortable game with the d5 pawn intact.

notes.text: The position is level.
notes.original: Level position.

notes.text: Castle to safety, then undermine the c5 pawn with b6; White has no lasting edge.
notes.original: You are fully developed with a safe king after castling, and the c5 pawn can later be undermined with ...b6. White has no lasting edge.

notes.text: You reach the same position by transposition.
notes.original: The same position by transposition.

notes.text: You are fully developed and can castle, while ...b6 can later undermine the c5 pawn.
notes.original: You are fully developed and can castle, while c5 can later be undermined with ...b6.

notes.text: Castle for an easy position, then undermine White's c5 pawn with b6.
notes.original: After castling you have an easy position. The c5 pawn can later be undermined with ...b6.

notes.text: Grabbing the pawn is possible, but it costs time and White's pieces gain ground.
notes.original: Grabbing the pawn is possible but costs time and White's pieces gain ground.

notes.text: Grabbing the c4 pawn was playable, but it cost you time.
notes.original: Grabbing the pawn is playable but you lose time.

notes.text: Grabbing the c4 pawn also works, but White gets time against your queenside pawns, so it is slightly less clean.
notes.original: Grabbing c4 also works and the knight lands on d5, but White gets time against your queenside pawns, so it is a shade less clean.

notes.text: Keep developing normally; don't react to a threat White hasn't played yet.
notes.original: Simple and solid - Black keeps developing normally rather than reacting to a threat that hasn't been played yet.

notes.text: White's g4 hits your bishop and expands on the kingside, aiming for a strong attack later.
notes.original: g4 strikes at the centre immediately and expands on the kingside. The extended pawns are useful later, since White will proceed with a powerful kingside attack. The question is what happens if the attention shifts and Black is the one attacking.

notes.text: White's pawn storm gains kingside space, but it commits the structure and can leave e5 and f4 weak.
notes.original: Now White follows up with the pawn storm, gaining space on the kingside at the cost of real structural commitments (the g- and h-files will be easier for Black to use later, and e5/f4 can become weak).

notes.text: White plans h5 next to trap your bishop on g6.
notes.original: White will usually harass the light-squared bishop further, and here is clearly planning to trap it with h5.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Be3 develops first, supports the d4 pawn and prepares queenside castling before h4.
notes.original: 7.Be3 develops before committing to h4, supporting d4 and preparing queenside castling.

notes.text: Against White's g4 and h4 pawn push, hit the centre with ...c5 and meet h4 with ...h5.
notes.original:
Idea: White throws the kingside pawns forward with g4 and h4. Drop the bishop back to g6, hit the centre at once with ...c5, and meet h4 with ...h5. Counterattack in the centre rather than wait.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 Bg6 6.Nge2 c5 7.h4 h5
Watch out: ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Bxf2+? loses material on move 12.
Next: 🔵 13 continues the Advance Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 07. Model game: 🟡 Game 04.

notes.text: Your h-pawn stops White's h-pawn; ...h6 would let White castle long and attack your king.
notes.original: ...h5 is needed because White is going to expand on the queenside. White would usually castle queenside and attack Black's king if ...h6!? is played instead of ...h5, and Black may have to sacrifice a pawn.

notes.text: White answers with Be3 and then f4, which gives White a comfortable position.
notes.original: h6!? Looks like a safer option but in case you missed Be3 followed by f4! Would give white a very feasible position indeed.

notes.text: You can't leave the bishop on g6: the knight would take it and your kingside would suffer.
notes.original: Black cannot leave the bishop alone on g6, since the knight would take it and Black's kingside would deteriorate further.

notes.text: You gave up the h-pawn on purpose; it opens the h-file for your rook.
notes.original: Black gives up the h-pawn on purpose. It opens the h-file for Black's rook, and the pawn would have come under pressure anyway.

notes.text: Your bishop is safe on h7; strike at d4 right away with the c-pawn or after developing the knight.
notes.original: The key tactical point: White grabs the h5-pawn, but the bishop is completely safe on h7 and Black has two move orders here that both work well, as the game below shows (Aabling Thomsen vs Schandorff, Denmark 2010). The common idea in both: meet Nxh5 with an immediate strike on d4, either right away with ...cxd4 or after first developing the knight to c6.

notes.text: White pushes g5 at once, trying to shut your bishop on h7 out of the game.
notes.original: 9.g5 pushes through immediately rather than trading on g6 first, trying to lock the bishop out of the game entirely.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Take on d4, then develop with the knights and keep your king flexible.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays 4.Nc3 or 4.g4 against 3...Bf5.
Idea: The same 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 set-up as 🔵 12, but here you take on d4 with 9...cxd4. Develop with ...Nc6 and ...Ne7 and keep your king flexible. The 4.g4 lines are covered at move 4.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 Bg6 6.Nge2 c5 7.h4 h5 8.Nf4 Bh7 9.Nxh5 cxd4
Watch out: ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 4 to 6.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White had to take on c5; otherwise ...cxd4 gives you the better game.
notes.original: White had to exchange on c5, for two reasons. The knight on c3 stops him from supporting d4 with c3, and if he leaves the pawn alone Black plays ...cxd4 and gets the better game.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Bb5 loosens White's grip on the centre; Bg2 was more accurate.
notes.original: A necessary move to suppress black's attack on the center. Loosening up the grip eh? Bg2 is more accurate.

notes.text: Don't grab on e5: White's knight takes g7 with check and you end up losing.
notes.original: Trap: 12...Nxe5? 13.Nxg7+ Kf8 14.Nxe6+ fxe6 15.Bxd8 Rxd8 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on e5 with the knight falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 12...Nxe5? 13.Nxg7+ Kf8 14.Nxe6+ fxe6 15.Bxd8 Rxd8 and Black is losing.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Take back with the f-pawn, then bring your knight to b4 to hit c2.
notes.original: The knight on g7 is nearly trapped, so White cashes it in for the e6 pawn with check. The plan is to fix your structure with fxe6 and then use the queen on d2 to trade bishops. You have the knight on b4 to hit c2. The material is gone and the position is balanced.

notes.text: You keep the slightly better pawn structure.
A kingside pawn storm is tempting, but it leaves White worse.
notes.original: A kingside pawn storm is tempting but it leaves White worse.

notes.text: White does best to take on c6 with check, easing your pressure on the centre.
notes.original: White does best to exchange bishop for queen to loosen up black's pressure on the center.

notes.text: White wins a pawn but loses the knight: after ...Kf8, Nh5, ...d4, the move ...Qa5 forks king and bishop.
notes.original: This wins a pawn for White but loses the knight in exchange. Black's tactic is ...Kf7, forcing Nh5, then ...d4 to evict the knight, and ...Qa5 wins the bishop, forking the king on e1 and the bishop on b5.

notes.text: You recapture with the queen and keep your central pressure.
notes.original: The threat now is ...d5, and Black would be winning.

notes.text: White's queen move is the only good way to hold the position together.
notes.original: Qf3 is forced because of the ...d5 threat; it is the only good move that holds for White.

notes.text: Castling long is the most accurate move; ...Be4 is also playable and about as good.
notes.original: 13...O-O-O is the most accurate move. The alternative 13...Be4 is also playable: it is about as good.

notes.text: Black is winning.
This knight move is playable, but putting the knight on e7 instead would have been more accurate.
notes.original: Playable, but Ne7 is more accurate.

notes.text: With White's dark-squared bishop gone, your bishop tactic on e4 now works and White is lost.
notes.original: The tactic Be4 does not work only because of the dark-squared bishop, which can come to help in an assault. With that bishop gone, White is lost.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Recapturing with the f-pawn is White's best try, stronger than taking with the bishop.
notes.original: White's strongest try here, stronger than Bxe3.

notes.text: You control the open d-file, White's king is stuck and the kingside is weak.
notes.original: Black's pressure is so strong that White can hardly hold: Black dominates the d-file, White's king is stuck and the kingside is weak.

notes.text: White wants to open the h-file, but you take the bishop on e3 and swing your rook to d2.
notes.original: White wants to open the h-file for the rook on h1 against your rook on h8, and the knight on g7 supports that attack. But you take the bishop on e3 and bring the rook into the seventh rank with ...Rd2. White's pawns on e3 and c2 become targets.

notes.text: Your king is safe on b8 and all your pieces are working.
Your queen takes the bishop on a7 with check, keeping your big advantage.
notes.original: Taking the a7 pawn only wins a pawn for a moment, since the bishop falls.

notes.text: Black is winning.
White offers a rook trade to ease the pressure, but your rook on d2 is your most dangerous attacker.
notes.original: White wants to trade a pair of rooks to relieve the pressure on the second rank; your rook on d2 hits c2 and f2, so it is the most dangerous attacker. After the rooks go off, the queen trade on f1 leaves you with the better pieces and an ending White cannot save.

notes.text: You win the queen trade and keep a big advantage.
notes.original: You win the exchange of queens and keep a big plus.

notes.text: Your bishop takes the queen on f2 with check, so White loses material.
notes.original: Kicking the queen with the pawn opens the g1-a7 diagonal for the check and White loses material.

notes.text: White is losing: your pawn on e2 and queen on f3 are too much to handle.
notes.original: White is losing: the pawn on e2 and the queen on f3 are too much to handle.

notes.text: White had to remove the e2 pawn; retake with the queen, then ...Be3 and d-file threats decide.
notes.original: White has to remove the advanced pawn that attacks f1 and prepares to queen. Your queen on f3 and the rook on d8 are ready to attack the king on g1, and the g4 pawn is a free target. After ...Qxe2 the threats on the d-file and Be3 are decisive.

notes.text: You win an extra piece and keep the attack.
notes.original: You get an extra piece and keep the attack.

notes.text: Your rook checks on the g-file, and White's queen sacrifice for a pawn leads to a forced loss.
notes.original: Giving up the queen for a pawn leads to a forced loss.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Trade off the c3 knight, then push d4 to open the long diagonal against White's king.
notes.original: Your plan is to remove the knight on c3 so you can play ...d4 and open the long diagonal against White's king, since you are down material. The checks on h1 and e4 keep you in the game.

notes.text: Your queen checks keep the position level.
notes.original: The queen checks keep the position level.

notes.text: Retreating your bishop passively lets White's extra material count, giving White a clear edge.
notes.original: Retreating the bishop passively makes White's extra material count, which gives White an edge.

notes.text: Your king is safer and your pieces are more active, so you stay a little better.
notes.original: Your king is safer and the pieces are more active, so you stay a little better.

notes.text: Your rook takes with check; White's natural queen move earlier lost to the bishop check on b4.
notes.original: This natural queen move just loses to the check on b4.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the knight on c3, and your queen's diagonal now hits the rook on h1.
notes.original: Attacks the rook and the knight!

notes.text: Take on c3, then bring your queen to f3 and bishop to e4 to threaten mate on g2.
notes.original: White castles to save the rook from the diagonal, but the d4 fork gets there first. After ...dxc3 you add the pressure on f2, and ...Qf3 with ...Be4 would threaten mate on g2. White grabs the g7 pawn but his queen is too far from his own king.

notes.text: Your extra pieces tell here, and you are winning.
notes.original: The extra pieces tell.

notes.text: The Nd5 deflection fails: you take the knight, everything stays defended, and White is just a piece down.
notes.original: Nd5 tries to deflect the queen from the long diagonal, but you take it and everything stays defended, so White just loses a piece.

notes.text: Black is winning.
White's knight hits your queen, but you take on b2 and keep the queen trade on your terms.
notes.original: White attacks the queen and wants to trade it so that the extra material (a piece for you, a few pawns for White) becomes less relevant. But you take b2 and keep the queen trade on your terms. Then the passed d-pawn runs and the bishops dominate.

notes.text: Your d3 pawn cramps White, and you are a bishop up.
notes.original: The d3 pawn cramps White and you have an extra bishop.

notes.text: This defensive try only delays the loss, and you stay winning.
notes.original: Defending with the bishop only delays the loss.

notes.text: Be3 costs White a tempo; now b2 is weak and ...Qa5 would breach White's position.
notes.original: 10.Be3 is another option, but it costs a tempo. After 10...cxd4 the b2 pawn is weak and ...Qa5 would breach White's position.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Your queen hits b2; castle long next and aim at b2 and a2, since your lead in development outweighs White's…
notes.original: White is a pawn up and the knight on h5 eyes g7, but your queen on b4 attacks the b2 pawn and the d4 bishop. After the bishop retreats you castle long and aim at b2 and a2. White's extra pawn means little compared with your lead in development.

notes.text: Your queen picks up pawns while your pieces are active.
notes.original: The queen picks up pawns while your pieces are active.

notes.text: Your knight joins in; White's greedy pawn grab cannot make up for lagging development.
notes.original: The greedy pawn grab cannot save White, who lags in development.

notes.text: Had White taken on h5 earlier, ...dxc3 and the bishop trade would leave you winning.
notes.original: Trap: 10.Nxh5? dxc3 11.Bb5+ Nc6 12.Bxc6+ bxc6 13.bxc3 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on h5 with the knight falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 10.Nxh5? dxc3 11.Bb5+ Nc6 12.Bxc6+ bxc6 13.bxc3 and White is losing.

notes.text: White's g5 plan is too slow; your central counterplay with ...cxd4 comes faster.
notes.original: 9.g5 pushes through immediately rather than trading on g6 first, trying to lock the bishop out of the game entirely. ...and Black's central counterplay with ...cxd4 proves faster.

notes.text: White's rook lift comes too late, because your central counterplay is faster.
notes.original: Trap: 10.Nxh5? dxc3 11.Bb5+ Nc6 12.Bxc6+ bxc6 13.bxc3 and White is losing. ...and Black's central counterplay with ...cxd4 proves faster.

notes.text: White wants the rook on b3 to hit b7.
notes.original: White is trying to use the rook on h3 to swing to b3 and hit b7, while the knights on d4 and f4 are well placed. You develop with ...Ne7 and ...Nbc6 so you can trade off the strong knights with ...Nf5. After the exchanges on f5 you keep a clear edge.

notes.text: Develop your knights, then trade White's strong knight with ...Nf5 to keep a clear edge.
notes.original: White is trying to use the rook on h3 to swing to b3 and hit b7, while the knights on d4 and f4 are well placed. You develop with ...Ne7 and ...Nbc6 so you can trade off the strong knights with ...Nf5. After the exchanges on f5 you keep a clear edge.

notes.text: Your knight develops and supports ...Nbc6 and ...Nf5, so White's rook lift comes too late.
notes.original: The knight develops and supports ...Nbc6 and ...Nf5, so White's rook lift on h3 comes too late.

notes.text: White's rook eyes b7, so your queen covers it and keeps pressing the e5 pawn.
notes.original: Rb3 hits b7, so cover it and keep the pressure on e5.

notes.text: You have the more active pieces and a safe king.
Your pieces are better placed and White's rook lift achieved nothing, so you are clearly better.
notes.original: Your pieces are better placed and White's rook lift on h3 has not led to anything. You are clearly better.
