notes.text: White has won the h5 pawn back, so you are only a little better.
notes.original: This allows White to win the h5 pawn back, so you are only a little better.

notes.text: This greedy try is less accurate, because White gets counterplay.
notes.original: A greedy try that is less accurate, since White gets counterplay.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
You regained the pawn, and your bishop now offers to trade White's best piece, the dark bishop.
notes.original: You regain the pawn immediately, because White's pawn on c5 is attacked by both the bishop and the knight, and trading the dark bishops removes White's best piece. Then ...Ne4 trades off the strong knight, and Bg2 faces the bishop on e4.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge now the bishops are gone, but your position is safe.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge with the bishop pair gone, but the position is safe for you.

notes.text: Recapturing with the knight lets White open the position against you.
notes.original: Taking with the knight lets White open the position against you.

notes.text: Black is winning.
White prepares Nb5, but your queen and bishop both press on f2 beside the king.
notes.original: White castles and prepares Nb5, which threatens Nc7+ forking king and rook. You answer with ...Nge7 and ...O-O, then ...Nxb4 hits the loose queenside. Your queen on h4 and bishop on c5 keep everything pointed at f2 and the king.

notes.text: You are a pawn up and still have the attack.
notes.original: You are a pawn up with an attack.

notes.text: White's natural queen move walked into the knight jump to d4 and the trade on f2.
notes.original: A natural queen move walks into the knight jump to d4 and the trade on f2.

notes.text: You hold the balance in this line.
notes.original: 7.Be3 develops before committing to h4, supporting d4 and preparing queenside castling. ...and Black holds the balance.

notes.text: Your knight heads for f5 to hit the d4 knight and the e3 bishop, then you regain c5.
notes.original: Your idea is to regain c5 and keep the extra pawn on g4 under pressure. The knight heads for f5 to hit the d4 knight and the e3 bishop. The bishop trade on d3 lets your queenside develop with ...Nc6 and ...Bxc5.

notes.text: Your knight guards the g4 pawn and heads for f5, hitting White's knight and bishop.
notes.original: The knight guards the g4 pawn and heads for f5 where it hits the knight on d4 and the bishop on e3.

notes.text: Your knight challenges the one on d4 and prepares to take on c5 with the bishop.
notes.original: Challenge the knight on d4 and prepare ...Bxc5.

notes.text: You regain the pawn, and the opened files are fine for you.
notes.original: You regain the pawn and the opened files are fine for you.

notes.text: You have won back the c5 pawn and White's kingside pawns are wrecked, so you are slightly better.
notes.original: You recover the c5 pawn and White's pawn structure on the kingside is wrecked. Black is slightly better.

notes.text: This also holds, but gives White extra counterplay on the g-file.
notes.original: This also holds, but gives White the extra counterplay on the g-file.

notes.text: White wins material back with Nxe6 tactics, so you lose some of your advantage.
notes.original: A tricky line where White returns material with Nxe6 tactics and you lose some of your advantage.

notes.text: Keeping the tension with a later ...c5 break in mind is equally playable, a matter of style.
notes.original: Keeping the central tension instead, with a later ...c5 break in mind, is equally playable - a matter of style rather than necessity.

notes.text: Simply take the pawn; White must spend real time winning it back.
notes.original: Simplest and most reliable response - just take the pawn. White has to spend real time winning it back, and Black gets a free, comfortable structure in return.

notes.text: Against a3, take the pawn and then hit the centre with c5.
notes.original: A well-prepared opponent may play a3; Plan B is to take the pawn and then play ...c5.

notes.text: White keeps its pawn structure intact instead of letting you damage it.
notes.original: White does not want to ruin the pawn structure.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White opens the position for its bishop pair; you answer by stopping h4 and Nh3 with h5 and f6.
notes.original: White opens the position to use the bishop pair, and queens come off on d5. Then h4 and Nh3 aim to shut your bishop out with g-pawn play. You neutralise this with ...h5 and ...f6.

notes.text: White has a small edge with the bishops, but your position is solid.
Offering the queen trade is another try for White.
notes.original: Offering the queen trade is another try.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White wants g4 to trap your f5 bishop; answer with h6 so it can retreat to h7.
notes.original: White wants to play g4 and trap the bishop on f5. You answer with ...h6 so the bishop can retreat to h7. The a3 move then forces you to decide about the bishop on b4. After the trade on c3 the pawn break ...c5 gives you fine play.

notes.text: You keep a slight edge.
The position is equal.
White's queen hits your a8 rook and the bishop pins your d7 knight.
notes.original: White has grabbed b7 and now attacks the rook on a8 while pinning the knight on d7. Your reply is ...Rc8, moving the rook out of danger and unpinning the knight indirectly, and then ...Bc5 and ...Bd3 harass the white pieces that wandered out.

notes.text: Everything is balanced here.
notes.original: Everything is balanced.

notes.text: Taking a second pawn is risky for White and gives you play.
Your bishop stays active in the centre; after f3 kicks it again, White has loosened e3 and the kingside.
notes.original:
4...Be4 keeps the bishop active and centralized rather than retreating passively. The point is that after 5.f3, the bishop is kicked again, but Black has already provoked White into weakening the e3-square and slightly loosening the kingside.
Trap: 4...Qa5+? 5.Bd2 Qb6 6.gxf5 Qxd4 7.Nf3 Qe4+ and Black is losing.

notes.text: Bg6 is the natural retreat: the bishop stays on its diagonal and avoids a further f3 tempo.
notes.original: 4...Bg6 is the most natural retreat - the bishop stays on the same diagonal and steps back one square, without inviting the further f3 tempo-gain that 4...Be4 allows.

notes.text: The modest retreat tucks the bishop in, avoids the tactics and keeps things simple.
notes.original: 4...Bd7 is the most modest retreat - the bishop gives up its active diagonal entirely and tucks in next to the king, but in exchange Black avoids all the immediate tactics of the other two retreats and keeps the position simple.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 4...Qa5+? 5.Bd2 Qb6 6.gxf5 Qxd4 7.Nf3 Qe4+ and Black is losing.

notes.text: Retreating the bishop is right; the tempting ...Qa5+ instead is a trap that leaves you losing.
notes.original: Trap: 5...Qa5+? 6.Bd2 Qb6 7.fxe4 Qxd4 8.Nc3 e6 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Your bishop retreats to g6; avoid the tempting queen check on a5, which loses.
notes.original: Trap: 5...Qa5+? 6.Bd2 Bxc2 7.Qxc2 Qb6 8.e6 Qxd4 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 5...Qa5+? 6.Bd2 Qb6 7.fxe4 Qxd4 8.Nc3 e6 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 5...Qa5+? 6.Bd2 Bxc2 7.Qxc2 Qb6 8.e6 Qxd4 and Black is losing.

notes.text: White sacrifices the e-pawn to open the centre and f-file; you can take it or decline with the queen.
notes.original: The thematic pawn sacrifice of this whole system: White offers the e5-pawn to rip open the center and the f-file while Black's king is still uncastled. Black has two ways to answer it, both fully playable.

notes.text: White sacrifices a pawn to rip open your kingside before your bishop on g6 can retreat safely.
notes.original: 7.e6 sacrifices a pawn to rip open Black's kingside before the bishop on g6 can retreat safely.

notes.text: You have enough compensation for the pawn; keep your light-squared bishop to keep the initiative.
notes.original: With the open h-file and the bishop pair, Black has enough compensation for the pawn. The pawn is a sacrifice for the initiative, so keep the light-squared bishop to maintain both the initiative and the bishop pair.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White develops the bishop to d3 and the knight to e2 to harass your bishop on h4.
notes.original: You took h4 with check. The tempting Rxh4 fails to Qxh4+, so the king has to move. Kd2 is the best square because Ke2 lets you take on h5 with the rook. White then develops with Bd3 and Ne2 to harass your bishop on h4, while you play ...Nh6 and ...c5.

notes.text: Everything is balanced here.
notes.original: Everything is balanced.

notes.text: White's king step to e2 allowed ...Rxh5 and leaves you slightly better.
notes.original: The king step to e2 allows ...Rxh5 and leaves you slightly better.

notes.text: After accepting the pawn accurately, you are already better.
notes.original: 7.e6 sacrifices a pawn to rip open Black's kingside before the bishop on g6 can retreat safely. ...and Black is already better after accepting the pawn accurately.

notes.text: The gambit is over and material is level; White's pawns on f3, g4 and h4 are loose.
notes.original: The e6 gambit is over and material is level, but you own the bishop pair and White's pawns on f3, g4 and h4 are loose. White develops the bishop to e3 and brings the queen to d2, while you answer with ...Nd7 and ...e5 to open the centre. After ...hxg4 the h-file is yours too.

notes.text: Now your central pawn mass is strong.
Offering the queen trade does not solve White's problems.
With the h-pawns fixed, g4 is a long-term hole for White; trade your light bishop and break with c5.
notes.original: Black's plan in this whole system: the h4/h5 pawns are now fixed, which means the g4-square is permanently weak for White and the h4-pawn itself is a long-term target once rooks and knights get active. Black's recipe is almost always the same regardless of which fifth move White chooses: trade off the light-squared bishop or reroute it to a safe square (h7 or g6), meet the center with the freeing ...c5 break at the right moment, and look to land a knight on f5 or use the half-open h-file/g4 hole in the middlegame. None of this requires memorizing forcing lines - it is a structural plan, and the two main branches below (5.Bd3 and 5.c4) both show it in practice.

notes.text: Your h-pawn move gives the bishop an escape square on h7.
notes.original: Instead, black makes an escape square for the bishop with h6. Also playable is h5, but I prefer the less committal h6, and so does Stockfish.

notes.text: Bg5 is a real theoretical try, but with precise play you equalise comfortably.
notes.original: A real try from established theory, not just a blunder. The bishop develops actively and rules out ...Qb6 for a move, but the critical test below shows Black equalises comfortably with precise play.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White offers to trade light-squared bishops: very safe, but it gives up any hope of a quick attack.
notes.original: The calmer, more positional approach - White offers the trade of light-squared bishops rather than letting Black keep the good bishop. Very safe for White, but also gives up any hope of a quick attack.

notes.text: White develops and prepares c4 to hit your centre, while the h4 pawn supports a kingside attack.
notes.original: White finally develops and prepares c4 to hit your centre, while the pawn on h4 stays as support for an attack on the kingside. It is a common move after this pawn push. So White wants to open the centre while you have not castled.

notes.text: White's c4 hits your d5 pawn, opening the centre while your king is still uncastled.
notes.original: The sharper, more aggressive try - open the center immediately while Black's king is still uncastled, rather than trading pieces off.

notes.text: Your queen strikes at b2 and d4 at once.
notes.original: Striking at b2 and d4 at once, exactly as in the simpler 5.Bd3 and 5.c4 lines.

notes.text: Bd3 is White's only real try; defending with b3 is well met by ...e6 and ...c5.
notes.original: White's only real try. Defending b2 with 6.b3?! is well met by 6...e6 followed by ...c5, which is very bad for White.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Retaking is right; checking on a5 with the queen instead would leave you clearly worse.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Qb6 8.Bxf5 e6 9.Bd3 Qxd4 and Black is clearly worse.

notes.text: Simply trade bishops; grabbing d4 with the queen leads to complications you don't need.
notes.original: Simplest. Grabbing the pawn with 6...Qxd4?! allows 7.Nf3 Qg4, and after the trades 8.Bxf5 Qxf5 White castles with 9.O-O, which produces the sort of tangle Black's opponents would gladly steer clear of; Black may well be fine there too, but there is no need to go looking for complications when the position is already comfortable.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are clearly worse.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Qb6 8.Bxf5 e6 9.Bd3 Qxd4 and Black is clearly worse.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn supports d5 and reinforces the centre.
notes.original: ...e6 reinforces the central pawn.

notes.text: Your queen chases White's queen off d3 and offers a trade, a typical Caro-Kann resource.
notes.original: The point: the queen chases White's queen off d3 and offers a trade, a thoroughly Caro-Kannesque resource. (7...Qxb2?! is dangerous here because of 8.e6!, hitting f7 with real force; stick with 7...Qa6.)

notes.text: This move order avoids heavy theory; the c4 main line runs into well-known theory after ...c5.
notes.original: This move order avoids heavy theory: c4 is the main line but runs into well-known theory after ...c5. Both are covered here, but this set-up is the one preferred. c5 was stronger.

notes.text: The queen move is playable, but ...c5 was stronger.
notes.original: c5 was stronger.

notes.text: The position is equal.
A queen trade would only allow Nxa6, and an endgame is also acceptable for Caro-Kann players.
notes.original: A queen trade would only allow Nxa6, which would favour both sides; still, an endgame is also acceptable for Caro-Kann players.

notes.text: White's c4 blocks the queen diagonal and hits your d5 pawn; ...Bb4 then ...c5 and ...Nc6 answer.
notes.original: Your queen on a6 faces the queen on d3, so c4 blocks that diagonal and hits d5. After ...Bb4 pins the knight on d2, b3 supports the pawn, and you counter with ...c5 and ...Nc6.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's pawn asks your bishop to decide; trade on d2, then play ...Nd7, ...Rac8 and ...Qb6.
notes.original: White asks the bishop on b4 to decide. After ...Bxd2 Nxd2 White has traded your active bishop and plans c5 to gain space. Your plan is ...Nd7 and ...Rac8, followed by ...Qb6 to hit the c5 pawn.

notes.text: White has more space but no clear attack.
The ...c5 break is your main resource in this line.
notes.original: The ...c5 break is your main resource.

notes.text: After Nd2 your main reply is ...c5; White usually expects c3, so this sharper c4 is covered with extra lines.
notes.original: The Tal Variation has been expanded with a new idea: after Nd2 the main recommendation is ...c5. White typically expects to play c3; the sharper c5 is highly theoretical, so extra variations have been added to cover it.

notes.text: Your a-pawn controls b4, so White can't comfortably play b4.
notes.original: This discourages White from playing b4.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's a-pawn stops your ...a4 and fixes your a5 pawn.
notes.original: White stops ...a4 and fixes your a5 pawn. The idea is to trade knights and take the d4 square. You castle and take the c-file with ...Rfc8, so queen and rooks come into play.

notes.text: Castle, then put your rook on the c-file so queen and rooks join the game.
notes.original: White stops ...a4 and fixes your a5 pawn. The idea is to trade knights and take the d4 square. You castle and take the c-file with ...Rfc8, so queen and rooks come into play.

notes.text: You hold comfortably here.
notes.original: You hold comfortably.

notes.text: Taking on c5 instead is also level.
notes.original: Taking on c5 is also level.

notes.text: The rook attacks your queen, but you can take on d4, trade queens and stay two pawns up.
notes.original: 10.Rb1 attacks the queen, but 10...Qxd4 is possible: the queens come off and Black is up two pawns.

notes.text: Nb3 is a highly theoretical line; the central tension is complicated, so take care to avoid errors.
notes.original: Nb3 is another variation, a highly theoretical line in the Tal Variation. The pressure on the centre from both sides makes it very complicated, so Black must take care to avoid errors in the opening.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
You are two pawns up; push ...d4 to gain space while White's queen holds things together.
notes.original: White is two pawns down and calls on the queen to hold the position together. You push ...d4 to take space from the knight on f3, then trade White's dangerous bishop with ...Bxg5 so your king can walk to e7.

notes.text: You hold on to the extra pawns.
notes.original: You hold the extra pawns.

notes.text: The e6 break is White's only way to open lines, but you stay ahead.
Your knight aims for b4 next.
notes.original: ...Nc6! Black's plan is ...Nb4, forking the king and the rook.

notes.text: You can't play Nb4 here, because White's queen would answer with check on b5.
notes.original: Black cannot play Nb4 because of Qb5+! A horrible position for white in this particular position.

notes.text: Taking a2 wins a second pawn; White is better developed but can't easily use it.
notes.original: 12...Qxa2 grabs a second pawn. White has more pieces developed, but cannot easily make that count.

notes.text: Taking on c5 works because a queen check on a5 would let White win back pieces.
notes.original: Bxc5 is made possible because Qa5+! with a fork on the king and knight would give his pieces back.

notes.text: White must cover d4, since your knight could land there later.
notes.original: White needs to cover up the d4 pawn since the knight would later land in there.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's rook hits your queen and wants the open c-file; your pieces are tangled.
notes.original: White hits the queen at once and wants to use the open c-file, since you are two pawns up but your pieces are tangled in the centre. You give the check with ...Qb5+ and then bring the knight into play with ...Nh6, aiming to trade queens.

notes.text: Check with your queen on b5, then bring the knight to h6, aiming to trade queens.
notes.original: White hits the queen at once and wants to use the open c-file, since you are two pawns up but your pieces are tangled in the centre. You give the check with ...Qb5+ and then bring the knight into play with ...Nh6, aiming to trade queens.

notes.text: It is an equal, double-edged position.
White's e6 push does not work.
notes.original: The e6 push does not work.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White's rook supports the d4 break, which would open the c-file against your queenside.
notes.original: White has traded a pawn for activity. The rook on c1 supports the central break d4, which would open the c-file against your queenside. You respond with ...a5 to stop b4, develop the knight on d7 and regroup the bishop to f8. You are a pawn up, so a calm position is enough.

notes.text: Stop b4 with ...a5, develop the knight to d7 and regroup the bishop to f8.
notes.original: White has traded a pawn for activity. The rook on c1 supports the central break d4, which would open the c-file against your queenside. You respond with ...a5 to stop b4, develop the knight on d7 and regroup the bishop to f8. You are a pawn up, so a calm position is enough.

notes.text: You keep the extra pawn and a safe position.
notes.original: You keep an extra pawn and a safe position.

notes.text: A quieter choice than the queen check: you simply finish development in a safe, well-tested structure.
notes.original: The quieter alternative to 6...Qa5+ - simply completing development. A very safe, thoroughly tested structure. Both choices are fine; 6...Qa5+ is included in more depth above because it leads to a clearer middlegame.

notes.text: Stop the h-pawn with h5, trade bishops, check with your queen, then play e6.
notes.original:
Idea: Meet 4.h4 with 4...h5 so the pawn can't go any further. Trade bishops with ...Bxd3, then play ...Qa5+ and ...e6. The Bayonet Attack, 4.g4, has its own branch at move 4.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.h4 h5 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.Qxd3 Qa5+
Watch out: ...Qxd2+? loses material on moves 7 to 8. ...Nxd4? loses material on moves 10 to 12.
See also: 🟢 07 covers more of the Advance Variation. Plans: 🟠 Plan 04, 🟠 Plan 07. Model games: 🟡 Game 07, 🟡 Game 08.

notes.text: Your queen checks the king, gaining a tempo and keeping your options open.
notes.original: The critical, most-tested continuation - and the one both real games below actually chose over the quieter 6...e6. The check gains a tempo and keeps options open for where the queen and king want to be.

notes.text: White's knight supports d4 and prepares c3 or Bg5, keeping a slight lead in development.
notes.original: A natural developing move that supports d4 and prepares c3 or Bg5. White keeps a slight lead in development.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge here.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: With the queens off, you take on d4 and equalise.
notes.original: If the queens come off you hit d4 and equalise.

notes.text: Develop the bishop with ...Bg4, then ...Nh6-f5, and strike at d4 with ...c5.
notes.original: You support the d5 pawn and open a retreat for your bishop on f5. Your plan is ...Bg4 or ...Be7, ...Nh6 and ...Nf5 to put a piece on f5, and ...c5 to attack d4. Avoid ...Qb6 too early, which loses time.

notes.text: White's queen and bishop target b7 and e6; cover b7 with ...Qc8 or ...Nc6.
notes.original: After the queen comes to b3 you play ...Qc8 or ...Nc6 to cover b7 and keep your king in the middle for one more move. White's other approach is 6.Bd3 instead of c4, and then you take the bishop with ...Bxd3 and settle into a solid structure. You are fine and roughly equal, but be careful about the b7 pawn. This is a semi-open position after the h-pawn push: your pawns on c6, e6 and h5 face White's centre, and your bishops are active. Your king may stay in the centre for a move or two. Your plan: protect b7 with ...Qc8, bring the knight with ...Nf5 or ...Nd7, trade bishops on g5 with ...Bxg5 when useful, and then castle short. White wants to attack b7 and e6 with Qb3 and Bc4 and use the h4 pawn as a hook. Meet that with ...Qc8 or ...Nc6. The risk is the b7 pawn and a sacrifice on e6. If White plays Bd3 instead of c4, take with ...Bxd3.

notes.text: Queen to d2 is playable for White, but slightly less accurate.
notes.original: This is also playable but slightly less accurate.

notes.text: White is a pawn up for now, but you can chase both the c5 and e5 pawns.
notes.original: Perhaps the most testing try here. White gives up the centre and is a pawn up for the moment, but Black can go after both the c5 and e5 pawns, and White will have to give one back or overreach.

notes.text: White supports the centre, but you take on d4 and develop with your knight and bishop for a real fight.
notes.original: White supports the centre with c3, but Black takes on d4 and follows with ...Nc6 and ...Bg4. A real fight lies ahead.

notes.text: White develops at once without deciding how to handle the tension on c5 and d4.
notes.original: 5.Nc3 (instead of the usual 4.c3 or 4.Nf3 plans) - develops immediately without first deciding how to meet the tension on c5/d4.

notes.text: White checks at once, hoping to disrupt your development before settling the centre.
notes.original: 5.Bb5+ - an immediate check, trying to disrupt Black's development before dealing with the pawn tension on c5/d4.

notes.text: White strikes on the queenside at once, trying to open the position before you consolidate.
notes.original: 4.c4 strikes immediately on the queenside instead of developing the knight first, trying to open the position before Black can consolidate the extra space.

notes.text: White's knight now guards d4, so it can recapture there if you take the pawn.
notes.original:
4.Nf3 allows 4...cxd4 and prepares to recapture the pawn with the knight. 5.Nxd4 Nc6 (e5 is loose) 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 prevents Black from developing their light-square bishop actively.

=4.Nf3 · Caro-Kann Defence - Advance Variation, Botvinnik-Carls Defence=

5.Nf3 can lead to more complications that 5.dxc5.Black can respond in a number of ways, such as 5...cxd4, where the knight will usually recapture, or 5...Nc6 forcing White to commit to a decision in the center.

notes.text: Your knight hits the e5 pawn; either that pawn or the c5 pawn will fall.
notes.original: ...Nc6 - either the e-pawn or the c-pawn will fall.

notes.text: Choose this move to win the c5 pawn back at once; your bishop takes it next.
notes.original: Choice guide: 4...e6 or 4...Nc6? Choose 4...e6 (this section) IF you want to win the c5-pawn back at once and reach a healthy position with a simple plan (the ...f6 break, ...Ne7-g6); it needs less memorisation. Choose 4...Nc6 (the main line of this chapter) IF you want to keep more tension and accept heavier theory. Risk level: low to medium. After 4...e6 Black intends ...Bxc5 next, so White has to pick a way to deal with that. The main tries are 5.a3, 5.Nf3, 5.Be3, 5.b4, 5.Bd3 and 5.Qh5; each is covered below with the practical answer.

notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
This odd move is dubious: it lets you play Nh6 and weakens White's kingside.
notes.original: This may sound odd, but it has been played. It is a bit dubious because it allows ...Nh6 and weakens White's kingside.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
This is the typical Caro-Kann reply; your bishop hits the f3 knight, and White chooses c3 or Bb5.
notes.original: This is the typical reply in the Caro-Kann. White has two choices, c3 or Bb5, and both are reasonable.

notes.text: White's bishop targets your c6 knight, one of the best attackers of its central pawns.
notes.original: White wants to eliminate one of black's finest attacker of his central pawns. Once the knight falls the e5 pawn could be kept defended.

notes.text: White can now protect c5 with b4 or clear the way for the queen to b3.
notes.original: Another alternative move which falls unto this idea of either b4 to protect the c5 pawn or to make way for the queen Q-b3.

notes.text: White may try to keep the c5 pawn with b4, though that move is dubious.
notes.original: White has two ideas here: try to keep the c-pawn with b4?!, or make room for the queen with Qb3.

notes.text: Or White makes room for the queen with Qb3.
notes.original: White has two ideas here: try to keep the c-pawn with b4?!, or make room for the queen with Qb3.

notes.text: White's bishop guards the knight against the pin, and White plans c4 to break up your centre.
notes.original: White develops and prepares castling, keeping a solid structure. The bishop on e2 supports d3 and protects against the pin on f3. The pawn on c5 is not under direct attack, so White is in no hurry, but he intends c4 to break up your centre.

notes.text: Develop fast with your knight, bishop and queen, then win the pawn back and go after e5.
notes.original:
Idea: 3...c5 attacks the pawn chain right away. After 4.dxc5 develop fast with ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...Qa5+, then win the pawn back and go after e5.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.dxc5 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.Bb5 Qa5+
Watch out: ...Nxe5? loses material on move 5.
Next: 🔵 14 continues the Advance Variation. See also: 🟢 05 to 07. Plan: 🟠 Plan 03. Model game: 🟡 Game 12.

notes.text: Your queen checks and hits the b5 bishop, so White must block with Nc3 or lose a piece.
notes.original: Forcing white to play Nc3 or otherwise lose a bishop. Dislodging white from ever playing Nd2 to defend the f3 knight since the f3 knight is quite valuable since it holds unto the e pawn.

notes.text: This is White's strongest try here, stronger than Na4.
notes.original: White's strongest try here, stronger than Na4.

notes.text: Castling long looks odd, but your rook reaches the d-file and the d5 pawn gets extra protection, so ...d4 becomes…
notes.original: An odd-looking move, since Black usually avoids castling queenside, but here it is useful: the rook reaches the d-file with counter-chances in the middlegame or endgame, and the d-pawn gets extra protection, making ...d5-d4 possible.

notes.text: White has to let go of the pawn; your Qa5 check wins the bishop or the knight.
notes.original: White has to let go of the pawn or otherwise suffer the inevitable. Qa5! And either the light square bishop or the knight falls.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White lines up a rook on your d5 pawn and will play c4; your bishop can trade on c5.
notes.original: White aims a rook at your isolated pawn on d5 and prepares c4. The pawn on c5 is attacked by your bishop, but the knight on a4 guards it, so you trade it off.

notes.text: Your king steps off the c-file, out of the way of any rook on c1.
notes.original: Your king steps off the c-file out of the way of Rc1 ideas.

notes.text: Your f-pawns are doubled, but you get the g-file and a solid centre.
notes.original: Doubled f-pawns, but you get the g-file and a solid centre.

notes.text: White is only slightly better; guard your d5 pawn, your main weak point.
notes.original: White has only a small edge: the isolated d5 pawn is your weak point, so keep it protected.

notes.text: White's bishop tried to hit f6, but your d-pawn chased it away and the queen trade left things equal.
notes.original: The bishop move tries to hit f6, but ...d4 kicks it first and the queen trade leaves the position equal.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the c3 knight, which your queen pins to the king, so White cannot save it.
notes.original: 11...d4 attacks the knight on c3, which is pinned to the king by the queen on a5. White cannot save it.

notes.text: Your d4 pawn attacks the pinned c3 knight, so White loses a piece whatever it does.
notes.original: Your pawn on d4 attacks the knight on c3, and that knight is pinned to the king by your queen on a5, so it cannot move. White loses a piece whatever he does, which is why 11...d4 works.

notes.text: You remove the defender first; if White retakes with the g-pawn, its structure is wrecked.
notes.original: Black removes the defender first. If White recaptures with the g-pawn, the pawn structure is wrecked.

notes.text: White grabbed a pawn with check, but you are still ahead in material.
notes.original: White picks up a pawn with check, but you are a piece ahead.

notes.text: White's recapture does not rescue the lost knight; you stay ahead in material.
notes.original: Taking a piece back does not rescue the knight; you stay a piece up.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's bishop pins your c6 knight to the king, so the b4 pawn is safe for now.
notes.original: The knight recaptures and the bishop stays on b5, where it pins your knight on c6 to the king, so the b4 pawn is immune for now. White keeps the bishop pair and a pawn chain that shuts in your bishop on f8.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop, and ...Ne7 will then break the pin.
notes.original: Kicks the bishop and prepares to unpin with ...Ne7.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge thanks to the bishops, but your position has no weaknesses.
notes.original: White still has a small edge thanks to the bishops, but your position has no weaknesses.

notes.text: The bishop left b5, so the pin is gone and your knight wins a pawn.
notes.original: The bishop was doing a job on b5: moving it releases the pin and wins you a pawn.

notes.text: After the trades you come out ahead in material.
notes.original: You are a clean pawn up.

notes.text: Keep it simple: take the knight, and you win the pawn back after the recapture.
notes.original: Other approaches prefer ideas such as ...a6 or even ...e6, but simplicity works here: take the knight, recapture on the pawn, and the pawn is regained.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
This is a blunder: after 7.Nxe5 Bxd1 8.Bb5+ White comes out ahead.
Taking on e5 with the knight falls into a trap: you lose material.
notes.original: Watch out: ...Nxe5? loses material on move 5.

notes.text: Grabbing on e5 is a blunder: White retakes, you win the queen, but Bb5 check comes out ahead for White.
notes.original: This is a blunder: after 7.Nxe5 Bxd1 8.Bb5+ White comes out ahead.

notes.text: White is slightly better.

notes.original: Choice guide: 4.c3 Nc6 (safe to balanced). Choose this if you want a French-style Advance structure with a good bishop on f5: ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Bg6, then break with ...cxd4 at the right moment. The main line 5.Be2 and the sidelines 5.Bb5, 5.f4, 5.a3 and 5.Be3 are shown. 4.c3 Nc6 invites White to build a classical Advance centre. White's usual choice is 5.Be2, but 5.Bb5, 5.f4, 5.a3 and 5.Be3 all appear.

notes.original: 11.h3 attacks the bishop and looks sharp, but it's actually a normal, roughly equal try, not a mistake. This is a closed Advance structure with White's pawns on d4 and e5, you with c6 and d5, and your light bishop already out on g4. White has more space but your pieces are active. Kings will probably stay in the centre for a while before you castle. Your plan: keep the pin with ...Bg4, develop the rook to c8 with tempo, then aim at d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Qd7 and prepare ...f6 or ...Nf5 to undermine e5. White wants to hold d4 and break with c4 or push on the kingside. You meet it by trading pieces. The risk is castling too early or releasing the tension with ...cxd4 before your pieces are ready. If White deviates, stay calm and keep the c-file in mind.

notes.original: The knight attacks the queen with gain of time and heads for the f5 square.

This is an open, gambit-style position where material is level, White's king is still on e1 and his queen on h3 is exposed. Your pieces are active with Nd7, Nh6 and the bishop on f7. Your plan: play ...Nf5 to hit the queen and d4, then ...e6, ...Be7 and ...Qc7, and castle long when safe. White wants Bd3 and Ne5 to trade your active pieces, and to open the h-file with h5. The mistake is grabbing pawns with your queen and neglecting development. If White plays Bd3, meet it with ...e6 and keep trading the most dangerous attackers.

Avoid ...h5 immediately, because f5 would then trap the bishop on h7 and leave you short of squares.
