notes.text: Your h-pawn hits the g4 pawn and opens the g-file.
notes.original: This breaks open the g-file.

notes.text: Chances are equal; aim to strike the centre with c5 once the kingside opens.
notes.original: The position is dynamic, with equal chances, and your task is to keep the bishop active and strike at the centre with ...c5 once the king side opens.

notes.text: Your queen and h8 rook both pressure the h4 pawn along the open h-file.
notes.original: This is an open, tense position after the bayonet g4 line: you have an open h-file with a rook on h8, and White's king is stretched. Your plan: develop with ...Ne7 and ...Nd7, then strike with ...c5 against d4, and put pressure on the h4 pawn with ...Rh8. Your king can go long or stay for now. White wants to play f5 to open the centre and bring his queen to g4 and g7. Meet f5 with ...exf5 and the queen. The risk is leaving g7 and the h-file loose and grabbing h4 hastily. If White plays f5 first, recapture and pile up on d4.

notes.text: Strike at d4 with c5 once your knights are developed.
notes.original: This is an open, tense position after the bayonet g4 line: you have an open h-file with a rook on h8, and White's king is stretched. Your plan: develop with ...Ne7 and ...Nd7, then strike with ...c5 against d4, and put pressure on the h4 pawn with ...Rh8. Your king can go long or stay for now. White wants to play f5 to open the centre and bring his queen to g4 and g7. Meet f5 with ...exf5 and the queen. The risk is leaving g7 and the h-file loose and grabbing h4 hastily. If White plays f5 first, recapture and pile up on d4.

notes.text: This is too slow: your bishop is stuck on h7 and White has the initiative.
notes.original: This is too slow, since after f5 your bishop is stuck on h7 and White is the one with the initiative.

notes.text: White backs up e5 with f4 and wants Nf3 and Be3, keeping a big grip on space.
notes.original: White backs up the e5 pawn with a second pawn and plans Nf3, Be3 and a knight or bishop to a good square, keeping a big grip on space. The cost is that the king side is stretched: the f4 and g4 pawns can become targets and d4 is guarded only by pieces. So attack the base of the chain at once. The move is common in practice (played in about 106,000 games).

notes.text: Attack the base of the chain at once with ...c5, hitting the d4 pawn.
notes.original: White backs up the e5 pawn with a second pawn and plans Nf3, Be3 and a knight or bishop to a good square, keeping a big grip on space. The cost is that the king side is stretched: the f4 and g4 pawns can become targets and d4 is guarded only by pieces. So attack the base of the chain at once. The move is common in practice (played in about 106,000 games).

notes.text: White just develops, since there is less to gain from ripping the position open now.
notes.original: White develops naturally rather than committing to an immediate pawn sacrifice - since the bishop is no longer on an exposed diagonal, there is less to gain from ripping the position open early.

notes.text: Challenge the g4 pawn with h5 before White can consolidate it.
notes.original: Black's plan in this branch: challenge the overextended g4-pawn directly with ...h5 before White can consolidate it with h3/Nf3.

notes.text: The other main try: strike in the centre at once instead of playing h5 first.
notes.original: The other main try: strike in the center immediately rather than committing to ...h5 first. Both approaches are fully playable.

notes.text: Strike at the d4 pawn right away, while White's kingside pawns are stretched.
notes.original: Striking in the center immediately, while White's kingside pawns are stretched out and the rook on h5 needs a moment to get back into the game.

notes.text: Your active rook and the c-file pressure make up for its awkward placement.
notes.original: A sharp, roughly balanced position where Black's activity (the h5-rook, the half-open c-file pressure) compensates fully for the slightly awkward-looking rook placement.

notes.text: Take the e5 pawn that holds White together; the knight exchange keeps your rook active.
notes.original: White's pawn on e5 is the only thing holding the position together, so take it. The knight exchange keeps your rook active and the exchanges favour you.

notes.text: White's queen attacks your rook on e5.
notes.original: Qd4 attacks the rook on e5.

notes.text: Give up the exchange: your rook was hit anyway, and the recapture wrecks White's structure.
notes.original: Give the exchange: the rook is hit anyway, and recapturing on e3 wrecks White's pawn structure.

notes.text: You won the c5 pawn back, and your king is safer, so the position is balanced.
notes.original: You win the c5 pawn back, and White's doubled e-pawns are weak. The position is balanced, with your king safer.

notes.text: Passive development let White take the g7 pawn.
notes.original: Passive development lets White take the g7 pawn.

notes.text: Your queen hits the c5 pawn, so you win the pawn back at once.
notes.original: Regaining the pawn immediately rather than letting White consolidate the extra material.

notes.text: You win a pawn back next move and keep a healthy, low-theory position with no weaknesses.
notes.original: Black regains the pawn next move with ...Qxc5 and stands at least equal, with a healthy structure and no weaknesses - a clean, low-theory way to meet the Bayonet Attack for players who would rather not memorize the sharper 4...Be4/4...Bg6 tactics.

notes.text: You win back the e5 pawn, and your bishop on f8 now eyes the c5 pawn.
notes.original: White's c3 prepares to protect the bishop on b5, but you win back the e5 pawn that cramps you and take the queen to the centre. The pawn on c5 is also under fire from ...Bxc5.

notes.text: White's queen and bishop pile up on your pinned knight, so your a-pawn hits the bishop to break the pin.
notes.original: Qa4 piles up on the pinned knight, so break the pin at once.

notes.text: Both kings are safe and the position is balanced; your knight on e7 guards the c6 knight.
notes.original: Both kings are safe and the position is balanced. Your knight on e7 guards c6 and prepares ...Nd5.

notes.text: Asking the bishop a question at once is slower: White gets f4 in and you are slightly worse.
notes.original: Asking the bishop a question at once is slower: White gets f4 in and the lines open while you are underdeveloped. You are slightly worse here.

notes.text: Your c-pawn hits d4 before White finishes development; follow with ...Nc6 and ...h5 to question g4.
notes.original: This is the thematic break: you hit d4 before White finishes development. After 6.dxc5 you answer ...e6, rebuilding a solid centre and preparing ...Bxc5 to win the pawn back with a good bishop. Your plan is bishop to c5, knight to c6 or e7, and ...h5 to question the g4 pawn. If White declines with 6.Nf3, just keep adding pressure with ...Nc6.

notes.text: White covers d4, but your h-pawn attacks g4, and if White ignores it, ...hxg4 opens the h-file.
notes.original: White covers d4 but you do not mind, because ...h5 attacks g4. If White ignores it, ...hxg4 opens the h-file for your rook.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop, the c5 pawn is doomed, and you are slightly better.
notes.original: Now your pawn kicks the bishop and the c5 pawn is doomed. After 9.Bf2 Bxc5 your bishop eyes f2, and you follow with ...Ne7 and ...Nc6. Avoid dropping back with ...e5 ideas; the point is to keep White's pawns overextended. White has more space but a loose pawn chain, and you are slightly better.

notes.text: You are a little better, but d4 is heavily attacked, so add a defender with ...Nc6 first.
notes.original: This is an open, sharp position with a loose white pawn chain on e5, f4 and g5, against your active bishops on c5 and d7 and a pawn on d4. You are a little better. Your plan: defend d4 with ...Nc6, then play ...Nge7 and ...Qb6, and castle long once the queen has moved. White wants to win d4 with Nxd4 and Bxd4, and use his space on the kingside with h4. The risk is that d4 is attacked twice and defended once, so add a defender at once before anything else. If White plays Bxd4, recapture with the bishop and keep the c5 bishop active.

notes.text: This is playable but slower: White gets Nf3 and g5 in undisturbed and you must defend a cramped position.
notes.original: This is playable but slower: White gets Nf3 and g5 in without being disturbed and you are the one who has to defend a cramped position instead of striking at d4.

notes.text: A sound alternative, though White is a touch more comfortable with extra central space.
notes.original: A sound alternative, though White is a touch more comfortable with the extra space in the centre.

notes.text: White's c4 tried to open lines, but your queen took d4 and the queen trade leaves you comfortable.
notes.original: c4 tries to open lines, but your queen takes d4 and the queen trade leaves you comfortable.

notes.text: White must live with a weakened kingside, but the position is level and your pieces have easy squares.
notes.original: White has to accept the weak pawn structure on the kingside. The position is level and your pieces have easy squares.

notes.text: Playing ...h5 first is just as good and cramps the kingside immediately.
This is solid too, but White got f4 in for free.
notes.original: Solid too, but White gets f4 in for free.

notes.text: You play the usual d5, supported by your c-pawn; this normally transposes into familiar Caro-Kann lines.
notes.original:
After Black plays 2...d5 (which, as after 2.d4, is almost always the move) this usually transposes to the:

Black plays the usual Caro-Kann move, 2...d5, supported by the pawn on c6.

3.exd5, which after 3...cxd5 4.d4 Nc6 transposes into an exchange variation, normally seen in the move order 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nf3 Nc6. Alternatively, 4.Ne5!? is the Apocalypse attack.

notes.text: White delays d4; after you take on e4, White's knight must recapture and White loses a tempo.
notes.original: The Two Knights Attack: White develops a second piece first and delays d4. In these chapters Black takes on e4, so White's knight has to recapture and White loses a tempo. Black then follows with ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6, as in the Karpov Variation.

notes.text: This transposes to the Two Knights Attack, which has its own chapters.
notes.original: 2.Nf3 is the Two Knights Attack. See 🔵 15 to 17 and 🟢 08 to 10 for the full treatment (Tartakower, Karpov, Classical, Dano-Russian and ...a6 Variations, and rare third-move tries). No new content here. ...transposing to the Two Knights, covered from 🔵 15.

notes.text: White's e5 reaches an Advance-style structure, which if anything is a small plus for you.
notes.original: 3.e5 - White delays Nc3 and instead transposes directly into an Advance Variation structure a tempo down for Black compared with the main lines (since the knight isn't yet committed to c3), which if anything is a small plus for Black.

notes.text: If White later tries Ne5, the trappy Apocalypse Attack looks scary but has no real venom once you know the…
notes.original: 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Ne5!? is sometimes called the Apocalypse Attack - a trappy try that looks scary (the knight eyes f7 and c6) but has no real venom once Black knows the refutation.

notes.text: A quiet try: White keeps d3 flexible for either a c4 or a Nbd2 setup.
notes.original: 3.d3 - a quiet try that avoids committing the knight to c3 yet, keeping d3 flexible for either c4 or Nbd2 setups.

notes.text: Bg4 is also popular here, but taking the pawn is the main line.
notes.original: Bg4 is also popular here.

notes.text: Your light-squared bishop hits the f3 knight, trying to loosen White's grip on the centre.
notes.original: This is the Classical System of the Caro Kann Defence against the standard "Two Knights Attack". Black's suppressive light square bishop is trying to loosen white's grasp on the center.

notes.text: A waiting move against the Two Knights: your a-pawn keeps White's pieces off b5.
notes.original:
Extra: an optional waiting reply, 3...a6, against the Two Knights. The core repertoire does not need it.
Idea: 3...a6 is a waiting move that keeps White's pieces off b5. After 4.d4 pin with ...Bg4, take on f3, and play ...e6, ...Nf6 and ...dxe4.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3 a6
Next: 🟢 10 continues the Two Knights Attack.

notes.text: Your a-pawn watches b5, denying White's pieces that square while you wait to see what White commits to.
notes.original: The ...a6 system. This chapter covers a flexible ...a6 idea for sidestepping memorised theory against the Two Knights Attack. First and foremost, a6!? is a waiting move: rather than committing immediately, Black keeps an eye on the b5 square, denying White's pieces that outpost, and waits to see whether White occupies the centre with d4 or resolves the tension with an early exchange on d5. If White plays d4, the game usually transposes into normal Two Knights structures a tempo down for White's would-be b5 ideas; if White exchanges on d5 instead, Black recaptures freely and reaches a comfortable, no-theory position. The idea of the line is practical: it is easy to remember, hard for White to punish, and it steers the game away from whatever sharp theory White may have prepared. Playable, but Bg4 is more accurate.

notes.text: Choose Nf6 for a repertoire that works in every Two Knights line; Bf5 runs into Ne5 and Qh5 tactics.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose 4...Nf6 (as in 🔵 15 to 17 and 🟢 08) if you want a repertoire that works in every Two Knights line. 4...Bf5 is shown mainly as a warning: with White's knight on f3 the standard Bf5-g6-h6 plan runs into Ne5 and Qh5 tactics, which is why this repertoire avoids it against 2.Nf3. The 5.Ng3 h5 gamble is shown as well. Risk level: high. After 4.Nxe4 Black normally develops with 4...Nf6; the alternatives below show why.

notes.text: Nf6 usually reaches a Classical Caro-Kann after the knight trade, the recapture and then d4.
notes.original: A further option is ...Nf6, which usually ends up in a Classical Caro-Kann after the knight trade and the recapture, followed by d4. That central push is the natural continuation.

notes.text: Nd7 avoids Nf6, where White can ruin your pawns, and prepares to support a knight on f6.
notes.original: The book move here is typically Nf6. However, this doesn't appeal to me, as white can immediately ruin black's pawn structure. Instead, I prefer to support the knight on f6 via d7. It's a similar concept to the Karpov Variation in classical lines of the opening.

notes.text: This move order runs into Ne5 and Qh5 tactics against 2.Nf3, so avoid it.
notes.original: 4...Bf5 5.Ng3 Bg6 6.h4 h6 7.Ne5 Bh7 8.Qh5 g6 9.Bc4 leaves Black in trouble. Avoid this move order against 2.Nf3.

notes.text: White avoids the usual knight trade; the queen on e2 backs up the knight on e4.
notes.original: 5.Qe2 - sidesteps the main 5.Nxf6+ trade entirely, pinning the e4-knight's retreat square and preparing to meet ...Nxe4 with a recapture that keeps the queen centralized.

notes.text: White retreats the knight to safety instead of trading on f6, keeping more pieces on.
notes.original: 5.Ng3 retreats the knight to safety rather than trading on f6 immediately, keeping more pieces on the board.

notes.text: White retreats the other knight, offering to repeat moves or head for a quieter structure.
notes.original: 5.Nc3 retreats the other knight back, offering to repeat moves or head into a quieter structure.

notes.text: White's d3 pawn quietly supports the knight on e4, instead of trading or retreating it.
notes.original: 5.d3 supports the knight on e4 quietly rather than committing it to a trade or a retreat.

notes.text: Against the Two Knights, take on e4, play Nf6 and recapture with the pawn for an easy set-up.
notes.original:
Idea: Against the Two Knights, take on e4 at once and play ...Nf6. After 5.Nxf6+ exf6 you get the same easy set-up as 🔵 08: ...Bd6, ...O-O and ...Re8. Against 5.Qe2, remember that ...Nbd7?? allows Nd6 mate.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6
Watch out: ...Bxc4? loses material on moves 11 to 14. ...Bxh2+? loses material on moves 8 to 10.
Next: 🔵 16 continues the Two Knights Attack. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11. Model game: 🟡 Game 14.

notes.text: Recapturing with the g-pawn opens the g-file; plan bishop to g4, e6 and rook to g8.
notes.original:
Extra: an optional sharper reply, 5...gxf6, against the Two Knights. The core repertoire does not need it.
Idea: 5...gxf6 against the Two Knights. You get the open g-file and play with ...Bg4, ...e6 and ...Rg8. It is sharper than 🔵 15, and White keeps an edge with good play.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ gxf6
Watch out: ...Qxd2+? loses material on move 4. ...Qxd4? loses material on move 6.
Next: 🟢 09 continues the Two Knights Attack.

notes.text: You accept doubled pawns for the open g-file and play against White's kingside.
notes.original: The Bronstein-Larsen Variation of the Two Knights Attack, also called the Dano-Russian Variation. Black accepts doubled pawns and a weakened kingside in return for the open g-file and a flexible position, with play aimed at White's kingside. Playable, but exf6 is more accurate.

notes.text: White's bishop develops actively, straight at your f7 pawn.
notes.original: 6.Bc4 develops actively toward f7 immediately after the trade, rather than the calmer d4/Nf3 setups.

notes.text: The c4 push is White's strongest try here, stronger than Qd2.
notes.original: White's strongest try here, stronger than Qd2.

notes.text: The c5 push hurts White's queenside and light squares; Qc2 was stronger.
notes.original: White can push on with c5, but the queenside will suffer: d4 is isolated and weak, the c5 pawn can be broken up once d4 is pressured, and the light squares from d5 to h1 are weakened. 12.Qc2 was stronger.

notes.text: The opening phase is over, and your rooks are active on the d- and e-files.
notes.original: The opening phase is over and Black stands very well: the rooks are active on the d- and e-files, the bishop pair is in place, and Black has an extra knight available for defence.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's b3 is less accurate than Be2.
notes.original: Be2 is more accurate.

notes.text: Queen to c2 is White's best try here, stronger than b3.
notes.original: White's strongest try here, stronger than b3.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White lines the queen up behind d4 and plans d5 to gain space.
notes.original: White lines up the queen behind d4 and plans d5 to gain space.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the f3 knight, so White's d5 push would cost time.
notes.original: The pin on f3 means d5 will cost White time.

notes.text: You lock the centre; your bishop is a little passive, but your knight gets f5 and e7.
notes.original: You lock the centre. The d6 bishop is a little passive, but your knights get the f5 and e7 squares.

notes.text: Your knight on f5 is well placed, and the h-pawn can still go to h4.
notes.original: You keep a small edge, with the knight on f5 well placed and ...h4 still in reserve.

notes.text: White playing d5 at once opens the position for you.
notes.original: Playing d5 at once opens the position for you.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Be2 adds a defender to f3, so your bishop taking there can be answered by Bxf3.
notes.original: This is White's best try, since Bg4 threatens to take on f3. His motive is to add a defender to f3 so that ...Bxf3 can always be answered with Bxf3, and to get the bishop off the d3-h7 diagonal.

notes.text: Your h-pawn gains space, and White's pieces are awkward.
notes.original: Your h-pawn gains space and White's pieces are awkward.

notes.text: Your knight is heading for f5, and White still has no plan.
notes.original: You keep the edge: your knight is heading for f5 and White still has no plan.

notes.text: White's c5 push looks active but hands your knight the d5 square, and the d4 pressure is gone.
notes.original: Pushing the pawn looks active but it hands you the d5 square and the pressure on d4 is gone.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White opens the c-file and wants d5 next, hitting your bishop on e6.
notes.original: White opens the c-file and the centre. His motive is the d5 break, which would attack your Be6 and try to pin the b5 pawn and the Bc7 together.

notes.text: Both queens raid the other camp and material stays even; your bishop and knight keep a small edge.
notes.original: Both sides grab pawns and queens run through the other camp. Material stays even and your bishop on d5 and the knight on e6 keep a small edge.

notes.text: Your queen offers a queen trade, and White's d5 pawn becomes a weakness.
notes.original: The queen invasion looks scary but you trade queens and the d5 pawn is a weakness.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White trades rooks to ease the pressure from your two bishops aimed at his kingside.
notes.original: White trades a pair of rooks because your Bd5 and Bc7 are aimed at his kingside and the c5 pawn is fixed, so fewer pieces means less pressure.

notes.text: You keep a small edge: your knight and bishop dominate, and White has no active plan.
notes.original: You keep a small edge. The knight on e6 and the bishop on d5 dominate the board and White has no active plan to speak of.

notes.text: Your pawn threatens h4, and White's bishop on g3 has no good square.
notes.original: The pawn push threatens ...h4 and the Bg3 has no good square.

notes.text: Your pieces are better placed, and White's doubled f-pawns are a weakness.
notes.original: Your pieces are better placed and the damaged f3 pawn is a weakness.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's h-pawn takes g4 from your bishop, and the knight will return to f3.
notes.original: White takes the g4 square away from your bishop and prepares to bring the knight back to f3. His motive is to keep the c4/d4 pair and slowly make something of your doubled f-pawns.

notes.text: Your bishop hits White's bishop on e3 and forces a decision about the dark-squared bishops.
notes.original: Hitting the Be3 forces a decision about the dark-squared bishops.

notes.text: Most minor pieces are traded; aim for a knight on e6 and a rook on d8, keeping queenside pawns together.
notes.original: You trade off most minor pieces. White keeps a small edge, so aim for ...Ne6 and ...Rad8 and keep your pawns together on the queenside.

notes.text: White's g3 weakened the kingside, which let your bishop reach h3 with a tempo on the rook.
notes.original: Weakening the kingside this way lets your bishop jump to h3 with a tempo on the f1 rook and stay there, which is why h3 comes first.

notes.text: White develops quickly, but the position stays balanced.
notes.original: 6.Bc4 develops actively toward f7 immediately after the trade, rather than the calmer d4/Nf3 setups. ...and the position remains balanced, with White's slightly easier development offset by Black's extra central pawn presence.

notes.text: With queens off, your king is safe in the centre, so develop quickly.
notes.original: With the queens off, your king is safe in the centre and you keep both bishops available. Your plan is quick development: ...Rd8, ...Nd7 and ...Ne5 to hit the Bc4.

notes.text: White trades before you can hit the bishop on c4; recapture with the bishop or the f-pawn and you are…
notes.original: White trades before you can hit the bishop on c4. Recapture with the bishop or the f-pawn and you are fine; the position stays level to a small White edge.

notes.text: This is playable, but your king stays on e8 and White gets a free hand with Nd4.
notes.original: Also playable, but the king stays on e8 and White gets a free hand with Nd4.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Your knight meets the Nd6 mate threat and heads for c7, preparing to take on e4.
notes.original: 5...Na6!? is the cleanest reply: the knight heads for c7 or b4 rather than committing to d7, and sidesteps any awkward pin along the e-file once White recaptures on e4. Choice guide: choose this if you want a surprise weapon against 5.Qe2: it sets a trap at once (the e7-pawn is pinned, so ...Nbd7?? loses to Nd6#) and often drags the game into quiet structures where Black is perfectly fine. Risk level: medium. If you prefer a completely safe structure, answer 5.Nxf6+ exf6 as in 🔵 15 and answer 5.Qe2 with 5...Nxe4 6.Qxe4 Qa5. After 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 White threatens Nd6 mate, because the e7-pawn is pinned against the king. 5...Na6 solves that problem and prepares ...Nc7 and ...Nxe4.

notes.text: White supports a later d4 push and keeps its options open instead of settling the centre with d3.
notes.original: 6.c3 - supports a later d4 push and keeps options flexible instead of resolving the center with 6.d3 right away.

notes.text: White trades off the centralized knight at once, with check, instead of retreating it first.
notes.original: 6.Nxf6+ - trades off the centralized knight immediately rather than retreating it with d3 or c3 first.

notes.text: White takes the centre; you trade knights on e4, and the queens often come off.
notes.original: 6.d4 is the principled reply. Black trades knights and the queens often come off.

notes.text: White's a-pawn stops your knight reaching b4, so trade on e4 and head for c7.
notes.original: 6.a3 prevents ...Nb4 ideas and keeps a bishop pair option. Black trades on e4 and plays ...Nc7 and ...Qd5.

notes.text: Trading knights removes White's strong central knight before it becomes a lasting asset.
notes.original: 6...Nxe4 simply trades off the strong centralized knight before it becomes a long-term asset for White.

notes.text: Your e-pawn claims the centre and equalizes comfortably; your pieces have natural squares and there is little to memorize.
notes.original: 7...e5 stakes out the center immediately and equalizes comfortably; Black's minor pieces have clear, natural squares (Be7/Bc5, Nc7-e6 or b4) and there is nothing to memorize beyond normal development.

notes.text: White offers a queen trade and aims to win your e5 pawn with the knight.
notes.original: White offers the queen trade and aims to win the e5 pawn after Nxe5.

notes.text: Your knight regains the pawn and attacks the bishop on d2 and the f2 pawn at once.
notes.original: The knight regains the pawn and attacks the bishop on d2 and the f2 square at once.

notes.text: Your knight takes the bishop on d2 and also hits the bishop on c4.
notes.original: White wins the e5 pawn with Nxe5, but your knight regains it with tempo.

notes.text: Qe3 is the more cautious choice for White, and your f6 pawn keeps your centre solid.
notes.original: Qe3 is a more cautious alternative where ...f6 keeps your centre solid.

notes.text: Your queen centralizes and hits the knight on e4, forcing White to untangle before you finish developing.
notes.original: 6...Qd5 centralizes the queen, attacking e4 and g2 at once and forcing White to untangle before Black finishes development.

notes.text: White takes the knight your queen was attacking, with check, and takes the sting out of your play.
notes.original: White removes the knight that your queen was attacking, and takes the sting out of your play, with a slight pull for White.

notes.text: Your pawn heads to h4 and your rook takes the g-file.
notes.original: The pawn heads to h4 and your rook uses the g-file.

notes.text: Your bishop eyes the c1 bishop behind the d2 pawn, and the half-open g-file is yours.
notes.original: Your bishop attacks c1 and the open g-file is yours.

notes.text: White gets a pleasant position, but your pieces come out quickly and your queen on d5 is active.
notes.original: 6.c3 Qd5 7.Nxf6+ gxf6 gives White a pleasant position but Black's pieces come out quickly and the queen on d5 is active.

notes.text: The queens come off and your pieces are active, with your bishop pinning the knight on f3.
notes.original: The queens come off and your pieces are active, with the bishop pinning the knight on f3.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
A trick line: White wins your a6 knight, but you took the g5 knight too, and your bishop hits the…
notes.original: This is a trick. White trades knights and wins your knight on a6, but you took the g5 knight too and Bf5 hits the queen, so the line ends in a repetition.

notes.text: Recapturing with the g-pawn gives your rook an open g-file, at the cost of doubled f-pawns.
notes.original: 6...gxf6 recaptures toward the center, giving Black the bishop pair and an open g-file for the rook in return for a slightly disrupted kingside structure, a standard and comfortable trade-off in this family of structures.

notes.text: White supports a d4 push and is ready to answer ...Qd5 with g3.
notes.original: White solidifies d4 and prepares to meet ...Qd5 with g3.

notes.text: Your queen centralizes and attacks the knight on f3.
notes.original: The queen centralises and attacks g2 and the knight on f3.

notes.text: Your bishop comes out with check, and White's king is stuck in the centre.
notes.original: You get your pieces out with check and your bishop pair is strong. White's king is stuck in the centre.

notes.text: You accept doubled f-pawns for the half-open g-file and harass White's kingside with your h-pawn; it's balanced.
notes.original: After 6.Nxf6+ gxf6 Black accepts doubled f-pawns for an open g-file and plays ...h5-h4 to harass the king's side. A messy but balanced game.

notes.text: Pushing your h-pawn to cramp White's kingside is also possible.
notes.original: Pushing the h-pawn to cramp the kingside is also possible.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Your a-pawns are doubled, but your bishops are active and the structure is sound.
notes.original: An endgame with doubled a-pawns that is perfectly playable: Black's bishops are active and the structure is sound.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
Your h-pawn gamble is double-edged and risky, so you must play exactly.
notes.original: The h-pawn gamble: 5.Ng3 h5 6.Bc4 h4 7.Ne2 b5 is double-edged and Black must be exact. risky.

notes.text: White castles and the position stays level, with a balanced middlegame ahead.
notes.original: 5.Ng3 retreats the knight to safety rather than trading on f6 immediately, keeping more pieces on the board. ...and the position stays level with a normal, balanced middlegame ahead.

notes.text: Your fianchetto continues with the bishop going to g7.
notes.original: You develop with a fianchetto. The plan is ...Bg7 and later ...b6 and ...Bb7, so that your pieces cover the long diagonal and the d5 square before White gets organised.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight and threatens to trade, which would double White's pawns.
notes.original: Pinning the f3 knight and getting ready to trade it, which would double White's pawns.

notes.text: White's knight eyes e6 and f7, but your e6 pawn blocks the bishop and keeps f7 safe.
notes.original: Ng5 eyes e6 and f7. Playing ...e6 blocks the Bc4 and keeps f7 safe in one move, so there is nothing to fear.

notes.text: You traded a pair of knights, which eases your game, and your light bishop is ready for b7.
notes.original: You have traded a pair of knights, which eases your game, and the queenside bishop is ready for b7.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes f6, but the position is level; keep developing with ...Bb7 and castling.
notes.original: White gets a pin on f6 to play with, but the position is level and your structure is healthy, so continue with ...Bb7 and ...O-O.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
A natural developing move; if the knight jumps to h4, your bishop goes to g6, so don't shut it in…
notes.original: A natural developing move. Your plan is ...Nbd7 and ...e6 or ...e5, followed by ...Bc5 and kingside castling. If the knight from f3 jumps to h4, the bishop goes to g6. Avoid shutting the bishop in with ...e6 before it has a safe square.

notes.text: White's retreat invites a quieter game, and the position is dead level.
notes.original: 5.Nc3 retreats the other knight back, offering to repeat moves or head into a quieter structure. ...and the position is dead level.

notes.text: White offers a bishop trade; take it, develop, and keep your structure.
notes.original: White offers to trade the light-squared bishops. His motive is a calm Queen's Gambit type of position in which Ne4 and Bf4 later press on f6 and c5, so there is nothing to fear: trade, develop and keep your structure.

notes.text: A modest developing move: White keeps Bd3 in reserve and leaves the pawn structure intact.
notes.original: A modest developing move: White keeps the option of Bd3 and meets ...h6 with a calm retreat. His motive is to keep the structure intact and to castle queenside.

notes.text: White's knight eyes your f6 knight and the c5 square; just keep developing.
notes.original: The knight eyes f6 and c5 and aims to remove your best defender; just keep developing.

notes.text: Your queen hits b2 and d4, preparing ...c5 or ...Nd5; the position is level, so choose your plan.
notes.original: The queen hits b2 and d4 and prepares ...c5 or ...Nd5. Neither side has a target and the position is level, so you are free to choose your plan.

notes.text: A useful waiting move: your h-pawn takes the g5 square away from White's bishop.
notes.original: A useful waiting move that stops Bg5.

notes.text: You trade off White's good bishop.
notes.original: Trading White's good bishop.

notes.text: Your queen watches the long diagonal toward g3 and the h2 pawn.
notes.original: Qc7 keeps an eye on the g3 and h2 diagonal.

notes.text: White's other bishop move only transposes into the same kind of position.
notes.original: Be2 only transposes into the same kind of position.

notes.text: The kings are on opposite wings: castle, then push in the centre while White storms.
notes.original: White has castled long and the kings are on opposite wings. The position is level. Your plan is ...O-O, ...c5 or ...Nd5 and then pushing in the centre while White starts a pawn storm.

notes.text: White's knight retreats to g3, and White keeps a small, pleasant edge.
notes.original: 5.d3 supports the knight on e4 quietly rather than committing it to a trade or a retreat. ...and White keeps a small, pleasant edge.

notes.text: Your bishop retreats to safety, guards the h5 square and stays on the long diagonal.
notes.original: Retreat the bishop to keep it safe and protect the h5 square. It stays on the b1-h7 diagonal, and White's edge is small.

notes.text: White's knight hit your bishop, so it retreats to g6 and stays on the diagonal.
notes.original: Ng3 attacks your Bf5, so the bishop has to move or be traded; ...Bg6 keeps it on the diagonal.

notes.text: A solid move that opens the diagonal for your bishop on f8.
notes.original: Solid, opens the bishop on f8.

notes.text: Send the awkward knight back and re-route it toward d7.
notes.original: Re-route the awkward knight toward d7.

notes.text: The a6 knight had no real destination, so it returns and can go to d7 later.
notes.original: The knight on a6 had no real destination, so bring it back and develop it to d7 later.

notes.text: Your queen challenges White's queen and keeps the b7 pawn safe.
notes.original: Challenging the queen so that b7 is safe.

notes.text: Your position is solid and the knight on d5 is great; White keeps only a tiny pull.
notes.original: You have a solid position and the knight on d5 is great. White keeps a tiny pull but there are no immediate threats.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge, but your position is solid; be patient and develop with Nd7, Bd6 and castling.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge, but your position is solid and your Nd5 is a fine blockader. Be patient and aim at ...Nd7, ...Bd6 and ...O-O.

notes.text: Your bishop on e6 blocks your central play and lets White develop freely, giving White a small edge.
notes.original: Placing the bishop on e6 blocks your central play and lets White develop freely, which gives a small White edge.

notes.text: Your bishop on e6 is passive, and White has a free hand in the centre.
notes.original: The bishop is passive on e6 and White has a free hand in the centre.

notes.text: White retreats the knight to c3 to stay solid; it is very common and the position is level.
notes.original: White retreats the knight from e4 to c3 to keep the position solid and avoid exchanges; the knights on c3 and f3 help control d5 and e4. It is a very common choice, played in about 304,000 games, and the position is level.

notes.text: White's quiet set-up keeps the e4 knight supported; it isn't a refutation, so aim for ...e5 and a healthy centre.
notes.original: White opens the bishop on c1 and prepares g3 and Bg2, a quiet set-up in which he keeps his knight on e4 supported by the d-pawn. It is very common in practice (played in about 234,000 games). So White is not trying to refute you, so you can aim for ...e5 and a healthy centre.

notes.text: White develops and lines up on your f5 bishop, so keep it protected.
notes.original: White develops and attacks your f5 bishop twice over, since the bishop and the e4 knight both look at it. He hopes to win the bishop pair or force concessions. It is very common in practice (played in about 214,000 games). So the bishop must stay protected.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
White's h-pawn stops ...Bg4, and the knight on h4 hits your bishop, planning to trade it.
notes.original: White prevents ...Bg4 and eyes your bishop on f5 with the knight, planning to trade it.

notes.text: Your bishop stays active on g6; if White takes it, recapture with the h-pawn and enjoy the open h-file.
notes.original: The bishop retreats to g6 where it stays active, and White may take it with Nxg6 if he wishes, after which you recapture with the h-pawn and gain an open h-file. Do not be afraid of the doubled pawns.

notes.text: Strike in the centre: the e5 pawn gains space and opens the road for your f8 bishop.
notes.original: Strike in the centre. The pawn on e5 gains space and opens the f8 bishop.

notes.text: Develop your bishop and aim at f2; you have a comfortable game, so castle short and avoid careless pawn pushes.
notes.original: Develop and aim at f2. You have a comfortable game with all your pieces out and a flexible centre; keep castling short and avoid pushing pawns carelessly.

notes.text: Bring your queen to e7 and knight to b6, then castle long; the open h-file is yours.
notes.original: This is a semi-open position with doubled g-pawns, so you have an open h-file and a flexible centre with pawns on c6 and e5. White has a solid structure and a g3 fianchetto. Your plan: bring the queen to e7 and knight to b6, keep the bishop active on c5 aiming at f2, put a rook on h8 against the h3 pawn, and castle long, since the h-file belongs to you. White wants Bg2, then f4 or d4 to undermine e5. Meet d4 by ...exd4 and ...Bb6, and meet f4 with ...exf4. The risk is a hasty ...Rxh3 or a rushed kingside castle; the doubled pawns are fine, but do not leave f2 and h3 stuff loose.

notes.text: Your bishop eyes the e4 knight, White's only active piece; trade it off and keep the e7 pawn guarded.
notes.original: You develop the knight and prepare ...e5 and ...Ngf6 in a way that avoids doubled pawns. The e4 knight is White's only active piece, so your plan is to trade it off and play ...e5 and ...Bd6. Do not allow Nd6+ ideas by neglecting the e7 pawn.

notes.text: Your e-pawn takes the centre and gives your bishop on f5 a retreat.
notes.original: You take the centre and give your bishop f5 a retreat.

notes.text: Your active queen guards both the e5 pawn and your bishop on f5.
notes.original: Your queen is active and supports e5 and f5.

notes.text: Your bishop takes a good diagonal, and next your king will castle short.
notes.original: Your bishop takes a good diagonal and your king will castle short.

notes.text: White may play Nh4 to trade your bishop; answer with ...Bg6, and keep your e5 pawn protected.
notes.original: You have a solid and active position with a space advantage in the centre and a plan of ...O-O and ...Rae8. This is an open, active position where White's knight on d2 has been moved and you have a space advantage in the centre with pawns on c6 and e5, and both kings castle short. Your plan: castle short, then play ...Rae8 and keep your bishop on f5 and queen on f6 coordinated. When ready, push ...e4 to gain space, or play ...Nf6 to bring the last knight in. White wants to play a4-a5, trade your bishop with Nh4 or Nd2-c4 and pressure e5. Meet Nh4 by ...Bg6 and Nxg6, hxg6. The risk is a loose e5 pawn, so keep it protected and never push ...e4 without checking that d3 is covered.

notes.text: Castling here is also a playable choice for you.
notes.original: This is also playable.

notes.text: Your pawn now guards the bishop and opens the f8 bishop; White keeps only a small edge.
notes.original: This protects the bishop with a pawn and opens the f8 bishop. Your plan is ...Nf6, ...Nbd7 and ...Be7 or ...Bxd6. If White plays Nd6+ you can recapture with the bishop. Avoid ...Nd7 too early because White gets Nd6+ ideas that damage your structure. White keeps only a small edge here.

notes.text: Your knight challenges White's knight on e4.
notes.original: Challenge the e4 knight.

notes.text: Develop the knight; your f8 bishop already covers the d6 square.
notes.original: Develop and cover the d6 square.

notes.text: Taking the knight is a good trade for you.
notes.original: Take the knight, a good trade for you because you get the bishop pair.

notes.text: Castle first; your e6 pawn can take the bishop on f5 afterwards.
notes.original: Do not recapture hastily; castle first.

notes.text: White's bishop on h3 hits your e6 pawn; don't let it pin your d7 knight.
notes.original: You keep a healthy structure and White has only a slight initiative. This is a semi-open position in which White has two bishops against your one after the exchanges, but your pawn structure is healthy and you are solid. Both kings will castle short. Your plan: recapture sensibly and play ...e5 or ...c5 to challenge the d4 pawn, then ...Qe7, ...Rfe8, and bring the knight to f8 and g6. White wants to open the game for the bishop pair and use the weak light squares such as e6 and f5. The risk is those light squares and the bishop on h3 attacking e6: do not let a bishop pin your knight on d7, and avoid weakening g6. If White deviates with Ng3 earlier, play ...Bg6.

notes.text: Challenge the centre with ...e5 to keep your structure healthy.
notes.original: You keep a healthy structure and White has only a slight initiative. This is a semi-open position in which White has two bishops against your one after the exchanges, but your pawn structure is healthy and you are solid. Both kings will castle short. Your plan: recapture sensibly and play ...e5 or ...c5 to challenge the d4 pawn, then ...Qe7, ...Rfe8, and bring the knight to f8 and g6. White wants to open the game for the bishop pair and use the weak light squares such as e6 and f5. The risk is those light squares and the bishop on h3 attacking e6: do not let a bishop pin your knight on d7, and avoid weakening g6. If White deviates with Ng3 earlier, play ...Bg6.

notes.text: This gives White a free bishop trade, but it is still playable.
notes.original: This gives White a free trade of his bishop but is playable.

notes.text: Also study White's play with Bc4 instead of this move.
notes.original: It's important to also review and understand white's play after 5. Bc4, which is discussed below.

notes.text: White threatens Nd6 checkmate because of the e-file pin; answer with ...e6 and develop calmly.
notes.original: White is aiming for the opening trap of Nd6 checkmate. Either ways this isn't white's one any only plan. White also wants to dominate the e file once white castles kingside or queenside followed by either rook to e1. White is going to develop is pieces with ease. Black should also do the same, just beware of checkmating ideas.

notes.text: Be2 is another White try; it looks passive, but White wants a solid, positional game.
notes.original: Be2 another alternative for White. Although this move may appear passive. White is aiming for a positional and solid gameplay rather than a dynamic game.

notes.text: g3 is another option for White, a positional and solid way to meet the Caro-Kann.
notes.original: g3 is another option for White, a positional and solid way to meet the Caro Kann.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes f7 for a moment; calm development with e6, Be7 and castling solves it.
notes.original: Here White tries another way to keep to the e4-e5 principle. This line is less challenging than others, causing Black only a temporary problem with f7. Black plays ...e6, ...Be7 and ...0-0 to maintain equality.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White aims for d5 and a central initiative, helped by the bishop and knights.
notes.original: White aims for d4-d5 and a central initiative, with the Bf4 and the knights helping.

notes.text: This is a sacrifice: if you take the knight, White's queen wins the bishop back and wrecks your structure.
notes.original: The point is a sacrifice: if you take with 13...exf5 then 14.Qxe7 wins the bishop back, and your structure is damaged.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen, and the position stays near equal.
notes.original: Your knight hits the queen and the position stays near equal.

notes.text: The position is equal.
After taking d4 and trading bishops, your rook is better placed on the c-file.
notes.original: Taking the d4 pawn and trading bishops leaves you better placed on the c-file.

notes.text: Avoid the natural-looking knight move here: it allows a knight check on d6 that is mate.
notes.original: Black must now avoid the natural looking Ngf6, as...

notes.text: White may keep the tension in the center and avoid trading minor pieces to complicate the game.
notes.original: White may even try to keep the tension on the center and avoid exchanging minor pieces to further complicate the game.

notes.text: Don't check with the queen here: White blocks with c3 and you end up worse.
notes.original: Trap: 9...Qa5+? 10.c3 b6 11.Nd2 Bb7 12.Nc4 Qd5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: White starts a kingside pawn storm, so answer with your own queenside pawn storm; it is a race.
notes.original: Once White launches a pawn storm on the kingside, Black should also attack on the queenside with a pawn storm of his own; it is a race, and both sides must watch out for mating threats.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's b3 shuts your queen's diagonal to a2 and keeps his king safe.
notes.original: Your queen on d5 hits a2, so White closes the diagonal and keeps his king safe, while Qe5 and the h5 pawn keep your kingside cramped.

notes.text: You start your own queenside play.
Your knight forks both White rooks.
notes.original: A knight fork: ...Nxf2 attacks both rooks.

notes.text: The position is sharp but balanced, and White's knight on e7 keeps things complicated.
notes.original: White must see that the knight on e7 comes with check before you take a rook. The position is sharp but balanced.

notes.text: The calm alternative leaves White a tiny edge, and your bishop on f5 is active.
notes.original: The calm alternative gives a tiny White edge and your bishop on f5 is active.

notes.text: Both kings will come under fire: you expand on the queenside while White storms the kingside.
notes.original: Both sides will attack the other's king here. Black has to expand on the queenside to find counterplay, while White may start a pawn storm on the kingside.

notes.text: White's knight hits your d7 knight and f7 pawn, and Ng6 would keep the h-pawn storm going.
notes.original: White's knight jumps in to hit the d7 knight and the f7 pawn; his motive is to keep the h-pawn storm alive with Ng6 ideas before your queenside play arrives.

notes.text: White offers a trade, hitting your bishop on e7 and rook on f8; answer calmly.
notes.original: A trade offer that attacks e7 and f8; answer calmly.

notes.text: You gain queenside space, which is your counter to White's h-pawn.
notes.original: You gain space on the queenside, which is your counter to the h-pawn.

notes.text: You keep a small edge, with a4 and b3 coming against the white king on c1.
notes.original: You keep a small edge and have ...a4 and ...b3 coming, aimed at the white king on c1.

notes.text: White's bishop is aiming at your f7 pawn.
notes.original: White is aiming for the f7 pawn.

notes.text: Your queen and bishop line up toward h2, ready to attack once the diagonal opens.
notes.original: Black has created a battery of Bishop and Queen. This can unleash a potential attack after black opens up the b8-h2 diagonal.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's bishop hits your d7 knight, so you have to answer actively.
notes.original: A forcing way to trade pieces: Bg4 hits the d7 knight, so you have to answer actively.

notes.text: Material is level, and your queen on b2 attacks the a1 rook, giving you the last tempo.
notes.original: The flurry of captures leaves material even and the position equal. Your queen picks up b2 and attacks the a1 rook, which gives you the final tempo.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White prepares c3 and b4 to chase a knight from c5; his bishop on a4 is a little loose.
notes.original: White unpins and prepares c3 and b4 to harass the c5 knight. His bishop on a4 is a little loose, which is the thing to remember.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks the queen and forces c3, which leaves a hole on d3.
notes.original: Forcing c3 makes d3 a hole.

notes.text: The a4 bishop is traded off and the position is level.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
White's king guards h3, and White will slowly use the bishop pair with Bd2, Qe2, a4 and Rae1.
notes.original: Kg2 prepares Bd2 and Qe2, keeps the h3 pawn safe and lets White use the bishop pair slowly with a4 and Rae1.

notes.text: Your a-pawn stops White's queenside expansion by blocking the a4 pawn.
notes.original: You stop the queenside expansion.

notes.text: Your center is solid, and ...Bb4 can trade White's dark bishop; the balance is level.
notes.original: Your centre is solid and you can play ...Bb4 to trade the dark bishop. The balance is level to a tiny White edge.

notes.text: Taking on f6 would be harmless; this knight move is much more challenging.
notes.original: Taking the knight on f6 here is completely harmless, whereas this perhaps synthetic move is much more challenging.

notes.text: White threatens bishop takes f7 with mate, so you must stop it; e6 does.
notes.original: White must prevent the threat of Bxf7#.

notes.text: White wants to take on f7 with the knight, because after ...Qe6+ you would get mated.
notes.original: White wants to take on f7 with the knight, because after ...Qe6+ Black gets mated.

notes.text: This knight sacrifice is unsound but often tried online, so it is worth reviewing.
notes.original: This knight sacrifice is unsound, but often attempted online, and definitely worth reviewing.

notes.text: Your knight on d5 covers against the Nxf7 idea; Nb6 does little, and Bf7 comes next.
notes.original: Black should play ...Nd5 to cover against the Nxf7 idea. ...Nb6 is an alternative, but the knight does little on the queenside; ...Nd5 followed by ...Bf7 is the better order.

notes.text: Black has fallen for the Nxf7 trap and is effectively lost.
This bishop move falls for the knight sacrifice on f7, and you are effectively lost.
notes.original: Black has fallen for the Nxf7 trap and is effectively lost.

notes.text: White threatens mate on h7; the only good defence is the d7 knight to f6.
notes.original: White threatens mate in one. The only good defence is ...N7f6; ...N5f6? would be a serious mistake since Black's position would be cramped.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's queen eyes e6 and h6, and g4-g5 will make it a direct kingside attack.
notes.original: White's queen eyes e6 and h6, and with Rae1 and g4-g5 to follow it is a direct kingside attack.

notes.text: Trade off the attacking knight.
notes.original: Trade the attacking knight.

notes.text: White keeps the initiative, so defend carefully with your king on h7 and rook on d8.
notes.original: White keeps the initiative, so you must defend carefully; the king goes to h7 and the rook to d8.

notes.text: Trading off the dangerous pieces calms White's attack.
notes.original: A slower move lets you trade the dangerous pieces.

notes.text: You take central space; White usually continues with Nf3, the Two Knights Attack.
notes.original:
After 2...d5 (near enough the only move, contesting the centre as Black prepared to do on move one), White may still play 3.d4 and transpose into the more common 2.d4 & 3.Nc3 Caro-Kann. However, the plan usually is to play 3.Nf3, the two knights attack. 3.Qf3 is the unusual Goldman variation.

Black takes space in the centre.

notes.text: This is the Two Knights Attack; your most common answers are ...Bg4 and ...dxe4.
notes.original:
3.Nf3 is the main move, the two knights attack.

= Caro-Kann Defence: Two Knights Attack = Black's two most common moves in this position are 3...Bg4 (the Mindeno Variation) and 3...dxe4.

notes.text: White trades at once, planning Nf3 and d4; your only question is which recapture keeps your structure healthy.
notes.original: White trades pawns at once to open the game. The idea is to use the knight already on c3 for quick development, then play d4 and Nf3 and hope you misplace a piece. It is very common in practice, so be ready for it. Your only question is which recapture keeps your structure healthy.

notes.text: White gains space with e5, planning d3, f4 and Nf3 to cramp you; your fight is for the center.
notes.original: White pushes the pawn to gain space and cramp your pieces, planning d3 and f4 and a quick Nf3 and d4. It is very common in practice and White is hoping for a closed game where you have no space. For you the fight is for the center.

notes.text: White's early queen move is harmless: trading on e4 neutralises the idea completely.
notes.original: 3.Qf3 - an early queen sortie, adding a second attacker to d5 and eyeing a future Qxf7-style idea if Black is careless. Trading in the center neutralizes the idea completely.

notes.text: White tries an odd early queen sortie; you meet it by striking the centre.
notes.original: 3.Qf3, full treatment in 🔵 19.

notes.text: Qe2 is unorthodox but logical: White wants to launch an aggressive kingside attack.
notes.original: Qe2 is an unorthodox reply but a logical one, as White wants to launch an aggressive kingside attack.

notes.text: White's queen adds pressure on e4 and d5 while keeping a later e5 push available.
notes.original: 3.Qe2 - a similar idea to 3.Qf3, adding pressure to e4/d5 and keeping options open for a later e5 push without blocking the f-pawn.

notes.text: An unorthodox but logical queen move, aiming to meet dxe4 with the queen centralized.
notes.original: 3.Qe2!?, an unorthodox but logical try aiming to meet ...dxe4 while keeping the queen centralized. Full treatment in 🔵 19.

notes.text: White's f4 grabs central space but weakens the e4 square and the diagonal toward its own king.
notes.original: 3.f4 - a more committal, gambit-flavored try that grabs extra central space at the cost of some structural weaknesses (the e4-square and the long diagonal toward White's own king).

notes.text: White transposes into the main-line Caro-Kann, normally reached by playing d4 first and Nc3 second.
notes.original: 3.d4 is a transposition to the main line Caro-Kann otherwise seen after 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.

notes.text: White doesn't want his pieces restricted, and you will find his centre hard to counter.
notes.original: Another interesting sideline: White does not want Black to restrict White's piece activity, and Black will find it hard to counter White's centre.

notes.text: White grabs the center at once, while your bishop's pin on f3 delays castling.
notes.original: 4.d4 (instead of the quieter 4.Be2 or 4.h3) - grabs the center immediately while the pin on f3 keeps White from castling right away.

notes.text: Recapture with the pawn and keep trading your bishop for the knight on f3.
notes.original: White opens the position and takes on d5, hoping your bishop on g4 is loose. White often follows with h3 to challenge it. For you the plan is to recapture with the pawn and keep trading on f3.

notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
notes.original: ...Bxf3, then play ...e6, ...dxe4 and ...Nf6

notes.text: The study warns of a trap where White grabs on d5 and ends up losing.
notes.original: Trap: 5.exd5? Bxd1 6.dxc6 Nxc6 7.Nxd1 e6 8.Bb5 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d5 with the pawn falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 5.exd5? Bxd1 6.dxc6 Nxc6 7.Nxd1 e6 8.Bb5 and White is losing.

notes.text: Pin with ...Bg4, give the bishop for the knight, then play ...e6, ...dxe4 and ...Nf6.
notes.original:
Idea: 3...Bg4 pins the knight. After 4.h3 give up the bishop with ...Bxf3, then play ...e6, ...dxe4 and ...Nf6. Fianchetto the other bishop and castle.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bxf3 5.Qxf3 e6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 7 to 11. ...Qxa5? loses material on move 12.
See also: 🟢 08 covers more of the Two Knights Attack. Plan: 🟠 Plan 01. Model games: 🟡 Game 03, 🟡 Game 09.

notes.text: Your position is very solid and hard to crack; White is ahead in development, but you have queenside chances.
notes.original: A very solid position, black's solid position would have been a very difficult task to crack. White sure do have the advantage due to his piece development but black do have some attacking chances on the queenside.

notes.text: The d4 push is another option for White here.
notes.original: Also possible: d4.

notes.text: This is the same position as before, and your existing repertoire choice here is correct.

notes.original: Also possible: g3.

notes.original: Your solid structure holds and ...e5 is the break.

notes.original: Not taking back leaves White a knight down.

notes.original: White accepts the structural damage in exchange for the bishop pair and open b-file.

notes.original: The bishop on a3 prevents castling because it covers f8.

notes.original: White gets an edge, but you can still play ...Bb7.

notes.text: You took White's queen; White's d-pawn now hits your queen, so White must recapture.
notes.original: Ignoring the recapture loses material.

notes.text: White fianchettoes at once, before you can block the long diagonal with ...c5 or ...Bc5.
notes.original: 8.Bg2 - fianchettoes immediately instead of the main 8.Qe3, aiming the bishop at the long diagonal before Black can block it with ...c5 or ...Bc5.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White castles and keeps the bishop pair, planning d4 to open the long diagonal.
notes.original: White castles and keeps the bishop pair. His motive is to open the long diagonal with d4 and c3 and to use the extra space, while the Qe4 hits the b7 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen and gains a tempo.
notes.original: The knight hits the queen with tempo.

notes.text: Your queen eyes b2 and d4 and is well placed for ...c5.
notes.original: You aim at b2 and d4, and the queen is well placed for ...c5.

notes.original: White has the bishop pair for a small edge, but your pieces are active and ...c5 is a natural break; do not rush it, first complete development with ...Rfe8.

notes.text: This is a slower route that reaches the same structure.
notes.original: A slower alternative that reaches the same structure.

notes.text: Your bishop develops actively and prepares castling without committing you to anything.
notes.original: 8...Bc5 (Solid & Optimal) - develops to an active, flexible square and prepares to castle without any immediate commitments; straightforward and easy to play.

notes.text: Your pawn grabs space in the centre, steering for a sharper, more committal structure.
notes.original: 8...d4 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - grabs space in the center right away, closing the long diagonal and steering for a sharper, more committal structure rather than quiet development.

notes.text: White finishes development before you can strike with ...d4, which is now less attractive.
notes.original: White finishes development before you can strike with ...d4, which is less attractive now that the Bg2 looks down the long diagonal.

notes.text: You castle at once and your king is safe.
notes.original: You castle at once and the king is safe.

notes.text: Your e-pawn takes the centre.
notes.original: You take the centre and block the Bg2 diagonal.

notes.text: White has to reroute the knight from b1; finish your development and watch the c5 bishop.
notes.original: White wanted Qe2 and d3 to support e4 and now has to reroute the knight from b1. The position is balanced with a small White edge, so complete development with ...Rad8 and ...Rfe8 and watch the c5 bishop.

notes.text: White's Na4 chased your bishop, but nothing has changed and the position is balanced.
notes.original: Na4 chases the bishop but you retreat with tempo and nothing has changed.

notes.text: White's knight hits your d4 pawn at once, wanting to remove it before you support it.
notes.original: White attacks d4 at once. His motive is to remove the pawn that cramps him before you can support it, and the Qf3 also eyes the b7 pawn.

notes.text: Your queen defends the d4 pawn and hits the b2 pawn at once.
notes.original: Defends d4 and hits b2 in one move.

notes.text: Your knight hits White's queen and takes a lasting central square.
notes.original: The knight hits the queen and takes a central square for good.

notes.text: Your bishop supports the e5 knight, so you are not forced to give it up.
notes.original: Bd6 supports e5 so you are not forced to give up the knight.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the knight away and you keep your space; just watch the weaknesses g5 leaves.
notes.original: The knight on f4 is kicked away and you keep the d4 pawn that gives you space. White is about level and you have the easier game, the only worry being the weaknesses ...g5 leaves behind.

notes.text: White's castling lost a knight to your d4 pawn, and the rook on b1 doesn't repay a whole piece.
notes.original: Castling leaves the c3 knight en prise to the d4 pawn, and the rook on b1 does not repay a whole piece.

notes.text: White's d3 keeps up the pressure on the centre.
notes.original: d3, white wants to keep the pressure on the center.

notes.text: A French-type structure has arisen, with White's pawns on d4 and e5.
notes.original: A French-type structure has arisen.

notes.text: White's Nd6 check would be a mistake: you take the knight and White ends up in big trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 10.Nd6+? Bxd6 11.Bxf3 Bc7 12.c4 Nc6 13.cxd5 and White is in big trouble.

notes.text: Checking with the knight on d6 falls into a trap: White is in big trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 10.Nd6+? Bxd6 11.Bxf3 Bc7 12.c4 Nc6 13.cxd5 and White is in big trouble.

notes.original: A horrible decision which fall short after Nc6

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's pawn hits d5 to undermine it, and he has the bishop pair.
notes.original: White's idea is to undermine d5 and use the bishop pair.

notes.text: Your pawn gains space with a tempo on White's queen.
notes.original: Gaining space with tempo on the queen.

notes.text: White can take your b7 pawn, but the open lines then give you compensation.
notes.original: White can grab the b7 pawn, but the open lines give you compensation.

notes.text: This is another try for White; you answer by castling.
notes.original: Another try.

notes.text: You plan Nc6; if White then grabs d4 with his queen, he is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 12.Qxd4? Nc6 13.Qxd5 exd5 14.exd6 Nce5 15.c3 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d4 with the queen falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 12.Qxd4? Nc6 13.Qxd5 exd5 14.exd6 Nce5 15.c3 and White is losing.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White opens lines to make up for the pawn, with the d6 pawn as his spearhead.
notes.original: White tries to open lines to compensate for the pawn; the d6 pawn is his spearhead.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop out; Rf7 follows and the d6 pawn will fall.
notes.original: Kick the Bg5 out; ...Rf7 follows and the d6 pawn will fall.

notes.text: With the rook on f7 you are clearly better.
notes.original: Black is clearly better.

notes.text: Your queen wins the c3 pawn.
notes.original: The c3 pawn drops.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White builds a Queen's Gambit structure and targets your doubled f-pawns.
White's knight attacks your bishop on g6 and will take it unless you act.
notes.original: The knight attacks your bishop.

notes.text: Your g-pawn takes the f5 square away from White's knight, and your position is solid.
notes.original: ...g6 stops Nf5 and your position is solid.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Simply finish development behind a solid structure; the pin still costs White a move before castling.
notes.original: 4...e6 is simplest: finish development and meet White's center with a solid structure; the pin means White still needs an extra move (Be2 or h3) before castling.

notes.text: White unpins and prepares to castle; the pin made him spend this extra move first.
notes.original: White unpins and prepares to castle; the pin means he needs this extra move first.

notes.text: White has a little extra space, but you have no weaknesses; develop, castle and play c5.
notes.original: White has a little extra space, but you have no weaknesses. Play ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c5 and the position is fine.

notes.text: Grabbing the d4 pawn is safe here; White's only compensation is development.
notes.original: Grabbing the d4 pawn is safe here, White's only compensation is development.

notes.text: Take back with the pawn, trade on f3 once h3 comes, and avoid ...Nf6 now.
notes.original: Recapture with the pawn. Plan: ...Bxf3 when White plays h3, then ...Nf6 and ...Nc6, ...e6, and castle short. Your break is ...e5 later. Avoid ...Nf6 now, because White gets the center with d4 and a free game.

notes.text: Developing the knight is tempting, but White takes on c6 and gets a big lead.
notes.original: Tempting but loses a pawn structure battle: White takes on c6 and gets a big lead.

notes.text: Your knight on c6 puts pressure on the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Your knights hit d4 and pressure the position.

notes.text: Your knight pressures d4 and heads for b4, while White's queen has few good squares.
notes.original: Now your knight pressures d4 and heads for b4, and White's queen on f3 has few good squares.

notes.text: The position is equal; jump your knight to b4, hitting the bishop on d3 and the c2 pawn.
notes.original: You have a solid setup, with all pieces developed and castling short next. If White tries to avoid trades with Bg5 or Qe2 you still play ...Be7 and ...O-O, and keep ...Rc8 for the open c-file. The long-term plan is to pressure the pawn on d4 with ...Nc6 and ...Rc8, while White tries to hold the isolated-looking center with Rd1. Equal. This is a Caro-Kann Exchange position with symmetrical pawns on d4 and d5 and a half-open c-file for you. White has a slight space advantage, but you can challenge it. Your plan: play ...Nb4 to hit the bishop on d3 and the pawn on c2, then ...Be7 or ...Bd6, castle short, and ...Qd7 and ...Rc8. White wants a3 to kick the knight and then Bb5 or a minority attack with b4. If a3 comes, take ...Nxd3+ and recapture. The mistake is playing ...Nb4 without a follow-up, so know your next move. If White plays Bb5+, block with ...Nc6.

notes.text: Recapture with the c-pawn: you keep a solid d5 pawn and a half-open c-file.
notes.original: Recapture with the c-pawn. You keep a solid pawn on d5 and a half-open c-file for a rook later. Because the knight stands on c3, White cannot support d4 with c3, so the center is a little less stable. Plan: ...Nc6, then ...a6 to stop Nb5 jumps, then ...e6 and ...Bd6 or ...Be7, and castle short. Your breaks are ...e5 and ...f6 against a pawn on e5.

notes.text: The natural developing move tempts, but White takes on c6 and leads in the center and development.
notes.original: The natural developing move is the tempting reply, but White takes on c6 and gets a lead in the center and in development.

notes.text: You have nothing to fear: blocking in your c-pawn does not favour White.
notes.original: Black has nothing to fear here, blocking in the c-pawn is not in white's favour.

notes.text: Playing your knight to c6 first is the preferable move order here.
notes.original: Another move order is ...Nc6, which is preferable to ...Nf6.

notes.text: Trade White's knight on e5; it is his most active piece and you don't want it jumping further.
notes.original: When White puts a knight on e5, trade it. It is White's most active piece and you do not want it jumping on to other squares.

notes.text: The e5 pawn is cramped and becomes a target: hit it with ...Nd7, ...Qc7 and ...f6.
notes.original: Now the e5 pawn is cramped and becomes a target. Hit it with ...Nd7, ...Qc7 and the lever ...f6, and bring your bishop out to d7 or pin the knight with ...Bb4. Your structure is healthy and the plan against e5 is easy. This is a Caro-Kann Exchange structure with White's pawn on e5 locked against your pawns on d5 and e6, and the bishops of both sides still on the board. White has a small space edge, but the pawn on e5 can become a target. Your plan: develop the knight with ...Nd7, bring the queen to c7 to hit e5, and play ...f6 to undermine it, with ...Bb4 or ...Bd7 for your bishop. White wants Bg5, Qg4 or Qh5 for a kingside attack, and h7 is the target. The mistake is playing ...f6 before you are developed, since Qh5+ becomes annoying. If White plays Qh5, answer calmly and keep your king flexible.

notes.text: Kick the knight and gain space; support d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6.
notes.original: Kick the knight and gain space at once. Plan: ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Bd7 and ...e6, then castle short. Your pawn chain on c5-d4 gives you a space advantage, and your pieces can use e5 and f5. Aim for the break ...f6 or ...Qb6 to hit b2. Avoid leaving the pawn on d4 without support, and avoid trading all your pieces, because the space you gain is your main trump. If White plays d3 early you can strike with ...c5 and ...Nc6 at once, and if White castles you can safely do the same. White's usual alternative is to play f4 and Nf3, and then you hold d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6.

notes.text: Bf5 is also a good move here, and it keeps your d5 pawn.
notes.original: Also playable and keeps the d5 pawn.

notes.text: Your center is solid and the position is balanced; hit b2 with ...Qb6 and use e7, f5 and g6.
notes.original: Your center is solid and your pieces go to e7, f5 and g6 as needed. Balanced with a clear plan. This is a closed centre where your pawn chain c5-d4 gives you space on the queenside, and White has the pawn chain e5-f4. Both kings are likely to castle short. Your plan: play ...Nge7, then ...Qb6 to hit b2, and ...Nf5 or ...Ng6 to hold your centre. White wants c3 to undermine d4, Bb5 and h4 to attack your king, so you hit back with ...Qb6 and ...f6. The mistake is leaving d4 unprotected; after c3 take with ...dxc3. If White deviates with Bb5, keep the knight on c6 protected with ...Be7.

notes.text: Your c6, d5 and e6 pawns form a solid Semi-Slav style center.
notes.original: e6, this variation has a Semi Slav taste against the Fantasy Variation. First of all you create a very solid and fortified center. This is another alternative choice against the Fantasy Variation if you like positional and solid gameplay. You are going to try and set up a Solid Semi Slav like structure. This can even transpose into a French Defence like position if white were to advance his central pawn forward.

notes.text: Your queen presses on b2 and d4 at once, forcing White to react right away.
notes.original: 3...Qb6!? (Aggressive Alternative) - instead of meeting 3.f3 with the structural ...e6 or ...dxe4, Black immediately presses on b2 and d4, forcing White to react right away rather than Black settling into a slow structure. Choice guide: choose 3...Qb6 if you are happy to play a more active, slightly unusual line that puts the queen on the b6-g1 diagonal and meets f3 with immediate counter-pressure on d4 and b2 (medium risk). For a calmer game stick with 3...dxe4 (🔵 18) or 3...e6 (the main line of this chapter). 3...Qb6 puts pressure on d4 and b2. White's main tries are 4.Nc3, 4.a3, 4.a4 and 4.c3.

notes.text: White develops at once instead of recapturing on e4, a gambit-style idea.
notes.original: 4.Nc3!? - a Milner-Barry-style gambit idea, developing immediately rather than recapturing the pawn on e4 right away.

notes.text: White ignores the weakened e1-h4 diagonal, since the f2 pawn is gone; your queen can use it.
notes.original: White shores up d4 and prepares to meet ...exd4 with cxd4, hoping to open the centre while the king is still on e1. The trouble is that it ignores the weakened e1-h4 diagonal, since the f2 pawn is gone.

notes.text: Take on e4, strike back with e5, then develop fast: knight to f6, bishop to d6 and castle.
notes.original:
Idea: Take on e4 and strike back with 4...e5. White's king is a little loose after f3, so develop fast: ...Bg4, ...Nf6, ...Bd6 and castle.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4 e5 5.Nf3 Bg4
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on move 4.
See also: 🟢 11 covers more of the Fantasy Variation. Plan: 🟠 Plan 05.

notes.text: If White grabs the e5 pawn, your bishop takes the queen and you end up winning.
notes.original: Trap: 6.Nxe5? Bxd1 7.Kxd1 Qxd4+ 8.Nd3 Na6 9.Nc3 and White is losing.

notes.text: White threatens to take on f7, then win your bishop on g4 and strand your king.
notes.original: 6.Bc4 prepares O-O and Ng5 once the queen is out of the pin. White is happy to give a pawn for quick development, and it also threatens Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe5+ Ke8 Qxg4, winning the bishop on g4 and leaving the black king stuck in the centre.

notes.text: Develop as actively as possible here.
notes.original: Theory note: Black should develop as actively as possible here.

notes.text: Taking on e5 with the knight falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6.Nxe5? Bxd1 7.Kxd1 Qxd4+ 8.Nd3 Na6 9.Nc3 and White is losing.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes f7, and a knight and rook can join. Grabbing e5 here still loses for White.
notes.original:
A knight, a bishop and, once White has castled, a rook can all bear down on f7. Watch what White is planning, as hidden dangers lurk in the opening.
Trap: 7.Nxe5? Bxd1 8.Nxf7 Kxf7 9.Bc4+ Ke8 10.Kxd1 and White is losing.

notes.text: White develops quietly: castle, then h3 to deal with your bishop on g4.
notes.original: White keeps the bishop on e2 instead of putting it on c4. The idea is quiet development: castle, then play h3 to deal with your bishop on g4. If you take on f3, White recaptures with the bishop and keeps a healthy structure with the bishop pair. This is a calmer way to play than 7.Bc4, and the pin on the knight is less annoying here.

notes.text: White's bishop looks natural, but it blocks the queen's protection of the d4 pawn.
notes.original: White puts the bishop on d3, eyeing your kingside and the h7 pawn. The drawback is that the bishop blocks the queen's protection of the d4 pawn. Many club players play this because it looks natural.

notes.text: Taking on e5 with the knight falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 7.Nxe5? Bxd1 8.Nxf7 Kxf7 9.Bc4+ Ke8 10.Kxd1 and White is losing.

notes.text: Your bishop adds a defender to f7. Other moves run into Qb3, hitting b7 and f7 together.
notes.original: 7...Bh5 adds a defender to f7. Other moves, such as ...Nbd7, run into 8.Qb3, which hits b7 and f7 together. Black can only defend one of them, and White gets a lot of play on the seventh rank.

notes.text: White threatens Qxb7, but ...b5 stops it and costs White a tempo.
notes.original: Qb3 doesn't work because of b5 thus eliminating white's threat of Qxb7 and at the same time lose one tempo.

notes.text: This pawn is poisoned: you are undeveloped, and White's Qe1 combination on the open e-file wins.
notes.original: The e-file is open and Black, still uncastled, is on the verge of losing. Poisoned pawns should not be taken: with so little development, Black lacks the pieces to hold against White's strong winning combination starting with Qe1.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop and gives your light-squared bishop room if White plays g4.
notes.original: 9...h6 kicks the bishop and also gives Black's light-squared bishop some breathing room in case White plays g4.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
You have castled and finished your development in the Fantasy Variation.
notes.original: The Fantasy Variation.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
Rf5 harasses your bishop on h5, but Ngf6 holds everything together; White keeps a small edge.
notes.original: White opens the a-file with axb5 and drops the bishop back to c2 to support e4. Your counter is ...Ng4, aiming at h2 and e3, followed by ...exd4 and ...Be5 to put your bishop on a strong central square. Rf5 harasses the bishop on h5, but ...Ngf6 holds everything together. White keeps a small, annoying edge.

notes.text: With the quieter bishop to f2 and knight to h4, you are fully equal.
notes.original: The quieter plan, with the bishop retreating to f2 and the knight to h4, leaves you fully equal.

notes.text: White can also take on d5 here, though you stay slightly better.
notes.original: Bxd5 is also possible for White here.

notes.text: White's bishop, d5 pawn and h2 are all loose, and your bishop and queen already line up on h2.
notes.original: White has too many hanging pieces - the bishop, the d5-pawn and h2 - and is on the verge of collapse.

notes.text: Your bishop takes with check, and your queen covers h2, so the king cannot take it.
notes.original: Nd2 attacks the pawn on e4 and opens the f-file against your knight, but it comes too late: the bishop takes with check, and the queen on c7 covers h2, so the king cannot take it.

notes.text: White sacrifices a knight to land a pawn on e6, but taking it leaves you better.
notes.original: White's last tactical try: a knight sacrifice to get a pawn to e6 hitting your knight on d7.

notes.text: The sacrifice runs out of steam: you keep an extra pawn and White's king stays exposed.
notes.original: The sacrifice runs out of steam: you keep an extra pawn and the white king is still exposed.

notes.text: Trading bishops does not stop the bleeding: h2 is gone and your e-pawn rolls on.
notes.original: Trading the bishop does not stop the bleeding: the h2 pawn is gone and the e-pawn rolls on.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White's last bishop is nearly trapped. Your pawn hits the knight on f3 and opens your bishop's diagonal.
notes.original: Here is the point: White's last bishop is nearly trapped, and every retreat costs a tempo. Your pawn push attacks the knight on f3 and opens the diagonal for the bishop on h5.

notes.text: You are clearly better: your e4 pawn cramps White, your knights are centralised and the a5 bishop is far away.
notes.original: You are clearly better: the pawn on e4 cramps White, your knights are centralised and the bishop on a5 is far from the action.
