notes.text: Rd1 looks natural but backfires: after your knight and e-pawn advance, White loses material and you come out ahead.
notes.original: Rd1 looks natural, but after ...Nf5 and ...e4 everything goes your way: White's rook has to take on d7 and ends up a piece down.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn is isolated: no neighbouring pawns can support it.
notes.original: Black has an isolated pawn.

notes.text: Qf5 is the more testing try: the queen stays central and pressures your slightly exposed king.
notes.original: Instead of Qg4 in the main line, the more testing try is Qf5, keeping the queen more centrally placed and creating immediate threats against Black's slightly exposed king.

notes.text: Your position is very unpleasant here, so defend carefully.
notes.original: This is just a horrendous position for Black.

notes.text: Your bishop guards the e5 pawn and prepares h5; get your pieces out and look for a queen trade.
notes.original: The bishop supports the e5 pawn that White's queen and bishop are eyeing, and prepares ...h5 later. The numbers say White is only modestly better, so the plan is to get your pieces out and look for a queen trade.

notes.text: Next, ...h4 kicks White's queen off g3 and takes the g4 square from White's pieces.
notes.original: A useful resource: ...h5-h4 would kick the queen off g3, and it takes the g4 square away from White's pieces.

notes.text: Your queen on g4 offers a queen trade and gives you a solid defensive set-up.
notes.original: You offer a queen trade on g4 and reach a solid defensive set-up.

notes.text: Pushing the pawn only creates a target: White's rook and knight pile onto e4.
notes.original: Pushing the pawn only creates a target: rooks and knights pile onto e4, and White's pieces are better placed.

notes.text: Taking on d4 here would be a blunder: Qxf8 would be checkmate.
notes.original: Trap: 13...exd4? 14.Qxf8# and Black gets mated.

notes.text: Taking on d4 here runs into a mating attack against your king.
notes.original: Trap: 14...exd4? 15.cxd5 h5 16.Qf7+ Kh7 17.Qxh5+ Kg8 18.Qf7+ Kh7 19.Rh3# and Black gets mated.

notes.text: White keeps a lasting initiative here, and this is the critical test of the whole line.
notes.original: White keeps a lasting initiative here that the main line's Qg4 understates. This is the critical test of this whole sharp line.

notes.text: Your queen on c4 stopped guarding the knight on d7, so White simply took it.
notes.original: This is the point of White's initiative: when your queen went to c4 it stopped guarding the knight on d7, so that knight falls. The rest of the line is damage control.

notes.text: White is a knight up for two pawns but undeveloped; use the tempi to push your d-pawn and activate your…
notes.original: White has an extra knight for two pawns, but the knight on b1 and bishop on c1 are still undeveloped, so you get a few tempi to push the d-pawn and bring the king and bishop into play. White must untangle first with Nd2 and Bf4.

notes.text: Pushing d5 instead is less testing, because you win time with ...e4.
notes.original: The alternative d5 lets you win time with ...e4 and is less testing.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
You must hold b5: White's a-pawn attacks it, and your a6 pawn supports it.
notes.original: You must hold b5: a4 attacks it directly, and ...a6 supports it so that axb5 axb5 does not open the a-file with tempo on your rook.

notes.text: If White trades on e5 and recaptures with the pawn, your bishop on d6 takes back.
notes.original: White tries Nxe5 Nxe5 dxe5 to open the d-file and the diagonals towards your king, but your bishop on d6 is waiting to take back on e5.

notes.text: Your check gains the tempo to save the bishop, and you can castle next with a balanced game.
notes.original: The check gains the tempo you need to save the bishop, and material is level; you will castle and the position is balanced.

notes.text: You answered the pin by trading bishops, and castling keeps the game level.
notes.original: Here you answer the pin by trading bishops, then take on e4 while White takes on c6, and the game is level.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
You keep the extra pawn, but White's rooks are active, so bring your knight into play and secure your king.
notes.original: This forced liquidation is White's best try: your queen is facing White's on the e-file with only your knight in between, and the bishop on d2 is attacked by both bishop and knight, so White trades everything. You keep the extra pawn, but White's rooks reach the open files before your knight and king are developed, so the position is balanced. Bring the king to safety and the knight into play.

notes.text: Castling would be too slow: you stay a clean pawn up and your rook takes the e-file.
notes.original: Castling is too slow: you remain a clean pawn up with the e-file in your hands.

notes.text: Develop calmly: your pieces head for d6 and c7, and your king goes short.
notes.original: Bring the last knight out and keep the centre solid. You do not need to hurry. Your pieces head for d6 and c7, and your king goes short.

notes.text: Your bishop supports the e5 pawn, so White's d4 break loses force.
notes.original: The bishop eyes the kingside and supports the e5 pawn, so White's d4 break loses force.

notes.text: Castle short, then play h6 to ask the bishop on g5 what it wants.
notes.original: This is a balanced centre where both sides have a pawn on e4 or e5 and the e5 pawn is yours to guard. Your plan: castle short, put a rook on e8 or d8, and play ...h6 to ask the bishop on g5 what it wants. Aim for ...Bxf3 only when it wins the bishop pair or wrecks White's pawn on f3 (it forces Nxf3). White wants d4 or Nc4, hitting the e5 pawn, and a later Qd3 or Qe3 with pressure on your king. Meet d4 with ...exd4 and ...Bxf3 so that the white queen is dragged out. The risk is greed: taking on e4 with ...Nxe4 looks free but after O-O and Nxe5 your knights lose their grip on the centre. If White plays Bc4 or Bd3 instead, keep the same set-up.

notes.text: This trade opens the centre while White is ahead in development; you can survive, but prefer the knight to d7.
notes.original: This trade opens the centre while White is a move ahead in development. You can survive, but you will have to defend the e-file, so prefer ...Nbd7.

notes.text: Take on d4 at once: White cannot simply recapture, because the queen no longer protects d4.
notes.original: Take on d4 straight away. White cannot simply recapture because the pawn on d4 has lost the queen's support.

notes.text: Your knight retreats to d7, ready to take the e5 pawn if it is loose.
notes.original: White pushes to gain a tempo and open the long diagonal for the bishop. Your knight retreats to d7 and is ready for ...Nxe5 if the pawn is loose.

notes.text: White has the bishop pair, but your position is solid and the e5 pawn is a target.
notes.original: This is an open position where White has the bishop pair and the open f-file, but your position is solid and the e5 pawn is a target. Your plan: play ...e6 to guard d5 and f5, then ...Nb6 or ...Qb6 to hit the pawns on d4 and b2. Castle short and put a rook on c8 or d8. White wants Bxh7, e6 or Qf3-f4, so keep your king safe and watch the h7 pawn and the f7 square. Meet e6 with ...fxe6 or ...Nb6 depending on what is hanging. The risk is castling too early into the attack on h7. If White avoids e5, play ...Be7 and ...O-O and sit comfortably.

notes.text: This quiet route also works, but taking on d4 is more ambitious.
This bishop sacrifice does not work: you take it and consolidate with ...Ngf6, and White has no follow-up.
notes.original: 7.Bxf7+ does not work. Black takes the bishop and consolidates with ...Ngf6, and White cannot follow with Ng5 because the black queen covers g5.

notes.text: White plans to open up the f-file.
notes.original: With plans of opening up the f file s

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
The position is equal.
Your knight lands on e6 heading for d4, your pieces are well placed, and the position is level.
notes.original: The e4-e5 push gains space and kicks the knight, but your pieces find good squares: the knight lands on e6 heading for d4 or g5, the bishop is safe on h5, and the rooks take the open files. The position stays level.

notes.text: The tactical point: taking on f3 pulled the knight away from d2, so the e4 pawn fell.
notes.original: Shows the tactical point: once Bxf3 deflects the knight from d2, the pawn on e4 hangs.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
You are a clean pawn up, so just finish your development.
notes.original: White's Qe2 allowed you to win a pawn on e4. Nbd2 attacks the knight, so you retreat it to f6 and keep the extra pawn. Then ...b5 gains a tempo on the bishop, and ...exd4 and ...Re8 pile pressure on the e-file. You are a clean pawn up and only need to finish development.

notes.text: Even the direct Qc2 hitting e4 is met by the same retreat, and you stay clearly better.
White repositions the bishop to b3, away from tactics on the long diagonal, before continuing the attack.
notes.original: Rather than the immediate Qf2, repositioning the bishop to b3 first is a cleaner try, keeping it safely out of tactics on the long diagonal before continuing the attack.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your king steps off White's bishop diagonal, and your knight eyes f4 to hold back the f4 break.
notes.original: White retreats the bishop to avoid ...Bxg5 and keep the bishop pair, advances the a-pawn for queenside space and wants the f4 break (f3-f4) to open the f-file. You aim your knight at f4 and tuck the king onto h8, away from the b3-g8 diagonal. If White plays f4 anyway, ...Nxf4 Bxf4 exf4 wins a pawn but White regains it with Qxf4. A modest White edge.

notes.text: White's knight tour fails to a tactic: you win a pawn and break the pin by taking the g5 bishop.
notes.original: The knight tour fails to a tactic: ...Nxe4 takes a pawn and the pin on g5 is broken by taking the bishop.

notes.text: This is a moderate improvement for White over the main line's try in this sub-line.
notes.original: A real, moderate improvement for White - not as sharp as the Main Line #1 note above, but still meaningfully stronger than the main line's original try in this sub-line.

notes.text: Your queen offers a trade that takes the sting out of White's play, leaving White only a modest edge.
notes.original: White is a pawn down, but has the g-file, the bishop on b3 aimed at f7 and the queen on the kingside: Rg1 and Bg5 threaten to remove your knight on f6 and then play against g7. Kh8 steps off the b3-g8 diagonal, and ...c5 and ...Bd4 gain space and activity. The queen trade on e6 takes the sting out of White's play, leaving a modest White edge.

notes.text: The same set-up with another move order lets you equalise.
Black is winning.
White's bishop sacrifice has no follow-up, so you are clearly ahead; just keep your king covered.
notes.original: White's Bxf7+ was a sacrifice that dragged your king out, but White has no follow-up: no more checks, and the open f-file is not enough. Taking on f3 first wrecks White's kingside pawns, and ...Qb6 hits b2 and d4 at once. You are clearly ahead in material and only have to keep the king covered.

notes.text: White's e6 pawn push does not help: your pieces swarm the white king.
notes.original: The intermezzo e6+ does not help: your pieces swarm the white king.

notes.text: White's e5 pawn only looks like a gambit; your active pieces will soon win it.
notes.original: This move looks aggressive and gambit-like, but it is not: the e5 pawn will soon fall because Black's pieces are active and White is cramped, so White must eventually give it up to develop. Lines where White tries to hold e5 need more detailed study.

notes.text: The material is back to level, and your more active rook gives you a clear edge.
notes.original: You are a pawn down on paper, but White's king is stuck in the middle and the pawn on e4 is weak. You pile on it with ...Rhe8 and ...Bg6, and when b4 tries to kick your knight, ...Ncxe4 only gives up a piece for a moment: after Nxe4 your bishop jumps to e5, the knight on e4 is attacked twice and d4 is hit as well, so the material comes straight back. You end with the more active rook and a clear edge.

notes.text: White's a-pawn push lost a tempo, so you pick up pawns while the king is exposed.
notes.original: Pushing the a-pawn loses a tempo and you pick up pawns while the king is exposed.

notes.text: Your bishop on h2 could be trapped, so White hits it with the knight at once and it must run.
notes.original: The bishop on h2 won a pawn but is in danger of being trapped by g3, so White hits it with the knight at once and it has to run.

notes.text: White's knights harass g7, but you answer with ...g6 and ...Rd7 and stay a pawn up.
notes.original: White's knights hunt for f5 and h6 to harass the g7 pawn and your rook; you answer with ...g6 and ...Rd7, then take the pawn on e4. You stay a pawn up with a small edge, because White's pieces are active and you must keep your king safe.

notes.text: The attempt to trap your bishop fails: it takes another pawn and escapes.
notes.original: The attempt to trap the bishop fails, because it takes another pawn and escapes.

notes.text: With queens off your king is safe in the centre, but opposite bishops make the extra pawn hard to convert.
notes.original: White's compensation for the pawn is the bishop pair: Be5 hits the knight on f6 and the rooks come off. You march the king to the centre, which is safe now that the queens are gone, and after the trade on f6 the bishops are of opposite colours. That is why the extra pawn is hard to convert and the position is only slightly better for you.

notes.text: Your check forces the king to move; blocking with g3 loses to ...Qxe4+, so the king gets stuck.
notes.original: This is the idea: the check forces the king to move. White cannot block with g3 because ...Qxe4+ wins material, so he plays Kd2 and the king is stuck in the middle. Your plan is to bring pieces with tempo, ...Nf6, ...Qf2+ or ...Nxe4+, and open the position with ...exd4. Keep checking only while it gains time; avoid pushing the queen alone far into the enemy camp. This is clearly better for you.

notes.text: Developing the knight misses the Qh4 check; after Nf3 and Bc4 White gets a comfortable, roughly equal game.
notes.original: Developing the knight is natural but misses the check; after Nf3 exd4 Bc4 White gets a comfortable game and the position is about equal. Do not play it.

notes.text: Open the centre while White's king is exposed and your pieces are better coordinated.
notes.original: Open the e-file and the centre while the king is exposed. Your knights and bishops are all better coordinated than White's.

notes.text: Bring your dark bishop out to hit the knight on d4, then chase it away with ...Nc6.
notes.original: White's king on c2 is the target, and you keep the initiative. This is an open position where White's king stands on c2 and your pieces are more active, so you keep the initiative. Your queen on f2 and knight on e4 are annoying, and it is your move. Your plan is, first, to bring the dark bishop out with ...Bc5 or ...Bb4, hitting the knight on d4. Second, develop ...Nc6 to chase it away. Third, keep checking and opening files toward the king rather than grabbing pawns. White wants to trade queens or to consolidate with Rd1 and Be3. The typical mistake is to play the queen alone to g2 and get trapped. If White trades pieces, keep the bishop pair active.

notes.text: Simply hold your extra pawn and develop; White lacks enough compensation for the lost tempo.
notes.original: 4...Nf6 is simplest: hold onto the extra pawn and develop normally. White's pawn on e4 is extra material, not enough compensation for the lost tempo.

notes.text: A safe way to avoid every gambit trick: you return the pawn at once.
notes.original: A safe way to avoid every gambit trick: Black returns the pawn at once.

notes.text: Against rare second and third moves, play d5, take on e4 when it is safe, and develop.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays a rare second or third move.
Idea: Everything else: rare second and third moves, each with a pointer to where it is covered. The answer is nearly always the same: ...d5, take on e4 when it's safe, and develop.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.f3 exf3

notes.text: Take the second pawn too; you plan to give one back later for a clean structural edge.
notes.original: Simplest and best: take the second pawn too, planning to give one back later for a clean structural edge rather than trying to hold onto both.

notes.text: Your extra pawn lasts only until White recaptures on e4, but you keep a healthy structure and an easy game.
notes.original: Strictly, your extra pawn lasts only until White recaptures on e4, and the knight is well placed there eyeing d6 and f6. What you keep is a healthy structure and an easy game.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your knight on f6; handle it calmly and do not give the pawn back for nothing.
notes.original: White pins the knight on f6 to the queen and wants to rid you of your best defender, intending to recapture on e4 with a good structure, or to follow with Qd2 and queenside castling. It is very common in practice (played in about 51,000 games). So the pin on f6 must be handled calmly, and you should not drop the pawn back without gaining something.

notes.text: This is the slow move: White develops the bishop but leaves the centre unprotected, and your pieces are free.
notes.original: This is the slow move: White develops the bishop but leaves the centre unprotected. The Fantasy position after the knight trades is tricky because White's e-pawn is gone and your pieces are free.

notes.text: It works, but you give up the extra pawn for nothing; taking on f3 scores better.
notes.original: A quiet position with only a tiny Black edge. It works, but you give up the extra pawn for nothing, and 4...exf3 scores clearly better.

notes.text: White's g-pawn lunge aims to harass your bishop, but it is safe on g6 and can drop back to h7.
notes.original: White's g4 lunge wants g5 and h4-h5 to harass the bishop, but the bishop is safe on g6; if h4-h5 arrives you drop back to h7, where it still eyes the long diagonal. You are a little more comfortable.

notes.text: You strike at the centre at once, hitting the d4 pawn while White's e-pawn is missing.
notes.original: You strike at the centre at once, taking advantage of the missing white pawn on e4.

notes.text: Develop the bishop, castle short and speed up development with Bg4 or Be6, but castle before grabbing pawns.
notes.original: This is an open position where you have a lead in the centre and good piece play. Your plan: bring the bishop to d6 or e7, castle short, and add ...Bg4 or ...Be6 to speed up development. White wants f4 or Nf3 to kick your queen and win time. Watch for tricks on the e-file when your king is in the centre. If White plays c3 and Bd3 or f4 early, trade queens only if it helps your structure, and keep the extra central pawn. The risk is grabbing too many pawns and leaving the king in the centre; castle first. If White deviates with Be3 or Bd3, take the d4 pawn only after checking that the queen still has an escape square.

notes.text: White adds a second guard to d4; you must decide how to settle the tension with your e5 pawn.
notes.original: White develops the kingside knight and adds a second attacker against d4, so that dxe5 or d5 both stay available next move. There is no trap here; it is the most natural move and it is very common in practice (played in about 71,000 games). So White is happy to wait, and you must decide how to settle the tension between your e5 pawn and the d4 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop on c4, a gain of time after the queen trade.
notes.original: The other recapture lets you strike with ...e5, trade queens and win the e4 pawn, and the bishop gets hit by ...Nb6.

notes.text: Take on d4 and accept the queen trade: you have no weaknesses and your bishop hits the knight with tempo.
notes.original: You take on d4 and accept the queen trade that follows. After Qxd4 Qxd4 Nxd4 you have no weaknesses, and your dark-squared bishop gets to hit the knight on d4 with tempo.

notes.text: This pin looks natural, but White plays dxe5 and trades queens with an easier game, so avoid it.
notes.original: Pinning the knight looks natural and many players choose it, but White just plays dxe5, trades queens with Kxd1 and has the easier game: the pin is not a real problem for White, and your bishop is misplaced. This leaves White a slight edge, so avoid it.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the knight on d4 at once.
notes.original: Hit the knight at once.

notes.text: Keep the bishop pressing the c3 knight, castle short, and bring the b8 knight out before rushing anything.
notes.original: Your plan is simple: keep pressure on the knight on c3 with the bishop, castle short, and bring the b8 knight to d7 or a6. You can aim for ...c5 or ...Nxe4 later when the c3 knight is overloaded. Do not rush the knight forward before your king is safe.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your b8 knight, so move it out first, then put a rook on e8.
notes.original: After the early queen trade you have a healthy structure and easy development, and you keep a small edge. You have reached a queenless middlegame with a healthy structure and an easy game, and you are a little more comfortable. The bishop on f4 attacks your knight on b8, so your first step is ...Nbd7 or ...Na6. Then put a rook on e8 to pressure the e4 pawn, and keep the bishop on b4 pinning the c3 knight. Your third step is to look for ...Bxc3 followed by ...Nxe4 when the pawn becomes loose. White wants to castle long, double on the d-file and push e5. The risk is rushing ...Nxe4 before the pin is built; if White plays e5, hit it with ...Nd7 and ...Nxe5.

notes.text: Take the f3 pawn now; then develop with Bg4 and bring the other knight out.
notes.original: Capture the f3 pawn before White can recapture on e4. After Nxf3 you play ...Bg4, pinning the knight in return, and ...Nbd7 to bring the second knight out. Your plans are ...e6 or ...e5 once the bishop on g5 is traded or when it leaves, castling short, and ...Qb6 pressure. This leaves you slightly better.

notes.text: Ask the bishop a question at once, and avoid Nxe4 because the pin and queen leave you exposed.
notes.original: Ask the bishop a question at once. Avoid ...Nxe4 here, because the pin on f6 and the queen on d2 leave you tactically exposed.

notes.text: White's knight attacks your bishop on g4 and the d5 pawn hits c6; you are slightly better.
notes.original: After the bishop trade you keep a solid structure, the bishop pair is not a worry, and you aim for ...Bf5 or ...e6 and ...Be7 next. This is an open position after the bishop trade, with White's pawn on d5 attacking your c6 pawn and your bishop on g4 attacked by the knight on e5, and you are slightly better. Your plan is, first, to move the bishop with ...Bf5, keeping it protected. Second, challenge d5 with ...cxd5 or ...e6. Third, complete development with ...Qc7, ...e6 and ...Be7, castling on the side that is safe. White wants to use the knight on e5 and the d-pawn to cramp you, and checks Nxf7 tricks. The risk is dropping the bishop or leaving f7 loose. If White plays Nxg4, recapture with the knight.

notes.text: White's main choice is whether to allow a queen trade; Nd2 avoids it by unpinning the d-pawn.
notes.original:
The usual 2...d5 is almost always the move. White plans to allow Black to take into them, and then recapture on e4 with the d-pawn. If 3.Nf3, then after 3...dxe4 4.dxe4 the queens see each other and are traded. To avoid the early endgame, the main reply is 3.Nd2: this unpins White's d-pawn from the queen and so prepares for 3...dxe4 4.dxe4. The mainline is to leave the tension with 3...e5. An alternative after 3.Nf3 dxe4 is to gambit the pawn with the sharp trap line 4.Ng5!?.

Black plays 2...d5, supported by the pawn on c6. The main choice White faces is whether to allow a queen trade or not.

After 3.Nf3 dxe4, White still has an opportunity to avoid the endgame by gambitting a pawn: 4.Ng5!? exd3 5.Bxd3 is a sharp line that affords White some practical success.

Usually Black leaves the tension with 3...e5 and the game continues resembling a King's Indian Attack, where White plays Nf3, g3, Bg7 and O-O. This is the mainline Breyer variation.

3.exd5?! would be strange: when White played 2.d3, they prepared to allow Black to take on e4 and recapture with the d-pawn if they did. After 3.exd5?! cxd5 White will eventually want to play d4 and so has lost a tempo compared to playing 2.d4.

3.Nc3 is interesting: after 3...dxe4 White can retake with the knight instead and avoid the queen trade that way. 3...d4 kicks the knight and Black can take more space in the centre, but is playable for White.

notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
White eventually wants a King's Indian-type setup with knight f3, g3, bishop e2 and castling.
notes.original: White is eventually aiming for a King's Indian-type structure with Ngf3, g3, Be2 and 0-0.

notes.text: White prepares Nf3 and a kingside fianchetto without touching the center pawns yet.
notes.original: The main King's Indian Attack move order - White prepares Ngf3 and a kingside fianchetto without touching the center pawns yet.

notes.text: White grabs central space but loosens the kingside; nothing to fear, just develop your knight.
notes.original: 3.f4!? - a more ambitious try than the main 3.Nd2, grabbing extra central space at the cost of some kingside structure. Nothing to fear: just develop.

notes.text: An unusual developing move: the queen guards e4, so it can recapture there and stay central.
notes.original: 3.Qe2!? - an unusual developing move, preparing to meet ...dxe4 with a recapture that keeps the queen centralized.

notes.text: White heads for a Two Knights-style setup, a tempo behind the usual order since d3 is already played.
notes.original: 3.Nc3 - transposes toward a Two Knights-style setup a tempo behind the usual move order, since White already spent a move on d3.

notes.text: A quiet developing move that keeps White's options open instead of going for the main King's Indian Attack plan.
notes.original: 3.Be2 - a quiet developing move, keeping options flexible rather than committing to the main 3.Nd2 King's Indian Attack plan.

notes.text: This alternative move order, with Nf3 instead of Nd2, is sometimes called the Leela set-up.
notes.original: The alternative move order, sometimes called the 'Leela' set-up, after the engine that made the early Nf3 (instead of Nd2) popular.

notes.text: White voluntarily lets you take over the centre, and you should seize it.
notes.original: White is voluntarily giving Black the chance to take over the centre, and Black should seize it.

notes.text: Grab the center at once: if you are slow, White chooses the structure and the setup works.
notes.original: Grab the center immediately - this is the single most important practical lesson against a King's Indian Attack setup as White: if Black is slow, White gets to choose the structure; if Black grabs the center first, White's whole setup loses most of its point.

notes.text: This transposes to the 2.d3 lines, which have their own chapters.
notes.original: Transposing to the 2.d3 lines. Full coverage in 🔵 19 and 20; a short version is given here.

notes.text: Taking the pawn at once is the simplifying alternative to building the same structure with e5.
notes.original: The simplifying alternative: just take the pawn at once rather than building the same King's Indian Attack structure Black gets anyway after 3...e5.

notes.text: White develops naturally before committing its dark-squared bishop.
notes.original: White's most natural follow-up, developing before committing the dark-squared bishop.

notes.text: White fianchettoes at once, and it usually transposes to the same structures.
notes.original: Also natural, fianchettoing immediately; transposes to the same structures after a normal developing sequence.

notes.text: Against the quiet d3, take the centre with d5 and e5, then play knight f6 and castle.
notes.original:
Idea: Against 2.d3, take the centre with ...d5 and ...e5. Put the bishop on d6 or c7, the knight on f6, and castle. You get an easy, roomy position.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 e5 4.Ngf3 Bd6
Next: 🔵 20 continues the 2.d3 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

notes.text: Build a classical set-up: knight to f6, castle, rook to e8, then ...a5-a4 for queenside space.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want a classical, symmetrical set-up against the King's Indian Attack: ...e5, ...Bd6, ...Nf6 and ...O-O, with ...Re8 and ...a5-a4 for queenside space (low risk, easy to learn). Against 5.d4 you can also play the open structures shown below. White's main set-ups are 5.g3 (King's Indian Attack) and 5.d4 (transposing to an open game).

notes.text: Your bishop takes its most natural diagonal before you castle.
notes.original: The standard developing scheme: the bishop takes its most natural diagonal before Black castles.

notes.text: Playable, but developing the bishop to d6 is more accurate.
notes.original: Playable, but Bd6 is more accurate.

notes.text: White wants castling, c3, queen to c2 and b4, looking for queenside play.
notes.original: White is settling for some sort of an "Inverted Hanham Structure". This involves Be2 0-0 c3 Qc2 and b4! Trying to find some play on the queenside.

notes.text: White's d4 break is fine, but answering with f6 is the easier, more natural reply.
notes.original: 5.d4 is an energetic break and fine for White. Black can take on d4, but ...f6 is the easier and more natural reply.

notes.text: White's g3 is safer than d4: it plans Bg2 and short castling.
notes.original: Other options include d4, but g3 is much safer for White; Bg2 followed by short castling is fine for White.

notes.text: White prepares the long fianchetto: the bishop heads to g2, the heart of the King's Indian Attack.
notes.original: Preparing the long fianchetto, the point of this whole King's Indian Attack set-up.

notes.text: Your central pawns give you more space than White has.
notes.original: Black maintains his spacious advantage.

notes.text: White's b4 pawn push starts some play on the queenside.
notes.original: White finds play on the queenside.

notes.text: Your a-pawn hits the b4 pawn so White cannot build a queenside attack.
notes.original: Black must not allow a White counter-attack on the queenside.

notes.text: Your centre is solid enough and you keep a small edge.
notes.original: Black's centre is manageable.

notes.text: Your knight heads for g6 to support the e5 pawn without blocking your light bishop.
notes.original: With ideas of Ng6 to support the e5 pawn without having to block the light square bishop.

notes.text: Your h-pawn covers g5, so White's bishop cannot pin your knight.
notes.original: This prevents any hasty pin.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Your pieces are active and White's are passive; keep improving and open the position only when it suits you.
notes.original: Black has everything going: the knights head for f4, the rooks double on the a-file and ...c5 prepares ...d4 and ...Bd7. White's pieces are passive and the queenside pawn storm with b4 has run out of steam. Your plan is to keep improving (...Bd7, ...Rea8) and only open the position when it favours you.

notes.text: This is another way to meet White's queenside pawn push.
notes.original: Another way to meet it

notes.text: Taking on d4 is a safer choice that simplifies the centre and avoids heavy theory.
notes.original: A safer option, black exchange central pawn aiming for a less theoretical simplification in the opening.

notes.text: This reply is rather dubious; taking on d4 was stronger.
notes.original: Rather dubious, but maintain black's central advantage. exd4 was stronger.

notes.text: White takes on d5 at once, opening the centre and heading for a simple structure.
notes.original: 11.exd5 resolves the center immediately instead of recapturing with the knight first, trading into a simple structure a move early.

notes.text: White's h3 pawn stops any of your pieces from jumping to g4.
notes.original: Prevents any piece from jumping on the g4 square.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your knight leaves e7, so your rook now eyes e1 and can answer exd5 with a rook trade.
notes.original: White's idea is to prepare exd5 so that the e-file opens with a tempo on your rook. The knight on e7 blocks your own rook, so ...Ng6 unmasks it and lets you answer exd5 with ...Rxe1+.

notes.text: The queen steps off the d8-g5 diagonal where Bg5 was hitting it.
notes.original: The queen steps off the d8-g5 diagonal where Bg5 was hitting it. The knight on d5 is a fine central piece and the position stays level.

notes.text: White's bishop on g5 was hitting your queen, so the queen steps off that diagonal.
notes.original: The queen steps off the d8-g5 diagonal where Bg5 was hitting it. The knight on d5 is a fine central piece and the position stays level.

notes.text: White can open the centre at once, but ...c5 and ...h6 give you an easy game.
notes.original: White can open the centre at once, but ...c5 and ...h6 give you an easy game

notes.text: This opens the position with a symmetrical pawn structure, and you have no problems.
notes.original: 5.d4 exd4 6.exd5 cxd5 leads to an open position with a symmetrical pawn structure. Black has no problems.

notes.text: The position is calm and balanced, with roughly symmetrical chances.
notes.original: 11.exd5 resolves the center immediately instead of recapturing with the knight first, trading into a simple structure a move early. ...reaching a calm, balanced position with roughly symmetrical chances.

notes.text: Your bishop steps back to c7 before a knight can hit it, and it eyes h2.
notes.original: Black castles and puts the rook on the e-file, where Be2 and the white king are lined up. The bishop steps back to c7 before Nb5 can hit it, and it keeps an eye on h2.

notes.text: Your bishop and queen line up against h2, so White must spend time covering it.
notes.original: Bc7 and Qd6 now form a battery aimed at h2, so White has to spend time covering it.

notes.text: White regains the pawn and the game is level; develop your bishop to g4 and play for the e-file.
notes.original: White regains the d4 pawn but the position is level. Your plan is to finish development with ...Bg4 or ...Bf5 and play for the e-file; there is nothing to fear.

notes.text: This setup is equally good: you traded your bishop for the knight guarding d4 and planted a knight on e4.
notes.original: An equally good setup: you trade the bishop for the knight that guards d4 and plant a knight on e4

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White did not need to take on d5, since that gave you two strong central pawns.
notes.original: Pawn takes pawn would not be so necessary for white since this would give black two powerful central pawns.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your isolated d5 pawn is the main weakness; answer White's pressure with active pieces like Rfe8.
notes.original: Your isolated pawn on d5 is the whole story. White piles up on it with Qb3, Be3 and the rook, hoping to force a concession, and the e-file gives White an easy plan. You answer with active piece play: Na5 kicks the queen, Bc7 eyes the h2 diagonal and Rfe8 contests the open file. White keeps a small edge but you have no real weaknesses besides d5.

notes.text: Your d5 and e5 pawns are hard to keep, so you will probably give one up later.
notes.original: Black's two central pawns on d5 and e5 are isolated and hard to keep, so Black will probably have to give one up later.

notes.text: A surprising but playable move: your king heads for the safest square, since an attack would be easily refuted.
notes.original: A surprising, unorthodox move that is nevertheless playable. Black's kingside is not under threat and an attack would be easily refuted, so the idea is to place the king on the safest available square.

notes.text: Your queen guards the e5 pawn, and you plan to castle short next.
notes.original: Protects the e4 pawn, black intends to castle short now 0-0.

notes.text: This is also possible, but the overextended e-pawn could become risky.
notes.original: Also possible but the over extended e pawn could be risky.

notes.text: This thrust hits the f3 knight, keeps it off d4 and opens the f-file for your rook.
notes.original: You must play this thrust. It cuts the f3 knight off from d4 and gives your rook on f8 the f-file.

notes.text: White's knight on a7 is short of squares; keep c4 defended and aim your knights at the b-pawns.
notes.original: White's motive is the loose c4 pawn and the dark squares: Qxc4+ ideas are always in the air and Nb5 hits your queen and the a7 pawn at the same time. Taking on a7 is greedy, though, because the knight is now short of squares. Keep c4 defended and use ...Nd5 or ...Nb6 to hit the b-pawns.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
You hit the knight at once; if it moves, Qxb4 regains the pawn and hits the weak b-pawns.
notes.original: White is a pawn up for a moment, so you hit the knight at once. If it moves, ...Qxb4 regains the pawn and your queen lands on the weak doubled b-pawns.

notes.text: Your pieces are active: the knight on e5 heads for d3 or c6, and your rook holds the d-file.
notes.original: White's plan is to use the open lines and the bishop against your king, while the doubled b-pawns remain a target for you. Your pieces are active: the knight on e5 heads for d3 or c6 and the rook sits on the d-file. White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: White pushing the b-pawn gives your knights great squares.
notes.original: Pushing the b-pawn gives your knights great squares

notes.text: White castles first instead of retreating the knight, getting the king safe before answering your central expansion.
notes.original: Rather than retreating the knight to b3 as the main line does, castling first is White's more accurate try, getting the king to safety before deciding how to meet Black's central expansion.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
With your king stuck on f8, White opens lines; ...b5 loosened too much and handed White the a4 lever.
notes.original: White's motive is to blow the position open while your king is stuck on f8. a4 pries at b5, c4 opens the c-file towards your queen and Rc1, and the piece sacrifice on d4 lets the c-pawn run with tempo on Bd6 and then c6. This is why 13...b5 loosens too much: it hands White the lever. After the exchanges you are in trouble.

notes.text: This calmer try is less dangerous for you.
notes.original: The calmer try is less dangerous for you

notes.text: White keeps a clear edge with the safer king; this is its critical improvement in this sideline.
notes.original: This keeps a clear, lasting edge for White thanks to the extra central pawn and safer king - a meaningful improvement over the main line's Nb3, worth having as the critical line in this sideline chapter.

notes.text: White aims at the c-file and your king, which cannot castle; your bishop and knight try to cause trouble.
notes.original: White's point is simple: win the e4 pawn (Nxe4 and cxd5) and then play against a king that cannot castle. The extra pawn and the c-file are the trumps, so after ...Qxd5 White develops with tempo by Be3 and Rc1, while your bishop on g4 and the knight on a6 try to cause trouble. White keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: Even the Bxh2 shot does not rescue you in this line.
notes.original: 12.Ne2 is nearly as strong; even the shot ...Bxh2+ does not rescue Black

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your e7 knight keeps f6 free for the other knight, which can come via d7.
notes.original: Keeping f6 free for the other knight and preparing a timely ...f5 or ...Nf5 reroute later.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White has the bishop pair and wants exd5, then Ng4; your h5 pawn takes g4 away.
notes.original: White has the bishop pair, so the plan is to open the e-file with exd5 and then bring the knight round Nh2-g4 to hit your f6 knight and the e5 pawn. ...h5 takes g4 away from the knight, ...Qb6 hits b2 and the a-pawn moves fix the queenside. You are fine with the d5 and e5 pawns controlling the centre; the position is level.

notes.text: White can also hold its knight back instead of trading.
notes.original: White can also hold the knight back

notes.text: A balanced position: develop your bishop to g4 or rook to e8, and bring the other knight to f6.
notes.original: A normal, balanced King's Indian Attack structure. Black's simplest plan from here is ...Bg4 or ...Re8 and ...Nd7-f6 regrouping; there is nothing sharp or dangerous for Black to worry about.

notes.text: Your bishop invites h3, which would loosen White's kingside; then you can line up queen and bishop against that pawn.
notes.original: Black wants to provoke h3, which weakens White's kingside, and then build a bishop-and-queen battery against the h3-pawn.

notes.text: White offers the d4 pawn, having prepared a central tactic to win it back.
notes.original: White sacrifices a pawn but has prepared a tactical sequence that breaks through in the centre and wins the material back.

notes.text: Grabbing on d4 with the knight would have been a mistake: Bxd1 and Nd7 leave White losing.
notes.original: Trap: 9.Nxd4? Bxd1 10.Rxd1 Nd7 11.N2f3 Bc5 12.exd5 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d4 with the knight falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 9.Nxd4? Bxd1 10.Rxd1 Nd7 11.N2f3 Bc5 12.exd5 and White is losing.

notes.text: Your pieces are active, and White's advanced kingside pawns on g4 and h3 will be hard to defend.
notes.original: Black has the bishop pair and White's kingside pawns are overextended, so White will have a hard time defending.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your knight lands on d3 with tempo, hitting the bishop on f4; keep making threats rather than slow moves.
notes.original: White is a pawn up after the bishop sacrifice on h2, but the king on h2 is the target. You keep the initiative with checks: ...Rfe8 takes the open file and eyes the bishop's squares, ...Qd6+ and ...Qd5+ drive the king back and forth and ...Ne5-d3 plants a knight with tempo on the bishop. White's only way to cash the extra pawn is to run the king to safety with Kg2 and c3, so you should keep making threats rather than slow moves. The result is level.

notes.text: If White pushes e5, your knight simply retreats to g8; your structure stays sound and White's kingside is loosened.
notes.original: Simple development is enough; if White pushes 4.e5 the knight just retreats to g8 and comes back via f6 or h6 later, while Black's structure stays sound and White's kingside is slightly loosened.

notes.text: Your bishop hits White's queen and keeps the light squares under your control.
notes.original: White's motive after e5 is space: f4 backs up the e5 pawn and g4-g5 will cramp your pieces and kick your bishop. You answer with ...Bd7 and the counter-thrust ...h5, which undermines g4 and fixes the g5 pawn, and then ...Bg4 hits the queen and keeps the light squares under your control. You can follow up with ...e6, ...c5 and ...Ne7 to undermine e5. White keeps a small edge but his kingside is very loosened.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the queen and keeps the light squares under your control, while ...h5 fixes the g5 pawn.
notes.original: After e5 White wants space: f4 backs up the e5 pawn and g4-g5 will cramp your pieces and kick your bishop. You answer with ...Bd7 and the counter-thrust ...h5, which undermines g4 and fixes the g5 pawn, and then ...Bg4 hits the queen and keeps the light squares under your control. You can follow up with ...e6, ...c5 and ...Ne7 to undermine e5. White keeps a small edge but his kingside is very loosened.

notes.text: White's modest capture gives you an easy game.
notes.original: White's more modest capture gives you an easy game

notes.text: Retaking and playing e5 at once gives you an equal share of the centre.
notes.original: Taking back in the center and immediately answering with ...e5 is the cleanest equalizer: Black grabs an equal share of the center at once rather than letting White keep it.

notes.text: White simply develops, rather than trying the sharper f4 or Nc3 against your early e5.
notes.original: 5.Nf3 develops naturally instead of the sharper f4 or Nc3 tries against this early ...e5.

notes.text: Two White knights press e5, but with it covered your extra space and development lead give a lasting edge.
notes.original: 5.Nf3 develops naturally instead of the sharper f4 or Nc3 tries against this early ...e5. ...and Black's extra space and development lead give a real, lasting edge.

notes.text: After the trade on b6 you still hold the centre and have more space.
notes.original: Nc4 attacks e5 a second time, so ...Nbd7 adds the second defender and prepares ...b5 with tempo on the knight. White's Ba5 hits your queen, but Qb8 simply keeps everything protected and the pawn on b4 gets in the way of the bishop. After the trade on b6 you still hold the centre and have more space.

notes.text: After the trade on b6 you still hold the centre and have more space.
notes.original: Here Nc4 attacks e5 a second time, so ...Nbd7 adds the second defender and prepares ...b5 with tempo on the knight. White's Ba5 hits your queen, but Qb8 simply keeps everything protected. After the trade on b6 you still hold the centre and have more space.

notes.text: Blocking with Be6 left e5 short of defenders, so White won your h8 rook; Nbd7 was much better.
notes.original: Your e5 pawn is attacked twice (Nc4 and Nf3) and defended only once, so blocking with ...Be6 lets White take it and even pick up the h8 rook (...Nbd7 is much better)

notes.text: Simply take the pawn and develop normally; White's extra d3 move barely matters.
notes.original: 3...dxe4 is simplest: take the pawn and meet the recapture with normal development; the extra tempo White spent on d3 barely matters.

notes.text: White has more space, but your structure is stable; your knight on d7 is heading for c5.
notes.original: White has an easy edge in space, but you have a stable structure. The ...a5 move stops a b4 push, and ...e5 and ...Nfd7 prepare ...Nc5. A modest White advantage at most.

notes.text: Your knight heads for c5 to hit the e4 pawn, and your centre stays solid.
notes.original: Recapturing with the knight keeps White's castling rights, so do not expect a completely safe endgame. f3 props up e4 and stops ...Ng4, and a4 stops your a-pawn. You still have a solid centre with ...e5, and ...Nfd7 heads for c5 to hit e4. White has a slight edge.

notes.text: White's bishop has been kicked back, and you take the centre.
notes.original: The bishop is kicked and you take the centre.

notes.text: Take the pawn and develop normally; this is again the simplest way to equalize.
notes.original: 3...dxe4 again the simplest equalizer: take the pawn and develop normally against the recapture.

notes.text: White lost castling and the king must walk back; your bishop eyes d4 and you develop easily.
notes.original: The queen swap costs White the right to castle, so the king has to waddle back to e1. a4 stops ...b5 and grabs queenside space, but ...Bc5, ...Nf6 and ...a5 give you easy development and the d4 square. You have nothing to worry about here.

notes.text: The queen trade cost White castling; ...Bc5, ...Nf6 and ...a5 develop easily and give you d4.
notes.original: Trading queens costs White the right to castle, so the king has to walk back to e1. a4 stops ...b5 and grabs queenside space, but ...Bc5, ...Nf6 and ...a5 give you easy development and the d4 square. You have nothing to worry about here.

notes.text: White's space and tempo moves don't pay for the pawn: you lead in development and stay a pawn up.
notes.original: Grabbing space with tempo does not give White enough for the pawn: you keep a clear lead in development and the extra pawn

notes.text: Taking the pawn is simpler than d4 and returns to the main line of the Classical Caro-Kann.
notes.original: Taking the pawn is simpler than d4, which brings complications for both sides; it returns to the main line of the Classical Caro-Kann.

notes.text: This is the right reply: your pawn hits the centre at once.
notes.original: 2.Nc3 d5 3.Qf3 e5! is the right reply, hitting the centre at once.

notes.text: Nd7 avoids doubled pawns; with the knight on f6 instead, White's queen on f3 could create tactics.
notes.original: The Karpov Variation is a good way to play the Classical Caro-Kann, but here ...Nd7 is better, avoiding doubled pawns; the queen on f3 can create tactical ideas if ...Nf6 is played instead.

notes.text: Avoid the queen check on a5 here: White answers Bd2 and you end up in big trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 9...Qa5+? 10.Bd2 Qb6 11.fxg4 Nd5 12.Qe5 Qxb2 and Black is in big trouble.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are in big trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 9...Qa5+? 10.Bd2 Qb6 11.fxg4 Nd5 12.Qe5 Qxb2 and Black is in big trouble.

notes.text: White's g4 leaves the d4 pawn undefended, so your queen can simply take it.
notes.original: This allows ...Qxd4.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Know the Bxh7+ deflection trick; White wins a pawn back, but your active bishop and ...c5 equalise.
notes.original: Bxh7+ is a deflection: it drags the king to h7 so that Bg5 can pin the knight on f6 against the bishop on h5, and White regains the piece. You have to know this line so that you do not fall for it. White ends a pawn up, but the pawn on d4 is isolated and your bishop on f6 is active, so ...c5 equalises.

notes.text: White's quiet pin on your knight is met by ...Bg6.
notes.original: The quiet pin is met by ...Bg6.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's tempo moves chase your queen, but you stay a pawn up and the checks keep coming.
notes.original: White's tempo moves (Ne2, a3) chase your queen, but you stay a pawn up, the bishop trades itself off on g6 and the checks keep coming. The white king is stuck in the middle.

notes.text: The queen trade leaves you a pawn up and much better.
A much easier approach is to exchange pawns, then develop your bishop to f5.
notes.original: A much easier approach is the exchange of pawns followed by the move Bf5, end of Opening Preparation.

notes.text: Simply take the pawn and meet the recapture with normal development.
notes.original: 3...dxe4 is the simpler reply to 3.Qe2: just take the pawn and meet the recapture with normal development.

notes.text: White's c3 is a simple breakthrough idea, hitting your advanced d4 pawn.
notes.original: Another breakthrough idea is c3, which is neither complicated nor hard to understand.

notes.text: If White grabs the e5 pawn with the knight, you trade queens and White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 10.Nxe5? Bxe2 11.Nxd7 Nxd7 12.Kxe2 O-O 13.Ne3 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on e5 with the knight falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 10.Nxe5? Bxe2 11.Nxd7 Nxd7 12.Kxe2 O-O 13.Ne3 and White is losing.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's bishop pair is the long-term asset; keep e5 guarded, since f5 or an exchange on e5 opens the f-file.
notes.original: The knight reroutes to f2 and the bishop pair is the long-term asset. Your plan is to expand with ...a5-a4 and keep the e5 pawn guarded; White wants f4-f5 or the exchange on e5 to open the f-file. A small White edge.

notes.text: White's kingside space grab is met by your queenside counter.
notes.original: Gaining space on the kingside is met by your queenside counter.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Your d4 pawn cramps White; meet the b-file pressure with ...b6 and keep the c-file.
notes.original: Your advanced pawn on d4 cramps White, but it also needs defending, so you shore it up with ...Rfd8 and develop around it. White's plan is pressure on the b-file with Qb5 and Rfb1, so you answer with ...b6 and keep the c-file. You keep a small edge.

notes.text: It is the same plan as before, just with your queen on a different square.
notes.original: The same plan with a different queen square.

notes.text: Beware ...Qa5+ in this line: White answers Bd2 and you are in serious trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Bxe4 8.Bxa5 Bxh1 9.f3 h5 and Black is in serious trouble.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are in serious trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Bxe4 8.Bxa5 Bxh1 9.f3 h5 and Black is in serious trouble.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White has the bishop pair and a kingside pawn storm; you meet it with ...Bd6, ...h6 and ...Nf6.
notes.original: White plays g4-g5 and h4 for a kingside pawn storm, with the bishop pair as a bonus. You meet it with ...Bd6 and ...h6, break open g6 on your terms and develop the knight to f6.

notes.text: White's a-pawn push opens the a-file, but your structure is fine and the game is balanced.
notes.original: a4-a5-a6 opens the a-file, but your structure is fine and the game is balanced.

notes.text: Your d5 pawn, guarded by the c-pawn and queen, hits the bishop and forces it to move.
notes.original:
Black will almost certainly play 2...d5. Since Black's d5 pawn is defended by both the c-pawn and the queen, White's bishop will be forced to move away, either on the following turn or after 3.exd5 cxd5.

3.exd5 cxd5 is the more common move in the Lichess database. However, after the pawn trade, White will be down a tempo and a center pawn with little to show for it. 4.Bb5+ can be blocked by the opposing bishop, and if White trades, Black is comfortable. 4.Bb3 keeps a bishop on the f7 diagonal, but does not challenge much.

Any other move loses the bishop or makes the initial 2.Bc4 a waste of time.

notes.text: Taking on d5 is the main line.
notes.original: 3.exd5 is the main line.

notes.text: In the Hillbilly Gambit White sacrifices a pawn, hoping for a quick attack or mate.
notes.original: Another interesting idea is the Hillbilly Gambit, in which White sacrifices a pawn and aims for a quick attack or mate.

notes.text: The Hillbilly Gambit: White sacrifices a pawn hoping for a quick kingside attack.
notes.original: 3.Bb3!?, the "Hillbilly Gambit": White sacrifices a pawn hoping for a quick kingside kill. Full treatment in 🔵 19, deepened here with the critical trap and the 4.Nc3 alternative.

notes.text: All White has achieved is a misplaced light-squared bishop.
notes.original: All white has achieved here is to misplace the light-squared bishop.

notes.text: The Hillbilly Attack is rare among strong players and known to be a poor opening.
notes.original: The Hillbilly Attack is very rarely seen at anything above 2000 level, as it's known to be a pretty lousy opening. So I've trawled through the archives to find this miniature from a few years ago. My opponent did indeed follow Stockfish's recommendation here. But it didn't do him or her much good!

notes.text: Your d5 pawn attacked the bishop, so White saves it with check and gains a tempo.
notes.original: Your d5 pawn attacked the bishop on c4, so White saves it with check and a tempo. White hopes to follow with a4, d4 and Nf3 and reach a comfortable game with no weaknesses. It is very common in practice, so you should have a clear answer.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes your d5 pawn, so keep it defended while you develop with tempo.
notes.original: White develops the knight and keeps the bishop on b3 pointing at your d5 pawn and at f7. The idea is to follow with d4 and reach a comfortable isolated-pawn type of position. This is a very common choice (played in about 861,000 games), so expect it. For you, d5 is the target, so keep it defended while you develop with tempo.

notes.text: White's slow d3 spends a tempo while the bishop on b3 still eyes d5, so you get a free hand.
notes.original: White avoids sharp theory and plans a slow build-up with Nf3, c3 or Nbd2 while the bishop on b3 keeps eyeing your d5 pawn. It is very common, played in about 497,000 games, but d3 is a modest move that spends a tempo, so you get a free hand in the centre. You are slightly better here.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
After the bishop swap, your bishop on f6 and knight on c6 both press d4.
notes.original: White offers a bishop trade to remove your good bishop and aims the queen along the c-file. You accept, then gain queenside space with ...b5 and ask the dark-squared bishop what it wants with ...h6. After the bishops swap, your bishop on f6 puts pressure on d4 together with Nc6. Your plan is ...Rc8 and ...Qd6 with a slightly better, safe game.

notes.text: White's early Nbd2 let you hit the bishop with ...g5.
notes.original: The immediate Nbd2 lets you hit the bishop with ...g5

notes.text: Break with ...e5 at once, develop both bishops, and castle short. Avoid the slow ...e6 set-up.
notes.original: Nc6 adds a second defender to d5 and prepares ...e5, the central break this whole line is built on. Your plan is to play ...e5 at once, answer d4 with ...e4 to gain space and chase the knight, then bring the bishop to d6 and the other bishop to e6 and castle short. Avoid slow set-ups with ...e6, which lock in your c8 bishop and leave d5 weak and static. The numbers give you a small edge.

notes.text: Put the bishop outside your pawn chain first; the game is quieter but your structure stays healthy.
notes.original: A solid alternative. Put the bishop outside your pawn chain first, then play ...e6, ...Nc6 and ...Be7. It is a quieter game: you give up the quick ...e5 break but keep a healthy structure against 6.d4.

notes.text: White's pawn stops ...Bg4, but it is slow, so strike in the centre with ...e5 now.
notes.original: This stops ...Bg4, so you cannot pin the knight. It is slow, and that is why you can strike in the centre immediately.

notes.text: Your e4 pawn attacks the knight and is protected by d5, so White must decide where the knight goes.
notes.original: The pawn on e4 attacks the knight and is protected by d5. White must decide where the knight goes.

notes.text: Your bishop challenges the knight on e5; develop the other bishop, castle, and look for ...Qe7 or ...Nxe5.
notes.original: You challenge the knight at once; if White supports it with f4 you keep a firm grip on the light squares. Develop Be6, castle, and look for ...Qe7 or ...Nxe5 to remove the strong piece when it suits you.

notes.text: You have more space and easy development: castle short, bring the queen out, and challenge the knight with ...Nxe5 when…
notes.original: You hold more space in the centre and have easy development, while White has to prove the knight on e5 is not just overextended. This is a space-gaining position where you have e4 and d5 supported by pieces, and White's knight on e5 is strong but not unassailable. You have more space in the centre and easy development. Your plan: castle short, then ...Qd7 or ...Qe7, and challenge the knight with ...Nxe5 when it suits you, using ...Ng4 or ...Nd7 to bring pieces over. White wants Nxc6, then Bxd6, to ruin your structure, or f3 to break up the e4 pawn. The mistake is allowing Nxc6 bxc6 with a damaged structure; if White plays f3, answer with ...exf3 and keep control of d5.

notes.text: Your knight eyes d4 and prepares ...e5; then develop your bishops and castle, avoiding the passive ...e6.
notes.original: Develop with a purpose. The knight hits d4 and prepares ...e5, the break you want: with pawns on d5 and e5 you own the centre and White's pieces have little room. Your plan is ...e5, then the light-squared bishop to e6 or g4, ...Bd6 or ...Be7, and castle kingside. Avoid the passive ...e6 set-up that locks in your c8 bishop; you do not need it.

notes.text: Your h-pawn takes the sting out of Bg5 pins; do not drift, and keep the e5 break in mind.
notes.original: White stops ...Bg4, so you spend a move on ...h6 to take the sting out of Bg5 pins. Do not drift with ...Bf5 and ...e6; keep the e5 break in mind.

notes.text: You gain space with ...e4, which shuts out White's knight and cramps his position.
notes.original: White challenges the centre, and you gain space with ...e4, which shuts out his knight from e4 and cramps his position.

notes.text: Your bishop develops while keeping d5 protected, and your knight already challenges the strong knight on e5.
notes.original: The knight on e5 looks strong, but you can challenge it with ...Nxe5 or ...Nd7 and ...Bd6, and ...Be6 develops while keeping d5 protected. Avoid ...exd4, which opens lines for White. You hold a big centre and develop easily while White's pieces tie themselves to d4 and e5.

notes.text: You are slightly better with e4 and d5 held; trade White's strong knight with ...Nxe5.
notes.original: This is an open centre where you hold the e4 and d5 pawns and have space, so you are slightly better. Your knight on e5 is attacking, but White's own knight hits your c6 knight. Your plan is, first, to trade the strong knight with ...Nxe5. Second, play ...Bd6 to trade the dark bishops and castle short. Third, support the centre with ...Qd7 and ...Rd8. White wants c4 to undermine d5 and a quick attack on f7. The risk is playing ...Bd6 first, which lets White play Nxc6 with tricks. If White plays c4, answer with ...dxc4 and keep your centre solid.

notes.text: Trade on e5, play ...Bd6 to swap the dark bishops, then castle short.
notes.original: This is an open centre where you hold the e4 and d5 pawns and have space, so you are slightly better. Your knight on e5 is attacking, but White's own knight hits your c6 knight. Your plan is, first, to trade the strong knight with ...Nxe5. Second, play ...Bd6 to trade the dark bishops and castle short. Third, support the centre with ...Qd7 and ...Rd8. White wants c4 to undermine d5 and a quick attack on f7. The risk is playing ...Bd6 first, which lets White play Nxc6 with tricks. If White plays c4, answer with ...dxc4 and keep your centre solid.

notes.text: Even if White develops first, you still play ...e5 and answer Bg5 with ...Be7.
notes.original: If White develops first, you play ...e5 anyway and answer Bg5 with ...Be7.

notes.text: Block the check with the bishop and offer a trade; if White takes on d7, you recapture comfortably.
notes.original: Block with the bishop and offer a trade. If White retreats with Be2 you have gained time, and if White takes on d7 you recapture with the knight or queen and are comfortable. Plan: ...e6, then ...a6 to challenge the bishop, ...Bd6 and ...Ne7, and castle short. Your d5 pawn is well supported and the structure is sound. Avoid trading your light-squared bishop for no reason, because that leaves d5 weaker.

notes.text: A playable alternative, but your knight on d7 blocks your own bishop on c8, so it is a little worse.
notes.original: A playable alternative, aiming for an early ...e5, but the knight blocks your own bishop on c8 and is a little less good.

notes.text: You are slightly better thanks to White's lost time; castle, develop the knight, and accept a bishop trade on a3.
notes.original: White has spent several moves on the bishop and you have a compact setup. Castle, bring a knight to c6 and push ...f5 or ...b6 only when needed. Your later breaks are ...Nbc6 followed by ...e5 or ...f6. You are slightly better thanks to the lost time. This is a closed, compact position where White has spent several moves on the bishop and you hold a solid centre with pawns on d5 and e6. Your plan: castle short, bring the other knight out with ...Nbc6, then free your game with ...e5 or ...f6 once your pieces are placed. White wants Ba3 to trade your dark-squared bishop, or c4 to challenge d5. You are happy to trade bishops on a3, and you meet c4 with ...dxc4 bxc4. The typical mistake is drifting passively because the position looks quiet, so keep making useful moves. If White delays castling, you have time for ...Nbc6.

notes.text: The point of the gambit: queen and bishop both aim at your f7 pawn before you consolidate.
notes.original: The point of the gambit: the queen heads straight toward f7 before Black can consolidate.

notes.text: White heads straight for the e4 pawn instead of playing f3 first, because it cannot be held long-term.
notes.original: 4.Nc3 goes directly for the recapture on e4 rather than delaying with f3 first, since the pawn can't be defended long-term.

notes.text: White's knight hits the e4 pawn, trying to win it back through quick development.
notes.original: 4.Nc3, the sharper alternative mentioned above: instead of chasing the pawn back immediately with the queen, White tries to regain it through faster development.

notes.text: You need ...e6 to secure your kingside; ...g6 would allow a quick, unpleasant White attack.
notes.original: ...e6 is needed to secure Black's kingside. ...g6 is another option, but White can launch a quick and unpleasant kingside attack.

notes.text: The most accurate reply: your pawn hits the queen and blocks its route to f7.
notes.original: The most accurate response, hitting the queen and blunting its route to f7 in one move.

notes.text: Watch out: this natural developing move walks straight into the point of the whole gambit.
Developing the knight walks into Qxf7 with check, and your king gets stuck in the center.
notes.original: Watch out: this natural developing move walks straight into the point of the whole gambit.

notes.text: You give the pawn back, but get faster development and the better position.
notes.original: Black has to give the pawn back, but in exchange gets faster development and the better position.

notes.text: This is also fine, just a little less precise than playing g6 earlier.
notes.original: Also fine, and our original recommendation: just a little less precise than 4...g6.

With queens off you have the bishop pair, and White's doubled b-pawns are a lasting weakness.
notes.original: White's queen is hunting the c5 and g7 pawns, but each harassing move is answered by a useful pawn push: ...f6 gives the queen a kick and ...e5 builds a centre. In the queenless ending you have the bishop pair and the doubled b-pawns of White are a lasting weakness. Your king on d7 is perfectly safe with the queens gone.

notes.text: Castling first let you meet Ng5 with ...h6, and the knight on e4 is harmless after ...Bc7.
notes.original: Castling first lets you meet Ng5 with ...h6 and the knight on e4 is no problem after ...Bc7

notes.text: Simply develop and let White prove the piece play is worth a pawn.
notes.original: Simplest: just develop and let White prove the piece play is worth a pawn.

notes.text: White's f-pawn attacks your e4 pawn, trying to blast the center open before you consolidate.
notes.original: The critical try, trying to blast the centre open before Black consolidates.

notes.text: You are already clearly and comfortably better.
notes.original: 4.Nc3 goes directly for the recapture on e4 rather than delaying with f3 first, since the pawn can't be defended long-term. ...and Black is already clearly, comfortably better.

notes.text: You are a pawn up; offer trades to remove White's attackers and don't leave your king in the middle too…
notes.original: You are a pawn up, and White's compensation is development plus the Bb3 bishop aimed at f7 and the knight on e5. Close the diagonal with ...e6, develop with ...Bd6 and offer trades with ...Bg6 and ...Nbd7: every piece that comes off removes an attacker. Do not grab anything else and do not leave your king in the middle too long. You remain clearly better.

notes.text: This is White's strongest try here, stronger than g3.
notes.original: White's strongest try here, stronger than g3.

notes.text: Against this set-up, finish with castling and ...Re8, and watch for White's d4 break.
notes.original:
Idea: Against the King's Indian set-up with g3 and Bg2, use the same plan: ...e5, ...Nd7, ...Ngf6, ...Bd6, ...O-O and ...Re8. Watch for White's d4 break.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 e5 4.Ngf3 Nd7 5.g3 Ngf6 6.Bg2 Bd6
Watch out: ...Bxg3? loses material on move 12.
Next: Plan: 🟠 Plan 11.

notes.text: A comfortable position: your bigger center gives you at least a slight edge.
notes.original: A natural, comfortable position where Black is already doing at least fine, arguably slightly better, thanks to the bigger central footprint.

notes.text: With queens off, your active rook and well-placed knights are at least as good as White's pieces.
notes.original: A realistic continuation showing the point: once the center clarifies and queens come off, Black's pieces (bishop pair, active rook, well-placed knights) are at least as good as White's, if not better - proof that grabbing the center early pays off well into the middlegame and endgame.

notes.text: Your pieces are more active; ...g6 and ...Kg7 give you a safe ending.
notes.original: White's motive for f3 is to drive away your strong bishop on f5 and win the e4 square back. You accept: ...Bxe4 fxe4 and the knight hops into c3 with tempo, forcing e5 and then ...Ne2+ wins the bishop pair. After the trades you are slightly more comfortable with the more active pieces; the plan is ...g6 and ...Kg7 with a safe, equal ending.

notes.text: White's knight jump looks active, but your pieces take over and you are clearly better.
notes.original: The double-knight jump looks active but ...Nb4 hits c2 and takes over: you are clearly better

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your isolated d5 pawn is no real weakness; ...Nf6 and ...Bg4 give easy piece play.
notes.original: Nf5 hits the bishop on d6 with tempo. You step back to e5 and, after Nf3, offer a knight trade with ...Ne7 so that White's active knight disappears. You then have an isolated d5 pawn but no real weaknesses, and ...Bc7, ...Nf6, ...Bg4 give easy piece play. White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Castling is a quiet move that tests White less.
notes.original: The quiet move is less testing

notes.text: The position is equal.
Develop normally and wait for White to commit.
notes.original: Black develops normally and waits for White to commit.

notes.text: The a-pawn prepares ...Na6 and ...Nc5; White's queenside play is slow and you are comfortable.
notes.original: 8.b3 a5 prepares ...Na6 and ...Nc5. White's queenside play is slow and Black gets a comfortable position.

notes.original: 8.Nh4 Bg4 hits the queen and the bishop pair is not important here.

notes.original: 8.Re1 Nbd7 and ...a5 and ...Nc5 give Black a standard, safe plan.
