Trading in the center at once is the simplest practical answer.
notes.original: By far the simplest practical answer - trade in the center immediately, before White gets a chance to recapture with a piece and keep some initiative.

notes.text: Your queen hits h2 along the diagonal, discouraging e5; White keeps only a small, normal edge.
notes.original: 3...Qc7!? - an 'Endgame Offer' trick: the queen eyes h2 along the long diagonal and discourages White from ever playing e5, since after an eventual ...dxe4 the position can simplify toward an endgame where Black's structure is at least as pleasant. White still keeps a small, normal edge with careful play, but has to find it rather than being handed one automatically.

notes.text: Against a quiet 3.d3, your queen stays active and you avoid the drawish queen trade.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want to answer a quiet, non-committal 3.d3 with ...Qc7 and simple development (low risk, little theory): the plan is ...dxe4 and ...Nd7, then ...e5 or ...e6 and ...Ngf6. Against 3.d3 the alternative is 3...dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ which leads to a drawish endgame. Risk level: low. After 3.d3 Qc7 Black keeps the queen active and avoids the symmetrical endgame. White's main moves are 4.Nc3, 4.Nbd2, 4.Qe2, 4.e5 and 4.exd5.

notes.text: The common recapture leads to a queen trade and an even position.
notes.original: 4.dxe4, the most common move, leads to a queen trade and an even position after 4...Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1.

notes.text: This unorthodox gambit trades a pawn for quick development; develop normally and disrupt White's set-up.
notes.original: This is an unorthodox gambit in which White trades a pawn for fast development. It is not a cause for concern: Black should develop normally and try to disrupt White's set-up.

notes.text: White recaptures with the king, but this simple, symmetrical position costs you nothing.
notes.original: Believe it or not, this simplification is completely fine for Black. Yes, White has to recapture with the king, but the position is so simple and symmetrical that this costs nothing concrete - no real attack is possible on an open board with almost no pieces left to attack with.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the knight to the king, and your position is comfortable with no theory.
notes.original: Pin the knight right away. Black already has a very comfortable, easy position with no theory to memorize.

notes.text: Trading the dark bishop is fine, but avoid the tempting knight check on f4 in this line.
notes.original: Trap: 13...Nf4+? 14.Nxf4 Bxf4 15.Bxf4 Nh5 16.Be3 g5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the knight on f4 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 13...Nf4+? 14.Nxf4 Bxf4 15.Bxf4 Nh5 16.Be3 g5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: You reach a safe, balanced middlegame with no weaknesses and no real winning try for White.
notes.original: A sample line all the way into a simple, balanced middlegame: Black trades the light-squared bishop for a knight, then the dark-squared bishop as well, reaching a position with no weaknesses and no real winning try for White - the kind of safe, low-maintenance equality this line is meant to offer against an opponent trying to avoid main-line theory.

notes.text: White gains queenside space, but you hold it shut with ...c5 and ...b6 and counter with ...h5.
notes.original: White's plan is to gain space on the queenside with a4, c4 and b5 and to fix your pawns there, hoping that the knights end up passive. You hold the queenside shut with ...c5 and ...b6, give the king room with ...f6 and ...Kf7 and then counter on the kingside with ...h5. Your knights have good squares on e6 and d7 and White has no breakthrough, so the position stays a small, safe plus for White.

notes.text: You are a pawn up, but after Bxd3 a natural Nf6 loses to the Nxf7 fork.
notes.original:
The most critical line is to accept the gambit with 4...exd3 and Black is up material but must be careful not to fall into any traps. After 5.Bxd3, White threatens attacks on h7 and f7. If Black is not careful and plays a natural move like 5...Nf6?? they are soon lost: 6.Nxf7! (forking queen and rook) Kxf7!? 7.Bg6+ hxg6 8.Qxd8 wins Black's queen for two minor pieces.

= Caro-Kann Defence, Endgame Offer =

White should capture with their bishop.

notes.text: Your queen stops Bf4; keep disrupting White's development or you end up cramped.
notes.original: This prevents Bf4. Black should keep disrupting White's ideal development, otherwise Black ends up cramped and difficult to play.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the queen, so White must move it to e1.
notes.original: White is forced to move his queen to e1. If f3 then his knight cannot go back to f3 anymore.

notes.text: You have a comfortable position; consolidate your central control and keep developing.
notes.original: Comfortable position for Black. Black should consolidate his central control and develop comfortably.

notes.text: Your bishop challenges White's on d4; White's f4 only weakens his own king.
notes.original: Bd4 aims at your f6 knight and the g7 pawn. ...Qa5 hits the c3 knight and keeps the queen active, and after Be5 you castle and challenge the bishop with ...Nd7 and ...Bf6. White's f4 only weakens his own king. You keep a small, comfortable edge.

notes.text: White's f-pawn lever opened the f-file, but you have the extra central space and your king is far away.
notes.original: White's f4-f5 lever opens the f-file, but your king on c8 is far from the action and you have the extra space in the centre

notes.text: White's knight retreats to g3, eyeing f5 and h5, but you have a free hand in the centre.
notes.original: White retreats the knight to a safe square instead of exchanging it, so he keeps an extra piece for the middlegame and eyes f5 and h5 for later. The move is simple development with no direct threat and it is very common (played in about 101,000 games). So the centre is yours to fight for: you have a free hand to play the usual pawn breaks.

notes.text: This is another way to trade queens, and it costs White the right to castle.
notes.original: Another way to trade queens that costs White castling

notes.text: Your c5 pawn stops White from comfortably playing d4. Follow with ...Nc6, ...e6, ...Be7 and castle short.
notes.original: Your plan is to take space in the centre and the queen side with ...c5, then ...Nc6, ...e6 and ...Be7, castling short. The pawn on c5 stops White from ever playing d4 comfortably and gives your pieces natural squares. Avoid rushing ...e5 and ...Bd6 without preparation, because White's knight on g3 then looks at f5 and e4 and can become annoying.

notes.text: Your knight pressures d4 and supports later ...e5 or ...d5 ideas.
notes.original: Develop with tempo-free simplicity: the knight on c6 pressures d4 and supports ...e5 or ...d5 ideas later.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn opens the bishop's diagonal and covers d5 and f5; if White tries Ng5, answer ...h6.
notes.original: Now the pawn on e6 opens the bishop's diagonal and defends d5 and f5. If White tries 8.Ng5 hitting f7 and h7, you answer ...h6 or ...Be7 and the knight has nowhere good to go.

notes.text: White's queen annoys your c6 knight; meet it with ...Qc7 or ...Bd7. You are slightly better.
notes.original: White wants to pin and annoy your knight on c6. You can answer with ...Qc7 and ...b5 ideas when needed. You have a comfortable, flexible game and are slightly better here. This is a flexible semi-open position: your pawns stand on c5 and e6, White has d3 and c3, both kings have castled short and neither side has a space edge. Your plan: first meet the queen on a4 with ...Qc7 or ...Bd7 so the knight on c6 is comfortable; then bring a rook to d8 and c8; then consider ...e5 or ...Nd4 to claim the centre. White wants to regroup with Nbd2-c2 or Re1 and play d4 at the right moment, so keep the c5 pawn solid. The risk is ...e5 played too early, when Nf5 and Ng3 pieces become annoying. If White deviates with d4, recapture calmly.

notes.text: White's last knight eyes e5 and d4, but your c8 bishop can still jump to g4 before ...e6.
notes.original: White finally brings out the last knight to eye e5 and d4. The motive is plain development: Bd3, castling and perhaps Ne5 follow. The key point for you is that your c8 bishop is still free to jump to g4 before you play ...e6, so use it.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your f6 knight and wants to trade it to wreck your pawns.
notes.original: White pins the knight on f6 to the queen's side and wants to trade it, doubling or weakening your pawns. This is very common (played in about 791,000 games). So every capture on f6 has to be recaptured sensibly, so decide early how you want to meet it.

notes.text: Your a-pawn stops White's knight from jumping to b5.
notes.original: Again, it's prudent to prevent the knight, in particular, from coming to b5, particularly once the bishop has been situated on the h2-b8 diagonal.

notes.text: White plays this to avoid being pinned by your bishop coming to g4.
notes.original: White may play this to prevent a ...Ng4 pin.

notes.text: When White delays Bd3 or c4, just develop with ...Nf6, ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...e6; ...a6 keeps White off b5.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays a 4th move other than 4.Bd3 or 4.c4.
Idea: When White delays Bd3 or c4 (4.Nc3, 4.Nf3, 4.Bf4 or 4.c3), just develop: ...Nf6, ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...e6. The early ...a6 keeps White's pieces off b5. There isn't much to memorise here.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Bf4 a6 6.Bd3 Nc6 7.Nf3 Bg4
Watch out: ...Nxd4? loses material on moves 7 to 14.

White has no real targets, so you simply improve your pieces.
notes.original: White has no real targets, so you improve your pieces.

notes.text: The ...b4 break comes once your pieces are well placed: it gains space and opens lines where you are better.
notes.original: The ...b4 break comes when your pieces are well placed: you gain space and open lines on the side where you are better.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White has the bishop pair and development for the pawn; you just finish developing with ...Nc6 and ...Bd6.
notes.original: The queen had to leave f3 because the Nd4 attacks it. White has the bishop pair and development, hoping activity pays for the pawn. You just finish development: ...e6, ...Nc6, ...Bd6.

notes.text: Trading the dark bishop removes White's compensation, and your d4 pawn cramps White's pieces.
notes.original: Trading the dark bishop removes White's compensation, and the d4 pawn cramps the knights.

notes.text: White's queen retreat wasted time, so you just keep developing.
notes.original: Retreating wastes time.

notes.text: Remember this bishop route: g4, h5, then g6 keeps your bishop alive.
notes.original: Always remember this bishop manoeuvre.

notes.text: The position is equal.
With your king still in the centre, your queen hits the d4 pawn and ties White down.
notes.original: Your king is still in the centre, so you tie White down first: the queen hits b2 and d4.

notes.text: You take the pawn and kick the c3 knight, which guards the centre, with your b-pawn.
notes.original: White's plan is g5 to open the h-file for the rooks. You take the pawn and kick the Nc3, which guards the centre, with ...b4.

notes.text: Your king steps off the dangerous files and sits behind your pawns; the game is level.
notes.original: The king steps off the dangerous files and sits behind your pawns. Level.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight to the queen and forces White to decide.
notes.original: Pin the knight and force White to decide. After h3 you trade on f3 and remove a key defender of d4. Plan: ...Nc6, ...e6, then ...Be7 or ...Bb4, castle short, and aim for ...Nb4 or a break with ...e5 at the right moment. Avoid playing ...e6 first, which locks your bishop behind its own pawn.

notes.text: This passive bishop move gives up the active jump to g4 and is a little less good.
notes.original: A passive try that gives up the active jump to g4 and is a little less good.

notes.text: Your knight hits the d3 bishop and c2 pawn; next develop the bishop and castle short.
notes.original: The knight jump hits d3 and c2, so White has to react at once, and if the bishop is traded you are happy with the knight on b4 and the structure. Next you play ...Be7 or ...Bd6 and castle short, with ...Qd7 and ...Rc8 supporting the central break. You have a solid, equal game with a clear plan. This is a Caro-Kann Exchange position where the pawn centres are symmetrical but you have the half-open c-file against White's c2 pawn. White has the bishop pair and the move. Your plan: use the knight on b4 to hit d3 and c2, trade on d3 if the bishop stays, then play ...Be7 or ...Bd6, castle short, and finish with ...Qd7 and ...Rc8. White wants a3 to kick your knight, then Qd1, Kf1 or a minority attack with b4. If a3 comes, take ...Nxd3+ and recapture. The mistake is leaving the knight on b4 loose without a plan. If White plays Bb5+, block with ...Nc6.

notes.text: Your knight adds pressure on d4 and eyes e5, keeping ...e6 in reserve.
notes.original: A natural developing move that adds to your control of d4 and e5 and keeps ...e6 in reserve. After 6.Nf3 play ...h6, and meet 7.Bh4 with ...Bg4, building the pin on the other side. Your plan is ...e6, ...Be7 and castling, followed by a pawn break at ...Ne4 or ...Qb6 later. If White plays Bxf6 you may recapture with the e-pawn or the g-pawn, choosing the one that keeps your centre healthy. Avoid grabbing material early or hurrying ...Ne4, which can leave the d5 pawn hanging. The numbers show equality, with a tiny edge for you.

notes.text: Also fine: a simple bishop trade after Be2, though Bxf6 would double your pawns.
notes.original: Also acceptable. The trade of bishops after Be2 is simple, and Bxf6 gxf6 leaves you with doubled pawns but the bishop pair is gone. Choose it if you like simple play.

notes.text: Your pawn asks the bishop; if it takes on f6, you recapture and get the bishop pair.
notes.original: Ask the bishop immediately. After 7.Be3 you have gained a useful tempo because ...h6 is a move you would often want to play anyway, and the bishop on e3 now blocks White's own plans. Your plan is ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Bd6 and castle short. If 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 gives you the bishop pair and an open game. Avoid answering the pin with ...Bg4 and then rushing ...e6 without ...h6: White can keep the pin with Be2 and Ne5.

notes.text: You developed with tempo and your bishop leans on the f3 knight; Be7 and short castling come next.
notes.original: You have developed with tempo and the pin on f3 is annoying for White. Your king goes short once Be7 is played.

notes.text: The position is equal; White's bishop pins your f6 knight, so trade on e5 with your knight.
notes.original: The position is equal; your piece play is clear, with no weaknesses, and you can aim for ...Nxe5 or ...Be7 with a solid, comfortable game. This is an open game where White's bishop on h4 pins your knight on f6 and his knight on e5 is trying to take over the centre. Your plan: trade on e5 with ...Nxe5, and after dxe5 play ...Qxd1+ to remove the pin and reach a safe ending. White wants dxe5 and then Bxf6 or e5xf6 to damage your pawns. The typical mistake is retreating the knight with ...Nd7 while the queen is still on d8, because Bxd8 wins it. If White recaptures on d1 with the rook or king, follow with ...Nd7 and attack e5. Do not hurry ...g5 before the queens are traded.

notes.text: White offers a bishop swap, steering toward a Horwitz-like structure.
notes.original: A bishop swap is possible here, steering the game into a Horwitz-like structure.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your h-pawn prepares ...g5 to chase White's f4 bishop, its only easy dark-square piece.
notes.original: The idea is to chase the Bf4, White's only piece with an easy dark-square job.

notes.text: Your knight heads for e4 and c4 and shields your position.
notes.original: The knight heads for e4 and c4 and shields your position.

notes.text: You have space and easy development, but your advanced g5 pawn leaves dark-square holes to watch.
notes.original: You have space and easy development. The advanced g5 pawn leaves holes on the dark squares, so keep an eye on them.

notes.text: If White castles at once, the same pawn advance comes with tempo.
notes.original: Castling at once lets the same pawn advance arrive with tempo.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your queen pressures b2 and d4, so White cannot expand calmly.
notes.original: You pressure b2 and d4, so White cannot expand calmly.

notes.text: White wants b4 and a minority attack, so your a-pawn takes control of b4 right away.
notes.original: White wants b4 and a minority attack against your queenside pawns, so ...a5 stops that plan before it begins.

notes.text: Your knight attacks White's active bishop on f4, aiming to trade off White's best-placed piece.
notes.original: Your knight challenges the active Bf4, aiming to trade off White's best-placed piece. Level.

notes.text: A quiet, low-risk setup: develop the bishop to f5 and play e6.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want to meet the quiet 4.Nf3 with simple development: ...Nc6, ...Bf5 and ...e6. It is positional and low-risk. The chapter also shows how to answer 5.Bb5 (the pin) and 5.Bf4. 4.Nf3 Nc6 is a natural developing reply. White can play 5.c3 to build a Carlsbad structure, or 5.Bb5/5.Bf4 to test Black's set-up.

notes.text: Answer the bishop with g6; e6 would let White force the Horwitz move order.
notes.original: White can force the Horwitz move order unless Black plays ...g6, which is the best reply (...e6 would allow it).

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's knight jumps into the center, eyeing your knight on c6 and the f7 pawn, daring you to challenge it.
notes.original: 5.Ne5 jumps into the center immediately, eyeing c6/f7 and daring Black to challenge it.

notes.text: White reinforces the center right away: the c3 pawn backs up d4.
notes.original: 5.c3 reinforces the center immediately rather than developing with Nc3 or Bb5 first.

notes.text: White develops the knight and prepares Bb5 or Bg5 to pressure your pieces.
notes.original: 5.Nc3 develops naturally, preparing Bb5 or Bg5 pressure against the newly-developed knight.

notes.text: Pin the knight at once, so White cannot play Bd3 for free and lose the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Black must pin the knight at once. This prevents white from moving his bishop to d3 for free: after 6.Bd3?! Bxf3 7.Qxf3 Nxd4, Black wins the d4 pawn and the knight hits the queen on f3, so White also loses time retreating it. White has to play h3 first instead.

notes.text: An early queen move like this does not work in this opening.
notes.original: Moves like Qb6 does not work in this particular opening.

notes.text: White's bishop mirrors yours; if c4 and c5 come, you get kingside play with knight e7 and f6.
notes.original: 5.Bf4 mirrors Black's set-up. After 6.c4 e6 7.c5 Black gets play on the kingside with ...Nge7 and ...f6.

notes.text: White supports d4 and the game becomes London-style, but you can still answer with g6.
notes.original: White supports the pawn, and the position transposes into a London-style setup. Meeting it with a Horwitz structure would be unappealing, but Black is not forced into that: ...g6 is still available.

notes.text: White gives up a pawn for the initiative that comes with the bishop pair.
The bishop pins your knight; if White trades it for your knight, you get the bishop pair.
notes.original: This pin is common at club level. White is prepared to spend a tempo or trade bishop for knight, which gives Black the dangerous bishop pair.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's pawn on h3 attacks your bishop on g4.
notes.original: Black tries to kick of the bishop

notes.text: White aims to break through in the centre, or to chase away your dark-squared bishop and switch to the kingside.
notes.original: A London-style set-up is possible here too, this time with the pin instead of ...Bf5. White aims either to break through in the centre or to chase away the dark-squared bishop and then switch to the kingside.

notes.text: Whatever White does, you can still play g6 in this setup.
notes.original: Black can still play ...g6 in every case.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Whenever White plays h3, you can answer by taking the knight on f3.
notes.original: Always remember that the move h3 would always be met with the move Bxf3

notes.text: An unusual idea: your bishop invites a trade on h6, and your knight can recapture.
notes.original: An unusual idea. ...Bh6 invites White to trade on h6. After ...Nxh6 the knight sits on the rim, but Black's light-squared bishop can drop back and trade itself for White's.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
Your pawn stops Nh4 and gives your bishop on f5 the g6 square.
notes.original: White wants to trade or pin the c6 knight, which guards d4, and then use the space on the kingside. ...g5 gives your Bf5 the g6 square and stops Nh4.

notes.text: Your position is solid; aim for the knight to f7 to untangle your pieces.
notes.original: White has a pleasant edge, but your position is solid. Aim for ...Nf7 to untangle the awkward knights.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
A useful waiting move that also covers the b5 square.

notes.original: An interesting sideline that provokes ...Nf6, since ...Bf5 would only lead to something like Ng3.

notes.text: A simple developing move that easily transposes to the Capablanca variation with h6 included.
notes.original: Simple developing move, yet it easily transposes to the Capablanca variation with h6 on the board.

notes.text: Another common move, which easily transposes to the Capablanca variation with ...Bf5 and ...e6.
notes.original: Another move variation that is mostly played. Yet easily transposes to the Capablanca variation with Bf5 then e6.

notes.text: White wants Ng3 to kick your light-squared bishop off its diagonal.
notes.original: White wants to play Ng3 and kick off the light square bishop forcibly evicting it.

notes.text: This rare but sound optional reply trades light bishops; the core repertoire does not need it.
notes.original:
Extra: an optional reply, 4...h6, against 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4. The core repertoire does not need it.
Idea: 4...h6 is rare but sound. In the main line you trade the light-squared bishops, then give up the other bishop with ...Bxc5 to double White's c-pawns, and play against them with ...e6, ...Ne7 and ...O-O.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 h6 5.Bd3 Bf5 6.Nc5 Bxd3
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 4 to 7. ...Qxh2+? loses material on moves 10 to 11.
Next: 🟢 04 continues the 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines. Plan: 🟠 Plan 02.

notes.text: White forced the bishop trade, which may show your h6 was a wasted tempo.
notes.original:
White forces black to exchange bishops possibly showing that the move h6 is a waste of tempo.
Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Qb6 8.Bxf5 e6 9.Bd3 Bxc5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qa5+? 7.Bd2 Qb6 8.Bxf5 e6 9.Bd3 Bxc5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Had White grabbed the b7 pawn instead, your queen would have punished it and White would be in trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 7.Nxb7? Qb6 8.Qxd3 Qxb7 9.Nf3 e6 10.Ne5 and White is in serious trouble.

notes.text: Taking on b7 with the knight falls into a trap: White is in serious trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 7.Nxb7? Qb6 8.Qxd3 Qxb7 9.Nf3 e6 10.Ne5 and White is in serious trouble.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Trading your bishop for the knight is good: White loses the c5 outpost knight that was hampering you.
notes.original: Exchanging the bishop for knight is beneficial since now white does not have an outpost on c5 with a knight which is affecting black's development.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's doubled c-pawns give a bishop a firm outpost on d6.
notes.original: White's doubled c-pawns give the Bd6 a firm outpost, and the queen eyes your c8 square.

notes.text: Your b-pawn now challenges White's c5 pawn.
notes.original: Challenge the c5 pawn.

notes.text: Your knight hits the d6 bishop and your pieces get active; White keeps a small edge.
notes.original: You hit the d6 bishop and your pieces get active; White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Your b6 is forced here; otherwise you simply lose the b7 pawn.
notes.original: ...b6 is forced: there is no other way to continue, and otherwise Black loses a pawn and the game.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White has castled long and wants Qb4 to hit your b6 pawn before you untangle.
notes.original: White has castled long and wants Qb4 to hit b6 and e7 before you can untangle.

notes.text: The c5 break is your equaliser: it hits the queen and opens lines against White's king.
notes.original: The ...c5 break is your equaliser, since it hits the queen and opens lines against the White king.

notes.text: You castle with a healthy structure and good play on the c-file.
White's knight jump is no more dangerous; you castle safely.
notes.original: The knight jump is no more dangerous

notes.text: Your knight develops and covers d5 and h5; you are up a knight for a pawn, so avoid tricks.
notes.original: Develop and cover d5 and h5; you are a knight for a pawn up, so just avoid tricks.

notes.text: White's f-pawn hits e6 to rip open your uncastled king; take it.
notes.original: White tries to rip your uncastled king open.

notes.text: You give a pawn back to complete your development.
notes.original: You give a pawn back to complete development.

notes.text: You are a knight for a pawn up with a big edge.
notes.original: You stay a piece up with a big edge.

notes.text: Trading your bishop for the knight is good: it no longer has to shuffle and lose a tempo.
notes.original: Exchanging the bishop for knight is beneficial, black now does not have to shuffle his bishop thus losing a tempo.

notes.text: Bring your queen to c7, then castle long to tuck your king away.
notes.original: Black plans ...Qc7 followed by ...0-0-0.

notes.text: The e6 move is also fine if you want to avoid complications on the e-file.
notes.original: e6 is also possible for those who want to avoid complications on the e file.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White offers a pawn to open lines toward your king; the bishop on f3 already hits c6.
notes.original: White offers a pawn to open lines toward your king on c8, with Bf3 already aiming at c6.

notes.text: Taking the pawn opens the queenside, so you must keep your king covered.
notes.original: The pawn grab opens the queenside and you must keep the king covered.

notes.text: White wins the pawn back and keeps a clear edge.
notes.original: White regains the pawn with the pin on c6 and keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White prepares b4 and c5 to gain space on the queenside.
notes.original: Rb1 prepares b4 and c5 to gain queenside space.

notes.text: Strike at the d4 pawn first.
notes.original: Strike at d4 first.

notes.text: A pawn sacrifice that gains a tempo by hitting White's queen.
notes.original: A pawn sac to gain a tempo on the queen.

notes.text: You rebuild solidly, but White keeps the bishop pair and a slight edge.
notes.original: You rebuild and play ...Qc8 with a solid position; White keeps the bishop pair and a slight edge.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White castles long and offers a queen trade; your doubled f-pawns are the structural problem.
notes.original: White castles long and offers a queen trade; the doubled f-pawns are your structural problem.

notes.text: Your knight is heading to c7 and then e6.
notes.original: The knight goes to c7 and e6.

notes.text: You trade pieces and your doubled pawns are solid; White keeps a small edge.
notes.original: You trade pieces and the doubled pawns are solid; White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: White castles long and prepares g4 against your h6 pawn and kingside.
notes.original: White castles long and prepares g4 against your h6 and kingside.

notes.text: You take the pawn and are a pawn up.
notes.original: You take the pawn.

notes.text: Your f-pawn guards the g4 knight and kicks the e4 knight, so you hold on.
notes.original: f5 supports the g4 knight and kicks the e4 knight, so you hold on; White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: White's knight and bishop both attack e6, which only your f-pawn defends.
notes.original: The knight attacks e6, which is also attacked by Bc4 and defended by f7 and the queen.

notes.text: Develop your bishop and prepare to castle short.
notes.original: Develop and prepare O-O.

notes.text: Your bishop becomes active on g5, and the game is level.
notes.original: You trade the f6 knight and get your bishop active. The game is level.

notes.text: White's f5 pawn shuts in your h7 bishop for now, but your e5 and c5 pawns free it.
notes.original: f5 shuts in the h7 bishop for a moment, but ...e5 and ...c5 free it.

notes.text: White can answer with c3 to blunt your bishop's long diagonal.
notes.original: Here, 3...g6 may be answered 4.c3, mitigating the pressure Black's bishop will be able to impose on the long diagonal.

notes.text: After your capture, White retakes with the knight and reaches the main Nc3 line.
notes.original:
This encourages the main move, 3...dxe4, and after 4.Nxe4 this transposes into the same line as if 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 had been played.

4.Nxe4, retaking the pawn and defending d4, transposes into the main line 3.Nc3 variation of the Caro-Kann.

notes.text: Your queen attacks the d4 pawn, but White simply defends it with c3.
notes.original:
A minor sideline is 3...Qb6, the Edinburgh Variation. Black develops their queen and attacks the undefended d4 pawn, though this can be answered with 4.c3.

This is a minor sideline of 3.Nd2, where Black attacks the undefended d4 pawn.

4.c3 is the main and best move. White defends their pawn with another pawn, forming a solid b2-c3-d4 pawn chain.

4.Ngf3 is another good move. White develops their g-knight to its most active square and defends the d-pawn.

notes.text: This is the most accurate reply, though few humans would play it.
notes.original: c5 is the most accurate. Not a move most humans would play. Kochyev, Alexander - Titov, German, 1-0, URS-ch sf, 1985

notes.text: Against 3.Nd2 or 3.Nc3 you can fianchetto with ...g6, the Gurgenidze set-up; it is optional.
notes.original:
Extra: an optional reply, 3...g6, against 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2. The core repertoire does not need it.
Idea: Against 3.Nd2 (and 3.Nc3) you can fianchetto with 3...g6, the set-up named after the Georgian grandmaster Bukhuti Gurgenidze. Take on e4, castle, and after Nxf6+ exf6 use the e-file and the bishop on g7.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 g6 4.Ngf3 Bg7 5.c3 dxe4 6.Nxe4 Nf6
Watch out: ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 9 to 13. ...Bxd4? loses material on move 6.
Next: Plans: 🟠 Plan 02, 🟠 Plan 09.

notes.text: Your doubled f-pawns are no real weakness: g6 keeps them connected, and ...f5 gains space.
notes.original: Black's doubled f-pawns aren't a real weakness here: the g6 pawn keeps them connected, and the follow-up ...f5 gives Black real central and kingside space rather than a target.

notes.text: Your rook takes control of the open e-file.
notes.original: Controls the e-file.

notes.text: Your knight is heading to f8, a safe square.
notes.original: Black is planning to tuck the knight to f8! For safe measures.

notes.text: Your queen hits the b2 and d4 pawns, and White tries to win a pawn too.
notes.original: White tries to win that pawn.

notes.text: White has to hold this pawn, since your queen is pressing it.
notes.original: White has to hold this pawn rather than let it go for activity: trying to generate counterplay by invading the 7th rank instead just runs into ...Qxc3, and Black's kingside is solid enough that White's own attack never gets started.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's bishop guards d4 against your queen, and White is ready for Nd2 and g3.
notes.original: The bishop goes behind the d4 pawn, which your queen on b6 is hitting, and White is ready for Nd2 and g3.

notes.text: Your f-pawn push prepares ...g5 and opens the kingside, though it weakens e6.
notes.original: You push the f-pawn to kick the knight on f3 and open the kingside for ...g5, though it also weakens e6.

notes.text: Both kings are loosened; your pawns gain space, but White's queen is active on h5, so it is level.
notes.original: Both kings are loosened. Your pawn advance gains space, but White's queen is active on h5, so the position stays level.

notes.text: White's a5 only gained a tempo: the queen retreated, the rooks come off and your plan stays the same.
notes.original: Kicking the queen with a5 gains only a tempo: it retreats, the rooks come off and you play the same ...f5 plan.

notes.text: White grabs the pawn; your compensation is development, and the c5 pawn will be hard to keep.
notes.original: White grabs the pawn. Your compensation is development and the fact that the c5 pawn is isolated and hard to keep.

notes.text: Your knight hits the e4 pawn and develops with tempo.
notes.original: You hit e4 and develop with tempo.

notes.text: White's king has lost the right to castle, and the c5 pawn is weak.
notes.original: White's king has lost castling rights and the c5 pawn is weak.

notes.text: You are ready to win the c5 pawn back with ...Ne4 and ...Nd7, though White keeps a small edge.
notes.original: You are ready for ...Ne4 and ...Nd7 to win the pawn back, and White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Qb3 hit b7 and d5 together, but taking on d4 solved that and the queens came off.
notes.original: Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together, but taking on d4 solves it and the queens come off.

notes.text: White's h3 pawn covers g4, so your bishop cannot pin the knight there.
notes.original: Prevent the pin immediately.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White gained a tempo for d4, so expect a slow fight for that pawn; your bishop already presses it.
notes.original: This is a Two Knights Attack, but Black has fianchettoed the bishop instead of playing ...Nf6 or ...Bg4. That takes two moves, giving White an extra tempo for d4. White will play c3 to support d4, so the c3 knight must move, which returns the tempo to Black. The result is a slow positional fight for d4. Black will castle kingside and then attack on the queenside.

notes.text: White's h3 stops Bg4 for now, but it weakens the kingside pawns and develops nothing.
notes.original: Most played move here. It prevents Bg4 for the moment. But it also weakens the king-side pawns, and if White castles queen-side later, c3 isn't so attractive anymore. Also, it doesn't develop a piece.

notes.text: White's bishop stops the pin and clears the way to castle; White has three pieces out to your one.
notes.original: An alternative to prevent the pin. Also develops the bishop, and enables king-side castling. Note that White has already developed three pieces, and they can castle. Black has only one piece developed.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
This exchange gives a very open game with many trades and a high chance of a draw.
notes.original: The exchange here leads to a very open game with lots of material trades and a high chance for a draw.

notes.text: Take in the centre, trade knights and recapture with the e-pawn, which opens the e-file for you.
notes.original: The pawn on h3 stops ...Bg4, so you take in the centre and recapture with the pawn on f6. That gives you the e-file and the pawn controls e5.

notes.text: Unlike the Two Knights Attack, White's c3 knight can simply take your knight on e4 here.
notes.original: Similar to the Two Knights attack, but here White can take that knight.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Avoid the queen check on a5 here; after White blocks, you end up in a lost position.
notes.original: Trap: 7...Qa5+? 8.Bd2 Qb6 9.Nc3 Qxb2 10.Rb1 Qa3 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 7...Qa5+? 8.Bd2 Qb6 9.Nc3 Qxb2 10.Rb1 Qa3 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Your knight on c6 cannot be pinned here, unlike in many other Caro-Kann lines.
notes.original: Note that this knight cannot be pinned, in contrast to many other CK variations.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your rook pins the d4 pawn to the queen, preparing an attack on the e4 knight.
notes.original: Pin the pawn for an attack on e4.

notes.text: Your active pieces and White's exposed king are worth more than White's extra material.
notes.original: (White's three extra pawns aren't enough compensation here - Black's activity and the exposed White king are worth more, the same pattern as the Qxa8 lines later in this chapter.)

notes.text: The calm king move is White's best try, sidestepping tactics on the long diagonal.
notes.original: Rather than Qf3, the calm king move Kf2 is actually White's best try here, sidestepping tactics on the long diagonal before continuing.

notes.text: Resist taking the e4 knight with your rook; it loses for you.
notes.original: Trap: 19...Rxe4? 20.axb4 Bb7 21.Bc2 Re1+ 22.Kxe1 Bxf3 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on e4 with the rook falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 19...Rxe4? 20.axb4 Bb7 21.Bc2 Re1+ 22.Kxe1 Bxf3 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Your bishop pair and open lines outweigh White's extra material.
notes.original: (Two extra pawns isn't enough against the bishop pair and Black's open lines here - the same pattern shows up again a few moves later.)

notes.text: Black is winning.
White's king is too exposed and your pieces too active for the extra material to count yet.
notes.original: (Even four pawns up, White's king is too exposed and Black's pieces too active for the material to count for much yet.)

notes.text: Taking on b2 is best; the other checks and captures here throw away most of your edge.
notes.original: Watch out: several other checks and captures look tempting here too, and all of them throw away most of that edge: 24...Qxf6, 24...Qd6+, 24...Qh5+, 24...Qd4+ and 24...exf6. Even the mildest of them, 24...Rd4+, gives back most of it. Reference lines: 24...Qxf6 25.Qxc8+ Kh7 26.Qc3 Qg5 27.Qd2 Qg3; 24...Qd6+ 25.Kc1 Qc7+ 26.Kb1 Kh7 27.fxe7 Bf5+; 24...Qh5+ 25.Kc1 Qc5+ 26.Kb1 exf6 27.Ka2 Rc4; 24...Qd4+ 25.Kc1 Kh7 26.Qxc8 Qe3+ 27.Kb1 Qxb3; 24...exf6 25.Qxc8+ Kg7 26.Qc3 Qg5 27.Qd2 a5; 24...Rd4+ 25.Kc1 Rd8 26.Bc2 exf6 27.Kb1 Kg7

notes.text: Taking on b2 is the move; the other checks and captures here throw away most of your edge.
notes.original: Watch out: several other checks and captures look tempting here too, and all of them throw away most of Black's edge: 25...Qxf6, 25...Qd6+, 25...Qh5+, 25...Qd4+ and 25...exf6. Even the mildest of them, 25...Rd4+, gives back most of it. Reference lines: 25...Qxf6 26.Kc1 b4 27.axb4 Rf2 28.Qc3 Qg5+; 25...Qd6+ 26.Kc2 Qxf6 27.Kb1 a5 28.Qc3 e5; 25...Qh5+ 26.g4 Qg5 27.Bxf7 Rd4+ 28.Kc2 Rd2+; 25...Qd4+ 26.Kc1 Qe3+ 27.Kb1 Qxb3 28.fxe7 Qd3+; 25...Rxf6 26.Qc3 Qg5 27.g4 a5 28.Kc2 Qf4; 25...Rd4+ 26.Kc1 Qe3+ 27.Kb1 Qxb3 28.Qc3 Rd1+; 25...exf6 26.Bxf7 Rd4+ 27.Kc2 Qe4+ 28.Kb3 h5

notes.text: Taking on a1 is best; the other captures and checks are worse than they look.
notes.original: Watch out: the other captures and checks here are worse than they look: 26...Rxf6 and 26...exf6 are close to lost for Black, 26...Rd4+ isn't much better, and even 26...Qxf6 gives back most of the advantage. Reference lines: 26...Rxf6 27.Qxb2 Rf5 28.g4 Rf3 29.Bc2 Rf2; 26...Rd4+ 27.Ke2 Qxc2+ 28.Bxc2 exf6 29.Rac1 Kg8; 26...Qxf6 27.Ra2 a5 28.Kc1 a4 29.Bd5 Qe5; 26...exf6 27.Qxb2 Kg7 28.Qc3 h5 29.Qc7 Rc4

notes.text: Your queen wins the rook on a1 with check, and you decline the queen trade.
notes.original: You win the rook with check and are happy to decline the queen trade that Qc2 offered.

notes.text: Taking on f6 with the queen is right; recapturing with the rook or pawn lets White consolidate.
notes.original: Watch out: 27...Rxf6 and 27...exf6 both let White consolidate and win, and 27...Rd4+ still throws away most of the edge. Reference lines: 27...Rxf6 28.Qxa1 a5 29.Qe5 Kg7 30.Qxe7 Rf2; 27...Rd4+ 28.Kc2 Qxc1+ 29.Rxc1 exf6 30.Kc3 Rf4; 27...exf6 28.Qxa1 a5 29.Qc3 Kg7 30.Qxa5 Rd4+

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
You have three pawns for the bishop, and your safe king and queenside pawns give you better chances.
notes.original: You have three pawns for the bishop, and the safe king plus the queenside pawns give you the better chances.

notes.text: White answers your check with Kb2, which keeps everything protected.
notes.original: Your last move was ...Qf5+, so White is in check, and Kb2 is the move that keeps everything protected.

notes.text: Your rook pins the bishop on c2 to the king, and rook and queen both hit g2.
notes.original: The bishop is pinned along the second rank, and the rook and queen now both hit g2.

notes.text: You won the g2 pawn; in this queen ending your four extra pawns and kingside majority are the trump.
notes.original: You have won the g2 pawn and in the queen ending you have four pawns for the bishop, with the kingside majority as the long-term trump.

notes.text: A king step to d1 here would lose the bishop on b3 to a queen check that forks.
notes.original: Kd1 loses the bishop on b3 to ...Qd3+ with a fork.

notes.text: Putting the king on c3 walks into queen checks that win the g2 pawn.
notes.original: Kc3 walks into a series of checks that win the g2 pawn.

notes.text: White must take the bishop with check, or your rook check on f1 or queen capture on a1 decides.
notes.original: White has to take the bishop with check, since any other move lets ...Rf1+ or ...Qxa1+ decide.

notes.text: Your king steps off the back rank and out of check.
notes.original: The king steps off the back rank, out of the check.

notes.text: Your a-pawn attacks the bishop on b3, and you keep the initiative.
notes.original: The a-pawn attacks the bishop on b3 and you keep the initiative.

notes.text: White's queen offer failed to your rook capturing on f3.
notes.original: Offering the queens fails to ...Rxf3.

notes.text: Bb7 is the most crushing choice; the other captures are fine but less strong.
notes.original: Xiong, Jeffery - Shabalov, A., 0-1, ch-USA 2017 22...Bxf5, 22...Qxf6 and 22...exf6 are not mistakes either. 22...Bxf5 (after 23.Qxa8+ Kh7 24.Qf3 Bd3+ 25.Ke1 Qa5+) is dead equal; 22...Qxf6 (after 23.Qxa8 Qxf5+ 24.Ke2 Qe5+ 25.Kf1) keeps a modest Black edge; and 22...exf6 (after 23.fxg6 b4 24.gxf7+ Kf8 25.Qxa8 Rf4+) keeps a somewhat bigger one. They are just less crushing than 22...Bb7, which is close to winning outright.

notes.text: White offers queens and eyes h6 and f7, hoping for threats, but it does not work.
notes.original: White offers the queens and eyes h6 and f7, hoping the pawn on f6 and the bishop on b3 produce threats. It does not work.

notes.text: Taking the pawn removes White's attacking pawn on f6.
Your rook hits the bishop on b3 and keeps your pieces together.
notes.original: The rook hits the bishop on b3 and keeps your pieces together.

notes.text: The checks run out, and you stay clearly ahead.
notes.original: The checks run out and you stay clearly ahead.

notes.text: Taking on f6 walks your king away from the chase and keeps the extra material.
notes.original: Bxf7+ tries to drag the king to g6 where Qg3+ can chase it, but ...Kxf6 simply walks away with the extra material.

notes.text: This line comes from the game Ibragimov versus Stangl, Dortmund 1992.
notes.original: Ibragimov, Ildar - Stangl, Markus, 1-0, Dortmund op-A, 1992

notes.text: White's king steps off g1 to avoid your rook and bishop checks.
notes.original: White is up the exchange, but the king on g1 is exposed to ...Rd1+ and ...Bc5+ tricks, so Kh2 steps out of them first.

notes.text: You win the f4 pawn, and your rook stays active along the fourth rank.
notes.original: You win the f4 pawn, and the rook stays active along the fourth rank.

notes.text: You have two pawns for the exchange and active bishops; White is slightly better, but it is balanced.
notes.original: You have won two pawns for the exchange and your bishops are active. White is slightly better but the position is dynamically balanced.

notes.text: Bd5 looked natural, but your rook on d2 attacks g2 and your queen checks the king.
notes.original: Bd5 looks natural because it blocks the d-file, but ...Rd2 opens an attack on the king and g2.

notes.text: Your rook takes on h1, but White's rook recaptures, so material ends up level.
notes.original: Black's rook grabs the rook on h1, but it's hanging back to White's rook on a1 - the point of the whole sequence is that material ends up level, not that Black nets an extra exchange here.

notes.text: With material level, the position is equal; this is a safe way for White to defuse your complications.
notes.original: With material level again, the position is about equal. This is a safe way for White to defuse Black's complications, not a winning try.

notes.text: A sensible follow-up that keeps the position balanced rather than tipping either way.
notes.original: A sensible follow-up, included to show the position stays balanced rather than tipping either way.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks the knight on e4, which only White's king protects, so White cannot dawdle.
notes.original: White wants the rook on the seventh rank hitting a7 and b7, and the knight on e4 is protected only by the king, so White cannot dawdle.

notes.text: Your bishop guards the dark squares, and after ...e6 it will also hit the b4 pawn.
notes.original: The bishop covers the dark squares and, once ...e6 is played, also hits the pawn on b4.

notes.text: Your bishop takes White's strong knight on e4.
notes.original: gxf4+ forces the recapture, and ...Bxe4 removes White's strong knight.

notes.text: Your rook is the more active piece and hits b2, so the position is balanced.
notes.original: Your rook hits b2 and is the more active piece, so the position is balanced.

notes.text: A quieter route: the knights come off and you keep the same balance.
notes.original: A quieter route: the knights come off and you hold the same balance.

notes.text: Both tempting captures, Nxe4 and Bxb5, backfire for White.
notes.original: Watch out: the two obvious tries here, 12.Nxe4 and 12.Bxb5, both backfire for White. Reference lines: 12.Nxe4 bxc4 13.Be3 Bf5 14.Nc3 Bd3 15.Qa4; 12.Bxb5 Qa5+ 13.Bd2 Qxb5 14.Rc1 Na6 15.Qe2

notes.text: White is clearly better.
White's h-pawn backs the knight; knight and bishop both hit f7, so ...h6 would run into h5.
notes.original: White supports the knight on g5. The Ng5 and the Bb3 both aim at f7, so ...h6 now runs into h5 and an open h-file against your king.

notes.text: Your knight hits d4 and e5, and next heads to a5 to trade White's strong bishop.
notes.original: You hit d4 and e5 at once and prepare to trade off White's strong bishop on b3, the second attacker of f7.

notes.text: The h-file is open and White's rook looks toward your king; White is clearly better.
notes.original: The h-file opens and White's rook on h1 looks at your king. You must find defensive resources; White has a clear edge.

notes.text: Opening lines with e6 looks natural, but it is much less effective than h4.
notes.original: Opening lines with e6 looks natural, but it is a lot less effective than h4.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White stops ...b5 and prepares Bd2 against ...Qa5; the doubled c-pawns are its weakness.
notes.original: White stops ...b5 and gets ready to answer ...Qa5 with Bd2, since the doubled pawn on c3 is the weakness of the structure.

notes.text: Your queen hits c3 and a4 together, so White must keep c3 protected.
notes.original: The queen hits c3 and a4 together, so White must keep the pawn on c3 protected.

notes.text: You gain space, kick White's bishop and fix its pawn structure.
notes.original: You gain space, kick the bishop and fix White's pawn structure.

notes.text: White's bishop on d2 guards the c3 pawn.
notes.original: Bd2 guards c3.

notes.text: Your king goes queenside; your g7 bishop covers h6, and White's doubled c-pawns stay a liability.
notes.original: Your king goes to the queenside; Bd2 and Qc1 aim at h6 but your bishop on g7 covers it. The doubled c-pawns remain White's long-term liability.

notes.text: A move-order alternative that reaches the same structure.
White is slightly better.
Offer a rook trade so White cannot invade on the seventh rank after f5.
notes.original: Black should try to exchange the rooks, so White can't invade on the 7th rank once Black plays ...f5.

notes.text: Too early: it gives White's rook the chance to reach your seventh rank.
notes.original: Too early, it gives White a chance to push the rook to the 7th rank.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White opens the centre before your knight settles on b4, hits c6 and prepares Bf4 and Rd2.
notes.original: White opens the centre before your knight can settle on b4 for good, hitting the c6 pawn and preparing Bf4 and Rd2 on the open d-file.

notes.text: Your bishop covers the c6 pawn and the long diagonal.
notes.original: The bishop covers c6 and the long diagonal.

notes.text: You take two pawns, but the open d-file points White's rook and queen at your queen.
notes.original: You take two pawns, but the d-file is open and the rook on d2 and the queen on d1 point at your queen.

notes.text: You are a pawn up, but White is active; keep your king covered and aim your knight at d5.
notes.original: The bishop recaptures with tempo on the queen. You are a pawn up, and White has open lines and activity for it. Keep the king covered and aim for ...Nd5.

notes.text: White's bishop on c3 already pressures your knight on b4.
notes.original: The calmer way: Bd2 hits the knight on b4 and Bc3 keeps the pressure on it.

notes.text: Don't grab on d4 with your bishop: White wins with Bxd8 and Nxd4.
notes.original: Trap: 13...Bxd4? 14.Bxd8 Rxd8 15.Nxd4 Nd5 16.Bxd5 cxd5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d4 with the bishop falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 13...Bxd4? 14.Bxd8 Rxd8 15.Nxd4 Nd5 16.Bxd5 cxd5 and Black is losing.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
Your queen goes to d6 and hits White's rook on e7 again.
notes.original: Your queen is attacked by the rook on e7, and because the bishop on g5 guards that rook you cannot simply take it. Qd6 moves with a counter-threat: it hits the rook again and takes the d-file.

notes.text: Your pawn hits d4, so White's rook must retreat or the centre dissolves.
notes.original: You hit d4 so the rook must retreat or the centre dissolves.

notes.text: Your bishop offers a trade that removes the piece shielding White's rook.
notes.original: Trading bishops removes the piece that was shielding White's rook.

notes.text: White is clearly better, but you can fight on by winning back the c5 pawn.
notes.original: White keeps a clear edge with better pieces, but you are not lost: trade queens and fight to win back c5.

notes.text: Playing Nd7 here runs into Ne5, with tricks on f7 and d8.
notes.original: The knight on d7 is attacked twice and Ne5 brings tricks on f7 and d8.

notes.text: Blocking with the bishop runs into Ne5 and leaves your kingside weakened.
notes.original: Blocking with the bishop runs into Ne5 and a weakened kingside.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your bishop fights for e4 and your rook keeps the e-file contested.
notes.original: The bishop leaves c8 and fights for the e4 square. Your rook on e8 keeps the e-file contested, so White cannot simply invade with rooks.

notes.text: Your centralised bishop hits the knight on f3 and eyes c2.
notes.original: The bishop is centralised and hits the knight on f3 and the c2 square.

notes.text: A central counterstrike: your pawn hits d4 and blunts White's bishop on c3.
notes.original: A central counterstrike: it hits d4 and takes the sting out of the bishop on c3.

notes.text: Your knight hits the c5 pawn and the pieces are active; White's edge is small.
notes.original: You pressure the c5 pawn with ...Nd7 and ...Bc6, and the pieces are active on both sides. White's edge is small.

notes.text: Offering the rook trade is playable, but it lets White gain space with c4.
notes.original: Offering the rook trade is also playable, but it lets White play c4 with extra space.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White trades rooks before you can double on the e-file or use Bf5 and Qd7.
notes.original: White trades the rooks before you can double on the e-file or use ...Bf5 and ...Qd7.

notes.text: White gains space and takes d5 away from your pieces.
Your bishop offers the light-bishop trade at once, so c4 cannot be backed by d5.
notes.original: You offer the trade of the light-squared bishops at once, so that the c4 pawn cannot be backed by a d5 push.

notes.text: With c5 you have freed your position; only White's small space edge remains.
notes.original: You have freed the position with ...c5, and the only thing left is White's small edge from the extra space.

notes.text: If White lets you trade the light bishops on e6, you equalise.
notes.original: If White lets you trade on e6, the doubled pawns are repaired and you equalise.

notes.text: Your light bishop has no other good square, so it goes to g4 anyway.
notes.original: anyway. There is no other good square for Black's light-squared bishop.

notes.text: Not recommended: White's knight recaptures and lands on a better square in the centre.
notes.original: Is not recommended, because it improves White's knight.

notes.text: White threatens e5, which would cramp you, so take on e4 now.
notes.original: Is probably the most accurate here. Now it's time to get Black's knight to f6 to enable castling. However, e5 by White would be very uncomfortable, so Black has to take e4 now.

notes.text: Your extra pawn doesn't cancel White's small edge: White gets faster development and open lines for it.
notes.original: (Black's extra pawn doesn't cancel White's edge here - White gets the usual compensation for this kind of early pawn-grab: faster development and open lines, worth more than one pawn this soon.)

notes.text: Your e6 is worth considering and transposes into a Grunfeld-Slav setup.
notes.original: Worth considering, transposing into a Grunfeld-Slav Defence.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
This position comes from a game in which you, as Black, beat Arkell's opponent in 2012.
notes.original: Brown, Martin - Arkell, Keith C, 0-1, GBR-ch 99th, 2012

notes.text: Trade the bishop for the knight so that ...e5 hits the bishop and d4 loses a defender.
notes.original: You trade the bishop for the knight so that ...e5 comes with a tempo on the bishop and the d4 pawn loses the Nf3 as a defender.

notes.text: Your central pawn break hits both the d4 pawn and the bishop on f4.
notes.original: Your central break hits both d4 and the bishop on f4.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop on g5, which was eyeing your queen.
notes.original: The pawn kicks the bishop, which was eyeing your queen.

notes.text: Your king steps off the diagonal, so White's queen check gains nothing.
notes.original: The king steps off the diagonal and the check gains nothing for White.

notes.text: White's pieces are active: the queen hits b7 and a bishop hits your knight, so keep both protected.
notes.original: White's bishops are active and Qb3 hits b7, so you must keep your knights protected and your b-pawn watched.

notes.text: This retreat is solid, but White's g-pawn push has already won extra space.
notes.original: A solid alternative, but White gets g4 in with extra space.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
You trade your attacked bishop for the knight, and White's e4 knight will take on f6 next.
notes.original: You trade before h3 can chase the bishop, and the knight on e4 will take on f6 next.

notes.text: Your knight hits c4 and d5, so White cannot comfortably take over the centre with c4.
notes.original: The knight hits c4 and d5, so White cannot comfortably take over the centre with c4.

notes.text: White has the bishop pair and the d-file, but you have no weaknesses and ...c5 is your counter.
notes.original: White has the bishop pair and the d-file, but your position has no weaknesses and ...c5 is your counter.

notes.text: Trading your knight for a bishop is tempting, but White gets the bishop pair and the open h-file.
notes.original: Tempting because it trades a knight for a bishop, but after hxg4 White has the bishop pair and the open h-file.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White grabs space and prepares d5 and Qb3 against your doubled f-pawns.
notes.original: White grabs space and prepares d5 and Qb3 against your doubled f-pawns, and the pawn on c4 takes d5 away from your pieces.

notes.text: Your rook takes the open file and presses the bishop on e3.
notes.original: The rook takes the open file and presses the bishop on e3.

notes.text: After h3 your bishop retreats to f5 instead of being given up for a knight.
notes.original: The bishop on g4 is asked a question and retreats rather than being given up for a knight.

notes.text: Your bishop covers e7 and the dark squares, and makes room for the knight to reach c7.
notes.original: You cover e7 and the dark squares and make room for ...Na6-c7.

notes.text: Your knight can reach e6 or d5; White's small edge is structure, with no direct threat.
notes.original: The knight reaches e6 or d5 and the position is solid. White's small edge is the better structure, with no direct threat.

notes.text: White's d5 break opened the centre, but your bishop keeps its diagonal.
notes.original: White's d5 break opens the centre, but your bishop keeps its diagonal.

notes.text: Had White grabbed on d5 instead of recapturing, you would have been winning.
notes.original: Trap: 8.exd5? Bxd1 9.dxc6 Nxc6 10.Nxc6 bxc6 11.Rxd1 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d5 with the pawn falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 8.exd5? Bxd1 9.dxc6 Nxc6 10.Nxc6 bxc6 11.Rxd1 and White is losing.

notes.text: White plays f3 before castling, solidifying the centre and taking e4 and g4 from your pieces.
notes.original: Before castling, White does slightly better inserting f3 first, solidifying the center and taking the e4 and g4 squares away from Black's minor pieces.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White's f3 props up the e4 pawn so the knight on e5 keeps a stable post.
notes.original: White supports e4 so that the knight on e5 has a stable post, and the centre stays intact.

notes.text: Your knight challenges the one on e5, the piece that makes White's setup work.
notes.original: You challenge the Ne5, the piece that makes White's setup work.

notes.text: Your c-pawn strikes at d4 and opens the diagonal for your bishop on g7.
notes.original: You open the position for your Bg7 and strike at d4.

notes.text: White wins a pawn, but your d-pawn hits the bishop and knight with tempo.
notes.original: White wins a pawn, but this push hits both Be3 and Nc3 with tempo and your bishop on g7 comes to life.

notes.text: Your b-pawn hits c5 and wins the pawn back, so the position is level.
notes.original: You win the pawn back and the position is level.

notes.text: Your queen hits b2 and d4, so the Bg5 pin does not impress and you are slightly better.
notes.original: Pinning the knight with Bg5 does not impress: ...Qb6 hits b2 and d4 and you get the slightly better chances.

notes.text: This move order keeps White's usual small edge; your plan stays the same.
notes.original: A small improvement that keeps White's usual small edge. Nothing changes in Black's plan; just know the move order.

notes.text: Bd2 breaks the pin and also prepares castling long.
notes.original: Your queen pins the knight on c3 to the king, so White's first job is to unpin, and Bd2 also prepares castling long.

notes.text: Your queen pins the knight on c3 to the king, so White must react.
notes.original: Your queen pins the knight on c3 to the king, so White's first job is to unpin, and Bd2 also prepares castling long.

notes.text: You challenge the centre before White is ready.
White's knight is centralised, but your queen steps away and gives White nothing to hit.
notes.original: The knight is centralised, but your queen steps away and gives White nothing to hit.

notes.text: White has more room, but you are solid and can contest the open d-file.
notes.original: White has the freer game, but you are solid and can target the open d-file with ...Rfd8.

notes.text: White's e5 aimed to trap your queen with b4, but your trades came first and came out even.
notes.original: The point of e5 is that b4 would trap the queen on a5, but you take on c3 first and the trades come out even.

notes.text: Taking on f3 can win a pawn for now, but it costs development and is not recommended.
notes.original: Black can win a pawn here temporarily, at the cost of development. This is not recommended.

notes.text: You want to trade this bishop for White's good light-squared bishop rather than for a knight.
notes.original: Is the more precise move order here. Black wants to trade this bishop for White's good light-squared bishop rather than for a knight.

notes.text: White puts the rook on the e-file against your doubled f-pawns and prepares Bf4 and a4.
Your queen leaves the d-file and eyes f4, where White's bishop wants to go.
notes.original: You step off the d-file and eye the bishop on f4 if it arrives.

notes.text: White gains space and stops b5, so your knight heads for c5.
notes.original: White gains space and stops ...b5, so your knight heads for c5 or b4.

notes.text: Or your knight can head for b4 instead.
notes.original: White gains space and stops ...b5, so your knight heads for c5 or b4.

notes.text: Your bishop guards the dark squares and frees the a8 rook to reach d8.
notes.original: The bishop guards the dark squares and prepares ...Rad8 and a ...e5 break.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge, but your position is sound and you can aim for a central break.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge but your position is sound, with ...Bg6 and a central break as your plan.

notes.text: You trade a pair of rooks, and your knight on b6 blocks the queen's route to b7.
notes.original: Bf4 and Qb3 aim at b7 and d6, but ...Nb6 covers both and you trade a pair of rooks.

notes.text: You are a pawn up for the moment, but White has counterplay.
notes.original: But White has counterplay.

notes.text: White threatens Nd6+, which is not easy to deal with.
notes.original: With the threat of Nd6. It's not so easy to deal with that.

notes.text: White has the pawn back, your queenside is wrecked, and the bishop pair gives a lasting edge.
notes.original: White has won the pawn back and stands clearly better: Black's queenside is wrecked, and White's bishop pair and safer king add up to a lasting edge.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your loose c6 pawn, and the rook hits your bishop on d4.
notes.original: And this rook will enter the 7th rank now. Also, c6 is hanging.

notes.text: White has collected a second pawn, and your pieces stay passive.
notes.original: An illustrative line (not from a real game): 13.Rd1! keeps hammering the loose bishop on d4, and after 13...Bb6 14.Bxc6 White collects a second pawn while Black's pieces stay passive.

notes.text: Before a pawn push can chase it, your knight cashes in for the c2 pawn; White's bishop recaptures.
notes.original: The knight cannot stay on b4 for long, since a2-a3 would drive it away, so you cash it in for the c2 pawn and force the bishop to recapture.

notes.text: Material is level again, but White keeps the bishop pair and the more active pieces.
notes.original: You take back the knight on b7, so material is level again, but White keeps the bishop pair and the more active pieces.

notes.text: Your bishop covers d8 against rook checks there and stays active.
notes.original: The bishop covers d8 against Rd8+ ideas and stays active.

notes.text: White holds the d-file, so activate your king and rook to trade the rooks.
notes.original: White plants a bishop on c6 and holds the d-file. You must activate the king with ...Ke7 and ...Rd7 to trade the rooks.

notes.text: Hitting the bishop with f5 is too slow: White traps your knight and comes out well ahead.
notes.original: Hitting the bishop is too slow: Bf4 and c3 trap the knight and White comes out well ahead.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
You offer the knight trade; taking back with the e-pawn opens the e-file and eases development.
notes.original: You invite the exchange. The pawn recaptures on f6 and gives you the e-file and an easy development.

notes.text: A useful waiting move: your a-pawn stops White from gaining space with a4 and a later a5 clamp.
notes.original: A useful waiting move that stops White from gaining space with a2-a4 and a later a5 clamp.

notes.text: White leads slightly in development, but your structure is fine; head for d7 and b6 with the knight.
notes.original: White has a slight lead in development but your structure is under no real pressure. Aim for ...Nd7 and ...Nb6.

notes.text: Bf5 loses time because Ng3 gains a tempo, so it is a little less accurate.
notes.original: ...Bf5 loses time here, since Ng3 comes with a gain of a tempo; this is a little less accurate.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White keeps the e5 wedge, frees f3 for the knight and invites you to trade bishops.
notes.original: White does not want the Bg4 pin to bite on f3, so Nd2 keeps the e5 wedge, frees f3 for the knight and invites the bishop trade.

notes.text: Your knight guards c6 and backs the ...c5 break; with White's light bishop gone, e6 is no longer weak.
notes.original: The knight supports c6 and the ...c5 break, and with the light-squared bishop gone the e6 pawn is no longer a weakness.

notes.text: Your freeing break hits the d4 pawn, and ...Nbc6 will add more pressure.
notes.original: Your freeing blow: e5 is guarded only by the knight and d4 is attacked by c5 and soon ...Nbc6.

notes.text: You are fully developed and keep pressure on d4, so White's space is more a target than a trump.
You castle and follow the same plan, bringing a knight to c6 to hit d4.
notes.original: After Nh4 you trade first and play the same plan, hitting d4.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your rook takes the open e-file at once.
White has the slightly better structure, but you have a sound king and active pieces.
notes.original: White has the slightly better structure but you have a sound king and active pieces.

notes.text: A playable alternative: White has doubled c-pawns but a solid centre.
White is clearly better.
Your queen hits b2 and leans on d4, so White must answer instead of finishing development.
notes.original: You hit b2 and lean on d4, so White must answer with Qc1 or similar instead of finishing development.

notes.text: White's queen covers b2 and keeps the e3 bishop protected.
notes.original: Qc1 covers b2 and keeps the bishop protected.

notes.text: Your knight attacks the e3 bishop and the d4 pawn together, so White must spend a tempo.
notes.original: The knight attacks Be3 and d4 together, so White spends a tempo on the bishop.

notes.text: Your bishop hits the f4 pawn, the head of White's chain, so ...fxe5 can open the f-file later.
Your knight presses f4 and d4; White has more space but no threat, so keep ...fxe5 in reserve.
notes.original: The knight on e6 presses f4 and d4. White has more space but no direct threat, so you wait with ...fxe5 in reserve.

notes.text: Taking on e5 at once is a shade less accurate: the ...d4 push runs into Bc4 and a strong knight…
notes.original: Taking at once is a shade less accurate: the ...d4 push runs into Bc4+ and a strong knight on e4.

notes.text: After a3 stops ...b4, play settles into normal central play; White has a modest edge, not a refutation.
notes.original: After 4.a3 (stopping ...b4) the position usually settles into standard central play. White has a normal, modest edge; it is a real try, not a refutation of Black's idea.

notes.text: In this illustrative line White develops naturally and keeps a small edge, but it is no refutation of your counterattack.
notes.original: An illustrative line, not from a real game: White develops naturally and keeps a small edge thanks to Black's slightly loose light squares on the kingside after ...exf6. Nothing dramatic, and certainly not a refutation of Black's counterattack.

notes.text: White lines up queen and bishop on h7, aiming at your king rather than just developing.
notes.original: White lines queen and bishop up on h7, so the point is to attack your king, not to develop.

notes.text: Your g-pawn shuts the diagonal at once, blocking the bishop's path to h7.
notes.original: This shuts the diagonal at once.

notes.text: Your f-pawn shuts the bishop's diagonal to g6 and gives your king room.
notes.original: Stops Bxg6 ideas and gives the king room.

notes.text: White is slightly better, but your position is solid and the f6 weakness is covered.
notes.original: White has a small edge, but you are solid and the f6 weakness is covered.

notes.text: White's bishop on h6 is not dangerous; it only provoked your bishop to d6.
notes.original: Bh6 only provokes ...Bd6 and is not dangerous

notes.text: This keeps the tension on d4 instead of resolving it right away.
notes.original: (Solid & Optimal: keeps the tension on d4 rather than resolving it immediately.)

notes.text: Taking on d4 at once is a full alternative to ...Bg4, leading to sharper, more open play.
notes.original: 4...cxd4 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - resolves the tension at once instead of pinning first, heading for sharper isolated-pawn-style structures where both sides' pieces have more open lines to work with. This is a complete alternative main system, not just a sideline, so a reader who prefers this character can adopt it as their primary answer to 4.Nf3 instead of 4...Bg4.

notes.text: White strikes the centre at once, and you have to take the d4 pawn.
notes.original: Another complicated idea which strikes the center right away. Black has to take the d pawn and further play would have been made with e6 and onwards.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White defends the d4 pawn to keep the centre together, though it could still give it up later.
notes.original: White defends the pawn to keep the centre together, though the centre could still be given up later.

notes.text: White wants to recapture on f3 with the bishop, then play c4 against your d5 pawn.
notes.original: White develops and wants to answer ...Bxf3 with a bishop recapture, then play c4 to undermine your d5 pawn. It is very common in practice (played in about 279,000 games) and avoids the sharper moves. So you can pick your own set-up calmly.

notes.text: White's pawn hits your bishop and will take it unless you trade on f3 or retreat.
notes.original: White asks your bishop a direct question: trade on f3 or retreat. He is happy to give up the knight, hoping to recapture with the queen and then use the open lines in the centre.

notes.text: Learn the forcing moves: queens come off, White's knight chases your a8 rook, but you get a strong d3 pawn.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White meets 3...c5 with 4.Nf3 or 4.c3.
Idea: Other ways for White to meet 3...c5, such as 4.Nf3 and 4.c3. The main line gets tactical fast: after 5.c4 cxd4 6.cxd5 Qxd5 7.Nc3 Bxf3 both queens come off and White's knight goes after your rook on a8, but you get a strong pawn on d3. Learn the forcing moves.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.c4 cxd4 6.cxd5 Qxd5 7.Nc3 Bxf3
