notes.text: Your king attacks the c7 knight, and you will get two pieces for a rook and a pawn.
notes.original: White's knight is trapped. Black gets two pieces for a rook and a pawn, which is a good exchange for Black.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White develops first, then brings the rook to c1 to hit your bishop on c2.
notes.original: The knight on a8 is stuck in the corner, so White first develops and then brings the rook to c1, which lines up against your bishop on c2.

notes.text: Your d3 pawn protects the bishop on c2 and cramps White.
notes.original: The pawn protects the bishop on c2 and cramps White.

notes.text: The knight escapes via c7; if you take it, White's rook wins your bishop.
notes.original: The knight gets out via c7, because taking it loses your bishop.

notes.text: White's knight escaped and material is balanced; the game is dynamic with a small White edge.
notes.original: The knight has escaped and the material is balanced, so the game is dynamic with a small White edge.

notes.text: The rook on c1 pins your bishop on c2 to your king, so the bishop is lost.
notes.original: The rook on c1 pins your bishop on c2 to the king on c7, so it is lost.

notes.text: White's e6 break opens lines for your pieces and gives White no more than equality.
notes.original: Throwing in e6+ opens lines for your pieces and is no better than equal for White.

notes.text: Your a-pawn stops White's Bb5, which would try to eliminate your knight.
notes.original: Prevents white from playing this pesky move Bb5! An attempt to try and eliminate the knight.

notes.text: White's b4 pawn is the main weakness; aim at the queenside to provoke more weaknesses.
notes.original: The b4 pawn is the main weakness in White's position. Black should aim at the queenside and try to provoke more pawn weaknesses.

notes.text: Your rook takes the e-file, and you accept that the knight on c6 will be traded.
notes.original: Your rook takes the e-file, where White's pieces crowd around e5, and you accept that the knight on c6 will be traded.

notes.text: You get the half-open b-file against White's b4 pawn.
notes.original: Your pawns are doubled, but you get the b-file against the pawn on b4, which has no pawn neighbours to support it.

notes.text: White's c4 break and bishop on d6 give White a slight edge, but your pieces are active.
notes.original: White breaks with c4 and Bd6 takes the dark squares, so you are slightly worse but your pieces are active.

notes.text: Regrouping your knight loses time and a4 hits b5, so you are worse.
notes.original: Regrouping the knight loses time and a4 hits b5: you are worse.

notes.text: White gives up the centre, so trade your bishop for the f3 knight; otherwise e5 keeps a defender.
notes.original: White gives up the center, black has to eliminate white's knight or otherwise the e pawn would have a defender.

notes.text: White keeps it simple and develops the bishop, following basic opening principles.
notes.original: Others prefer to keep things simple and would have decided to just stick to his opening fundamental and principle.

notes.text: White's bishop supports the f3 knight, so it can answer your bishop trade by recapturing with the bishop.
notes.original: White develops the bishop to support the knight on f3 and prepare short castling, avoiding any tricks with the knight pinned. It is a common choice in practice. It means White wants to hold the center solidly and answer ...Bxf3 with the bishop.

notes.text: White's queen hits your g7 pawn, and defending it with the king or g6 would be horrible, so you let…
notes.original: Black has to sacrifice the g pawn or otherwise Kf8 or g6 would have been a horrible move.

notes.text: You give up the g pawn for quick development, and the e5 pawn is your key target.
notes.original: Black temporarily gives up the pawn for rapid development; the e5-pawn is the key target.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's queen answers with a threat of its own: it attacks your knight on e5 and eyes the h7 pawn.
notes.original: Your knight on e5 hit the queen on f3, so it moves with a threat of its own: Qh5 attacks the knight and eyes h7.

notes.text: Your knight retreats to g6, where your h and f pawns protect it.
notes.original: Your knight retreats to g6, where the h- and f-pawns protect it.

notes.text: Your queen centralises on e5.
notes.original: The queen centralises and hits b2.

notes.text: You castle and your king is safe, but White keeps a small edge.
notes.original: You gave up the bishop pair, but White's doubled e-pawns are a long-term weakness and your king is safe; White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Giving up the bishop leaves you with active pieces, and the position is level.
notes.original: Giving up the bishop doubles your pawns but gives you active pieces; level.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's queen is offside on a4 and the f4 bishop backs e5; despite the rook on c1, you have the…
notes.original: White's queen is a little offside on a4 after the earlier check, and the bishop on f4 supports e5. White puts a rook on the c-file, but you have the easier game.

notes.text: Your a-pawn takes b5 away and prepares your queen to go to b6.
notes.original: Takes b5 away and prepares ...Qb6.

notes.text: This pawn lever attacks White's e5 pawn.
notes.original: The lever against e5.

notes.text: The trades leave a balanced structure where you are slightly better.
White's g4 kicked your knight but weakened the kingside, and your c4 pawn now gains space.
notes.original: Kicking the knight with g4 is the tempting try, but it weakens the kingside, and ...c4 gains space for you.

notes.text: Trade now, then play Nc6, take on d4 and aim your queen at b2; delaying lets White gain time.
notes.original: You trade the bishop for the knight, which removes a defender of the d4 pawn and of the e5 pawn. Your plan is to play ...Nc6, then take on d4 and use the queen on b6 to put pressure on the b2 pawn. Your structure is healthy, and White has nothing special. Avoid delaying the trade, because then White can play Ne5 or d4 with gain of time.

notes.text: Your queen attacks the d4 and b2 pawns at once, and White must decide how to defend.
notes.original: Your queen attacks the d4 and b2 pawns at once. White has to decide how to defend.

notes.text: This simple endgame is equal, but it gives you less to play for.
notes.original: This leads to a simple endgame that is equal, but it gives you less to play for.

notes.text: Your pawn and knight both hit d4, so trade on d4 and avoid ...c4, which drops that pressure.
notes.original: You add pressure to d4 and e5, develop a piece and keep the option of ...e6. Your plan is to trade on d4, take on e2 when it helps, and use the light squares left by the exchanged bishops. Be careful with the d5 pawn: if White takes on d5 you want to recapture with the queen or the pawn without losing time. Avoid ...c4 here, which gives away your pressure on d4.

notes.text: This is also fine: everything is protected, and after c4 you recapture on d5 with the queen.
notes.original: This is also fine and keeps everything protected; White again plays c4 and you recapture with the queen.

notes.text: You swap off White's bishop; if the king recaptures, it ends up awkwardly placed.
notes.original: You swap off White's bishop so that his king has to recapture.

notes.text: White's king is awkward, and your d5 and e6 pawns give you a solid centre.
notes.original: Now the king is awkward and you have a solid centre.

notes.text: Your queen now guards the c6 knight, which White's queen was pinning.
notes.original: This defends the pinned knight and keeps the c6 piece safe.

notes.text: The position is balanced and White's king is awkward, but watch the pin on your c6 knight.
notes.original: The position is balanced, your king will castle long or short, and White's king on e2 gives you targets. This is a semi-open position where your pawns are on c5, d5 and e6 against White's pawns on d4 and e5, with White's king on e2 and no castling for him. You have the more comfortable game because his king is awkward. Plan: recapture on d5 with ...exd5, trade on d4 with ...Nxd4 only when it works, then develop with ...Nf6, ...Bc5 and castle short, aiming at his king along the e-file. White wants to hide the king and play Nc3 or Rd1 with pressure on d5. The risk is the pin on c6: if the knight moves carelessly, Qxd7 wins material. If White plays Nc3 first, recapture ...exd5 anyway.

notes.text: Trading is right: White's queen comes out early, while retreating the bishop would waste time and a good piece.
notes.original: Trading is the right answer. After Qxf3 White's queen is out early and you can take on d4. Your plan is ...cxd4, ...Qd7 to stop Qb3 from hitting b7, then ...Nc6 and ...e6, followed by short castling. Avoid retreating with the bishop, which loses time and a good minor piece.

notes.text: Your queen defends b7, so White's queen has no target there and you stay compact.
notes.original: You defend b7 and stay compact.

notes.text: White's queen wanders while your pieces are fine and your pawns sounder; next bring the bishop to e7.
notes.original: White's queen wanders around, but your pieces are fine and you have the sounder pawn structure. You develop the bishop to e7 and castle short.

notes.text: You hold a slight edge; watch g7, where White's queen aims, and develop your knights.
notes.original: If White plays 8.Nc3 or 8.Nd2 instead of the queen move, you reply with ...e6 and ...Nc6 and take the pawn on d4 once it is safe. The pawn on d4 will often fall because White has no easy way to defend it. You hold a slight edge, with no weaknesses. This is a semi-open position in which you hold a small but real edge, with pawns on d5, e6 and the tension in the centre; you will probably castle short once g7 is safe. Your plan: protect the d4 pawn with ...Nc6, develop ...Nge7 and ...Nf5 to hit the queen, then ...Bc5 and ...Qd7. White wants to take on d4, play Bd3 and use his queen on g3 against g7 and h7. The risk is leaving g7 loose: do not let Qxg7 come with tempo, and do not let a knight take on d4 for free. If White uses Nd2 instead, still play ...e6 and ...Nc6.

notes.text: Retreating the bishop was clearly worse: White takes space and you gave up your better bishop.
notes.original: The retreat is clearly worse because White takes space and you have given up the better bishop.

notes.text: Recapturing with the knight is White's most natural choice; Qxd4 is the other main try.
notes.original: 5.Nxd4 is White's most natural recapture (5.Qxd4 is the other main try, transposing to similar structures after 5...Nc6).

notes.text: White's queen recaptures, but your knight comes to c6 with tempo, forcing it to move again.
notes.original: 5.Qxd4 - recaptures with the queen, the other of the two main tries alongside 5.Nxd4; the queen is immediately hit by ...Nc6 so White has to pick a square for it right away.

notes.text: Choose this for solid, forgiving piece play with ...e6 and ...Nc6; White's tries are c4, Nxc6, f4 and Bb5.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want solid piece play with ...e6 and ...Nc6 and no early queen adventures: the lines here are positional and fairly forgiving. It covers 6.c4, 6.Nxc6, 6.f4 and 6.Bb5, the tries White uses to avoid the Qxd4 structures. Risk level: low to medium. After 5.Nxd4 Nc6 White chooses between hitting the centre with c4, simplifying with Nxc6 or testing Black with f4/Bb5.

notes.text: White grabs central space with c4, but normal development keeps the position balanced.
notes.original: 6.c4 is White's most ambitious try, grabbing extra central space; Black continues with normal development (...Nxd4, ...Qxd4-style exchanges, or ...e6 and ...Bc5 depending on move order) and the position stays balanced.

notes.text: White's bishop pins your knight on c6, but with no queen on d4 the position stays calmer.
notes.original: 6.Bb5 - pins the knight as in the 5.Qxd4 line, but here there is no queen on d4 to win back material, so the position stays calmer.

notes.text: White trades knights at once, which spoils your queenside pawns but costs White time.
notes.original: 6.Nxc6 trades off immediately rather than retreating or developing, damaging Black's queenside pawn structure in exchange for giving up a tempo and the bishop pair.

notes.text: White's f4 is rare and a little loosening, and your knight gets a comfortable game.
notes.original: 6.f4 is rare and a little loosening. After ...Nh6 and ...Nf5 Black gets a comfortable game.

notes.text: The solid answer: your e-pawn supports d5, and your bishop can pin a knight on c3 from b4.
notes.original: The solid answer. You support d5, develop, and prepare ...Bb4 to pin the knight if it goes to c3.

notes.text: The centre is liquidated and queens are off; White's king has lost its castling rights.
notes.original: You liquidated the centre and the queens are off; White's king has lost castling rights, while your doubled c-pawns give you the b-file.

notes.text: Qg4 looks aggressive, but ...d4 hits the knight and you take over.
notes.original: 9.Qg4 looks aggressive but ...d4 hits the knight and Black takes over.

notes.text: You accept an isolated d5 pawn for active bishops and easy development; the position is equal.
notes.original: Black has accepted the isolated-looking central pawn in exchange for active bishops and easy development; equal.

notes.original: Grabbing c4 looks tempting, but the knight trade forces a queen swap and White regains the pawn with Ne4.

notes.text: Your bishop unpins the knight, and you can follow with ...a6 or ...Nxd4.
notes.original: 6...Bd7 unpins directly and prepares ...a6 or ...Nxd4 next; this is the natural, fully sound reply here (the long-diagonal tactic that refutes Bd7 in the 5.Qxd4 line doesn't exist in this version).

notes.text: White takes your knight; after you retake, White develops quickly with Bd3 and Qe2.
notes.original: Your bishop has unpinned the knight, so White cashes in the knight for the one on c6. After ...Bxc6 White aims at quick development with Bd3 and Qe2.

notes.text: Your pawn gains space and takes c3 and e3 away from White's knight.
notes.original: You gain space and cramp the white knight.

notes.text: Your bishop grabs the g2 pawn and hits the rook on h1.
notes.original: The pawn grab hits the rook on h1.

notes.text: Your rook isn't really threatened: if you take it, you walk into a check.
notes.original: The rook is not lost: if you take it, you walk into a check.

notes.text: Your pawn blocks the bishop's diagonal to h7. You're a pawn up, but your bishop is out of play.
notes.original: This blocks the bishop's diagonal to h7. You are a pawn up but your bishop is out of play and White is ahead in development.

notes.text: Your bishop on h1 is trapped and your king is exposed, so this is losing.
notes.original: The bishop on h1 is trapped and your king is exposed, so this is losing.

Retaking is forced, and you get the half-open b-file plus quick development.
notes.original: 6...bxc6 is forced; the resulting doubled c-pawns are a long-term structural concession, but Black gets the half-open b-file and quick development to compensate.

notes.text: White develops the bishop, eyeing your h7 pawn along the diagonal.
notes.original: 7.Bd3 develops naturally, eyeing the e4-h7 diagonal and preparing to meet ...Qb6 or ...Ba6 ideas.

notes.text: Your pawn solidifies the center and prepares to develop with ...Bd6 and ...Ne7.
notes.original: 7...e6 solidifies the center and prepares ...Ne7/...Bd6 development.

notes.text: White castles to get the king safe before deciding between c4 and Nd2.
notes.original: 8.O-O gets the king safe before deciding on c4 or Nd2 plans.

notes.text: White's knight heads for f3 or c4, one move earlier than in the main castling line.
notes.original: 9.Nd2 reroutes the knight toward f3 or c4 one move earlier than the main 9.O-O line.

notes.text: Your knight heads for f5 or g6, a flexible square.
notes.original: 8...Ne7 heads for g6 or f5, a flexible square that also eyes the long diagonal via ...Ba6.

notes.text: White's knight reroutes toward f3 or e4, keeping c4 in reserve.
notes.original: 9.Nd2 reroutes the knight toward f3 or e4, keeping c4 in reserve.

notes.text: White's rook lines up behind the e5 pawn, supporting it.
notes.original: 11.Re1 centralizes the rook immediately, preparing e5-e6 ideas or supporting a knight on e5 later.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes a7 and supports a later queen to e2 and f4.
notes.original: 11.Be3 develops toward c5/a7 immediately, supporting a later Qe2 and f4 plan.

notes.text: Your a-pawn starts queenside expansion and prepares ...Ba6 to trade White's good bishop.
notes.original: 9...a5 starts queenside expansion and prepares ...Ba6 to trade off White's good bishop.

notes.text: White's knight returns to f3, heading toward d4 to add pressure on the center.
notes.original: 13.Nf3 heads back toward d4/e5 rather than staying on d2, adding pressure to the center.

notes.text: White's queen supports a later f4 push rather than hurrying the knight to f3.
notes.original: 13.Qe2 supports a later e5-e6 break or f4 push rather than routing the knight to f3 immediately.

notes.text: White strikes on the queenside at once, trying to open lines before you finish developing.
notes.original: 13.c4 strikes on the queenside immediately rather than rerouting the knight to f3 first, trying to open lines before Black finishes development.

notes.text: White challenges your center, but you hold the balance with accurate play.
notes.original: 13.Nf3 heads back toward d4/e5 rather than staying on d2, adding pressure to the center. ...and Black holds the balance with accurate play.

notes.text: Your queen guards c6 and frees the rook to return to a8, while c4 undermines d5.
notes.original: The rook on a6 is awkward after the bishop trade, so the queen guards c6 and frees the rook to return to a8. White's c4 now tries to undermine your d5 pawn.

notes.text: You give ground on the kingside, but your knight still holds f5 and e6 stays firm.
notes.original: You give back ground on the kingside but hold f5 and e6 firmly.

notes.text: White has more space, but nothing concrete yet.
notes.original: White has more space but nothing concrete.

notes.text: With your rook offside, Qg4 and exf6 now open lines against your king.
notes.original: Opening the centre with ...c5 while your rook is offside lets White open your king with Qg4 and exf6.

notes.text: White pushes the h-pawn, but the position stays balanced with chances for both sides.
notes.original: 13.Qe2 supports a later e5-e6 break or f4 push rather than routing the knight to f3 immediately. ...and the position remains balanced with chances for both sides.

notes.text: Castle before the h-pawn gets going: White wants h5 to kick your knight off g6.
notes.original: Castle before the h-pawn gets going. White's plan is h5, which kicks your knight off g6, and then Nf3-e5 for a kingside squeeze.

notes.text: Your knight has few squares, but after ...f5 it can head for f7.
notes.original: The knight has few squares, but it heads for f7 once you break with ...f5.

notes.text: White's knight on e5 is strong, but you can trade it off; White keeps a small edge.
notes.original: The knight on e5 is strong but you can trade it off with ...Nxe5; White keeps a small edge.

notes.text: Bg5 hits your queen, and your knight on h8 is stranded.
notes.original: Starting the break at once is too loose: Bg5 hits your queen and the knight on h8 is stranded.

notes.text: White regains the pawn with the bishop, and the position stays balanced with chances for both sides.
notes.original: 13.c4 strikes on the queenside immediately rather than rerouting the knight to f3 first, trying to open lines before Black finishes development. ...and the position stays balanced with chances for both sides.

notes.text: Your bishop guards the queen, so Qxd8+ can be met by ...Bxd8 with a healthy structure.
notes.original: The bishop protects your queen, so you can answer Qxd8+ with ...Bxd8 and keep a healthy pawn structure.

notes.text: Your bishop will go to b6 to hit f2 and trade off White's active pieces.
notes.original: This bishop will go to b6 to hit f2 and trade White's active pieces.

notes.text: White keeps a small edge: e5 takes space and the bishop eyes e6, but your bishop is well placed.
notes.original: White keeps a small edge: the e5 pawn takes space and Bc4 eyes e6, but your bishop on b6 is well placed.

notes.text: Trading queens early let White's knight jump to d4 and pressure c6; now it takes there.
notes.original: Taking the queens at once lets White's knight jump to d4 with pressure on c6.

notes.text: White's rook on e1 backs up the e5 pawn, and White keeps a lasting initiative.
notes.original: 11.Re1 centralizes the rook immediately, preparing e5-e6 ideas or supporting a knight on e5 later. ...and White keeps a lasting initiative.

notes.text: You develop actively: your bishop aims at f2, then you castle and prepare ...f6 against e5.
notes.original: You develop actively: the bishop aims at f2 and you prepare ...O-O and the ...f6 lever against e5.

notes.text: Your queen joins the attack on f2 and b2.
White's bishop hits your rook, but the position stays balanced with a small White edge.
With queens off and White's bishop taking on g6, you end up slightly worse.
notes.original: Here the queen on g4 eyes g6 and your h-pawn, and you end up slightly worse.

notes.text: With f4 in, White keeps a comfortable, lasting edge.
notes.original: 11.Be3 develops toward c5/a7 immediately, supporting a later Qe2 and f4 plan. ...and White keeps a comfortable, lasting edge.

notes.text: White's f4 prepares f5 to kick your knight, so you develop and aim to castle.
notes.original: White's f4 prepares f5, which would kick your knight on g6 and open the kingside, so you develop and aim to castle.

notes.text: Your c-pawn break takes control of d4 and cuts down White's light bishop.
notes.original: The break hits d4 and cuts down the scope of Bd3.

notes.text: Breaking too early lets White keep a pleasant game.
notes.original: The immediate break lets White play Bb5+ with a gain of time and then pile up on d4, so White keeps a pleasant game.

notes.original: 9.Nd2 reroutes the knight toward f3 or c4 one move earlier than the main 9.O-O line. ...and Black develops comfortably.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks Bd3, so White must decide whether to allow the bishop trade that eases your kingside.
notes.original: Your bishop attacks Bd3, so White has to decide whether to allow the trade of the light-squared bishops that would relieve you on the kingside.

notes.text: Your knight hits the e5 pawn and makes the bishop trade on g6 natural.
notes.original: Your knight hits e5 and makes the Bxg6 trade natural.

notes.text: Your doubled g-pawns are the price for the open h-file pointing at White's king.
notes.original: The doubled g-pawns are a price you pay for the open h-file against the king on g1.

notes.text: Your queen hits the knight on d2 and prepares to take on c4.
notes.original: The queen hits d2 and prepares ...dxc4.

notes.text: White's knight eyes e6 and f7, but the game is level and your h-file gives counterplay.
notes.original: The knight eyes e6 and f7, but the position is level and your h-file gives you counterplay.

notes.text: That was too slow: the g6 and h5 pawns loosen your king, and White's queen now hits h5.
notes.original: Too slow: ...c5 weakens d5 and the g6/h5 pawns loosen your king, while the queen swings to h3 to hit h5.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Your knight hits the queen with a gain of time, so White must move it.
notes.original: 5...Nc6 gains a tempo on the queen at once. White's two main 6th moves here are 6.Bb5 (pinning the attacker) and 6.Qf4 (sidestepping while eyeing g3/c7); both are covered below.

notes.text: White's bishop pins your knight to the king, so it cannot take the queen.
notes.original: 6.Bb5 - pins the knight to the king along the long diagonal; the knight cannot simply grab the queen because it is absolutely pinned.

notes.text: White's queen steps aside and hits f7; you choose between solid g6 and sharper f6.
notes.original: 6.Qf4 - sidesteps the attack on the queen while keeping an eye on c7 and preparing Nc3; this is the source course's own main recommendation at this exact fork. Choice guide: choose 6...g6 if you want a stable fianchetto set-up where White's queen struggles to find a good post (solid, positional, medium theory). choose 6...f6 if you are happy to loosen your structure for fast piece play and a direct attack on e5 (sharp, higher risk). After 5.Qxd4 Nc6 6.Qf4 White's queen eyes c7 and f7. Black has two serious answers, ...g6 and ...f6, and they lead to very different games.

notes.text: Only e6 holds here; next you can unpin with the light bishop.
notes.original: 6...e6 is the only fully sound reply (Bd7, Qa5+, a6 and Rb8 all run into tactics along that same diagonal or on a7/d5). Black unpins next move with ...Bd7 or ...a6 once the structure is clarified.

notes.text: White castles and keeps your c6 knight pinned; the plan is Bxc6+ to double your c-pawns.
notes.original: White castles and keeps the pin, so ...Nxd4 is still impossible. The idea is Bxc6+ to double your c-pawns, then c4 to hit d5.

notes.text: Your a-pawn hits the bishop and asks it what it wants to do.
notes.original: You unpin and ask the bishop what it wants.

notes.text: You now have both bishops and a half-open b-file as compensation.
notes.original: You get the bishop pair and the b-file as compensation for the doubled pawns.

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen, so you gain a tempo.
notes.original: Gains time on the queen.

notes.text: The game is level: White has more space, but you have the bishops and will play Be7 and castle.
notes.original: The game is level: White has more space, you have the bishops and the plan of ...Be7 and castling.

notes.text: White's queen eyes g7, but you have unpinned and traded the pinning bishop; the game is level.
notes.original: Qg4 eyes g7 and discourages ...Ng6 ideas, but you unpin with ...Bd7 and trade the pinning bishop; level.

notes.text: Your pawn prepares the bishop on g7, a solid, flexible setup against White's central pressure.
notes.original: 6...g6 fianchettoes and prepares ...Bg7, meeting White's central pressure with a solid, flexible setup; both ...Bh6 ideas and normal development are available depending on White's next move.

notes.text: Your f-pawn hits e5 at once; it's more aggressive but weakens e6 and your king's diagonal.
notes.original: 6...f6 hits e5 immediately and is the more aggressive option. It does weaken the e6-square and the king's diagonal, so it suits players who like open fights.

notes.text: White develops the knight naturally, adding pressure on your d5 pawn.
notes.original: 7.Nc3 develops naturally, adding pressure to d5 and preparing long castling.

notes.text: Bd3 is a mistake: your bishop goes to h6, hits the queen, and you take over.
notes.original: 7.Bd3 is a mistake: 7...Bh6 hits the queen and Black takes over.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the knight, and ...Bh6 will hit the queen next.
notes.original: The thematic push: the knight is attacked and ...Bh6 will hit the queen next. After 8.Nb5 Black keeps comfortable counterplay. White's initiative is real but modest.

notes.text: White is ahead in development, and that turns into a lasting initiative.
notes.original: 7.Nc3 develops naturally, adding pressure to d5 and preparing long castling. ...and White's development lead translates into a real, lasting initiative.

notes.text: Your d5 pawn is attacked twice but defended once, so castling lets White take it.
notes.original: White has a lead in development and the king is safe on c1. Your d5 pawn is attacked twice (Nc3 and Rd1) but only defended by the queen, so castling lets White take it. You hope to use the bishop on g7 and open lines for compensation.

notes.text: Your queen counterattacks the knight on d5 and the a2 pawn.
notes.original: Counterattack on the knight and the a2 pawn.

notes.text: White pushes the a-pawn so it no longer hangs to your queen.
notes.original: Saves the pawn.

notes.text: White's e-pawns are doubled, but White keeps the extra pawn.
notes.original: You traded the dangerous bishop and White's e-pawns are doubled, but the extra pawn stays.

notes.text: The f6 push just loses a pawn: White's knight takes it with check.
notes.original: The knight on e4 dominates f6 and d6, and ...f6 simply loses a pawn.

notes.text: You traded the dark-squared bishops and won the pawn back; the position is roughly equal.
notes.original: The liquidation: Black trades the dark-squared bishops, wins back material and reaches a roughly equal position.

notes.original: 7.Bb5 g5! wins a tempo on the queen: after 8.Qg3 Nh6 Black's pieces coordinate well and ...Nf5 follows. Black is fine, even slightly better after 9.Nd4 Qb6.

notes.original: 7.Nc3 a6 prepares ...fxe5 while keeping ...d4 in the air. White's best is the quiet 8.Bd3 and the position is balanced.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White is slightly better.
Your second knight recaptures on d4 and threatens to jump to c2.
notes.original: Your second knight recaptures and lands on d4 with a threat on c2.

notes.text: White is a pawn up, but your rook hits g2 and the white king is exposed, so it's level.
notes.original: White has won a pawn but your rook hits g2 and the white king is not entirely safe, so the game is level.

notes.text: With a white bishop traded off, d4 is a great square for your knight, and your queen covers it.
notes.original: Trading off a bishop gives your knight a monster post on d4 and White loses the bishop pair.

notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
The knight on b3 covers c5 and d4, so your c5 break is slightly harder.
notes.original: The point of the maneuver - the knight eyes c5 and d4 and makes Black's usual ...c5 break slightly harder to execute for free, since ...c5 can sometimes be met by Nxc5 tricks depending on the position.

notes.text: Against 4.Nd2, develop with e6, Qb6 and Ne7, then hit the centre with c5; avoid Bxc2 and Qxd4.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays 4.Nd2 or 4.c4 against the Advance.
Idea: Against 4.Nd2, develop normally with ...e6, ...Qb6 and ...Ne7, then hit the centre with ...c5. 4.c4 is covered as a side line at move 4.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nd2 e6 5.Nb3 Qb6
Watch out: ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 4 to 6. ...Qxd4? loses material on moves 7 to 8.

notes.text: Your queen develops with tempo, the most natural and testing reply.
notes.original: Hit straight back at the undefended b2 pawn and develop with tempo - the most natural and testing response.

notes.text: You castle into safety, and White's knight maneuver has left you with no real weaknesses.
notes.original: A realistic continuation showing what Black's setup is for: even though White's knight maneuver (Nb3-c5-d3) looks annoying, Black castles into safety and keeps the position balanced with no real weaknesses - which is what the 4.Nd2 sideline is trying, and failing, to avoid.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your queen; next comes f4 to hold e5, then Ng3 to chase your bishop.
notes.original: White develops with tempo on your queen. The bishop prepares f4 to hold e5, then Ng3 to chase your bishop off f5.

notes.text: Your queen steps away from the attacking bishop and stays near the e5 pawn.
notes.original: Step out of the bishop's attack and keep an eye on e5.

notes.text: Hit the e5 pawn with your f-pawn before White consolidates with Ng3 and castling.
notes.original: Your thematic break: hit the e5 chain before White consolidates with Ng3 and castling.

notes.text: Your knight reaches d6 and attacks the b5 bishop; your king is safe and White has no target.
notes.original: Your knight finally reaches d6 with a threat against the b5 bishop. Your king is safe and your pieces cover each other, so White has found no target.

notes.text: The ...d4 break opened the centre, so you win the e5 pawn back.
notes.original: Hitting the bishop at once is tempting, but ...d4 opens the centre and you win the e5 pawn back.

notes.text: Your knight lands on the excellent d5 outpost, a comfortable and sound structure.
notes.original: A perfectly normal, comfortable structure. White's small lead in development is balanced out by Black's extra pawn and completely sound position - the knight lands on the excellent d5 outpost right on schedule.

notes.text: White's bishop retreats from the coming ...a4 and still eyes e6 through your knight.
notes.original: The bishop steps back because ...a4 was about to harass it on b3. From a2 it still eyes e6 and f7. White's small edge comes from the h5 pawn, the knight on g3 and the d4 centre, so play accurately.

notes.text: Your pawn clamps the h5 pawn and takes f4 away from the knight on g3.
notes.original: Clamp down on the h5 pawn and take f4 away from the knight on g3.

notes.text: White offers to trade your best bishop, and you accept.
notes.original: White offers the trade of your best bishop, and you accept.

notes.text: White opens the position while your king is in the centre; avoid pawn grabs and finish development.
notes.original: White opens the position with f4 while your king is still in the centre, and the resulting tactics keep White somewhat ahead. Avoid extra pawn grabs and finish your development.

notes.text: White's rook and queen hunt your uncastled king; you survive, but it is a more uncomfortable version.
notes.original: Re1 and Qg4 hunt the king that has not castled yet. You survive, but it is a more uncomfortable version.

notes.text: Avoid the queen check on a5 here: White answers Nc3 and you end up losing.
notes.original: Trap: 8...Qa5+? 9.Nc3 c5 10.Nf3 cxd4 11.Nxd4 O-O-O and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the queen on a5 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 8...Qa5+? 9.Nc3 c5 10.Nf3 cxd4 11.Nxd4 O-O-O and Black is losing.

notes.text: Solid development lets you trade down and grab the loose b2 pawn; this sideline has no real venom.
notes.original: Simple, solid development pays off here: Black trades down comfortably and even grabs a loose pawn on b2 once the position opens up - a good demonstration that this sideline carries no real venom once Black knows the basic setup.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your queen on b2, and White wants to win the g7 pawn back.
notes.original: The bishop hits your queen on b2, and the point is to win the g7 pawn back in return, with your queen running around.

notes.text: Your queen steps aside and keeps the pressure on the c3 bishop.
notes.original: Your queen steps aside and keeps pressure on c3.

notes.text: White's queen attacks your h8 rook, so you move it to the safe f8 square.
notes.original: The rook on h8 was attacked, and f8 is a safe square.

notes.text: Offer a queen trade to ease the pressure from the open position.
Your queen is centralised and material is balanced, so you can play on freely.
notes.original: The queen is centralised and the material is back to balance, so you can play on freely.

notes.text: After the queen trade White has nothing for the missing pawn, so you are clearly better.
notes.original: Hitting the queen looks natural, but after the queen trade White has nothing for the missing pawn and you are clearly better.

notes.text: This reaches the same structure and tactical point as before; whatever White's move order, your reply is identical.
notes.original: This transposes back into the exact same structure and tactical point covered above (Nxh5 met by ...cxd4) - whichever move order White chooses to reach this pawn storm, Black's response is identical.

notes.text: The bishop pins your c6 knight to the king, so you add a defender and prepare a6.
notes.original: Bb5 pins your knight on c6 against the king, so you add a defender and prepare ...a6.

notes.text: Taking on c2 with the bishop falls into a trap: you lose material.
notes.original: Watch out: ...Bxc2? loses material on moves 4 to 6.

notes.text: You have the kingside initiative for just the pawn White grabbed earlier, a fair trade of assets.
notes.original:
Black already has an initiative on the kingside (the rook eyes g4/g2 down the g-file) for nothing more than the pawn White grabbed a few moves ago - a completely fair, often better, trade of assets.
Trap: 12...gxh6? 13.Nf6# and Black gets mated.

notes.text: Taking on h6 with the pawn falls into a trap: you get mated.
notes.original: Trap: 12...gxh6? 13.Nf6# and Black gets mated.

notes.text: White's queen defends the bishop on h6, but you keep the initiative.
notes.original: The queen defends the bishop on h6 and eyes the kingside squares, but you keep the initiative.

notes.text: Your b-pawn hits the bishop on a4, gaining space and time.
notes.original: Chase the bishop, gaining space and tempo.

notes.text: Your queen and rook now press on the c-file, and White's pieces are scattered.
notes.original: You have strong pressure on the c-file and kingside, and White's pieces are scattered.

notes.text: If White castles long here, ...Nb4 and ...Nxc2 win a pawn.
notes.original: Castling long runs into ...Nb4 and ...Nxc2, which costs a pawn.

notes.text: Developing the knight first and resolving the center later is equally comfortable; it is a matter of taste.
notes.original: The alternative move order - developing the knight first and only then resolving the center - reaches an equally comfortable position; a matter of taste rather than necessity.

notes.text: Your a-pawn threatens the b5 bishop, so White trades it off with check. This gives you a slight edge.
Your a-pawn hits the bishop on b5, so White trades it off with check.
notes.original: Your a-pawn threatens the b5 bishop, so White trades it off with check. This gives you a slight edge.

notes.original: Hit e5 and the c3 square.

notes.text: After the queen trade your pieces are active and White's knight on h5 is offside; you are a bit better.
notes.original: The queen trade leaves your pieces active and White's knight on h5 offside. You are a bit better.

notes.text: Queens are off and White's knight on h5 is offside, so you keep a small edge.
notes.original: The queens come off and White's knight on h5 is offside. You keep a small, pleasant edge.

notes.text: Grabbing the queen looks tempting, but your knight takes White's queen back.
notes.original: Grabbing your queen looks tempting, but your knight takes the white queen and you end up far ahead.

notes.text: Taking on c2 costs time, because White gains tempo and then finishes development.
notes.original: Taking c2 costs time, since Bg5 hits your queen with tempo and White finishes development.

notes.text: White gains queenside space, but your pieces are active and the b4 pawn is a target.
notes.original: White gains space on the queenside, but your pieces are active and the b4 pawn is a target. You are fine.

notes.text: Retreating the queen at once also holds, but White gains time with h4 against your bishop.
notes.original: Retreating the queen immediately also holds, but White gains time with h4 against your bishop.

notes.text: With the bishop out, White can castle quickly, though pushing the d-pawn was more accurate.
notes.original: 6.Bc4 is an alternative to 6.d4. White can castle quickly and follow up with Nc3, d5 or Be3. 6.d4 is more accurate.

notes.text: Your h-pawn pushes on to add to the kingside attack.
notes.original: Black has a strong kingside attack.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
White is clearly better.
Your king is stuck in the centre, so White takes your best defender and opens the position.
notes.original: Your king is stuck in the centre since ...Rg8 gave up castling, so White removes your best defender and opens the position.

notes.text: White's d5 pawn is a break to blast open the centre against your uncastled king.
notes.original: A break to blast open the centre against the uncastled king.

notes.text: White's rooks reach the c-file while your king is stuck; castle before ...Rg8 if you can.
notes.original: White is clearly better: the rooks come to the c-file while your king is stuck in the centre. If you can, avoid this setup and castle before ...Rg8.

notes.text: Castling long gets your king safe, and White's edge shrinks.
notes.original: This gives you time to castle long and White's edge shrinks.

notes.text: Your bishop on h3 stops White castling, so White must spend a tempo chasing it away.
notes.original: A sign of domination: Black finds a temporary outpost on h3 that stops White castling. White must bring the bishop back to f1, losing a tempo to get rid of the intruder.

notes.text: White must defend against a quick kingside attack, while you are flexible with long castling available.
notes.original: A pleasant feature of the Dano-Russian Variation: White has to defend against a quick kingside assault, and Black's play is comfortable and flexible, with queenside castling available.

notes.text: White plans a5 to kick your knight, then a6 to attack your long-castled king.
notes.original: White gains queenside space with a4-a5 to kick the Nb6, and with a6 to follow he hopes to attack the long-castled king.

notes.text: Your a-pawn stops a5-a6 ideas and controls the b5 square.
notes.original: Stops a5-a6 ideas and secures the b5 square.

notes.text: White castles long too, so both kings stand on the same wing.
notes.original: White castles long too.

notes.text: Your h-pawn rushes forward to start the attack.
notes.original: Your attack: the h-pawn hurries forward.

notes.text: The kings share a wing, so speed decides; your h-pawn and the g-file make a fast attack.
notes.original: The position is balanced and the kings are on the same wing, so everything depends on who is faster; your h-pawn plus the g-file is a fast attack.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn shuts the bishop's diagonal, so f7 is no longer hit by it.
notes.original: Now the Bc4 and the queen hit f7, which is why ...e6 comes.

notes.text: Your rook heads to the c-file.
notes.original: The rook takes the open c-file.

notes.text: The game is balanced: your structure is good, so play a6 and castle.
notes.original: Balanced: you have a good structure and the plan ...a6, ...O-O and ...d5.

notes.text: Another solid way for White to keep the balance.
notes.original: Another solid way to keep the balance.

notes.text: Taking on d5 gives up White's pressure on the centre and leads to a simple, equal game.
notes.original: Pawn takes pawn only leads to total equality for both opposing sides. White lets go of his pressure on the center pawn which would lead to a simple game.

notes.text: There is not much to address after h3; simply carry on developing.
notes.original: There's frankly not much to be addressed. Bg4 e6 Bd6 0-0 as usual if h3 isn't played.

notes.text: Next play e6, then slide the bishop back to h5 and g6, or trade it for the knight.
notes.original: With intentions of playing e6 then either sliding back the bishop to h5 - g6 or exchange bishop for knight.

notes.text: Your plan from here, one move at a time.
notes.original: ...e6, ...Nf6 and ...dxe4

notes.text: White rightly recaptures with the queen; taking on d5 instead would leave White losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6.exd5? Bxd1 7.Nxd1 cxd5 8.c3 Nc6 9.Bf4 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d5 with the pawn falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6.exd5? Bxd1 7.Nxd1 cxd5 8.c3 Nc6 9.Bf4 and White is losing.

notes.text: This is a Slav-like position without your light bishop, which helps because you have no bad bishop.
notes.original: This is a Slav-like position, but without the light-squared bishop, which is actually beneficial since Black has no bad bishop.

notes.text: White can now advance with e5, or simply develop and castle.
notes.original: White now has two choices: advance with e5, or develop or castle.

notes.text: The e5 push gives an Advance-like structure, but your light bishop is already out; aim to cut off White's central…
notes.original: e5, transposes into an improvised advance variation except the light square bishop is out. Black's goal is to try and cut off white's central pawns.

notes.text: Trading pawns avoids complications, and that is often the best choice.
notes.original: Exchange pawns to avoid complications, its often for the best.

notes.text: Now you can castle kingside comfortably.
notes.original: Black can now castle kingside comfortably.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White's queen and bishop line up toward h7, avoiding a queen trade and aiming at your kingside.
notes.original: Queen and bishop line up toward h7, and White avoids a queen trade. His motive is a kingside attack, backed by the bishop pair.

notes.text: Your knight eyes c4 and d5.
notes.original: The knight eyes c4 and d5.

notes.text: Your h-pawn takes g5 away from White's bishop and removes the h7 target.
notes.original: Stops the bishop attack on h7 and g5.

notes.text: White has the bishops and space, so close the h-file with g6 and aim for a blocked position.
notes.original: White has the bishop pair and space. Black should close the h-file with ...g6 and aim for a blocked position where the bishops are of little use.

notes.text: Your knight forks White's queen and bishop, and if White takes it, your other knight forks again.
notes.original: After the pawn capture, ...Nxe5 forks the queen and the light-squared bishop, and there is no defence.

notes.text: White must recapture on e5; taking on c5 instead would lose to your knight capturing the queen with check.
notes.original: Trap: 13.dxc5? Nxf3+ 14.gxf3 Bxc5 15.Bxc5 Qxc5 16.Nf4 and White is losing.

notes.text: Taking on c5 with the pawn falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 13.dxc5? Nxf3+ 14.gxf3 Bxc5 15.Bxc5 Qxc5 16.Nf4 and White is losing.

notes.text: Don't grab on b2 with your queen; White's rook swings to b7 and you'd be in serious trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 13...Qxb2? 14.Rfb1 Qa3 15.Rxb7 Nxe5 16.Qh5 Bd6 and Black is in serious trouble.

notes.text: Taking on b2 with the queen falls into a trap: you are in serious trouble.
notes.original: Trap: 13...Qxb2? 14.Rfb1 Qa3 15.Rxb7 Nxe5 16.Qh5 Bd6 and Black is in serious trouble.

notes.text: Take the bishop first; grabbing b2 with your queen would lose to White's queen taking on e5.
notes.original: Trap: 14...Qxb2? 15.Qxe5 c4 16.Rfb1 Qxa1 17.Rxa1 cxd3 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on b2 with the queen falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 14...Qxb2? 15.Qxe5 c4 16.Rfb1 Qxa1 17.Rxa1 cxd3 and Black is losing.

notes.text: You won a pawn and got your piece back, but keep an eye on your knight on d3.
notes.original: Black won a pawn and his piece back. Just keep an eye to that knight on d3.

notes.text: White's pawn hits your queen so White can win back the knight on d3.
notes.original: White hits the queen so that he regains the knight on d3.

notes.text: Castle at once; your king is safe there.
notes.original: Castle at once; the king is safe.

notes.text: White is slightly better with active rooks, but you have counterplay and a good bishop on d6.
notes.original: White is a little better with active rooks, but you have counterplay and the bishop on d6.

notes.text: You are winning here, so stay alert to White's tactics before pushing on.
notes.original: Ignoring the knight on d3 costs a lot, so deal with it first.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White prepares c3 and Bf4, and the knight move avoids your ...Nb4 hitting the queen.
notes.original: White prepares c3 and Bf4 and avoids ...Nb4 hitting the queen.

notes.text: A solid, natural developing move.
notes.original: Solid and natural.

notes.text: Bring a rook to the c-file, keep the d5 pawn protected, and play on the queenside.
notes.original: The position is equal and quite symmetrical. Play ...b5 and ...Rfc8 or ...Rac8, keep the d5 pawn protected, and try for a queenside play.

notes.text: The bishop backs up the e4 knight, so White can simply recapture if you take it.
notes.original: Rather than retreating with Ned2, White keeps more pieces on and more central control by playing Bd3 directly, meeting a future ...Nxe4 with a simple recapture.

notes.text: The position is equal.
You prepare ...Bb7 to put pressure on the e4 square.
notes.original: You get ready to play ...Bb7 and put pressure on e4.

notes.text: The position is equal: you have the c-file and an easy plan of castling and ...Rc8.
notes.original: Equal. White has traded one pair of knights, you have the c-file and an easy plan with ...O-O, ...Rc8.

notes.text: White keeps a small pull, and this line is the more testing option for you.
notes.original: A small, normal opening pull for White - fully within the range of what's expected from this system, and worth having on record as the more testing option.

notes.text: White takes your active bishop, and your queen cannot recapture on f5 yet.
notes.original: White removes your active bishop at once. His motive is to follow with Qb3 and hit b7, since your queen cannot recapture on f5 yet.

notes.text: Your queen checks the king and hits the bishop on f5, winning the piece back with tempo.
notes.original: A check that wins the piece back with tempo, because the c3 square is empty and White has to block.

notes.text: This frees your bishop on f8 and shuts the long diagonal against your queen.
notes.original: Opens the bishop on f8 and shuts the b1-h7 diagonal against your queen.

notes.text: Your queen offers a trade that removes the pressure on b7.
notes.original: Offers a queen trade that removes the b7 pressure.

notes.text: White keeps a small pull, but you are solid and can castle next.
By castling you decline the trade, which is slightly less annoying for you.
notes.original: Declining the trade is slightly less annoying for you.

notes.text: Odd moves like Qf3 are harmless: take on e4, develop, and hit the centre with ...e5.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays a rare third move such as 3.Qf3.
Idea: Odd third moves like 3.Qf3 don't create real threats. Take on e4, develop, and hit the centre with ...e5.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Qf3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.c3 e5
Watch out: ...Qxd2+? loses material on move 4.

notes.text: The endgame is level, and your doubled f-pawns are of no consequence.
notes.original: A completely level, slightly better for Black endgame - the doubled f-pawns are of no consequence since Black has the bishop pair and a sound structure everywhere else.

notes.text: Recapturing with the pawn undoes your doubled f-pawns.
notes.original: Recapture with the pawn: this unblocks the doubled f-pawns and opens the f-file.

notes.text: The position is level.
White's rook move leaves your king stuck.
notes.original: This pushes the pawn and leaves your king stuck.

notes.text: White's queen was kicked back with tempo, so you are already ahead in development for nothing.
notes.original: After the queen is kicked back with tempo by the natural developing move, Black is already comfortably ahead in development for nothing.

notes.text: Avoid the knight jumps to e2 or f3 here; White's replies leave you losing.
notes.original:
Trap: 12...Ne2+? 13.Nxe2 Qf5 14.Nc4 Qd7 15.h4 Bg7 and Black is losing.
Trap: 12...Nf3+? 13.Bxf3 Qf5 14.Re1 O-O-O 15.h4 Bh6 and Black is losing.

notes.original: Trap: 12...Ne2+? 13.Nxe2 Qf5 14.Nc4 Qd7 15.h4 Bg7 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the knight on f3 falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 12...Nf3+? 13.Bxf3 Qf5 14.Re1 O-O-O 15.h4 Bh6 and Black is losing.

notes.text: Your pieces develop naturally while White spent tempi on the queen, giving you a small lasting initiative.
notes.original: Black continues to generate easy, natural piece play (...c5, ...Bg4, ...Nd4) against a White setup that has spent multiple tempi with the queen instead of developing - a small but real and lasting initiative.

notes.text: Take with the pawn: it opens the h-file for your rook and keeps your pieces where they are.
You stay slightly better: your knights are active and White's king is a bit loose.
notes.original: You stay slightly better: the knights are active and White's king is a bit loose.

notes.text: Your king loses castling rights, and White gets the better game.
notes.original: The king loses castling rights and White gets the better game.

notes.text: Castling long was a serious mistake; White is now winning.
notes.original: Castling long is a serious mistake (more than +5 for White).

notes.text: Trading in the centre with ...dxe4 is always fine, and nothing needs memorising here.
notes.original: Trading in the center immediately is again the simplest answer. Black is already very slightly better here, and the position is easy to play with normal developing moves - no memorization needed beyond recognizing that ...dxe4 is always fine.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn shuts out White's bishop on c4; next you castle long.
notes.original: White's Bc4 and Qf3 aim at f6 and c6, so you first shut the bishop out and then castle long.

notes.text: Your queen move aims at a queen trade, since White has no attack.
notes.original: Offering a queen trade, since White has no attack.

notes.text: This move order reaches the same position as the main line.
notes.original: transposes

notes.text: The c5 break strikes at White's centre.
notes.original: The ...c5 break strikes at the centre.

notes.text: You are level to slightly better, and nothing needs memorising.
Don't take on d4 here; White's Bg5 and recapture leave you clearly worse.
notes.original: Trap: 9...cxd4? 10.Bg5 Qb6 11.Bc1 dxc3 12.Nxc3 d4 and Black is clearly worse.

notes.text: Taking on d4 with the pawn falls into a trap: you are clearly worse.
notes.original: Trap: 9...cxd4? 10.Bg5 Qb6 11.Bc1 dxc3 12.Nxc3 d4 and Black is clearly worse.

notes.text: Treat this like the main Advance lines: bishop to f5 and the usual structural plans.
notes.original: Just meet it exactly like the main Advance Variation chapters - develop the bishop to f5 and follow the same structural plans covered in 🔵 11 to 13 and 🟢 05 and our other Advance Variation material.

notes.text: Your f6 lever hits the e5 pawn that cramps you; strike before White supports it with f4.
notes.original: A quiet move: g3 takes f4 and h4 away from your pieces and prepares Bf1, which frees e2 for the queen. Your thematic answer is the lever ...f6, hitting the e5 pawn that cramps you; do not wait for White to reinforce it with f4.

notes.text: Your bishop on f6 rules the long diagonal, the doubled h-pawns matter little, and you have the bishop pair.
notes.original: Once e5 is gone, your fianchettoed bishop becomes a strong Bf6 on the long diagonal, and the doubled h-pawns matter little in this semi-closed position. White keeps a little more space on the queenside with b4 and c3, you have the bishop pair, so it is a small White edge at most.

notes.text: White's knight raid is meant to provoke weaknesses; answer calmly with Nc6 and keep a solid Carlsbad-type structure.
notes.original: Choice guide: choose this if you want a safe, structural answer to an unusual knight sortie: the plan is ...Nc6, ...a6 and ...e6, accepting a Carlsbad-type pawn structure. It is a low-risk line but demands care in the early moves. 4.Ne5 is an early knight raid aimed at provoking weaknesses. Black answers with the natural 4...Nc6 and keeps solid.

notes.text: White's knight adds pressure on d5; guard it sensibly and finish development with a clear plan.
notes.original: White adds a second attacker against d5, planning d4 and then Ne5, Bf4 or Bb5. It is a natural developing move and very common in practice. White is not trying to dodge theory, just to build a comfortable setup. For you the task is to guard d5 sensibly and finish development with a clear plan.

notes.text: White's check forces you to commit a minor piece now; since Nc3 isn't played yet, you have a flexible answer.
notes.original: White checks to force you to decide a minor piece at once. The idea is to continue with d4 and O-O, perhaps trading the bishop for your knight to wreck your structure. Because White has not yet played Nc3, you have a flexible answer.

notes.text: White's queen eyes f7, but you simply take the knight and reach a safe position.
notes.original: This queen sortie looks threatening (it eyes both f7 and the knight's follow-up ideas), but it's met by returning the piece for a pawn and consolidating - the resulting position is completely safe and, if anything, favors Black's better structure.

notes.text: The recapture is normal; a White check on b5 here would lose to Nc6 and a solid setup.
notes.original: Trap: 6.Bb5+? Nc6 7.d4 Bd7 8.Nc3 Nf6 9.Qd1 and White is losing.

notes.text: Checking with the bishop on b5 falls into a trap: White is losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6.Bb5+? Nc6 7.d4 Bd7 8.Nc3 Nf6 9.Qd1 and White is losing.

notes.text: White's knight hits your d6 bishop; keep finishing development and you reach a comfortable position.
notes.original: White has nothing better than to recapture the hanging knight - any other move just loses material outright. From here Black finishes development (...f6, ...Bd7, ...Nc6) and reaches a fully comfortable position with an extra central pawn majority to work with in the long run.

notes.text: Retreating avoids giving up your bishop for the knight, guards a7 and keeps the diagonal toward h2.
notes.original: The knight on b5 hits the bishop on d6 and eyes a7 and c7. Retreating to b8 keeps your bishop pair (Nxd6+ Qxd6 would give it up), guards a7 and stays on the b8-h2 diagonal. White's only active idea is the break c4: after dxc4 Bxc4 your knight hops to a5 with a tempo on the bishop, and you castle without worries.

notes.text: You are fully developed and the position is level.
notes.original: Bh6 only chases the rook sideways. You are fully developed and the position is level.

notes.text: Giving up your bishop for the knight is fine, and your king is safe enough on f7.
notes.original: Also holds: you give up a bishop for the knight and the king is safe enough on f7.

notes.text: White trades the knight, and you get a half-open b-file and a solid centre.
notes.original: White trades the knight and Black gets a half-open b-file and a solid centre. 8.Nd2 Nf6 9.Be2 Bd6 is fine for Black.

You get an easy position: follow up with e6 and Nf6.
notes.original: 5.Nxc6 gives Black the bishop pair-free but easy position: ...e6 and ...Nf6.

notes.text: A useful move: it stops Bb5 and Nb5 ideas so you can develop with Nc6 and Bf5.
notes.original: A useful move. It stops Bb5+ and Nb5 ideas and prepares ...Nc6 and ...Bf5 without worry. Plan: ...Nc6, ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, ...e6, ...Nf6 or ...Bd6, then castle short. Your break is ...e5 once the pieces are out. Do not let White pin your knight with a quick Bb5 while d5 is loose.

notes.text: Equally good, and it develops a piece at once.
Taking with the b-pawn gives you a half-open b-file, and the c6 pawn supports d5.
notes.original: Recapturing with the b-pawn gives you the half-open b-file and a flexible pawn center. The pawn on c6 supports d5 and your bishop is already outside the pawn chain.

notes.text: White's knight heads for c5 or b6, so develop with Nf6 and Be7, then castle.
notes.original: White heads for c5 or b6 with the knight, so keep your queen ready for ...Qa5 or ...Qd7 and play ...Nf6 and ...Be7 to finish development. Equal and your structure is healthy. This is a balanced Caro-Kann position with a pawn structure close to a French, where White has a knight on a4 that is a little offside. Your bishop on f5 is already outside the pawn chain. Your plan: develop with ...Nf6 and ...Be7, then castle short, using ...Qa5+ or ...Qc7 when it helps. White wants to bring the knight to c5 and use the bishop on f4 to build pressure on c7. Meet Nc5 by guarding b7 with ...Qc7. Remember that ...Qa5+ is answered by Nc3, so it is a resource, not a win. The mistake is ignoring the knight and leaving your king in the centre.

notes.text: Your bishop blocks the check and offers a trade; if White retreats with Be2, you gain time.
notes.original: Block with the bishop and offer a trade. If White retreats with Be2 you gain time, and if White takes on d7 you recapture with the knight or queen. Plan: ...Nc6, ...Bg4 to pin the knight on f3, ...Nf6 and ...e6, then castle short. Your break is ...e5 or ...f6 once the pieces are in place.

notes.text: This looks tempting because the knight guards c5 and b6, but it blocks your bishop and White gets the easier…
notes.original: Tempting because the knight guards c5 and b6, but it blocks your bishop and White gets the easier game.

notes.text: White wants b4 and b5 to hit your c6 knight, or Ne5 to trade your active pieces.
notes.original: White gains space with c5, but the pawn cannot easily be supported. Aim at it with ...b6 and ...Be7, and keep your knights on c6 and f6 ready to jump to e4. Avoid letting your pawn on d5 become isolated. Equal with a clear plan. This is a fairly closed position where White has gained space with c5 and d4, and your pawns stand on d5 and e6. Your bishop on g4 and knights on c6 and f6 are well placed. Your plan: play ...Be7, then undermine the pawn on c5 with ...b6, and castle short. White wants b4-b5 to hit the knight on c6, or Ne5 to trade your active pieces. Trade on f3 with ...Bxf3 when it helps, and keep a knight ready for e4. The mistake is letting your pawn on d5 become isolated. If White plays b4, answer ...b6 at once and open the queenside.

notes.original: 4.e5 Bg4 hits the knight and prepares ...e6, ...Nd7 and ...c5.

notes.original: White challenges d5 at once, hoping to exploit your queen on c7.

notes.original: Transposing into a Queen's Gambit-like structure; Black plays ...Bb4 and ...O-O comfortably.

notes.original: Your bishop develops and keeps Bf4 from gaining time on the queen.

notes.text: A calm alternative that keeps the position equal.
notes.original: A calm alternative.

notes.text: White develops the bishop to a quiet square before deciding how to recapture on e4.
notes.original: 6.Be3 - develops the bishop to a quiet square before deciding how to recapture on e4, rather than committing with the main 6.Nc3 right away.

notes.text: White develops the bishop actively to d3 instead of playing Nc3.
notes.original: 6.Bd3 - develops actively toward the kingside instead of 6.Nc3, planning to meet ...dxe4 by recapturing with the bishop.

notes.text: White grabs space at once, trying to punish your slower e6 setup before it consolidates.
notes.original: 4.e5 grabs space immediately rather than developing with Nc3 or Be3 first, trying to punish Black's slower 3...e6 setup before it's consolidated.

notes.text: White's c4 pawn hits your d5 pawn and grabs space, but the b1 knight is still undeveloped.
notes.original: White grabs space on the queenside and attacks d5 at once, hoping you will push or exchange and that his lead in the centre will grow before the f3 pawn becomes a liability. It is very common in practice (played in about 70,000 games). Note that the knight on b1 has not moved, so White is a little loose and you can use that.

notes.text: White supports d4 so it can meet ...dxe4 with fxe4, a quiet and solid choice.
notes.original: White supports d4 so that he can meet ...dxe4 with fxe4, and prepares Nd2 or Bd3 with a flexible set-up. It is a quiet, solid choice that is common in practice (played in about 48,000 games), and it avoids the sharp lines with Nc3. So a fight for a small positional edge, not a tactical melee.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
White develops the knight flexibly, keeping Nf4 or g3 available for later.
notes.original: 5.Nge2 - develops the second knight flexibly instead of committing the bishop yet, keeping Nf4 or g3 available later.

notes.text: Against 3.f3, play the calmer French-style setup: develop, then take on e4 and play e5.
notes.original:
Extra: only needed if White plays 3.f3 and you answer 3...e6 or 3...Qb6.
Idea: 3...e6 is a calmer, French-style answer. Develop with ...Nd7, ...a6 and ...Be7, then take on e4 and play ...e5 once White has committed. The sharp 3...Qb6 is covered here too.
Main line: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3 e6 4.Nc3 Nd7 5.Be3 a6
Watch out: ...Qxc3? loses material on move 13. ...Qxh2? loses material on move 14.

notes.text: Your a6 pawn covers b5 and prepares ...b5 to gain queenside space.
notes.original: The ...a6 idea again. The same ...a6 idea from the Two Knights Attack chapters shows up here too: a6 keeps an eye on the b5 square, ruling out any White piece landing there and preparing a future ...b5 expansion of Black's own queenside space. In this particular structure it also gains a tempo for development, since White's pieces are not yet ready to punish the small loss of time.

notes.text: Strike the center with ...e5 so White doesn't take over the game.
notes.original: Black strikes at the centre with ...e5 and does not let White take over the game.

notes.text: Taking on e4 with the knight is another option for White.
notes.original: Another option for White.

notes.text: The e5 pawn move lets your g8 knight develop easily to f6.
notes.original: e5 needs to be played in order to develop the knight with ease on Ngf6.

notes.text: The quiet Be2 keeps White's bishop safe from ...Nb6 or ...b5 ideas while still eyeing the kingside.
notes.original: The quieter Be2 (rather than Bc4 in the main line) is actually the more accurate try, keeping the bishop safely out of any future ...Nb6 or ...b5 ideas while still eyeing the kingside.

notes.text: Bc4 is playable, but Be2 is the more accurate bishop move for White.
notes.original: Be2 is more accurate.

notes.text: White has a small, normal edge, but you can handle it with careful play.
notes.original: A small, normal edge for White after the further simplification shown - manageable for Black with careful play, and a minor but real improvement on the main line.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
White's g-pawns end up doubled, while you take the e-file and your pieces stay active.
notes.original: The knight jumps to f5 to hit your queen and the g7 pawn; you take it, accept White's f5 pawn and castle. When White pushes g4 you check, trade queens and take the e-file with the rook, so White's pawns end up bent but the pieces stay active.

notes.text: Queens are off and your rook takes the e-file, pressing the e4 pawn.
notes.original: An easy line for you: queens come off and you take the open e-file.

notes.text: White's e4 pawn is isolated, with no friendly pawn beside it.
notes.original: White has an isolated pawn.

notes.text: White's e4 pawn is isolated, with no friendly pawn beside it.
notes.original: White has an isolated pawn.

notes.original: With the queens off you keep the bishop pair and a powerful bishop on d4. The h3 move kicks your bishop on g4, so you trade it for White's good bishop, which opens the f-file for you. Both sides castle long and your bishops give you the better of it.

notes.text: You traded queens with check and keep a lead in development.
notes.original: The knight jump hits your queen, but you trade queens with check and keep a lead in development.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Castling long puts a rook behind your d4 bishop, and you keep the bishop pair.
notes.original: The queen on d3 attacks your strong bishop on d4, so you develop with tempo: ...Be6 brings the last minor piece out, ...Qg5+ gains time with a check, and castling long adds a rook to the defence of d4 and takes the d-file. You keep the bishop pair and the better development.

notes.text: Even with queens traded, you keep both bishops and the better structure.
notes.original: The knight move allows a queen trade, but you keep your bishops and the better structure.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Your knight lands on d5 eyeing e3, so White's extra e5 pawn won't be easy to keep.
notes.original: The bishop on c2 and queen on d3 aim at h7, and the g5 pin on your knight adds to it; h4 followed by h5 is White's kingside plan. You block the h7 diagonal with ...g6 and hit the centre with ...e5, and the knight lands on d5 with an attack on e3, so White's extra pawn on e5 will not be easy to keep.

notes.text: White's pawn storm cost the g5 pawn, though White still has some play for it.
notes.original: The pawn storm gives up the g5 pawn, though White still has some play for it.

notes.text: Simple, solid development; nothing here needs memorizing beyond normal piece placement.
notes.original: 5...Ngf6 meets this with simple, solid development; nothing here needs memorizing beyond normal piece placement.

notes.text: Keep hitting d4 with your c-pawn and knight until White has to resolve the tension.
notes.original: This is an Advance French structure with f4 included: White gains space with e5 and f4, you kick back and reroute your knight to f5. Your queen hits d4 and b2, which forces Rb1, and the knight on f5 adds to the pressure on d4. The key plan is ...c5: keep hitting d4 until White has to resolve the tension. You are only a little worse.

notes.text: With White's bishop out, you answer by hitting the d4 pawn with your c-pawn.
notes.original: With the bishop out you answer in the same way.

notes.text: White has other good moves here, such as Bd2. This line is rare, so theory is thin.
notes.original: Several other moves also merit consideration, including Bd2. This variation is rarely played, and so theory remains relatively underdeveloped.

notes.text: Take the bishop with check; grabbing the d4 pawn with your queen instead loses.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qxd4? 7.c3 Qd8 8.cxb4 Ne7 9.Bc4 O-O and Black is losing.

notes.text: Taking on d4 with the queen falls into a trap: you are losing.
notes.original: Trap: 6...Qxd4? 7.c3 Qd8 8.cxb4 Ne7 9.Bc4 O-O and Black is losing.

notes.text: Trading on d2 first was right; an early knight to d7 would have let White win a piece.
notes.original: The critical position of the 3...e6 4.Nc3 Bb4 line. This particular branch (4...Bb4, pinning the knight before deciding on a central break) is not the line this course actually recommends - our main choice against 4.Nc3 is the simpler 4...Nd7, covered in 🟢 11. This is included purely as supplementary reference for a related, well-known try, along with a real practical warning worth knowing: if you ever reach this position and follow up carelessly with an immediate ...Nd7 before resolving the pin on b4, White wins material outright with Bxb4! - there is no way to recapture. The correct, sound continuation trades the bishop off first with ...Bxd2+, exactly as shown here, before continuing development.

notes.text: This is the best move; White has only a small, normal edge.
notes.original: The best move here. White has a small, normal edge, nothing alarming.

notes.original: Also fine: Nf6.

notes.original: Also fine: Ne7.

notes.text: White keeps a small, stable edge from extra space, but your position is fully playable.
notes.original: A small, stable White edge from the extra space and bishop pair, consistent with the overall known assessment of the Fantasy Variation - fully playable and well-trodden for Black.

notes.text: White storms with g4 and g5; you answer with knight d7, taking on e4, and ...e5 first.
notes.original: The queen develops and eyes e4, and it stays flexible for ...Nbd7. White's plan is a kingside pawn storm with g4 and g5; your counter is ...Nbd7, then ...Nxe4 and ...e5 so that your central play arrives first.

notes.text: White has a passed d-pawn, and you must watch the long diagonal.
notes.original: The structure is now dynamic: White has a passed d-pawn but also doubled pawns, and you must watch the long diagonal. You are slightly worse.

notes.text: Grabbing pawns cost time, and your queen on g4 is running short of squares.
notes.original: Grabbing pawns with the queen costs time and the queen soon runs short of squares.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
The queens are off, and White's b4 keeps the initiative and a clear edge.
notes.original: The queens come off first, because on the open d-file White's queen would otherwise take yours. White's doubled e-pawns are not weak yet, since e6 gains time; you meet it with the king on e7. White's initiative with b4 keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: By avoiding the trade, you let White keep the pawn on d6 as a thorn.
notes.original: Avoiding the trade lets White keep the pawn on d6 as a thorn.

notes.text: White is clearly better.
White's knight on d6 is an outpost you cannot easily remove, and the g4 storm follows.
notes.original: Kb1 prepares c4 and a grip on the d-file; your knight comes to d7 to cover f6 and e5, but the c4-c5 break opens lines and lets the knight jump to d6, an outpost you cannot easily remove. The g4 pawn storm comes with it. You are under pressure but your pieces are solid.

notes.text: This is another setup, but White's pieces are active here too.
notes.original: Another setup, but White's pieces are active here too.

notes.text: Take the pawn and meet the recapture with normal development; it is the simple, solid route.
notes.original: 6...dxe4 (Solid & Optimal) - simply takes the pawn and meets the recapture with normal development; the simplest route to a comfortable, slightly favorable structure for Black.

notes.text: Your queen keeps the tension and eyes b2, pushing White into an early decision.
notes.original: 6...Qb6 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - keeps the central tension and immediately eyes b2, provoking White into an early decision rather than resolving the pawn structure yet.

notes.text: Your queen checks from a5, and you end up with an extra pawn and a level game.
notes.original: White recaptures on e4, but your check with the queen lets you take that pawn as well. White's compensation is development: Qe2 defends the bishop on e3 and challenges your queen, and Bg2 hits it again. You answer by keeping the queen safe on f5 and checking on a5, ending with an extra pawn and a level game.

notes.text: Your queen goes to c7 to attack the c5 pawn and keep pressure on the centre.
notes.original: You keep the pawn and hit the centre with ...c5.

notes.text: Your f6 pawn undermines White's e5 pawn, and your pieces come to life.
notes.original: The queen on b6 attacks d4 and b2; b3 simply protects the pawn and Qd2 shores up d4. You take e4, hit the bishop with ...Ng4 and undermine the e5 pawn with ...f6, so your pieces come to life. The position is level.

notes.text: The pawn grab works because your queen returns to b6, though White gets some development.
notes.original: The pawn grab works because the queen returns to b6, though White gets some development.

notes.text: You take the pawn at once and reach a comfortable, well-tested structure with no memorization.
notes.original: 6...dxe4 (Solid & Optimal) - takes the pawn at once; after 7.Bxe4 Black develops normally and reaches a comfortable, well-tested structure with no memorization required.

notes.text: You strike at the centre at once, aiming for a sharper game with chances for both sides.
notes.original: 6...c5 (Complicated & Imbalanced) - strikes at the center immediately instead of resolving the e4-tension, aiming for a sharper, more unbalanced middlegame with chances for both sides.

notes.text: You are a pawn up, but White leads in development, so finish developing quickly.
notes.original: Taking on d4 is safe because the bishop on d3 blocks White's queen from defending it. The knight hit costs White time, so you retreat the queen and set up the e5 and Bg4 centre. White has a lead in development for the pawn and you must finish developing quickly.

notes.text: Your knight steps away from the bishop's attack, and you stay a pawn up.
notes.original: The bishop is hit and you stay a pawn up.

notes.text: Your bishop checks, forcing White to weaken the light squares with g3 or play the worse Kd2.
notes.original: c3 supports d4 against your c5 lever. You pile on with ...Nc6, take on e4 and play ...cxd4, and ...Bh4+ comes with check, forcing a concession in front of the king (g3 weakens the light squares, Kd2 is worse). You get comfortable play.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the bishop on d3 while White's king is stuck in the middle.
notes.original: The white king is in the middle and your queen takes a pawn with tempo.

notes.text: You are already comfortably better once you challenge White's centre.
notes.original: 4.e5 grabs space immediately rather than developing with Nc3 or Be3 first, trying to punish Black's slower 3...e6 setup before it's consolidated. ...and Black is already comfortably better once the center is challenged.

notes.text: Your queen recaptures on c5; the strike at d4 is the key to your position.
notes.original: Bb5 pins the knight and White hopes for Bxc6+ and dxc5. You hit the loose bishop with the queen; once it is supported by Qa4 you tuck the queen back, unpin with ...Bd7 and win time on d4. You are clearly better and the strike at d4 is the key to the position.

notes.text: Developing the bishop to e3 is another good route for White.
notes.original: Another good route.

notes.text: Take the pawn; after Nc3 pin the knight with ...Bb4, then undermine d4 with ...c5.
notes.original: Take the pawn. White cannot simply recapture and keep an easy game, because his pieces are not ready. After Nc3 you play ...Bb4, pinning the knight, then ...c5 to undermine d4. Do not feel you must hold the pawn on e4; giving it back in exchange for a clean structure and active pieces is fine.

notes.text: Your c5 pawn defends the bishop and hits d4, answering the threat with a counter-threat.
notes.original: The queen eyes b4 and b7, but ...c5 defends the bishop and hits d4 at once, so you answer the threat with a counter-threat. Then recapture on c5 and develop the knight to c6.

notes.text: Save your attacked bishop, trade knights with ...Nf6, then castle short; you are slightly better.
notes.original: You are fully developed, the bishop pair is active on c5, and you have a slight edge. Aim for ...Nf6 and short castling next. This is an open game with the centre cleared and both sides developed, and you are a little more comfortable. Your c5 bishop is attacked by the knight on e4, so your first step is to move it with ...Be7 or ...Bb6. Second, trade White's best piece with ...Nf6, recapturing on f6 with the queen or pawn as needed. Third, castle short and bring the rooks to the centre. White wants to use the queen on b3 against b7 and e6, so keep both pawns covered. The risk is leaving b7 or the bishop hanging in one move. If White plays Bg5 or Nf3, continue your development.

notes.text: Your e4 pawn threatens to take on f3 and strip White of his centre pawn.
notes.original: Take on e4 and then ...exf3, stripping White of his centre pawn. After Nd2 exf3 Ngxf3 you have the better structure, since e4 and f3 have gone. Your plan is ...Nf6, ...c5 to undermine d4, bishop to e7 or d6 and castle short. Avoid leaving the pawn on e4 under attack from too many pieces. The edge is small.

notes.text: This is fine, but White gets an easy position with Bd3 and Ne2, so the edge fades to about equal.
notes.original: A fine alternative, but White gets an easy position with Bd3 and Ne2, and the advantage drops to about equal.

notes.text: Strike at the centre now: your c-pawn hits d4 before White castles.
notes.original: Strike at the centre now, before White castles.

notes.text: Develop with Nc6 to hit the knight on d4, then Bd6 and castle; your structure is healthier.
