notes.original: Your pieces come out smoothly, you have a good structure, and you can aim for ...Bd6 and ...O-O with a comfortable game. This is an open, healthy position with the f- and e-pawns exchanged, so you have the better structure and a smooth, comfortable game. Your plan is, first, to complete development with ...Nc6 hitting the knight on d4. Second, play ...Bd6 and castle short, aiming at the h2 pawn. Third, use the half-open c-file and the knight on f6 to pressure White's centre. White wants Nf5 or Nxe6 with Bxh7 ideas against your king. The risk is leaving e6 loose or letting Bxh7 work when your f6 knight leaves. If White plays Nb3, answer calmly with ...Bd6 or ...Be7, but do not lose time.

notes.text: White's a4 is the most testing try; after ...e5 the position opens into a sharper fight.
notes.original: 4.a4 is White's most testing try, gaining a tempo on a future ...a5/...Qb4 ideas while defending b2 indirectly; after 4...e5 the position opens into a sharper fight than the main 3...e6 lines.

notes.text: White's c3 is the quieter try: it backs d4 and ignores the pressure on b2 for now.
notes.original: 4.c3 - the quieter alternative to 4.a4, supporting the center and ignoring the pressure on b2 for now.

notes.text: White simply develops and dares you to take the b2 pawn for real.
notes.original: 4.Nc3 - simply develops instead of committing to a3/c3 right away, daring Black to take on b2 for real.

notes.text: White's a3 stops Bb4 but wastes time; strike with e5 and you get a strong initiative.
notes.original: 4.a3 stops ...Bb4 but wastes time. 4...e5! gives Black a strong initiative.

notes.text: Your e-pawn hits d4, which lost support because f3 blocks the g1 knight, so White must resolve the centre.
notes.original: The lever hits d4 at once: the pawn has lost support because f3 blocks the g1 knight, so White has to resolve the centre right away. After exd5 you take on d4 with the queen, offer a queen trade, and the pawn count is soon level again.

notes.text: Your pawn on d4 cramps White, and the knight on a3 struggles to find a good square.
notes.original: Your pawn on d4 cramps the white pieces and the knight on a3 is trying to find a good square, so you are fine.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White is clearly better.
This calmer route costs you a queen tempo and leaves White a little more comfortable.
notes.original: The calmer route costs you a tempo with the queen and leaves White a little more comfortable.

notes.text: Your e-pawn strikes back in the centre at once, and you already stand slightly better.
notes.original: 4...e5! strikes back in the center immediately, exploiting the tempo White spent on move 2 (f3) rather than development; Black already stands slightly better here.

notes.text: White spent time chasing your queen while you won the e4 pawn; after the recapture it is level.
notes.original: The a4-a5 jab chases your queen back, but White has spent time on it while you take the centre pawns. You win a pawn on e4, which White recaptures quickly, and the position is level.

notes.text: This is a safe route into a queenless position where you stay comfortable.
notes.original: a safe route into a queenless position where you stay comfortable.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is winning.
Black is slightly better.
This is the calmest, best-scoring reply: finish development and let White prove the b2 pawn grab is worth anything.
notes.original: 4...e6 is the calmest and best-scoring reply: finish development and let White prove the pawn grab on b2 is worth anything (it generally isn't, since Qxb2 walks into Nb5 or Rb1 tricks).

notes.text: Your queen steps out of the knight's attack, and you have comfortable play for the pawn.
notes.original: White's a3 takes b4 from your bishop and queen and prepares Na4 to harass the queen. Your answer is to blast open the centre with ...e5 before White is ready: the pawn on d5 is given back for play, because f3 weakened the e1-h4 diagonal (...Bh4+ ideas) and your knight heads to f5 to hit d4. After Na4 the queen steps out of the attack. You have comfortable play for the pawn.

notes.text: Against the quieter Qd2 and b3 plan, you develop with Bg4 and equalise.
notes.original: The quieter Qd2 and b3 plan lets you develop with ...Bg4 and equalise.

notes.text: White keeps a big centre and wants Nf3, Bd3 and Qe2; you must hit it before it becomes a wall.
notes.original: White recaptures with the pawn and keeps a big centre on d4 and e4 with an open f-file. The idea is to build with Nf3, Bd3 and Qe2, and to attack with e5 and Bc4 later. It is common in practice (played in about 49,000 games in the online database). It means White has a big centre, so you must hit it before it becomes a wall.

notes.text: Your bishop pair is safe and your king can castle comfortably.
notes.original: The bishop pair is safe and Black's king can castle comfortably.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Strike the centre at once; a pawn on e4 backed by d4 gives White a free hand.
notes.original: Strike the centre at once. After dxe5 your queen is not hit, and after Nf3 exd4 you reach an easy ending. Your plan is simple: exchange queens, play ...Bd6 and ...Ne7 with your king on its home square, and enjoy the healthy pawn structure. Avoid delaying, since a pawn on e4 backed by d4 gives White a free hand.

notes.text: Developing the knight is a mistake here: e5 kicks it away, and White gets the centre and development.
notes.original: The natural developing move is a mistake here. White plays 6.e5 and the knight is kicked, so you lose the centre and fall behind in development.

notes.text: Your bishop comes to d6 and heads for e5 next.
notes.original: Your bishop comes to d6 and then e5 to hit the knight on c3 and the pawn on b2.

notes.text: Your bishop is strong in the centre; develop the knights, castle long, and the ending is level.
notes.original: The bishop is strong in the centre. Next you play ...Ne7, ...Nd7 and ...Nf6 or ...Bg4 and you can castle long, with a level ending.

notes.text: White's knight hits your bishop, so settle it first: trade on c3 or retreat, then develop. You are equal.
notes.original: After the queens go off you are equal, with ...Ne7 and ...Be5 to come and no weaknesses to worry about. This is an open, queenless position with no centre pawns for you and a lone e4 pawn for White, so activity matters more than structure. Your bishop on e5 is attacked by the knight on f3, so settle it first: trade with ...Bxc3+ bxc3 to wreck White's queenside pawns, or retreat to c7 or f6. Then play ...Ne7, ...Nd7 and ...Nf6 or ...Bg4, and castle long or short. White wants Bc4, Be3 and Rd1 to use the open d-file; put a rook on d8 to answer. The mistake is leaving the bishop to be hit with tempo. If White plays Bf4, trade bishops.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Retaking with the queen drops the d4 pawn, so punish it by taking with your queen.
notes.original: White retakes with the queen to develop quickly and hit the f-file, but this loses the d4 pawn. Nxf3 was the correct move, so you should be ready to punish this common mistake.

notes.text: You could pin the knight with Bg4, but there's no reason to hand White a sharper position.
notes.original: Black can also pin the bishop with Bg4, but I see no reason to immediately hand white the privilege of a sharper position.

notes.text: Bc4 is by far the most common try here, well ahead of Bd3.
notes.original: By far the most common try here, well ahead of 6.Bd3 above. The same position comes from the Von Hennig Gambit via 4.Bc4 Nf6 5.f3 exf3 6.Nxf3 (see Part Three's Von Hennig branch below, which transposes straight back here).

notes.text: White's bishop eyes c7 and prepares queen to d2 and long castling.
notes.original: A developing move that aims at c7 and prepares Qd2 and long castling.

notes.text: You are a clean pawn up, with a safe, comfortable position and no weaknesses.
notes.original: Black is just a clean pawn up, with a safe and comfortable position and no weaknesses to show for it.

notes.text: You keep the extra pawn and traded off White's best attacker; now play knight d7, queen c7 and castle.
notes.original: Black keeps the extra pawn and has traded off White's best attacking piece. The plan from here is simple: ...Nbd7, ...Qc7 and castle.

notes.text: Your bishop develops and prepares e6 while you keep the extra pawn.
notes.original: The same improving move as in the Rasa-Studier line. Black develops the bishop and prepares ...e6, keeping the extra pawn. White's sharpest try is 7.Ne5 e6 8.g4, to which Black must reply 8...Nfd7!, while 7.Nh4 Bg4 is harmless.

notes.text: This is solid but less ambitious than Bf5, and it gives back part of your edge for no reason.
notes.original: Solid but noticeably less ambitious than 6...Bf5 - safe, but gives back a good chunk of Black's edge for no real reason.

notes.text: Watch out: this looks like the same natural developing move as in the 6.Bd3 line above, but here it runs…
notes.original: Watch out: this looks like the same natural developing move as in the 6.Bd3 line above, but here it runs into a real tactic - a very common practical mistake.

notes.text: Developing the bishop here looks natural but runs into a real tactic: White sacrifices on f7.
notes.original: Watch out: this looks like the same natural developing move as in the 6.Bd3 line above, but here it runs into a real tactic - a very common practical mistake.

notes.text: White's most dangerous try: knight and bishop both hit f7, and your bishop on f5 has lost its retreat.
notes.original: The most dangerous try: the knight hits f7 and the bishop on f5 loses its retreat square.

notes.text: White's knight also hits your bishop, but this is less dangerous.
notes.original: A less dangerous alternative that also hits the bishop immediately.

notes.text: White's g-pawn attacks your bishop and will take it unless you act.
notes.original: White now attacks the bishop with the g-pawn.

notes.text: The only good reply: your knight challenges White's knight and keeps your bishop.
notes.original: The only good reply: Black challenges the knight and keeps the bishop.

notes.text: Hitting the bishop looks natural, but it walks into trouble.
notes.original: Hitting the bishop is natural, but it walks into trouble.

notes.text: White won a bishop for the pawn, but his king is stuck in the middle and you keep the initiative.
notes.original: White has won a bishop for the pawn but the white king is stuck in the middle and Black keeps the initiative.

notes.text: You won a bishop back, but your king is exposed on the open f-file as White's pieces flood forward.
notes.original: Black has won a bishop back but the king is exposed on the open f-file and White's pieces flood forward.

notes.text: Your bishop is safe on h5 and you keep the extra pawn; White has no good use of its lead.
notes.original: The bishop is safe on h5 and the extra pawn is intact; White has not found a good way to use the lead in development.

notes.text: White gives the bishop back to pull your king out, setting up a second strike with Ne5.
notes.original: The point: this sacrifices the bishop back, but opens the king up for a second strike.

notes.text: Taking the bishop was forced; there was nothing better.
notes.original: Forced - there's nothing better.

notes.text: This knight check is the only move that cashes in the sacrifice; other White tries hand the edge back.
notes.original: The only move that actually cashes in the sacrifice - White's other tries here (8.h3 or 8.Bd2, say) just hand the advantage straight back and leave White clearly worse instead.

notes.text: You can take a second pawn, but only accurately; the safe way is keeping your structure intact.
notes.original: Black can take a second pawn, but White's lead in development means it must be done accurately. The safe approach is to keep the structure intact with ...Nbd7 and ...Be7.

notes.text: Your queen lands in the centre hitting the knight; don't take more pawns and leave it offside.
notes.original: You take the pawn and your queen lands in the centre, attacking the knight and the b2 area. Your plan is ...Nf6 and ...Bg4 to develop with tempo, and ...e6 to castle. Avoid taking pawns further and leaving your queen offside.

notes.text: You are a clean pawn up; keep developing, castle short, and don't grab pawns with your queen.
notes.original: White may instead try 6.Nb5, hoping to catch the queen out of position, but your queen retreats with ...Qb6 or ...Qe5 while still being a pawn up. Do not rush and keep your king safe by castling soon. After the queen trade you only need to keep developing. You are a clean pawn up and White has little compensation. This is an open game where you are a clean pawn up and White has only some activity, with your queen in the centre and both kings short of safety. Your plan: develop with ...e6, ...Be7 and ...Nbd7, challenge the queen on h4 with ...Be7 at a good moment, and castle short. White wants to bring the pieces out and attack with Ng5, Bxh7 and Nb5 against your queen. Meet Nb5 by retreating ...Qa5 or ...Qd8 quickly. The risk is being greedy: do not grab b2 or d4 with the queen, because White gets tempi against it. If White plays Nb5 first, retreat and keep your extra pawn.

notes.text: This is a calmer path, but you are still clearly better.
Simplest and best: finish your development and meet whatever White tries next.
notes.original: Simplest and best: just finish development and meet whatever comes next.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop at once, a good alternative to Nf6.
notes.original: Kicking the bishop at once is a good alternative to 4...Nf6.

notes.text: This natural bishop move runs into White's g-pawn push, which hits your bishop.
notes.original: Natural-looking, but it runs into 5.g4!

notes.text: This natural developing move walks into a forced mate: Qh5 hits f7 and nothing guards it.
notes.original: Watch out: this natural-looking developing move walks straight into a forced mate.

notes.text: White's most natural try develops the last minor piece before deciding what to do about the missing pawn.
notes.original: White's most natural try, developing the last minor piece before deciding what to do about the missing pawn.

notes.text: You keep developing, a clean pawn up with no real weaknesses.
notes.original: Black continues developing, a clean pawn up with no real weaknesses.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the bishop and gains space, leaving White's knight on e2 awkward.
notes.original: Kicking the bishop gains space, and it leaves the knight on e2 awkwardly placed.

notes.text: White's knight on a4 is offside, and you keep the extra pawn comfortably.
notes.original: The knight on a4 is offside and Black keeps the pawn comfortably.

notes.text: This returns to the main Rasa-Studier position, so there is no need to learn it twice.
notes.original: Back into the main position of the Rasa-Studier Gambit (reached there via 4.f3 exf3 5.Nxf3 Nf6 6.Bc4) - see that branch above (under 3.Nc3) for the full tree, including the 6...Bf5! recommendation and the 6...Bg4? trap. There is no need to learn this twice; it is the identical position either way.

notes.text: Nothing covers f7, so White threatens mate in one.
notes.original: The point: nothing currently covers f7, so this threatens mate in one.

notes.text: This is forced: it stops the mate, chases the queen away, and you keep the extra pawn.
notes.original: Forced, and just about sufficient - the queen gets chased off and Black keeps the extra pawn.

notes.text: The losing mistake: this natural-looking developing move still does not cover f7.
Developing this knight is the losing mistake: it still does not cover f7.
notes.original: The losing mistake: this natural-looking developing move still does not cover f7.

notes.text: Checkmate: the bishop guards the queen on f7 and your king has no escape.
notes.original: Checkmate.

notes.text: You keep the extra pawn, and your queenside pawns have gained space.
notes.original: Black keeps the extra pawn and the queenside pawns have gained space.

notes.text: White gets real play for the pawn, so the position is level; 4...Nf6 is better.
notes.original: White gets real play for the pawn, and the position is level. Playable, but worse than 4...Nf6.

notes.text: White simply develops the bishop to d3, the most popular try in practice, with no immediate tactics.
notes.original: The most popular try in practice: simple development, no immediate tactics.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn stops the bishop check but not this knight check, and the safe square is narrow.
notes.original: The point missed above: e6 stops the bishop check but not this one. Very popular in practice, and for good reason - the only safe square is narrow and two natural-looking tries fail badly.

notes.text: Your e6 pawn blocks the bishop's diagonal, so this is no longer check.
notes.original: No longer check (the e6 pawn blocks the diagonal), just another developing try.

notes.text: White develops toward long castling and still keeps the Ne5 check in reserve.
notes.original: A developing move that heads for long castling and keeps the Ne5+ trick up White's sleeve.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
White tries the knight jump anyway, and it gives check, so your king must move.
notes.original: White tries the knight jump anyway, now that the bishop on d3 supports it.

notes.text: Your bishop on c5 hits f2, and your queen will come to a5 with check and tempo.
notes.original: White's pieces look active, but Black's bishop on c5 aims at f2 and ...Qa5+ will come with tempo, so Black remains clearly better.

notes.text: This is the only move that keeps your full advantage, and your king has no more checks to fear.
notes.original: The only move that keeps the full advantage. Simple and safe - the king has no further checks to worry about from here.

notes.text: This natural-looking king retreat gives back almost all of your advantage.
notes.original: Watch out: this natural-looking retreat gives back almost all of the advantage and then some.

notes.text: Watch out: this one loses material outright, not just the advantage - the king walks into a fork.
Stepping the king to e7 loses material outright: the knight forks it and the rook.
notes.original: Watch out: this one loses material outright, not just the advantage - the king walks into a fork.

notes.text: White develops first and keeps the knight jump to g6 in reserve.
notes.original: Develop first and keep the knight jump Ng6 in reserve.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your e6 pawn and eyes the diagonal to your king.
notes.original: Hitting the e6 pawn and trying to pile pressure on the king's diagonal.

notes.text: Meet unsound gambits actively: your c-pawn hits d4 and challenges White's structure at once.
notes.original: The best way to meet unsound gambits is to play actively: ...c5 invites a queen exchange and challenges White's structure immediately.

notes.text: Also fine: your queen attacks the knight on g6.
notes.original: Also fine: the queen attacks the knight on g6 and protects the rook on h8 from behind the king.

notes.text: White takes on c5 to trade queens; your queen can take on d1 down the open file.
notes.original: White trades queens to relieve the pressure.

notes.text: White's bishop piles onto your e6 pawn.
notes.original: Piling on the e6 pawn.

notes.text: Your pawn and knight both hit d4, so White must capture and you gain development.
notes.original: Black forces White to capture and gets ahead in development.

notes.text: White's king has lost castling, and your bishops and active pieces give you the better game.
notes.original: The white king has lost castling and Black has the bishop pair and the more active pieces.

notes.text: After the dust settles you have an extra piece for a pawn and a safe king.
notes.original: After the dust settles Black has an extra piece for a pawn and a safe king.

notes.text: Material is roughly level, but your knights are well placed and White's king is stuck in the centre.
notes.original: White has won the exchange back and material is roughly level, but the black knights are well placed and White's king is stuck in the centre.

notes.text: Your pieces are far more active, so you keep a clear edge.
notes.original: Material is now roughly level on paper (a rook and pawn for two knights), but Black's pieces are far more active and White's king is still in the centre, so Black keeps a clear edge.

notes.text: Your king is safe on g8 and White has nothing left to attack with.
notes.original: Black's king is safe on g8 and White has nothing left to attack with.

notes.text: White castled and traded knights, but your c6 and e6 pawns hold everything together and you are a piece up.
notes.original: White has castled and traded a pair of knights, but Black is still a piece for a pawn up and the c6 and e6 pawns hold everything together.

notes.text: This check forks your king and the rook on h8, and you cannot save both.
notes.original: The point: this check forks the king and the rook on h8 - there's no way to save both.

notes.text: White is winning.
Black is clearly better.
You are fully developed, and your king can tuck into g8 whenever needed.
notes.original: Black has finished development and the king can tuck into g8 whenever needed. White has pieces out but nothing to hit. The extra piece decides.

notes.text: Queens are off and you are a piece for a pawn up; bring your king and bishops into play.
notes.original: White has traded off the attacking knights and the queens come off. Black is a piece for a pawn up in a very simple ending and just needs to bring the king and bishop pair into play.

notes.text: White is winning.
Also playable, but it gives up about half a pawn because White can expand with tempo.
notes.original: Also playable, but it gives up about half a pawn compared with 7...c5 because White can now expand with tempo.

notes.text: You keep the extra piece and can bring your king to g8, but there is less to show for it.
notes.original: Black keeps the extra piece and can castle by hand with ...Kg8, but there is less to show for it than in the main lines.

notes.text: White checks with the knight first, gaining a tempo.
notes.original: The check comes first, with tempo.

notes.text: Ne5 check freed the knight, then it took your bishop: a pin on f3 fails against a king on f7.
notes.original: The knight escapes the pin with check, and the bishop that was pinning it is left hanging. The pattern to remember: with the king on f7 any pin on the f3-knight can be answered by Ne5+.

notes.text: You have developed everything with tempo and your king is safe; a clear edge, slightly smaller, for a calm game.
notes.original: Black has developed everything with tempo and the king is safe behind the pawns. It is still a clear edge, just slightly less than the main lines, so it is a reasonable choice if you prefer a calm game.

notes.text: Block the check with your other bishop, offering White a trade.
notes.original: Simplest: block the check by developing the other bishop, offering a trade on White's terms.

notes.text: Also sound: your pawn blocks the bishop's diagonal and keeps your king on f7.
notes.original: Also sound: the pawn blocks the diagonal and keeps the king on f7.

notes.text: White trades bishops with check rather than retreat, since the bishop has no better square anyway.
notes.original: White trades down rather than retreat, since the bishop has no better square anyway.

notes.text: Recapture with your king: it looks bold on e6, but White has no immediate checks and it is safe.
notes.original: Correct and only real choice: recapture with the king. It looks bold marching the king to e6, but there are no immediate checks available and Black's king is perfectly safe there with queens still on.

notes.text: Retreating instead of recapturing gives back almost your whole advantage for nothing.
notes.original: Watch out: retreating instead of recapturing gives back almost the entire advantage for nothing.

notes.text: Walking the king to g6 loses to a forced mate.
notes.original: Watch out: this one doesn't just give back the advantage, it walks straight into a forced mate.

notes.text: Your queen offers a trade into an ending where your extra piece is decisive.
notes.original: The king goes back to f7 as soon as the checks have run out, and Black trades queens into an ending where the extra piece is decisive.

notes.text: Checkmate: White's queen checks your king and it has no escape.
notes.original: Checkmate.

notes.text: The key reply: your bishop offers to trade White's only attacking piece, leaving White almost nothing against your king.
notes.original: The key reply. Black offers to trade off White's only attacking piece. Without the light-squared bishop White has almost nothing left against the king.

notes.text: White has spent its whole attack, and you keep all the extra material.
notes.original: White has spent its whole attack and Black has all the extra material.

notes.text: When the sacrifice is unsound, take the knight; declining just loses a whole rook.
notes.original: White keeps the sacrificed piece and wins a whole rook. The lesson for Black: when the sacrifice is unsound, take the knight. All the traps below come only after 6...Kxf7.

notes.text: You have the more comfortable ending, with the bishop pair and no weaknesses.
notes.original: Black has the more comfortable endgame, with the bishop pair and no weaknesses.

notes.text: You are a knight up for a pawn: White's knight had no retreat once you played h6.
notes.original: Black is a whole knight up for a pawn. The knight on g5 had no retreat once Black spent a tempo on ...h6, which is exactly why 6.Nxf7 or 6.N5f3 are the only real choices.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the g5 knight at once, and Nh3 is its only decent retreat.
notes.original: You kick the knight at once, and it has only h3 as a decent retreat. After Nh3 you play ...c5 and ...e6, hitting the centre while the White knights sit on poor squares on h3 and f4. Your plan is ...Nbd7, ...Be7, castle short and ...a6. Avoid blocking your own light bishop and avoid ...e5 early, because the d4 pawn is not yet weak. The small edge is yours.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes your f5 bishop and wants a trade; recapture with the e-pawn to keep your structure solid.
notes.original: Do not be afraid of Bb5+: you answer with ...Nbd7 and then ...a6 pushes the bishop back, since your king is safe in the centre until you castle. You have more active pieces, a healthy centre and an easy plan of ...Be7 and castling. This is an open-ish position where you hold a healthy centre and White's knights on f3 and f4 stand a little awkwardly, though your king is still in the middle. Your plan: complete development with ...Be7, castle short, and then play ...Qc7 and ...Rac8 so that ...cxd4 can come at the right moment. White wants to trade light-squared bishops with Bxf5 and open the centre with dxc5; recapture ...exf5 and keep the structure solid, or take back on c5 with a knight. The risk is the Nxe6 shot if your bishop leaves f5 carelessly. If White plays dxc5 at once, take back with ...Nxc5 and trade bishops.

notes.text: Finish development with Be7 and castle short before the queen and rook come to the c-file.
notes.original: Do not be afraid of Bb5+: you answer with ...Nbd7 and then ...a6 pushes the bishop back, since your king is safe in the centre until you castle. You have more active pieces, a healthy centre and an easy plan of ...Be7 and castling. This is an open-ish position where you hold a healthy centre and White's knights on f3 and f4 stand a little awkwardly, though your king is still in the middle. Your plan: complete development with ...Be7, castle short, and then play ...Qc7 and ...Rac8 so that ...cxd4 can come at the right moment. White wants to trade light-squared bishops with Bxf5 and open the centre with dxc5; recapture ...exf5 and keep the structure solid, or take back on c5 with a knight. The risk is the Nxe6 shot if your bishop leaves f5 carelessly. If White plays dxc5 at once, take back with ...Nxc5 and trade bishops.

notes.text: White trades your bishop and gets a stable centre, so you only equalise.
notes.original: This is the tempting reply many players choose, but White trades your bishop and gets a stable centre, so you only equalise.

notes.text: Your pawn gains space and keeps the bishop under pressure; after Bb3 you have no problems.
notes.original: The sharp 6.Bc4 b5! gains space and keeps the bishop under pressure. After 7.Bb3 e6 8.O-O Ngf6 Black has no problems.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
Your bishop pins the f3 knight and prepares ...e6; after h3 and g4 you are fine.
notes.original: 4.Nbd2 Bg4 pins the knight and prepares ...e6. After 5.h3 Bh5 6.g4 Bg6 Black is fine.

notes.text: The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
White is slightly better.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
The position is equal.
A clean, simple position, much like an Exchange structure but a tempo different, since White never played d4.
notes.original: A clean, simple position, similar in spirit to an Exchange-style structure but a tempo different since White never got round to d4.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is slightly better.
White's best try keeps the queen active, eyeing your e4 pawn.
notes.original: White's best try, pinning the e4-pawn to nothing in particular but at least keeping the queen active.

notes.text: After a5 White is a pawn down with a loose queen, so you stand slightly better.
notes.original: The Hillbilly Attack: 2.Bc4 d5 3.Bb3 dxe4 4.Qh5 g6 5.Qh4 a5 leaves White a pawn down with a loose queen.

notes.text: You keep developing, a clean pawn up with no weaknesses to show White for it.
notes.original: Black continues development, up a clean pawn with no weaknesses to show White for it.

notes.text: Black is clearly better.
Black is winning.
White's queen takes f7 with check and wins the pawn back, leaving your king stuck in the center.
notes.original: White wins back the pawn with interest and leaves Black's king stuck in the center for the rest of the game.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
You win a pawn, but White's bishop eyes g7 along the long diagonal, so be careful.
notes.original: 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 dxe4 wins a pawn but White gets compensation along the diagonal; careful.

notes.text: After taking on d4 and meeting Nf3 with Bg4, your pieces become active.
notes.original: 2.f4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nf3 Bg4 gives Black active pieces.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
You get a comfortable French-style position where your knight and light bishop develop easily.
notes.original: 2.Ne2 d5 3.e5 c5 gives Black a comfortable French-style position where ...Nc6 and ...Bf5 come easily.

notes.text: White is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is clearly better.
Black is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
White's e5 keeps the tension and reaches an Advance-style setup, but the g4 move wasted time.
notes.original: 3.e5 keeps the tension and transposes into an Advance-style structure, except White has spent a move on g4 instead of a useful developing move.

notes.text: Open the center at once while White's g4 pawn has already loosened the kingside.
notes.original: Simplest and strongest: open the center at once while White's kingside pawn is already loosened.

notes.text: Developing the knight is simplest; ...h5 first, hitting the overextended g4 pawn, is about as good.
notes.original: Simplest, just developing. 4...h5 first, hitting the overextended pawn immediately, is about as good.

notes.text: Your e5 break opens the centre while White's g5 pawn is cut off and White is undeveloped.
notes.original: Black attacks the overextended g-pawn at once with ...h5. After g5 the pawn is cut off from support, the f5 square is firm for Black, and the break ...e5 opens the centre while White is still undeveloped.

notes.text: White heads for an Advance-style structure, and h5 soon gives this sideline extra bite.
notes.original: 3.e5 transposes into an Advance Variation structure, and 4.h5 next actually gives this sideline a bit more bite than most of the others on this list by hitting the bishop's retreat square early.

notes.text: Open the centre and meet h4 with normal development.
notes.original: Simplest: open the center and meet h4 with normal development.

notes.text: White's d4 is the natural developing move; Bb5 with check is the other real option.
notes.original: The most natural try, developing. 4.Bb5+ is the other real option here, scoring almost identically.

notes.text: White gives a cheap check instead of quiet development, trading away the awkward tempo.
notes.original: The other real try, trading the awkward tempo for a cheap check instead of quiet development.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The simplest answer: your bishop blocks the check and prepares to trade White's bishop.
notes.original: Simplest, blocking and preparing to trade off the bishop.

notes.text: White's h5 pawn takes the g6 retreat square from your bishop, giving White a small edge.
notes.original: 3.e5 transposes into an Advance Variation structure, and 4.h5 next actually gives this sideline a bit more bite than most of the others on this list by hitting the bishop's retreat square early. ...and White gets a small, real edge, the one try on this list worth remembering by name rather than just dismissing.

notes.text: Grabbing space with d4 is direct, but simple development with ...Nd7 or ...e6 is just as sound.
notes.original: The most direct try, grabbing extra space at once while the h5 pawn has already committed White's kingside. Simple development (4...Nd7, 4...e6) is just as sound.

notes.text: Your c5 hits d4; if White takes on c5, you can win the underprotected e5 pawn.
notes.original: The idea is to hit d4 and, after dxc5, to take on e5 where the pawn is under-protected.

notes.text: White develops the knight; Bc4 would score almost the same.
notes.original: 4.Bc4 scores almost the same.

notes.text: You won the e5 pawn with check, and White's h5 push has bought nothing concrete yet.
notes.original: Black wins the e5 pawn with check and White's h5 push has not yet bought anything concrete. Slightly more accurate than 4...d4.

notes.text: The simplest and strongest reply: ignore the flank and just take the centre.
notes.original: The simplest and strongest reply: ignore the flank entirely and just take the centre.

notes.text: Attack the gambit pawn head-on: your a-pawn hits b4.
notes.original: A more direct challenge, attacking the gambit pawn head-on instead of ignoring it.

notes.text: White's e5 reaches an Advance-style structure, with an extra queenside pawn push instead of a developing move.
notes.original: 3.e5 transposes into an Advance Variation structure with an extra queenside pawn push thrown in instead of a useful developing move.

notes.text: Take the centre; White's b4 pawn does nothing useful and can become a long-term weakness.
notes.original: Simplest: take the center, White's b4 pawn does nothing useful here and can become a long-term weakness.

notes.text: White's knight eyes e5, but your quick ...Bg4 pin scores just as well.
notes.original: Simple development, eyeing e5 next. 4...Bg4, pinning the knight at once, scores just as well as the main try below.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
White's extra queenside pawn push wasted a tempo, so you are at least equal, maybe a touch better.
notes.original: 3.e5 transposes into an Advance Variation structure with an extra queenside pawn push thrown in instead of a useful developing move. ...and Black is at least equal, arguably already a touch better thanks to White's wasted tempo.

notes.text: White challenges the center and finishes development, the critical test of your setup.
notes.original: The critical test, directly challenging the bishop's square and completing development.

notes.text: Your a-pawn strikes at White's gambit pawn on b4.
notes.original: The thematic queenside counter-strike against the gambit pawn, exactly as in the main 2...a5 line above.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
The position is equal.
White pushes on instead of trading, because taking on a5 would hand you the open b-file.
notes.original: Keeping the chain rolling forward rather than trading; 3.bxa5 just hands Black an open b-file and an easy initiative for nothing.

notes.text: The position is balanced: White has queenside space, you have the central pawn and freer development.
notes.original: A roughly balanced position; White's queenside space is matched by Black's extra central pawn and freer development.

notes.text: White just develops normally.
notes.original: Continuing to develop normally.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
This resembles the Advance Variation, but f3 instead of a developing move is a real loss of time.
notes.original: 3.e5 transposes into an Advance Variation structure, but f3 (instead of a useful developing move) is a real loss of time here.

notes.text: Open the center right away while White's knight is still stuck behind its f-pawn.
notes.original: Simplest: open the center immediately while White's knight is still stuck behind its own f-pawn.

notes.text: White finally gets a real central pawn out, admitting that f3 lost time.
notes.original: The critical try, finally getting a real central pawn out while admitting f3 was a loss of time.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Develop your bishop outside the pawn chain; with f3 wasted, you are comfortably at least equal.
notes.original: 3.e5 transposes into an Advance Variation structure, but f3 (instead of a useful developing move) is a real loss of time here. ...and Black is comfortably at least equal.

notes.text: White completes the center, but f3 still costs a real tempo compared with a normal Advance.
notes.original: Completing the center, though f3 still costs a real tempo compared to a normal Advance Variation.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
The position is equal.
Simple development; White has nothing else to try.
notes.original: Simple development, there is nothing else to try.

notes.text: The position is equal.
The position is equal.
White just develops a knight; the best move was another waiting move, so h3 achieved very little.
notes.original: Simple development. Amusingly, the best move here is 4.a3, yet another pure waiting move, underlining just how little h3 achieved on its own.

notes.text: The position is equal.
Black is slightly better.
White finally gets a real pawn into the center; playing ...Bf5 first is about as good for you.
notes.original: Finally getting a real pawn into the center. 4...Bf5 first is about as good.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
Retreating the knight straight home is White's best; the alternatives score a little worse.
notes.original: Remarkably, the best move is retreating the knight straight back home. 4.Bb5+ and 4.Ng5 both score a little worse, since the knight has nowhere useful to go from h3.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Black is slightly better.
White builds a centre pawn and you simply keep developing, starting with your knight.
notes.original: The normal developing try.

notes.text: White retreats the queen, giving up the whole excursion, and you stay slightly better.
notes.original: The other near-equal try: simply retreating the queen all the way back home, giving up the whole excursion. See the note at 2.Nh3/4.Ng1 above, this transposes into the exact same position as that knight retreat, and into 2.Qg4's own queen retreat below.

notes.text: Black is slightly better.
Taking on d5 is a blunder: your bishop already eyes the queen on g4 and wins it.
notes.original: A natural-looking try, but it's a real blunder: capturing on d5 clears Black's own d-pawn off the c8-g4 diagonal, leaving the queen on g4 completely undefended on that same diagonal.

notes.text: Your bishop wins the queen outright, since nothing stands in its way.
notes.original: Simplest and strongest: the bishop just wins the queen outright, since nothing stands between c8 and g4 anymore.

notes.text: Also fine if you miss the tactic - Black keeps a safe, normal structural edge - but this gives back…
notes.original: Also fine if you miss the tactic - Black keeps a safe, normal structural edge - but this gives back almost all of the much bigger advantage 3...Bxg4! would have won outright.

notes.text: Recapturing on d5 is fine, but taking the queen with your bishop would have won much more.
notes.original: Also fine if you miss the tactic - Black keeps a safe, normal structural edge - but this gives back almost all of the much bigger advantage 3...Bxg4! would have won outright.

notes.text: White's pawn hits your bishop, but White is a whole queen down with no compensation.
notes.original: Desperately trying to dislodge the bishop and salvage something, but there is no saving this position, White is down a full queen for a single pawn with no compensation anywhere on the board.

notes.text: Your bishop just steps aside and keeps the extra queen safe.
notes.original: Simplest, the bishop just steps aside with the extra queen safely tucked away.

notes.text: White retreats the queen at once, reaching the same position as after other early retreats.
notes.original: Retreating at once, the exact same idea, and the exact same resulting position, as 2.Qh5's own queen retreat above (and as 2.Nh3's knight retreat before that), see those notes for the full comment.

notes.text: White throws in an annoying check rather than admit the queen trip failed.
notes.original: The more natural try in practice, most players would rather throw in an annoying check than quietly admit the queen trip failed.

notes.text: Blocking the check with your knight is stronger than the more natural-looking bishop move.
notes.original: Blocking with the knight is actually stronger than the more natural-looking 4...Bd7.

notes.text: Don't retake with the b-pawn; check with your queen first, then take the bishop.
notes.original:
White may be tempted to snap the knight off, 3.Bxa6?!, so that after Black recaptures 3...bxa6? they have doubled rook pawns. However this does not work in this instance: Black has the intermezzo 3...Qa5!+ followed by ...Qxa6. Their pawn structure is unaffected and then they are happy with the bishop pair.

White snap off Black's knight, thinking if 3...bxa6? they have ruined Black's pawn structure with doubled, isolated pawns on the a-file.

notes.text: You can prepare to develop your kingside bishop with ...g6.
notes.original: 3...g6 preparation for the development of the bishop on g7.

notes.text: Your queen checks the king and attacks the bishop, so you win it without spoiling your pawns.
notes.original: However, because Black has already opened up their queen with c6, they have the reply 3...Qa5+ 4.Nc3 Qxa6, and Black picks up the bishop pair without spoiling their pawns.

notes.text: White blocked the check with a knight, and your queen still attacks the bishop.
notes.original: Black gives a check and attacks the bishop, intending to capture it with the queen. White will most likely block the check using 4.Nc3.

notes.text: White blocked with the knight, and now your queen has taken the bishop.
notes.original: White blocks the check by developing a knight. Black plays 4...Qxa6 next.

notes.text: After White pushes g4 and f3, your bishop retreats safely to h7; then complete the pawn triangle with e6.
notes.original: Now if 5. g4, black forces white to commit the advance of its f-pawn, before retreating to the sanctuary of h7. Other playable moves here are h5 and c3, after which black should complete the pawn triangle with e6.

notes.text: This pawn thrust is rare at lower levels but appears more often the higher the rating.
notes.original: This move isn't seen often at beginner or even intermediate level. But it does appear on the board with more regularity, the higher that you climb the rating ladder.

notes.text: After Bd3 you trade off White's bishop and play for equality.
notes.original: White has two main moves here. The first is the relatively straightforward Bd3, after which black can snap this bishop off, and play for equality. 7. e6 is discussed above.

notes.text: Your c5 break hits d4; in the Advance Variation you must play it right away.
notes.original: Black almost always plays for this c5 break in the Advanced variation. I've picked f4 here as it's the most direct plan, but white could also play h5, Ne2, c3, or even the dubious Nc3. Regardless, black must break with c5 immediately.

notes.text: White's h5 is playable, but you have plenty of strong replies and a comfortable position.
notes.original: h5 is also playable here, but black's position is quite comfortable after this effort, with a plethora of strong replies available.

notes.text: Key Advance themes: the c5 break, knights to e7 and c6, and control of the c-file.
notes.original: Thematically, the c5 break, knights coming to e7, d7, c6, but rarely f6, controlling the c-file, and moves such as c5, Nc5, Rc8, etc, with this aim, are all important in the Advance Variation. We will also encounter them frequently in other Caro-Kann lines, and in our d4 repertoire.

notes.text: You stand well: castle kingside soon, and remember the c-file, where c4 and c3 can become your outposts.
notes.original: Black should be appreciative of this position, and should aim to castle kingside imminently. Rc8 is also a strong move, and common idea, here. Controlling the c-file is critical in the Advance variation, and for that matter in the Caro-Kann generally. Often the c4 and c3 squares can be liabilities for white, and valuable outposts for black.

notes.text: Recapturing is the natural reply, and you are marginally better even if White takes on d4.
notes.original: This seems the most natural riposte, and black is even marginally better after the natural Qxd4. Black can transfer the knight to c6 via e7, and can hope for a superior middlegame.

notes.text: Calm development is better for White: your d4 pawn is going nowhere and will soon be recaptured.
notes.original: Better for white is this calm knight development, as the d-pawn is going nowhere, and will soon be recaptured.

notes.text: You are comfortable; pushing a5 targets White's loose king, though Bc5, a6 and Rc8 also work.
notes.original: Nonetheless, black is very comfortable now, and has a choice of viable plans. Stockfish encourages the a5 push, in order to expose the slightly loose white king position, but the more positional Bc5, a6, and Rc8 are all possible. I would wish to keep queenside castling as an option here, though.

notes.text: Developing the bishop to c5 is a conservative but safe choice.
notes.original: So this is a conservative, but safe, choice.

notes.text: Castling queenside, you have comfortably equalised.
notes.original: Now black can castle queenside, having comfortably equalised.

notes.text: Taking the pawn leaves you cramped and weak on light squares; Nf6 is more sensible, though sharp.
notes.original:
Black can take this pawn, but its pieces will be awfully cramped, and the light squares will perilously weak. Suddenly, the black position appears worryingly permeable.
Thus, more sensible is to play Nf6, but this also leads to sharp play. This is one of the most critical lines.

notes.text: Your king looks exposed on f7 but is actually safe; still, you must play precisely to survive.
notes.original: White has several possible ideas here. Although the king looks poorly placed on f7, it is, in fact, perfectly safe. But black must play with precision in order to survive.

notes.text: The engine prefers the e5 break, but this knight move is easier to play and keeps things equal.
notes.original:
Stockfish states that the best move here is e5, but it's psychologically difficult for a human to make a pawn break in this position.
I would instead recomment Nbd7, after which black has complete equality after anything other than f4.

notes.text: The e5 break is more principled: White is undeveloped and has left space behind its advanced pawns.
notes.original: More principled, though is to make the e5 break immediately. This seems scary with your king uncastled, but white is very undeveloped and has left significant space with pawn advances, so it is quite logical.

notes.text: When White plays f4, answering with e6 is essential.
notes.original: If 11. f4 then 11...e6 is essential.

notes.text: You are uncomfortable and must untangle your pieces, but White has no direct attack.
notes.original: Black is uncomfortable here, and must untangle its pieces, but white has no direct attack. This is undoubtedly one of the most complicated and challenging positions in the entire Caro-Kann, and one that you will very rarely encounter, particularly at beginner level.

notes.text: If White attacks directly, you are quite comfortable and have positional pluses despite your weakened king.
notes.original: If white goes for a direct attack then black is actually quite comfortable here, and has some positional pluses in exchange for its weakened king position.

notes.text: This quiet knight move turns the tables; the position is double-edged, but you are doing quite well.
notes.original: This innocuous move begins to turn the tables for black. This is a profoundly double-edged position, but black is doing quite well.

notes.text: Highly dangerous for both sides; your king looks slightly safer, and the position is playable for you.
notes.original: This is now a highly dangerous position for both sides! If anything, black's king appears slightly safer, but white can gain tempi by harassing the black queen. There are many possible moves here, but this is definitely playable for black.

notes.text: After this razor-sharp line, you are at least equal and probably slightly better.
notes.original: Black is at least equal and probably slightly better after this razor sharp variation, in which white has to find several only moves.

notes.text: White's g5 was a mistake: your rook takes on h1, and White's compensation should not be enough.
notes.original: 10. g5 is a mistake here, allowing this neat combination. White has compensation for the lost material, but it shouldn't be enough to be equal with sound play from black.

notes.text: White could try the sharper c4 instead, and then Ne7 would be the prudent reply.
notes.original: A sharper try for white here is 8. c4, after which Ne7 is prudent.

notes.text: Your a-pawn move is useful prophylaxis: it stops White pieces from landing on b5.
notes.original: a6 is often a useful move in the Caro-Kann (not to mention other openings), prophylactically preventing the knight, bishop, or queen coming to b5 in many lines.

notes.text: Contest the c-file with b5 or knight moves, and aim your other knight at f5.
notes.original: This would be a very promising position for black. Often in the Advanced variation, the e5 pawn can become weak if white missteps slightly. Black should now contest the c-file, with moves such as b5, Rc8, Nc6, or Nd7 > c5, or Nd7 > b6 > c4, while black's other knight often belongs on f5.

notes.text: A pleasing position: you control the c-file, have no weaknesses, and keep long-term pressure on the e-pawn.
notes.original: This is a pleasing position for black, with strong c-file control, no structural weaknesses, and long-term pressure against the e-pawn.

notes.text: Developing the knight to c6 is the more logical choice, though Ne7 is another possibility.
notes.original: Ne7 is another possible try here, but the text move seems more logical.

notes.text: White castles to show off its lead in development and a very safe king, which is more principled than Nc3.
notes.original: Nc3 is also a strong riposte here, but it's more principled for white to castle in this system, emphasising the lead in development and ultra-safe king position.

notes.text: You have basically equalised, but developing your pieces is still awkward.
notes.original: Black has basically equalised here, but still faces a conundrum in terms of piece development.

notes.text: Your bishop has a strong diagonal and your knight a typical f5 post; you're two moves from castling.
notes.original: This would be my choice, which places the light-squared bishop on a strong diagonal, the knight on the typical f5, and ensures that, without disruption, black is two moves away from castling

notes.text: This is White's best try for a small advantage.
notes.original: This is white's best hope to play for a small advantage.

notes.text: Bxe7 is White's best; any other move leaves you slightly better.
notes.original: Black is slightly better after any other move.

notes.text: White may be slightly better here, which is why this system is a top-level weapon.
notes.original: White is perhaps slightly better here, hence the fact that this system has become a highly-regarded weapon at the highest level. However...

notes.text: You should be okay here; your only problem piece is the knight on f5.
notes.original: White is perhaps slightly better here, hence the fact that this system has become a highly-regarded weapon at the highest level. However... ....after this logical continuation, black should be okay, with its only problematical piece being the f5-knight.

notes.text: White is marginally better here; Rc8 and castling kingside was arguably stronger than castling long.
notes.original: White was probably marginally better here; arguably better is Rc8 and castling kingside. But my position was decent, and I went on to win in 27 moves after white underestimated my c-file pressure (see: https://lichess.org/EXHIO4Dt)

notes.text: You're fundamentally sound: bring the b8 knight to d7 and look for the c5 break.
notes.original: Black is fundamentally sound. Usually, the black knight on b8 will come to d7. c5 is a typical idea in this structure.

notes.text: White often puts a knight on e5, though Stockfish doesn't always rate it best.
notes.original: White will often put a knight on e5, even though Stockfish states that it's not always the best move.

notes.text: Your c5 break is in, and the middlegame is underway.
notes.original: Now we can play the c5 break, and the middle game is underway.

notes.text: White's Bc4 isn't impressive; you finish developing calmly and can claim a slightly better position.
notes.original: Bc4 is sometimes chosen here by white players, but it's not particularly impressive. Black can complete development in unflustered fashion, and can ultimately claim a slightly better position.

notes.text: White can also deviate here by developing the bishop to c4.
notes.original: Black can also deviate with Bc4 here.

notes.text: White may simply trade off your light-squared bishop; you needn't fear it, though it can force queenside castling.
notes.original: Another idea here is to simply exchange the light-squared bishop, as indicated in this line. Black doesn't need to fear this whatsoever, but it can sometimes necessitate queenside castling.

notes.text: You're fully developed, and the open h-file makes up for your doubled g-pawns; White has achieved little.
notes.original: Black has completed development, its pieces are superbly placed, and black also has excellent compensation for the superficially wounded pawn structure via the open h-file. White has really achieved nothing of note in the opening here.

notes.text: Playing e6 is the natural reply, and White will often castle kingside next.
notes.original: A natural response to this is e6, and white will often castle kingside.

notes.text: White's knight and bishop both eye e6, so a sacrifice there is coming and play gets sharp.
notes.original: While this line can be played positionally, white can also arrange a sacrifice on e6. This can be tricky to face, as play becomes particularly sharp, and black can easily deviate from the appropriate path.

notes.text: You've equalised and can even take the b-pawn; White has more space but you have nothing to fear.
notes.original: Black has definitely equalised here, and has a pleasant choice, including capturing the b-pawn, but white has a significant space advantage and can be reasonably satisfied with this position. Nonetheless, black has nothing to fear here.

notes.text: This solid line is also possible, though swapping a bishop for a knight this way isn't very principled.
notes.original: Also possible here is this solid line, although it's not particularly principled to swap bishop for knight in this fashion.

notes.text: You win another pawn, but White has a huge lead in development.
notes.original: There are many possible moves for white after Bg4, but this is a critical line. Black wins another pawn on d4, but now white has a huge lead in development.

notes.text: White's bishop to e3 was the most promising approach, though other moves also kept White better.
notes.original: White could go back with the queen, go straight to b4, or pin the bishop via e5, and still be better. But this is the most promising approach.

notes.text: You're better, but White's lead in development means an attack could appear fast if you go astray.
notes.original: Black is definitely better here, but, considering the lead in development, a gargantuan white attack could materialise in little time if black goes awry over the next few moves.

notes.text: White has many options here; this pawn push is just the most forcing one.
notes.original: There are so many possibilities for white here that it's impossible to predict how a human opponent would play, but this seems the most forcing variation.

notes.text: Stockfish prefers e6, but that needs a tactical melee; this quiet move is far more prudent.
notes.original: Stockfish favours e6 here, but that requires a tactical melee in order to work. This approach is far more prudent.

notes.text: You have been slightly better throughout, and castling would give you a superior position.
notes.original: Black has been better throughout this sequence, and if we can castle then we can see a superior position on the horizon.

notes.text: White's bishop steps aside so the rook on d1 hits your d7 knight; it's White's best try.
notes.original: Actually, there is little that white can do here in order to cause black problems, and this move, which opens up the rook on the d-file, appears the best try.

notes.text: Grabbing the a7 pawn isn't White's best, but it is the most likely human choice.
notes.original: Not the best move, but probably the most likely human response to the position.

notes.text: You are much better now, and would be better after the other bishop move too.
notes.original: Black is much better now, and would also be better after Bc5.

notes.text: Once White plays h3, your bishop can come out to f5.
notes.original: If h3 here then the bishop can come to f5.

notes.text: Castling is possible too, but humans almost always play this knight move.
notes.original: Castling is also possible, but this played by humans almost without exception.

notes.text: The engine prefers e6, but retreating the bishop to g6 is the more natural choice.
notes.original: Again, I'm going against Stockfish here. The Silicon behemoth prefers e6 here, but this seems far more natural.

notes.text: You could also play e6, but this queenside expansion with b5 is preferable.
notes.original: e6 is also possible here, but I believe that this queenside expansion is preferable.

notes.text: White won the pawn back, but you are well developed and slightly better.
notes.original: White has won back the pawn, but black is well-developed, has a strong position, and can be considered slightly better.

notes.text: Castling gives you a rock-solid position, familiar to any regular Caro-Kann player.
notes.original: This is a rock solid position for any regular Caro-Kann player.

notes.text: You are better, but you must still tread carefully.
notes.original: Black is better, but must still tread warily.

notes.text: Other options exist, but this knight move is supremely solid.
notes.original: Other options are available, but this approach is supremely solid.

notes.text: White has compensation for the pawn, but not enough.
notes.original: White definitely has compensation for the pawn. But not enough!

notes.text: Nd2 is another try for White; here is a game where it was played.
notes.original: In a win that I recently had against a 2299-rated player, my opponent chose Nd2 here. Play continued as follows.

notes.text: You lead slightly in development and can castle queenside, so this quiet line is comfortable for you.
notes.original:
Black has a small lead in development, and can again castle queenside in this line. White has several other positional plans available, but the positioning of the pieces shouldn't be too difficult for black in this line.
In fact, I relish facing this quiet and unambitious line, as I feel it's ideal in nature for experienced Caro-Kann players. Sorry Magnus, Fabi and Bobby!

notes.text: Your bishop happily steps onto the diagonal and challenges White's bishop on f4.
notes.original: Bf4 is playable here too, but this just seems an open invitation to the bishop to come to this diagonal.

notes.text: The b7 pawn is poisoned, and you have reached a good position.
notes.original: The b7-pawn is poisoned. Black has achieved a good position here.

notes.text: Castling kingside is perfectly fine for you here.
notes.original: It was perfectly fine for black to castle kingside here; I was quite satisfied with my position at this point.

notes.text: Rerouting the knight is playable, but the engine prefers simply centralising your other rook.
notes.original: I quite liked this rerouting of the knight, but Stockfish frigidly proclaims that simply centralising the other rook is better.

notes.text: Bg5 is a mistake: it allows your natural knight jump and gives you a nagging edge.
notes.original: This move was a mistake, allowing my natural looking response, which gives black a nagging positional edge.

notes.text: This natural queen-attack idea is disliked by engines; the c5 break was much stronger here.
notes.original: This seemed a natural way to potentially bring my queen into an attack on the kingside, but computers hate this move! The frequently played c5 break was much stronger here; again demonstrating the value of general moves in the Caro-Kann.

notes.text: The c5 break is strong again here, and you still stand better.
notes.original: My opponent makes a couple of sub-optimal moves, and again the c5 break is strong here, although black still stands better after my next move.

notes.text: At last you make the obvious pawn break.
notes.original: Finally, I made the obvious pawn break!

notes.text: You are much better, with easy play against White's weak pawns, such as the isolated d4 pawn.
notes.original: Here I was confident that I was much better, and that I would have elementary and decisive play against white's weak pawns. Which is exactly what happened in the game, which can be replayed here: https://lichess.org/JXnxup8m

notes.text: White threatens Qxa8, but your queen has a mating reply on c1.
notes.original: Bf4 now looks tempting, and it seems as if white will win the exchange by capturing the a8 rook, which cannot be prevented. However, sadly for white...

notes.text: Qc1 is mate, so White's Bf4 idea simply fails.
notes.original: Qc1 is mate! In short, the Bf4 idea doesn't work, so black can afford to airily administer this simple queen move.

notes.text: White's h3 stops your bishop from jumping to g4, an interesting positional idea.
notes.original: There are several valid moves for white at this point. a3 puts the question to the bishop immediately, while developing the dark-squared bishop to f4 is also logical. This is also an interesting positional idea, preventing Bg4.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the f3 knight to the queen. The position is fully equal.
notes.original: When finally developing the light-squared bishop, it is natural for black to pin the f3 knight. Again, we have achieved complete equality here, and Stockfish even claims that black stands microscopically better.

notes.text: Castling is natural here, though developing the knight to c6 is also fine.
notes.original: There is no reason not to castle here, but Nc6 is also playable.

notes.text: Your bishop challenges White's dark-squared bishop at once; Be6 is also logical.
notes.original: Challenging white's dark-squared bishop immediately. Be6 is also a logical continuation, and the e6 square is a natural place for the bishop if development to g4 is denied by white.

notes.text: After this big simplification, your position is very stable and comfortable.
notes.original: AFter this massive simplification of the position, black comes up for air in a very stable state.

notes.text: Exchanging on d6 is possible, but it doesn't lead to anything particularly promising.
notes.original: Black could also exchange on d6 here, but this doesn't lead to anything particularly promising.

notes.text: With your bishop on e7, White's plan of isolating your d-pawn becomes slightly stronger.
notes.original: If Be7 here then isolating the d-pawn becomes marginally stronger.

notes.text: You can't safely trade bishops: Bd7 just hands White a free tempo and a strong knight on e5.
notes.original: White has other ideas as well, but this check is a natural developing move, as black can't safely exchange off bishops. 8...Bd7 9. Bxd7 Qxd7 10. Ne5 simply hands white a free tempo, while the knight establishes itself on the juicy e5 square.

notes.text: White's knight jumps to e5 now; castling first is White's other main move.
notes.original: Castling kingside is white's other main move here, after which white will often put a knight on e5 anyway.

notes.text: The queen move is the best way to hold your pawn; sacrificing it for development doesn't suit this repertoire.
notes.original: This is the best way of holding the pawn. Black can also castle and sacrifice the c-pawn, hoping to gain counterplay from more rapid development, but this approach is inimical to the spirit of this repertoire.

notes.text: Stockfish likes Bd6, but developing your light-squared bishop seems more natural.
notes.original: Stockfish likes Bd6 here, but developing the light-squared bishop seems more natural.

notes.text: Your rook takes the c-file, as in most Caro-Kann lines; White is probably slightly better.
notes.original: The rook occupies the c-file, as is hugely common across all variations of the Caro-Kann. Black is okay here, but it seems fair to assert that white has a slight initiative, and is probably slightly better.

notes.text: This is why Bb4 is favoured, but White's edge stays small; g4 is the accurate move.
notes.original: This is why the Bb4 tends to be favoured, but, having said that, white's edge is nothing too serious, and players of this line must find the paradoxical looking g4 here in order to maintain an optimal advantage.

notes.text: Your bishop is better on e6 than g6, where h4 would be a threat.
notes.original: If this does occur, the bishop is considerably better on e6 than g6, otherwise h4 is threatened.

notes.text: White should now storm the kingside with f4; after anything else you are fully equal.
notes.original: A pawn storm should follow now from white on the kingside with f4. After anything else, black has complete equality.

notes.text: Your knight can take on e4 later, but White finds f5 more natural.
notes.original: Nxe4 is obviously playable here, but f5 seems more natural.

notes.text: You must kick the knight out of e5; White then has several options.
notes.original: Black must kick out the e5-knight, after which white has several options.

notes.text: You are okay despite White's space, and Bxa2 may even win a pawn.
notes.original: Black should be okay here, despite white's space advantage, and may even win a pawn with Bxa2.

notes.text: Pushing the a-pawn was a blunder; b6 was the better move here.
notes.original: This was a blunder. b6 was better here.

notes.text: White's b5 is the best reply; if you now play b6, White's c6 leaves you in a bad way.
notes.original: White plays accurately with the best response. Now after b6, white has the foreboding c6, and black's game is rather terrible!

notes.text: White went wrong with a4; you should strike in the centre with e5.
notes.original: White has gone wrong here, and black should counter-attack in the centre with e5. But I decided on a more dramatic (and unsound!) counterplay concept.

notes.text: This quiet queen move is rare; the author found it by playing a game against Stockfish.
notes.original: I have never faced this variation as black, so it's quite rare. In order to remedy the situation, I played a game against Stockfish level 6, and the computer chose Qd2 here.

notes.text: The engine prefers Nd7, but castling is quite safe here because White is still undeveloped.
notes.original: Stockfish's choice here is Nd7, but Black can castle quite safely in this position, with white still relatively undeveloped.

notes.text: White's e5 looks tempting, but your c5 break then leaves White's dark squares weak and you much better.
notes.original: e5 may appear tempting, but after the thematic c5 break black is much better, and white's dark squares are tangibly weak.

notes.text: The c5 break looks natural, but it invites a scary sacrifice from White.
notes.original: The classic c5 break also looks natural here, but this does invite the following scary riposte.

notes.text: White's big centre can become a target. You are ahead in development, but White has space, so it's balanced.
notes.original: White's centre appears visually imposing, but in reality the two central pawns can become targets. Black is slightly ahead in development, while white has problems deploying some pieces and is potentially castling into strife on the queenside. But white has a space advantage and some hope of a kingside attack, so the position is largely equal and dynamically balanced.

notes.text: This attack is why to avoid the c5 line and play the quieter dxe4 instead.
notes.original: This is why I would steer away from this line, and play the reassuringly quieter dxe4!

notes.text: White needs a perpetual after Rxg6+, so you can draw, but your king is close to being mated.
notes.original: White will have to rely on a perpetual here, after Rxg6+, so in a sense this is an effective drawing line for black. But it needs to be remembered with perfect accuracy in order to be utilised, as black's king teeters on the brink of being mated.

notes.text: White castles queenside here; start active play quickly, because the position is double-edged.
notes.original: Another line worth considering here sees white castle kingside. Black would be advised to initiate active play rapidly here, in what could become a highly double-edged position.

notes.text: Your attack has arrived first, and White must find enterprising play to survive.
notes.original: Black's attack has arrived first, and white will need to demonstrate some enterprising play in order to survive.

notes.text: The rook move looks odd, but it supports a g-pawn push while White plans to castle queenside.
notes.original: This is an unusual move, but bots are prone to such dalliances. Nonetheless, it is not entirely illogical, as white largely intends to castle queenside in this line, and the rook move can support a potential g-pawn assault.

notes.text: The c5 break seems natural, but the engine prefers dxe4 or e5 to stifle White's centre.
notes.original: The c5 break seemed natural here, but the microprocessor instead prefers dxe4 or e5, both of which more favourably stymie white's centre.

notes.text: This was a mistake: Be3 relieves much of the pressure on White, though you still stand comfortably.
notes.original: This was a mistake, as Be3 relieves a lot of the pressure on white's position. Despite this error, black has a comfortable game, and I was eventually able to defeat the computer in a fluctuating affair. You can see this far-from-perfect game here: https://lichess.org/LIPtC2l4

notes.text: Your bishop pins the knight on f3 to the queen; this is more principled than Bf5.
notes.original: Bf5 is also perfectly fine, but this knight pin seems more principled.

notes.text: You give up the bishop pair, but that is easier to play than retreating and facing g and h pawn…
notes.original: White can retreat the bishop here, but this can be troublesome after 8...Bh5 9. g4 Bg6...as the piece can become vulnerable to g-pawn and h-pawn advances. Relinquishing the bishop pair leads to a more practically playable position, even if it is not to be relished in principle.

notes.text: White is slightly better with the bishop pair and bigger centre, but your well-placed pieces make this easy to play.
notes.original: White has a slight edge here, due to the retention of the bishop pair, and a somewhat stronger centre. But black's position is not difficult to play, all of its pieces are well-placed, and we can now play for some of the established motifs in the Caro-Kann.

notes.text: A natural developing move; if White plays Be3, your knight goes to d5 with a very decent position.
notes.original: Stockfish prefers a5 here, but this is a natural developing move. If 12. Be3 then Nd5 gives black a very decent position.

notes.text: White's bishop thrust to g5 delays your c5 break.
notes.original: This disruptive bishop thrust delays black's c5 break.

notes.text: Your c5 break was only delayed; it arrives now anyway.
notes.original: But it's coming imminently anyway!

notes.text: White is still marginally better, perhaps with a queenside pawn majority, but your position is very playable.
notes.original: White is still marginally better here, and perhaps something could be made of the queenside pawn majority. But this is an eminently playable position for black.

notes.text: Your knight hits the bishop and wins a tempo, though the idea is less effective now.
notes.original: I managed to gain a tempo here anyway, but already this idea is less effective; underlying the importance of timing.

notes.text: White's h3 wastes time, since you cannot pin the knight anyway, and lets you equalise.
notes.original: This was completely unnecessary, as black cannot pin the knight due to my early e6, nor can I do anything useful on the g4 square with my f6 knight. This is simply a waste of time, and enables black to equalise.

notes.text: This push weakens your pawns and c5 was arguably better, but you stand about equal.
notes.original: This weakening push wasn't necessarily the best approach; arguably c5 is better. However, black stands pretty much equal.

notes.text: This wasn't necessary: the pin on your knight achieves little, so Bb7 would have kept your plan going.
notes.original: Not really necessary. I could have continued with my plan with Bb7, as the knight pin achieves little of note.

notes.text: White has the better centre, but your position is absolutely solid.
notes.original: White has a better centre, but black is absolutely solid.

notes.text: After your hesitant play, White has built an unsubtle but dangerous attack.
notes.original: After some hesitant and insipid play from black, white has achieved an unsubtle yet dangerous attack.

notes.text: White's rook lift is a mistake, because you can now strike at the centre with c5.
notes.original: This rook lift is a mistake, as black can now intrude on white's centre with c5.

notes.text: You retreated to protect your dark squares, but missed the simple c5 idea.
notes.original: But I was concerned about my dark squares, and missed this elementary idea.

notes.text: Finally the c5 break comes: it opens your b7 bishop and gives you at least equality.
notes.original: Finally! I manage to get in the c5 break, open up my b7 bishop, and have achieved completely equality at the very least here.

notes.text: You are better here, and the author won this game despite one huge blunder.
notes.original: Black is better now, and I managed to win the game from this position, despite one humungous blunder! See here: https://lichess.org/32dW77wX

notes.text: This game shows the c5 break, strong pawns and a bishop coming alive on the long diagonal.
notes.original: This game demonstrates some of the important ideas and positional considerations in this line, many of which (c5 break, strong c6 and e6 pawns, bishop coming alive on b7) should be familiar by now, and will become increasingly engrained as later sections unfold.

notes.text: Your h-pawn now attacks the knight and forces it back.
notes.original: Now h6 forces the knight back.

notes.text: Bd6 would be worse: White swaps on d6 and is much better.
notes.original: White is much better after Bd6, Nxd6, Qxd6, after which our opponent has myriad options.

notes.text: White has several plans and is possibly slightly better; Stockfish finds a less obvious approach.
notes.original: White has several possible plans here, and is possibly slightly better. Re1 and c3 are likely human moves, but Stockfish sees the potential of the following approach.

notes.text: Ne5 straight away is also playable; you can't trade it, because the e5 pawn becomes a thorn.
notes.original: The immediate Ne5 is also playable here. Black can't exchange, as the resulting e5-pawn becomes a thorn in the black camp.

notes.text: White has three equally good choices here; the top engine line follows.
notes.original: Bxd6, Ne5, and Nxf6 are all equally playable here. The number one computer line is as follows...

notes.text: You are slightly behind in development, but you should be fine.
notes.original: Black is slightly behind in development, but should be fine.

notes.text: Your c5 break hits White's d4 pawn and is strong and logical here.
notes.original: But the c5 break is strong and logical here.

notes.text: After this unsound sacrifice, taking the knight is your only choice.
notes.original: Black has no choice after this unsound sacrifice.

notes.text: You castled by hand, and White's speculative attack has fizzled out.
notes.original: Black has castled manually, and white's speculative attack has rapidly fizzled out.

notes.text: You can safely take the knight.
notes.original: Black can safely take the knight.

notes.text: Ke8 is more natural: it opens the diagonal for your dark-squared bishop instead of blocking it.
notes.original: Black has two decent squares here, but Ke8 seems more natural, as it opens up the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop, as opposed to blocking it.

notes.text: This looks scary, but the main thing is not to hang your queen.
notes.original: This looks quite scary, but the main thing here is not to hang your queen! Trust me, I've done it before!

notes.text: Your queen is ideal here: if Qe2 comes, you can answer Ne5, protected by the queen.
notes.original: This is the ideal square for the queen, as now Qe2 can be met by Ne5, which is protected by the queen, thus neutering the potential discovered attack.

notes.text: Your king is finally about to slip away from the centre to safety.
notes.original: Black's king is threatening to escape now...

notes.text: With queens traded, you should be better.
