notes.original: After the queen exchange, black should be better.

notes.text: The knight on d6 is checkmate. Playing Ndf6, Qc7 or e6 instead would have stopped it.
notes.original: This ends the game abruptly! Instead, 5...Ndf6, 5...Qc7, or 5...e6 eliminate this threat.

notes.text: If White ever plays e5 here, your knight jumps to d5 and it is a mistake.
notes.original: 6. e5 is a mistake here, after 6...Nd5!

notes.text: Whatever White tries here, you end up slightly better.
notes.original: White is going to be slightly worse here whatever is tried. Stockfish suggests 7. Ne1?!, but it's hard to imagine any human player ever choosing this.

notes.text: You are slightly better: a solid structure, no weaknesses, decent development, and castling still available.
notes.original: Black is just slightly better here, with a very solid structure, no weaknesses, a king that can still be castled, and decent development.

notes.text: This is a natural, practical choice, though Nc5 is also worth considering.
notes.original: 8...Nc5 also merits consideration here. But this is a pragmatic and natural choice.

notes.text: The engine likes this odd knight retreat; castling is your natural reply.
notes.original: Stockfish still wants this weird move. See the notes for other variations.

notes.text: The position is completely equal, and White's other options do no better.
notes.original: This is a position of complete equality. Other options fare no better for white.

notes.text: You are just better in this position.
notes.original: Black is just better here.

notes.text: This is very comfortable for you; White struggles to find any advantage or initiative.
notes.original: This is another supremely comfortable variation for black. White has an impossible job to achieve any advantage or initiative whatsoever in this line.

notes.text: Most opponents trade here, which hands you a lead in development; retreating to e2 is feeble.
notes.original: I have found that most opponents will exchange here, at which point black has been handed a lead in development on a silver platter. Equally, retreating the bishop to e2 represents pretty feeble play.

notes.text: You are simply better here, whatever sensible move White chooses.
notes.original: Black is just better with any sensible move.

notes.text: You lead in development and can build c-file pressure; White must play accurately to stay near equality.
notes.original: White is solid enough, but black has a lead in development, and can now continue with typical ideas in the Caro-Kann without being impeded at all. Black can now build up c-file pressure, and white must play accurately and resourcefully in order to retain anything approaching equality.

notes.text: Your a6 is not really necessary, but White has played so poorly that you are still better.
notes.original: This prophylactic move isn't really necessary, but white has so fundamentally abandoned sound opening play that black has time for such cautious play, while still being better.

notes.text: Be4 is White's best try here; any other move gives you complete equality.
notes.original: This is the best try for white here, as any other move leads to complete equality.

notes.text: The position is very drawish, and you have achieved equality, your main goal in this line.
notes.original: This is now a very drawish position, but it wouldn't be too bold to conclude that black's primary mission of achieving equality has been accomplished.

notes.text: If White takes on b7, the game just ends in a draw by repetition.
notes.original: Taking on b7 just leads to a dead draw by repetition.

notes.text: The b-pawn isn't hanging: your knight attacks the queen on b7 and threatens to take it.
notes.original: The b-pawn is emphatically not hanging, as Na5 traps the queen!

notes.text: If White takes on d5 and you recapture, you are slightly better and comfortable.
notes.original: If Nxd5 exd5 here, black is slightly better, and has enjoyed a pleasantly untroubled opening.

notes.text: White's play is anaemic; the engine likes the e5 thrust, but a quieter move keeps you comfortably better.
notes.original: White's play has been quite anaemic, and the computer already wants an aggressive pawn thrust here with e5. However, I chose a quieter response, after which black is still comfortably better.

notes.text: Castling was fine, but bringing your rook to d8 at once to hit the isolated d-pawn was stronger.
notes.original: I was perfectly content to castle here, delighted with the serene scene on the board. But Rd8, immediately ganging up on the isolated d-pawn, was stronger.

notes.text: Your knight eyes the b3 square.
notes.original: Eyeing the b3 square.

notes.text: You now hold the c-file, which Caro-Kann players covet.
notes.original: Black has the c-file presence that is so coveted by Caro-Kann players.

notes.text: Winning the b-pawn looks very tempting, but White gets counterplay for the first time in the game.
notes.original: This seemed a hugely tempting continuation; black wins a pawn. But white has counterplay now for the first time in the game.

notes.text: Your a-pawn looks dangerous but is an illusory threat; with accurate play this should be a draw.
notes.original: The a-pawn appears dangerous, but it is an illusory threat. White should be able to encircle the pawn with rook, knight and king, while black's e6 pawn is also particularly weak and vulnerable. The game should definitely be a draw with accurate play.

notes.text: White allowed you to gain important tempi, and you went on to win this game.
notes.original: White allowed black to gain some important tempi, and I went on to win. You can replay the whole game here: https://lichess.org/Pg9IfoqM

notes.text: You could have gained a big advantage with d4 earlier; now you are okay, but White is slightly better.
notes.original:
Black could have achieved a big advantage at any time with d4, but this move never occurred to me, and I instead chose more stereotypical development.
Eventually, black played d4 and is okay here, although white is probably slightly better.

notes.text: This bishop move makes little sense: it lets you undermine White's pawn structure, starting with axb4.
notes.original: This moves makes little sense, as it just allows black to fatally undermine white's pawn structure. White never really recovered from this mistake in the game.

notes.text: Simple, natural moves have left you much better.
notes.original: Simply by employing straightforward, natural moves black is much better.

notes.text: Knight to d3 was the stronger move here, winning the exchange.
notes.original: Nd3 winning the exchange was superior.

notes.text: You sacrifice your bishop by taking the h3 pawn.
notes.original: Here I took the liberty of sacrificing my bishop.

notes.text: A move to d3 was completely winning, and your pieces are far better than White's.
notes.original: d3 was completely winning, but observe the quality of black's pieces in comparison to the white army.

notes.text: Your knight forks the queen and rook, so you win the exchange.
notes.original: Finally, black wins the exchange. I must admit that I missed a hanging queen on the very next move! But black won handily, apart from this major oversight! You can replay this game here: https://lichess.org/Ekv4mXgh/black#38

notes.text: White's knight on e5 sits on a valuable outpost; learning to handle it is critical.
notes.original: As is so often the case, the e5 square is a valuable outpost for white. Learning to deal with this is a critical skill in the Caro-Kann.

notes.text: The computer prefers Bd7, but your move is fine too.
notes.original: The computer favours Bd7 here, but this is fine as well.

notes.text: This recapture invites your c-pawn break soon.
notes.original: This exchange practically invites an imminent c5 break.

notes.text: White's Na4 would try to support c5, but it achieves little and you keep developing.
notes.original: Na4 is an interesting attempt here to reinforce c5, but it doesn't achieve a great deal, and black can continue to develop without impediment.

notes.text: Your position is excellent; your light bishop can later go to b7.
notes.original: Black has an excellent position. The light-squared bishop can later be developed to b7, or sometimes a6.
